**Sūrat al-Baqarah**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ Its like and its counterparts are names whose referents are the spelled-out letters from which words are composed. The *alif* indicates the middle letter of *qāla* (he said), the *lām* indicates its last letter, and likewise for similar forms. The evidence that these are names is that each of them indicates a meaning in itself, and they undergo inflection through *imālah* (vowel-raising), *tafkhīm* (emphatic pronunciation), definiteness and indefiniteness, pluralisation and diminutive formation.

They are inflected (*mu'rabah*). They are vowelled with sukūn, as with Zayd and other nouns, in that inflection does not touch them because its governing cause is absent. It has been said that they are indeclinable (*mabniyyah*), like sounds, as in *ghāq*, imitating the cry of the crow. Then, the majority hold that they are the names of the sūrahs. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: Allah swore by these letters. Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) said: They are the Greatest Name of Allah. It has been said: they are among the ambiguous verses (*mutashābih*) whose interpretation no one knows except Allah. They were only called "unclear" (*mu'jamah*) because of their being obscure and ambiguous. It has been said: the occurrence of these names in the form of an enumeration is like an awakening for one who was challenged with the Qur'an, and like a stirring of attention to the fact that this recited text, which they have been unable to match from first to last, is speech composed of the very same material out of which they compose their own speech. This is so that reflection may lead them to become certain, if their capacity has not collapsed short of it, and their inability to produce its like has not become evident after lengthy deliberations, even though they are the masters of speech, except because it is not the speech of humans, and that it is speech of the One who created powers and destinies. This view is among the most readily accepted.

It has also been said: the sūrahs began with these letters so that the first thing to strike the ears would be something standing on its own with a kind of strangeness, and as a prelude to the signs of inimitability (*i'jāz*). This is because in pronouncing the letters themselves, the Arabs were equal in their ability, both the unlettered among them and the People of the Book. This is unlike pronouncing the names of the letters, which was restricted to one who wrote and read, mixed with the People of the Book, and learned from them. For an unlettered person, to speak these names was considered as unlikely as writing and reciting. So the ruling on pronouncing these, together with the well-known fact that he (ﷺ) was not one who had acquired anything from their people, is the same as the ruling on the narratives mentioned in the Qur'an, which Quraysh and those like them had no grasp of. In both cases it is evident that this knowledge came to him through revelation, and it is a witness to the truth of his prophethood (ﷺ).

Know that what is mentioned at the openings (*fawātiḥ*) is half of the names of the letters of the alphabet. They are: Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad, Ra, Kaf, Ha, Ya, ʿAyn, Ta, Sin, Ha, Qaf, and Nun, across twenty-nine sūrahs, corresponding to the number of letters of the alphabet. They comprise half of each class of letters. Of the whispered letters (*mahmūsah*), half are: Sad, Kaf, Ha, Sin, and Ha. Of the voiced letters (*majhūrah*), half are: Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra, ʿAyn, Ta, Qaf, Ya, and Nun. Of the plosive letters (*shadīdah*), half are: Alif, Kaf, Ta, and Qaf. Of the continuant letters (*rakhwah*), half are: Lam, Mim, Ra, Sad, Ha, ʿAyn, Sin, Ha, Ya, and Nun. Of the emphatic letters (*muṭbaqah*), half are: Sad and Ta. Of the open letters (*munfatiḥah*), half are: Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra, Kaf, Ha, ʿAyn, Sin, Ha, Qaf, Ya, and Nun. Of the elevated letters (*mustaʿliyah*), half are: Qaf, Sad, and Ta. Of the lowered letters (*munkhafiḥah*), half are: Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra, Kaf, Ha, Ya, ʿAyn, Sin, Ha, and Nun. Of the letters of *qalqalah* (echoing), half are: Qaf and Ta. The letters not mentioned from these classes are overwhelmed (*makthūrah*) by those mentioned from them. You know that the majority of a thing takes the place of its whole. So it is as if Allah, exalted is He, enumerated for the Arabs the letters from which their speech is composed, as an indication of the rebuke already mentioned, and of the establishment of the proof against them. They came scattered across the sūrahs, because repeating the admonition about what was challenged, composed of these letters and nothing else, is more effective in reaching the aim. Likewise every repetition that occurs in the Qur'an: what is intended by it is to fix what is repeated in souls and to confirm it.

They did not come in one uniform pattern. Rather, the numbers of their letters vary, such as: Ṣ, Q, N, Ṭā Hā, Ṭā Sīn, Yā Sīn, Ḥā Mīm, Alif Lām Mīm, Alif Lām Rā, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād, Alif Lām Mīm Rā, Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād, and Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf. Thus they occur in one, two, three, four, and five letters, in keeping with their habit of varying their speech. Just as the forms of their words are based on one to five letters, so this course was followed in the openings.

Alif Lām Mīm is a verse wherever it occurs, and likewise Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād is a verse. Alif Lām Rā (*Mar*) is not counted as a verse, and likewise Rā is not counted as a verse in its five sūrahs. Ṭā Sīn Mīm is a verse in its two sūrahs. Ṭā Hā and Yā Sīn are two verses. Ṭā Sīn is not a verse. Ḥā Mīm is a verse in all its sūrahs. Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf is two verses. Kāf Hā Yā ʿAyn Ṣād is a verse. Ṣād, Nūn, and Qāf, all three, are not counted as verses. This is the view of the Kufans, while all others do not count any of them as a verse.

This is a matter of revelation (*tawqīfī*), in which there is no room for analogy, like knowing the sūrahs. All of them are to be paused upon as a complete pause when they are taken to have an independent meaning, not needing what follows. That is the case when they are not made into names of sūrahs and are uttered as sounds are uttered, or when they are made by themselves into predicates of an omitted subject, as in His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 1], meaning: "This is Alif Lam Mim," and then He began: ﴿Allah — there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 2].

For these openings there is a place in grammatical inflection (*i'rāb*) according to the one who makes them names of sūrahs, because according to him they are like the rest of proper names, and their place is nominative as subject of a sentence, or accusative, or genitive, since they are valid for oaths, and their status is like "Allah," and "Allāh" in both dialects. As for one who does not make them names of sūrahs, he cannot conceive that they have any place in his doctrine, just as there is no place for an independent sentence, or for enumerated individual words.

That is the Book which they were promised through the tongue of Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both. Or, "that" is a reference to Alif-Lam-Mim.

The demonstrative (ism al-ishara, "that") is given in the masculine form although its referent, the sura, is feminine. This is because, if al-Kitab is its predicate (khabar), then "that" has the same meaning and the same referent as the predicate, so its masculine form may be applied to it. If al-Kitab is its attribute (sifa), then the demonstrative refers directly to the Book, because the demonstrative points to the category that stands as its attribute. You say: "Hind is that person (dhalika al-insan)," or "that individual (dhalika al-shakhs) did such-and-such."

As for the construction of "that the Book" together with "Alif-Lam-Mim": if you make "Alif-Lam-Mim" the name of the sura, then "Alif-Lam-Mim" is the subject (mubtada', "the topic"), "that" is a second subject, al-Kitab is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject. Its meaning is that this is the complete Book, as if every other book, in comparison with it, were deficient, just as you say: "He is the man (huwa al-rajul)," meaning the one who is complete in manliness, combining in himself the praiseworthy qualities found among men.

It is also possible that "Alif-Lam-Mim" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "These are Alif-Lam-Mim (a sentence); and that Book is another sentence." And if you treat "Alif-Lam-Mim" as being like a sound (bi-manzilat al-sawt), then "that" is the subject and al-Kitab its predicate, meaning: "That Book which was sent down is the complete Book."

﴿La rayb﴾, "there is no doubt," i.e., no uncertainty. Rayb is a verbal noun (masdar) from rabani, when doubt arises in you. The real meaning of rayb is the unease and agitation of the soul. From it is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt, for doubt is a source of unease, and truthfulness is tranquility." That is: the matter being doubtful is something that unsettles the soul and does not let it rest, while its being sound and true is something that calms the soul and makes it still. From the same root is "the misfortunes of time" (rayb al-zaman), which is what unsettles souls and presents itself vividly to hearts through its calamities.

He negated doubt in an absolute sense (ʿala sabil al-istighraq), although many have doubted it, because what is negated is its being an object of doubt and a cause for it. This is because of the clarity of its indications and the brilliance of its proof, such that a doubter ought not to fall into doubt concerning it. It does not mean that no one doubts. He did not say "there is no doubt in it" (la fihi rayb), as He said: ﴿There is no intoxication (ghawl) therein﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. This is because the purpose of placing the negative particle before doubt is to negate doubt from it, and to affirm that it is true and not false, as the disbelievers claim. Had the prepositional phrase been placed first, it would have strayed from the intended meaning, which would then be that another book contains doubt, but not this one. This is the same intention as in His statement: ﴿There is no intoxication therein﴾ [al-Saffat: 47], which praises the wine of Paradise over the wines of this world by saying that it does not confuse the intellects as the wines of this world do.

The pause (waqf) on "fihi" is the well-known one. Nafi' and Asim are reported to have paused on "la rayb," and the one who pauses must intend a predicate, the sense being: "there is no doubt in it." ﴿Fihi huda﴾ ("in it is guidance"), with the pronoun "fihi" having its final vowel lengthened in each case, is the reading of Makki. Hafs agreed with him in ﴿fihi muhanan﴾ [al-Furqan: 69], and this is the original form, as in your saying "marartu bihi" ("I passed by him"), "min ʿindihi" ("from him"), and "fi darihi" ("in his house"). Just as one does not say "fi darihi" and "min ʿindihi" without the lengthening, so one should not say "fihi" (without lengthening). Sibawayh said: What he (Makki) said leads to the combination of three consonants which are not vowelled (sawakin): the ya' before the ha', and the ha' itself, since the vowelled ha' in their speech is like the unvowelled one, because the ha' is hidden (khafiyya), and the hidden is close to the unvowelled, and then the ya' after it.

Huda is a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern fiʿl, like buka' ("weeping"). It is the indication that leads to the desired goal. The proof of this is that error (dalala) is set in opposition to it in His statement: ﴿These are those who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqara: 16]. And why was it said: ﴿guidance for the God-conscious (muttaqin)﴾, when the God-conscious are already guided? It is like saying to someone who is honoured and esteemed: "May God honour you and make you mighty," meaning that you seek an increase on what he already has, and its continuation, as in His statement: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6]. Also, He named them "God-conscious" when they were about to put on the garment of taqwa, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills a slain man, to him belongs his spoils." And the saying of Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both): "When one of you intends to perform Hajj, let him hasten, for the sick may fall ill." Thus he named the one about to be killed a "slain man" and the one about to fall ill a "sick man."

He did not say "guidance for the misguided (dallin)," because they are of two groups: a group whose remaining in error is known, and a group whose end is known to be guidance. And it (the Qur'an) is guidance only for the latter. Had the expression that clarifies this been used, it would have said: "guidance for those who will arrive at guidance after error." So the speech was shortened by applying it according to the manner we have mentioned, and it was said: "guidance for the God-conscious." Moreover, this sets forth at the beginning of the sura, which is the first of the two Zahrawayn (the two bright ones, i.e., al-Baqara and Al ʿImran) and the hump of the Qur'an (sanam al-Qur'an), mention of His friends.

The muttaqi (God-conscious) in language is an active participle (ism fa'il) from the saying of people: "waqahu fa-ittaqa" (he protected him, so he was protected). Its first radical is waw and its last is ya'. When you form from it the pattern ifta'ala, you change the waw into ta' and assimilate it into the other ta', so you say: ittaqa. Wiqaya is excessive protection. In the sacred law (shari'a) it means one who protects himself from engaging in what would make him deserving of punishment, whether by an act or by an omission.

The place of huda in grammar is the nominative case, because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a predicate together with "la rayb fihi" for that reason. Or it is in the accusative case as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "fihi."

What is most deeply rooted in eloquence (balagha) is to say that His statement "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a sentence in itself, or a group of letters of the alphabet standing independently by itself. "That the Book" is a second sentence, "la rayb fihi" a third, and "huda lil-muttaqin" a fourth.

The arrangement of these has reached the joint of eloquence (mafsil al-balagha), in that they have been brought together harmoniously in this way without a conjunction particle. This is because they come in mutual kinship, each one taking hold of the neck of the other. The second is united with the first and embraces it; and so on through the third and the fourth. The explanation of this is that He first drew attention to the fact that it is the speech with which challenge is made (al-kalam al-mutahadda bihi). Then it was pointed out to be the Book described with the utmost perfection, so that this established the aspect of the challenge. Then He negated from it that any trace of doubt should resemble it. This was a testimony and a recording of its perfection, because there is no perfection more complete than that which belongs to truth and certainty, and no deficiency more deficient than that which belongs to falsehood and dubiousness.

It was said to a scholar: "In what does your delight lie?" He said: "In a proof that struts about in its clarity, and in a doubt that shrinks in its disgrace."

Then He informed about it that it is ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾, thereby establishing that it is certainty, around which doubt cannot hover, and truth, ﴿to which falsehood cannot come from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42]. Then each of the four, after being arranged in this elegant order and composed in this graceful arrangement, is not devoid of a point of splendid force. In the first there is ellipsis and allusion to the sought-after meaning in the most subtle manner. In the second there is the majesty found in the definite form. In the third there is what is in placing doubt before the prepositional phrase. In the fourth there is ellipsis, and the placing of the verbal noun, which is huda, in the position of the attribute, which is hadin (guiding), as if it were itself guidance. And its being indefinite (munakkaran) carries the implication that it is guidance whose essence cannot be fully comprehended. The brevity in mention of the God-conscious is as already explained.

(p-41) ﴿Alladhina﴾ (those who) is in the nominative or accusative case, by way of praise (mad'h), meaning: they are ﴿those who believe﴾; or: I mean ﴿those who believe﴾; or it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿those are upon guidance﴾; or it is in the genitive, as a description (sifa) of ﴿the God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾. It is a description that comes to clarify and reveal the God-conscious, like your saying: Zayd the jurist, the investigator. This is because it includes that upon which the state of the God-conscious is founded: ﴿iman﴾ (faith), which is the foundation of good deeds, and the prayer and the charity. These two are the foundations (umm) of bodily and financial acts of worship, and they are the measure by which the others are judged. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) called prayer the pillar of the religion, made the dividing line between Islam and disbelief the abandonment of prayer, and called zakat the bridge of Islam? So it is in their nature to entail all other acts of worship. For this reason the speech was abbreviated, by dispensing with enumerating the acts of obedience and mentioning instead that which serves as their heading, along with what it reveals of the excellence of these two acts of worship. Or it is a described attribute appended to the God-conscious, conveying a benefit other than their own, like your saying: Zayd the jurist, the speaker, the physician. The intended meaning of the God-conscious is: those who refrain from evil deeds. ﴿Yu'minuna﴾ (they believe) means: they affirm as true (yusaddiquna). It is a form (if'al) derived from security (al-amn). The saying of them, "amanahu," means: he affirmed him as true; its underlying sense is: he gave him security from denial and opposition. Its transitivity with the preposition ba' is because it includes the sense of acknowledging and confessing. ﴿Bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen) means: that which is absent from them, of what the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them concerning the resurrection, the raising up, the reckoning, and other things. It is in the sense of the absent (al-ghA'ib), by way of naming with the verbal noun, from your saying: "ghaba al-shay'u ghayban" (the thing was absent). This is if you make it a complement to faith (iman). If you make it a circumstantial phrase (hal), it carries the sense of absence and concealment, meaning: they believe while absent from that in which they believe; its underlying sense is: they are clothed in the unseen. True faith (al-iman al-sahih) is that one acknowledges with the tongue and affirms with the heart, and that action is not included within faith. ﴿Wa-yuqimuna al-salat﴾ (and they establish the prayer) means: they perform it. He expressed performance by establishment, because standing (al-qiyam) is part of its pillars, just as he expressed it by qunut, which is standing, and by bowing, prostration and glorification, because these are present within it. Or it is meant that establishing the prayer is the straightening of its pillars, from "aqama al-'ud" (he straightened the stick) when he straightens it. Or it is constancy in it and guarding it, from "qamat al-suq" (the market became brisk) when goods sell well, because when it is guarded it is like a sought-after commodity toward which desires are directed, (p-42) and when it is neglected it is like a worthless commodity that no one desires. The word salat is a form (fa'la) from "salla," like zakat from "zakka." Its writing with a waw follows the emphatic pronunciation. The underlying meaning of "salla" is: he moved the two salawayn, that is, the two buttocks, because the one praying does this in his bowing and prostration. It was said of the one who supplicates that he is a musalli (one who prays), likening him, in his humility, to the one who bows and prostrates. ﴿Wa-mimma razaqnahum﴾ (and from what We have provided them) means: We gave them. The "ma" is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which). ﴿Yunfiquna﴾ (they spend) means: they give in charity. He introduced "min" (from) as partitive, to protect them from the extravagance (tabdhir) that is forbidden. He placed the object first to show that it is more important. What is intended by it is zakat, because it is joined with prayer, which is its sister; or it is this together with other expenditures in the ways of good, because it came unrestricted. Anfaqa al-shay' and anfadhahu are two siblings, like nafaqa al-shay' and nafida. Every word whose first radical is nun and whose middle radical is fa', and whose last is dal, indicates the sense of going out and departing. The verse indicates that deeds are not part of faith, since it conjoined prayer and zakat to faith, and conjunction requires difference.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 4:

﴿Those who believe﴾ are the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his like, from among those who believed in every revelation sent down from God, and who had certainty regarding the Hereafter, a certainty that removed from them what they had held, namely that none enters Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of counted days. Then, if you take them as conjoined (ʿatf) to "those who believe in the unseen," they enter into the category of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). But if you take them as conjoined to "the God-fearing," they do not enter it. So it is as if it were said: "a guidance for the God-fearing and a guidance for those who believe in what has been sent down to you." Or the intended meaning is a description of the first group. The conjunction (ʿatif, the particle of coordination) is placed in the middle, as it is placed between attributes in your saying: "He is the brave and the generous." And the poet's words:

"To the mighty king and the son of the valiant one, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

The meaning is: they are those who combine those attributes and these, ﴿and in what has been sent down to you﴾, meaning: the Qur'an. The intended meaning is the entire Qur'an, not only the portion that had been sent down at the time of their belief, because belief in all of it is obligatory. It is expressed in the past tense even though part of it was yet awaited, out of giving precedence to what exists over what does not yet exist, and because when part of it has descended and part of it is awaited, it is treated as though all of it has descended. ﴿And in what was sent down before you﴾, meaning: the rest of the books sent down to the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿And the Hereafter﴾: it is the feminine form of "the last" (al-akhir), which is the opposite of "the first," and it is an adjective whose noun is omitted, namely "the abode" (al-dar), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿That is the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. It is one of the adjectives that have become predominant, and likewise "the world" (al-dunya). It is related from Nafiʿ that he lightened it by dropping the hamza and placing its vowel on the lam. ﴿They are certain﴾: certainty (al-iqan) is the perfection of knowledge with the absence of doubt and uncertainty regarding it.

Those (are) upon guidance (from) their Lord. The clause is in the place of nominative (raf') if "those who believe in the unseen" is a subject (mubtada'); otherwise it has no place in i'rab. It is permissible that the first relative clause be an attribute (sifah) of "al-muttaqun" (the God-conscious), and that the second be nominative by way of beginning (ibtida'), with "ulaika" as its predicate (khabar). The restriction of them to guidance and success is made as an allusion (ta'ridh) to the People of the Book, who do not believe in the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while they suppose themselves to be upon guidance and hope that they will attain success with God.

The sense of elevation (isti'la') in "upon guidance" is a metaphor (mathal) for their being firmly established in guidance, persisting in it and holding fast to it, such that their condition is likened to the condition of one who has mounted a thing and ridden it. Similar is the expression: "he is upon the truth" and "upon falsehood." They have made this explicit in their saying: "he made error a mount, he rode ignorance, and he settled upon the back of desire."

The meaning of "guidance from their Lord" is: it was given to them from His presence. He made "guidance" indefinite (nakkara) to convey a kind of vagueness whose full extent cannot be reached, as if it were said: "upon what kind of guidance." Similar is the expression: "You have fallen upon meat," meaning upon great meat.

"And those are the successful" means: the ones who attain what they sought and escape what they fled from. Thus "falah" (success) is the attainment of the desired aim, and "muflih" (successful one) is the one who has won his aim, as if he is one for whom the faces of victory have been opened. The root (tarkib) indicates the meaning of splitting and opening, and so do its cognates in the fa' and 'ayn, such as: falaqa, falaTha, and falla. Here the conjunction (ataf) is used, unlike His saying: "Those are like cattle; nay, they are more astray. Those are the heedless" (al-A'raf: 179), because the two predicates require conjunction here, while the heedlessness is one and the comparison to beasts is there, so the second serves to confirm the first, and it is far from conjunction.

"Hum" is a separator (fasl), and its benefit is to indicate that what follows it is a predicate and not an attribute, and emphasis, and the affirmation that the benefit of the predicated is established for the subject alone and not for anything else. Or it is a subject (mubtada'), and "al-muflihun" is its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of "ulaika." So observe how God, Mighty and Majestic, repeated the alert to the exclusive status of the God-conscious in attaining what no one else attains, by many ways: the mention of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) and its repetition. Therefore there is an alert that just as guidance is established for them as a distinction, so success is established for them.

The definiteness of "al-muflihun" indicates that the God-conscious are the people of whom you have been informed that they will succeed in the Hereafter, just as when you are informed that a person from your town has repented, and you ask who he is, and it is said: "Zayd the penitent," meaning: he is the one of whom you were informed of his repentance. The insertion of the separator between it and "ulaika" is to make you perceive their ranks, to make you desirous of seeking what they sought, and to energize you to advance what they advanced.

O God, adorn us with the garment of piety, and gather us in the company of those whose mention You began the Surah al-Baqarah with.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 6:

When he (Allah) had mentioned His friends (awliya'), with their attributes that bring them near to Him, and had made clear that the Book is guidance for them, He followed this up by mentioning their opposites, who are the obstinate rebels (al-'utah al-maradah) on whom guidance has no effect, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. Kufr (disbelief) means concealing the truth through denial. The root (ta'kib) indicates concealment, and for this reason the farmer is called kafir (one who covers the seed), and so is the night.

He did not use a conjunction (al-'atif) here, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous are surely in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed, the wicked are surely in the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13-14], because the sentence here is brought to mention the Book as an explanation (bayan), not as a report about the believers, whereas the second sentence was brought to inform about the disbelievers with such-and-such. Thus there is a difference in the intended meaning between the two sentences, and they stand in a relation where there is no room for a conjunction. And if it is considered a subject (mubtada') by way of estimation, then it follows the same rule.

By "those who disbelieve" is meant particular individuals whom Allah knew would not believe, such as Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, and their likes. ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾, with two hamzas, (read by) Kufi. Sawa' (same) here means equality (al-istiwa'), and it is used as a description, as adjectives are described by verbal nouns (masadir). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to a word that is common (sawa')﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64], meaning equal (mustawiyah). Its nominative case is because it is the predicate of inna, and ﴿a'anzarta-hum am lam tunzir-hum﴾ is in the nominative position by way of agency (fa'iliyyah), as if it were said: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, your warning them and not warning them are equal for them." Or sawa' may be a predicate placed before, and ﴿a'anzarta-hum am lam tunzir-hum﴾ in the position of the subject (mawdi' al-ibtida'), meaning: "It is the same for them whether your warning or not," and the sentence is the predicate of inna. It is permissible to report about the verb (al-fi'l) even though it is always a predicate, because it belongs to the kind of speech in which the aspect of wording is set aside in favour of the aspect of meaning. The hamza and am are used merely for the meaning of equality, and the meaning of interrogation has been entirely stripped from them. Sibawayh said: "This has taken the form of the interrogative particle, just as the vocative particle is used in your saying: 'O Allah, forgive us, O group (al-'isabah).'" He means: this has taken the form of interrogation without being an interrogation, just as that has taken the form of the vocative without being a vocative.

Al-Inzar (warning) is frightening [people] of the punishment of Allah by restraining them from disobedience. ﴿They will not believe﴾ is a sentence emphasizing the sentence before it, or the predicate of inna, and the sentence before it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), or a predicate after a predicate. The wisdom in warning, despite knowing their persistence, is the establishment of proof, and so that the sending (of the Messenger) is general, and so that the Messenger ﷺ is rewarded.

﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-khatm (sealing) means covering, because when one secures something by pressing a seal upon it, this is a covering of it, so that nothing may gain access to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah has stamped (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts, so they do not understand the good. That is: Allah has stamped upon them, making them such that what is in them of disbelief does not come out, and what is not in them of faith does not enter.

The essence of the sealing and the stamping, according to us (the Ash'arites), is the creation of darkness and constriction in the breast of the servant, so he does not believe as long as that darkness is in his heart. According to the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), it is pure information placed upon the hearts, showing to the angels that they are disbelievers, so that they curse them and do not invoke any good for them. Some scholars said: the attribution of the sealing to Allah the Exalted is figurative (majaz, metaphorical usage), and the one who seals is in reality the disbeliever. However, since Allah the Exalted is the One who empowered him and enabled him, He attributed the sealing to Himself, just as an action is attributed to its cause. It is said: "The governor built the city," because an action has various connections: it is connected to the doer, the object, the verbal noun, the time, the place, and the one who causes it. Its attribution to the doer is literal (haqiqah, literal usage), but it may be attributed to these other things figuratively, because they resemble the doer in being connected to the act, just as a man resembles a lion in his boldness, so the lion's name is borrowed for him. This is a branch of the question of the creation of actions.

﴿and upon their hearing﴾: He made hearing singular, as He made the belly singular in the saying: "Eat in some of your belly, you will be healthy," for the sake of avoiding confusion, and because hearing (sam') is originally a verbal noun: one says "I heard the thing, sam'an and sama'an." A verbal noun is not made plural, because it is a generic noun that applies to the few and the many, so there is no need for dual or plural forms in it, and thus he kept to the original form. It was also said: there is an omitted genitive, that is, "and upon the places of their hearing." It was read as "upon their ears" (asma'ihim).

﴿and upon their sight is a covering﴾: this is read with a nominative (raf') as a predicate and subject. Al-basar is the light of the eye, that by which the seer sees, just as al-basirah is the light of the heart, that by which one perceives and reflects. It is as if they are two subtle substances that Allah the Exalted created, placing in them two instruments for seeing and for insight. Al-ghishawah means the covering, on the pattern fa'alah, from ghashshahu, when he covered it. This pattern denotes what wraps around a thing, like 'isabah (a bandage), 'imamah (a turban), and qiladah (a necklace).

The hearing falls under the ruling of the sealing, not under the ruling of the covering, as in His saying: ﴿And He has sealed his hearing and his heart, and placed over his sight a covering﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23], and because they stop at "upon their hearing" without stopping at "upon their hearts." Al-Mufaddal alone read ghishawah in the accusative, by supposing an implied verb ja'ala (He made). The repetition of the preposition in His saying ﴿and upon their hearing﴾ is evidence of the intensity of the sealing in both places.

The Imam Shaykh Abu Mansur, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the disbeliever, since he did not hear the word of truth, and did not look into himself and other created things to see the signs of having come into being, so that he would know that there must be a Creator for him, was made as if there were a covering over his sight and his hearing, even though this is not literally so. This is evidence that in his case the hearing falls under the ruling of the covering. The verse is an argument for us against the Mu'tazilah concerning what is best (al-aslah), for He the Exalted informed that He sealed upon their hearts, and there is no doubt that not sealing would be better for them.

﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾: al-'adhab (punishment) is like al-nakal (exemplary punishment) in form and meaning, because one says "a'dhaba 'an al-shay'" when he refrains from it, just as one says "nakala 'anhu." The difference between 'azim (great) and kabir (big) is that 'azim is the opposite of haqir (contemptible), while kabir is the opposite of saghir (small), so 'azim is above kabir just as haqir is below saghir. Both are used for bodies and for events alike; one says "a great man (rajul 'azim)" and "a big man (rajul kabir)," meaning his body or his importance. The indefiniteness (tankir) means that upon their sight there is a kind of covering other than what people commonly know, namely the covering of blindness to the signs of Allah. And for them, among the grievous pains, there is a great kind of punishment whose true nature none knows except Allah the Exalted.

And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and in the Last Day," (2:8). He, glorified and exalted, began with mention of those who sincerely made their religion for God, whose hearts agreed with their tongues in it. Then He followed with the disbelievers, whose hearts and tongues differed. Then He presented a third group, the hypocrites (munafiqun), who professed belief with their mouths while their hearts did not believe. They are the most wicked of the disbelievers, because they mixed disbelief with mockery and obstinacy. For this reason God revealed about them, ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire﴾ (4:145).

Mujahid said: Four verses at the beginning of the surah describe the believers, two verses mention the disbelievers, and thirteen verses concern the hypocrites. In them He censured their deceit, their wickedness, their foolishness, and their ignorance. He mocked them, ridiculed their actions, recorded their rebellion and their blindness, called them "deaf, dumb, and blind," and coined shameful parables for them.

The story of the hypocrites, from beginning to end, is coordinated with the story of those who disbelieved, just as one sentence is coordinated with another.

The original form of nas (ناس) is unas (أُناس), whose hamza was dropped for lightness. Its dropping together with the definite article (al-) is treated as obligatory, so one hardly says al-unas. Its original form is supported by insan (إنسان), anasi (أناسيّ), and ins (إنس). They were named thus for their visibility, and because they "perceive" (yu'nisun), meaning they see, just as the jinn (الجن) were named for their concealment (ijtinan). The morphological pattern of nas is fa'al, because the pattern is determined by the root letters; you say the pattern of qi (قِ) is if'al, and you have only the middle radical with you. It is one of the collective nouns (asma' al-jam'), and the definite article in it is for the genus.

Man (مَن) is a qualifying (mawsufa) relative, and yaqulu (يَقُولُ) is its descriptive clause, as if it were said: "Among the people are people who say such and such."

They specifically mentioned belief in God and in the Last Day, which is the time without limit, the everlasting eternity that does not end. It is called "the Last" (al-akhir) because it comes after the elapsed times, or because it is the appointed period from the resurrection until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire. They gave the impression in this statement that they had encompassed both sides of faith, its beginning and its end. This is because the sum of doctrinal matters (al-masa'il al-i'tiqadiyya) returns to matters of the origin (al-mabda', i.e., the beginning), which are knowledge of the Creator and His attributes and names, and matters of the return (al-ma'ad, i.e., the afterlife), which are knowledge of the resurrection, the raising from graves, the bridge (al-sirat), the scales (al-mizan), and all the other conditions of the Hereafter.

The repetition of the preposition "in" (bi, الباء) indicates that they claimed each of the two beliefs in its proper and firm form.

His words ﴿but they are not believers﴾ (2:8) correspond to their words ﴿We believe in God and in the Last Day﴾, although the first speaks of the state of the agent and the second of the state of the act, because the intention is to deny what they claimed and to negate it in the most emphatic and forceful manner, namely to remove their persons from being a group among the believers. A similar usage is His words: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it﴾ (5:37). This is more emphatic than saying "they do not come out of it."

He used the word "belief" without qualification in the second instance after qualifying it in the first, because it may be intended as qualified, the qualifier being omitted because the mentioned one indicates it, and it may also be intended as the negation of the very root of belief, which implicitly negates what was mentioned earlier.

The verse refutes the view of the Karramiyya (a sect that held faith to be mere verbal profession), that belief is only verbal affirmation with the tongue and nothing more, because it denies them the name of belief even though they verbally affirmed it. It supports the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the mainstream Sunni community) that belief is verbal affirmation with the tongue and assent of the heart.

The preposition "in" (bi) entered into the predicate of "ma" (ما) to emphasize the negation, because the listener derives the denial from it when he has forgotten the beginning of the sentence.

The word "say" (yaqulu) is singular in form, which is why it is said to be singular in its wording, but the plural was used in ﴿but they are not believers﴾ in view of its meaning.

They deceive Allah. That is, [they deceive] the Messenger of Allah, and the object is elided, as in His words: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This is what Abu ʿAli (may Allah have mercy on him) and others said. That is, they show what is not in their souls. So *khida ʿ* (deception, *khidāʿ*) is showing what is not in the self. Allah has elevated the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) by making his deception to be their deception, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ [al-Fath: 10]. It was also said that the meaning is: they deceive Allah in their own claim, because they suppose that Allah is one whose deception is valid. This usage is common with other than two parties, as in your saying: "I punished the thief." It has also been recited as *yakhdaʿūna Allāh* (they deceive Allah). The clause is an explanation of *yaqūlu* (they say), or it is a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "Why do they claim belief while lying? And what benefit do they gain from that?" It is then said: ﴿They deceive Allah﴾. Their benefit in that is their being spared the fighting that was with others among the disbelievers, the application to them of the rulings for believers, and their obtaining of spoils, and other things.

The author of *al-Wuqūf* said: the pause (*waqf*) on ﴿bi-mu'minīn (believers)﴾ is obligatory, because if it were joined, the sense would become: "And they are not believers deceiving," so the description would be negated, as in your saying: "He is not a lying man," while the intended meaning is the negation of belief from them and the affirmation of deception for them.

As for one who makes *yukhādiʿūna* (deceiving) a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *yaqūlu* (they say), with *yaqūlu* as its governing element, the sense is: "They say: we believe in Allah, while deceiving." Or [one who makes it] a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *bi-mu'minīn*, with the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) as its governing element, the sense is: "And they are not believers while in the state of their deceiving." It does not stop [at *bi-mu'minīn*].

The first opinion: ﴿And those who believe﴾, that is, they deceive the Messenger of Allah and the believers by showing belief and concealing disbelief. ﴿And they deceive only themselves﴾, that is, they do not deal in that dealing which resembles the dealing of deceivers except with themselves, because its harm reaches them, and the outcome of their deception, which is punishment in the Hereafter, returns to them. So it is as if they deceived themselves. *Wa-mā yukhādiʿūna* (and they do not deceive) was read by Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ and Makki for agreement (with the preceding verb form). The justification of the first group is that *khada ʿa* and *khādaʿa* here have one meaning.

*Al-nafs* (self) is the essence and reality of a thing. Then it was said of the heart and the spirit: *nafs*, because the self is by them. Blood also has a *nafs*, because its sustenance is by blood, and water has a *nafs* due to its extreme need for it. What is meant by *al-anfus* (the selves) here is their essences. The meaning of their deceiving their essences is that the deception clings to them and does not pass beyond them to others.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾, that the outcome of their deception returns to them. *Shuʿūr* (perception) is knowledge of a thing by sensation, from *al-shiʿār* (undergarment), which is the garment that is next to the body. *Mashāʿir al-insān* (a person's faculties) are his senses, because they are the instruments of perception. The meaning is that the reaching of the harm of that to them is like the perceptible, while they, because of the prolonged persistence of their heedlessness, are like one who has no sense at all.

**"In their hearts is a disease"** means doubt (*shakk*) and hypocrisy (*nifaq*, the concealing of disbelief behind a profession of faith). Doubt is wavering between two matters, and the hypocrite is wavering. In a hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like the likeness of a stumbling sheep between two flocks." A sick person is torn between life and death. Also, disease is the opposite of health, and corruption is the opposite of health, so "disease" came to denote every kind of corruption. Doubt and hypocrisy are corruptions in the heart.

**"So Allah increased them in disease"** means weakness in gaining victory and incapacity in exercising power. It was also said that what is meant is the trait of hypocrisy, which persists as long as its like persists, as is known regarding the increase of faith.

**"And theirs is a painful punishment"**: *alīm* is the form *fa'īl* in the sense of *mufʿil*, that is, painful (*mu'lim*).

**"Because they used to lie"**: this is the reading of the Kufans (*Kūfī*). It means: because of their lying in their saying, **"We believe in Allah and the Last Day."** Here *mā* with the verb is in the sense of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). Lying (*al-kadhib*) is reporting something contrary to what it actually is. The verb **"yakdhibūn"** [in the other reading, *yukadhdhibūn*], meaning other than them, i.e., by their denying the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he brought. It was also said that it is an intensive form of *kadhaba*, just as *ṣaddaqa* was intensified from *ṣadaqa*, and the parallels of these two are *bāna al-shay'* and *bayyana*.

(p-50)

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ is conjoined to "they say: We believe." For if you said, "Among the people are those who, when it is said to them, ﴿Do not cause corruption on the earth﴾," it would be correct. Corruption (al-fasad) is the departure of a thing from its state of soundness and its being beneficial, and its opposite is reform (al-salah), which is attaining the sound and beneficial state. Corruption on the earth is the stirring up of wars and strife, because in that is the corruption of what is on the earth, the loss of soundness in people's affairs, in the crops, and in religious and worldly benefits. The corruption of the hypocrites on the earth was that they would incline toward the disbelievers and back them against the Muslims by disclosing the Muslims' secrets to them and inciting them against the Muslims, and this leads to the stirring up of strife among them. ﴿They say: We are only reformers﴾. He made a distinction between the believers and the disbelievers through diplomacy (al-mudara). That is, the attribute of reformers belongs purely to us, and it is unmixed with any flaw that taints it from any aspect of corruption. For "innama" (إنما) is used either to restrict a judgment to a thing, or to restrict a thing to a judgment, like your saying: "Innama yantaliqu Zayd" (Only Zayd sets out), and "Innama Zayd katib" (Zayd is only a writer). And "ma" (ما) is *kaffa* (كافة), because it restrains (تكفها) the particle from operating (عن العمل).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 12:

﴿Verily, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive﴾ — that they are corrupters. He omitted the object (al-maf'ul) because its reference is known. Alā (ألا): it is composed of the interrogative hamza and the particle of negation, to give the sense of alerting attention to the certainty of what follows. When the interrogative enters upon a negation, it conveys affirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He Who is able to do that?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40]. Because it carries this force of emphasis, a sentence after it is never begun except with what introduces an oath. Allah has refuted, in the most eloquent and decisive way, what they claimed of being counted among the reformers, and this indicates His great wrath, and the intensity of it (p-51) from the standpoint of the resumptive construction (al-istdue'af), and the emphasis contained in alā and inna, the definiteness of the predicate, the placement of the separating pronoun (al-fasl), and His saying: ﴿but they do not perceive﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 13:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ They advised them in two respects. The first: denouncing what they were upon, because it is remote from the correct and leads to corruption. The second: showing them the straightest path, which is to follow those of sound judgment (*dhawu al-ahlam*). Their reply was to call the believers foolish (*sufaha*), because of the persistence of their ignorance. In this there is consolation for the scholar regarding what he suffers from the ignorant. The attribution of "it was said" (*qila*) to "tufsidu" and "amanu" is valid, although attributing a verb to a verb is not valid. This is because it is an attribution to the wording of a verb, whereas what is impossible is attributing a verb to the meaning of a verb. So it is as if it had been said: "When this statement was said to them." From the same usage: "they claimed" is the mount of falsehood. As for the *ma* in "kama": it is either *kaffa* (a restrictive particle, as in *rubbama*, "perhaps"), or *masdariyya* (a particle forming a verbal noun, as in ﴿with what [breadth] it was vast﴾ [al-Tawba 9:25]). The *lam* in "al-nas" (the people) is *lam al-ahd* (the *lam* of previous reference), meaning: as the Messenger ﷺ and those with him believed, and they are known people; or it refers to ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, meaning: as your companions and brothers believed. Or it is *lam al-jins* (the *lam* of the genus), meaning: as those perfect in humanity believed; or the believers are treated as if they alone are "the people" in reality, and whoever is other than them is like beasts. The *kaf* in ﴿kama amana﴾ is in the accusative position, because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a belief like the belief of the people. Its like is ﴿as the foolish have believed﴾. The interrogative in "anu'minu" is for denial. The *lam* in "al-sufaha" refers back to "al-nas". They called them foolish, although they were the intelligent and the superior, because in their ignorance they believed that what they were in was the truth and that anything else was false, and whoever mounts the back of falsehood is a fool. Sufah is the weakness of intellect and lightness of forbearance. ﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾ that they are the foolish. Here He said "they do not know" (*la ya'lamun*), whereas earlier He said "they are not aware" (*la yash'urun*), because He had mentioned foolishness, which is ignorance, so mentioning knowledge alongside it is a better antithesis to it. Also, faith requires reflection and inference, until the one who reflects acquires knowledge. As for corruption on the earth, it is a matter based on customs (p-52), so it is like the perceptible. "Al-sufaha" is the predicate of *inna* (indeed). "Hum" is a separator (*fasl*) or a subject (*mubtada'*), and "al-sufaha" is the predicate of "hum", and the sentence is the predicate of *inna*.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 14:

﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say: "We believe."﴾ Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) recited: (wa-idha laqaw) [وَإذا لاقَوْا]. It is said: "laqītuhu" and "lāqaytuhu," when you face him closely, near to him. The first verse explains the doctrine of the hypocrites and translates their hypocrisy, while this one explains what they used to do with the believers: mockery of them, meeting them with the faces of friends, and giving them the impression that they are with them. ﴿And when they go back alone to their devils﴾: "khalawtu bi-fulānin wa-ilayhi" means when you are alone with him. Using "ila" is more eloquent, because it implies both starting point and endpoint; that is, when they withdraw from the believers to their devils. It is also possible that "khala" here means "madā" (passed away). "Shayāṭīnuhum" refers to those who resembled the devils in their rebellion, and they are the Jews. It is reported from Sibawayh that the nun of "shayāṭīn" is original, as evidenced by their saying "tashayṭana" (acted like a devil). It is also reported from him that it is extra (a added letter). Its derivation is from "shaṭana," meaning "to be far off," because of its distance from righteousness and goodness, or from "shāṭa," meaning "to perish"; and among its names is "al-bāṭil" (falsehood). ﴿They say: "Indeed we are with you."﴾ That is, we are your companions and in agreement with you in your religion. They addressed the believers with a verbal sentence, and their devils with a nominal sentence confirmed by "inna," because in their address to the believers they were claiming that faith had newly arisen in them, not claiming that they were unique in faith; either because their own selves did not help them in it, since they had no incentive or motivator from their beliefs, or because it would not have been accepted from them had they said it in the form of emphasis and exaggeration. And how could they hope for its acceptance while they were among the Muhajirun and the Ansar? As for their address to their brethren, it was out of desire, and it was accepted from them and current among them, so it was a basis for affirmation and a sign of emphasis.

﴿Indeed we are only mockers﴾: this is an emphasis of their words ﴿Indeed we are with you﴾, because its meaning is persistence upon Judaism. Their words ﴿Indeed we are only mockers﴾ are a rejection of the greeting and a repudiation of it from them, because the one who mocks a thing, who belittles it, denies it and repudiates its being regarded as significant. Repelling the opposite of a thing is an affirmation of its firmness. Or it is a new sentence, as if they were objected to, when they said to them: "Indeed we are with you," "If you are with us, why do you agree with the believers?" So they said: ﴿Indeed we are only mockers﴾. "Al-istihza'" means ridicule and belittling; the root of the matter is lightness from "al-huzw," which is swift killing; and "haza'a yahza'u" means he died on the spot.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 15:

﴿Allah mocks them﴾, i.e., He requites them for their mockery. He called the recompense of mockery by its name, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Thus He called the recompense of an evil deed an "evil deed," and the recompense of aggression "aggression," though the recompense is not in itself an evil deed or aggression. This is because mockery is not permissible for Allah, Exalted is He, in its literal reality, since it belongs to the category of frivolity, and He is exalted above it. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the preferred interpretation.

The resumption of His saying, ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, without a conjunction, is of the utmost eloquence and grandeur. It implies that Allah, Exalted is He, is the One who mocks them with a more forceful mockery, one to which their mockery is not comparable, because of the punishment, humiliation and disgrace that befalls them. And since Allah's chastisements and afflictions descend upon them moment by moment, it was said ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ rather than "Allah is one who mocks them," so that it would correspond to His saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾.

﴿And He extends them﴾, i.e., He gives them respite. From al-Zajjaj: ﴿in their transgression﴾, in their excess in disbelief, ﴿wandering blindly﴾, a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), i.e., they are bewildered and vacillate.

This verse is a proof against the Mu'tazilah in the question of al-aṣlaḥ (what is best for the servant).

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (Those) is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿alladhīna ishtarawu al-ḍalāla bil-hudā﴾ (those who bought error in exchange for guidance). That is, they substituted it (*istabdalūhā bihi*) and chose it over it (*ikhtārūhā ʿalayhi*). Why did He say ﴿ishtarawu al-ḍalāla bil-hudā﴾ (bought error in exchange for guidance) when they were not upon guidance? Because the verse refers either to a people who believed and then disbelieved, or to the Jews who used to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and, when he came to them, disbelieved in him. Or, because of their capacity to attain it, guidance was treated as though it were present among them, and they abandoned it for error. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of sale by mutual conduct (*bay' taʿāṭī*, a sale concluded by exchange of goods without spoken words), because they did not pronounce the word for buying, but they abandoned guidance for error by choice, and this was called "buying" (*shirā'*). Thus it becomes evidence for us that whoever takes something belonging to another and leaves its equivalent in its place with his consent has bought it, even if he did not speak the word.

*Al-ḍalāla* (error) is deviation from the right course and the absence of guidance. It is said: "*ḍalla manzilahu*" (he lost his dwelling), and so the word is borrowed for going astray from what is correct in religion.

﴿Fa-mā ribiat tijāratuhum﴾ (So their trade did not profit). *Al-ribḥ* (profit) is the surplus over capital, and *al-tijāra* (trade) is the occupation of the merchant, who is one who buys and sells for profit. Attributing the profit to the trade is a metaphorical attribution (*al-isnād al-majāzī*), and its meaning is: "they did not profit in their trade," since trade itself cannot be profited. When the buying of error in exchange for guidance occurred metaphorically, He followed it with mention of profit and trade as *tarshīḥ* (a supporting embellishment for the metaphor), like the poet's saying:

*When I saw the eagle had overpowered Ibn Da'ah,*
*and had nested in its nest, my breast stirred for him.*

Because he likened grey hair to the eagle and jet-black hair to the crow, he followed it with mention of nesting and nest.

﴿Wa-mā kānū muhtadīn﴾ (and they were not guided) to the path of trade, just as merchants who manage affairs are those who know what they gain and lose by. The meaning is: the aim of merchants is the preservation of capital and profit, and these people have lost both. Their capital is guidance, and nothing remains for them with error. When nothing remains for them but error, they cannot be described as having achieved profit, even if they attain worldly aims, because the one who is astray is a loser, and because one whose capital has not been preserved for him is not said to have profited.

It has been said: *alladhīna* is an attribute (*ṣifa*) of *ulā'ika*, and ﴿fa-mā ribiat tijāratuhum﴾ up to the end of the verse is in the position of *raf'* (nominative) as the predicate of *ulā'ika*.

﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾. When He had mentioned the reality of their state, He followed it with a parable, as an increase in clarification and a completion of the explanation. Presenting parables (amthal, sing. mathal, "parable" or "example") has a clear effect in bringing out hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities. Such parables are abundant in the heavenly books. Among the chapters of the Gospel (Injil) is the Chapter of Parables (Surat al-Amthal).

In its original usage, the mathal is the mithl, meaning "equivalent" or "likeness." It is said: mathal, mithl, and mathil, like shabah, shibh, and shabih. Then the term mathal was applied to a widely circulated saying whose occasion of use is its source. They did not coin a mathal except as a saying that contains strangeness, and for this reason it is preserved and not altered. The word mathal has been used metaphorically for a state, a description, or a story when it has significance and contains strangeness. It is as if it were said: their state, which is of a wondrous nature, is like the state of the one who kindled a fire. Similarly is His saying: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: among the wonders We have related to you (p-55) is the story of the Garden, which is of a wondrous nature; then He began to explain its marvels. And His saying: ﴿To God belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning: the attribute that has greatness and majesty.

The word alladhi (the one who) is placed in the position of alladhina (those who), as in His saying: ﴿And you plunged in as those who plunged﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69]. Thus the comparison is not of a group to an individual, nor is the intent the species of those who kindle fire, nor is it meant as the group who kindled a fire. Rather, the dhawat (essences) of the hypocrites were not compared to the essence of the one who kindled the fire, so that it would follow that a group is compared to an individual. Rather, their story was compared to the story of the one who kindled the fire.

The meaning of istawqada is awqada (kindled). The wuqud (blazing) of fire is its flaring up. The nar (fire) is a subtle, luminous, hot, burning substance. Its derivation is from nara yanur, meaning "to flee," because in it there is movement and agitation. ﴿So when it illuminated what was around him﴾. The ida'ah (illumination) is the excess of lighting. Its corroboration is His saying: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light﴾ [Yunus: 5]. In the verse it is transitive. [It is possible that it is intransitive] with ﴿what was around him﴾ as its subject, and the feminine form is for agreement with the meaning, since the surroundings of one who kindles a fire are places and things.

The response (jawab) of "falamma" is ﴿God took away their light﴾. It is a temporal adverbial clause, and the governing element within it is its response, like idha. Ma is a relative pronoun, and hawlahu is in the accusative as an adverb of place, or it is an indefinite qualified noun, and the implied meaning is: when it illuminated a fixed thing around him. The pronoun is plural and singular, used sometimes for agreement with the wording and sometimes with the meaning. The nur (light) is the light of fire, and the radiance of every luminous thing. The meaning of adhhabahu is: he removed it and caused it to go away. The meaning of dhahaba bihi is: he took it along and departed with it. The meaning is: God seized their light and held it back. ﴿And whatever He withholds, none can release﴾ [Fatir: 2]. Thus it was more eloquent than causing it to go away. He did not say "God took away their brightness," because of His saying ﴿when it illuminated﴾, since mentioning the light is more eloquent, because the brightness (dau') implies an increase, while what is intended is the removal of light from them entirely. Had it been said "God took away their brightness," it would have suggested the going away of an increase while something still called light remained. Do you not see how He mentioned after it ﴿and left them in darkness﴾? The zulmah (darkness) is an accident opposed to light. Note how He made it plural, how He made it indefinite, and how He followed it with what indicates that it is a darkness in which two figures cannot be seen, which is His saying ﴿they do not see﴾. Taraka in the sense of "to cast off" and "to leave" when it takes one object; when it takes two objects, it is taken to include the meaning of sayyara ("to make"), and so it operates like the verbs of the heart. From this is ﴿and left them in darkness﴾; its underlying form is: they are in darkness, then taraka entered and governed both parts. The omitted object of ﴿they do not see﴾ belongs to the category of the abandoned and cast-off, not to the category of the implied and intended. As if the verb were not transitive at all. Their state was compared to the state of one who kindled the fire because, after the illumination, they fell into darkness and bewilderment. Indeed, the hypocrite is ever floundering in the darknesses of disbelief; but what is meant is that they were illuminated only briefly by benefit from the word spoken on their tongues, and behind their illumination by the light of this word lies the darkness of hypocrisy, which leads them to the darkness of everlasting punishment.

There is another interpretation of the verse: when they were described as having bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, He followed this with this parable, so that the guidance they sold is represented by the bright fire around the one who kindled it, and the misguidance they bought is represented by God's taking away their light and leaving them in darkness. The indefiniteness of "fire" is for magnification.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 18:

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾. That is: they are deaf. Their senses were sound, but when they sealed their hearing (masami'hum) against heeding the truth, and refused to let their tongues (alsinatahum) speak it, and to look and gain insight with their eyes, they were made as though their faculties had been destroyed (iyfat mash'iruhum). The method of this (tariqatuhu) among the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-bayan) is like their saying: "They are lions for the brave, and seas for the generous," except that this is in attributes (al-sifat) while that is in names (al-asma'). In the verse there is a eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), according to the more correct view, and not a metaphor (isti'arah), because the thing compared to (al-musta'ar lahu) is mentioned, namely the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). Metaphor is only used where the mention of the thing compared to is omitted and the speech is left free of it, suitable for it to be meant by what is transferred from and what is transferred to, were it not for the indication of the situation (dalalat al-hal) or the import of the speech (fahwa al-kalam). ﴿So they do not return﴾: they do not come back to guidance after having sold it, or away from error after having bought it, given the variety of "returning to something" and "returning from it." Or he meant that they are bewildered, remaining rigid in their places, not moving, and not knowing whether to advance or to fall back.

(p-٥٧)﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky, in which are darkness, thunder and lightning﴾. God, glorified and exalted is He, followed up their affair with another parable (tamthil) for greater disclosure and clarification. In the first parable He likened the hypocrite to one who kindles a fire, and the showing of faith to the light, and the cessation of his benefit to the extinguishing of the fire. Here He likens the religion of Islam to the rain-cloud (sayyib), because hearts live through it as the earth lives through rain. Also related to it are the doubts of the disbelievers, likened to the darkness; what it contains of promise and threat, likened to the thunder and lightning; and what afflicts them of terror and calamities from the side of the people of Islam, likened to the thunderbolts. The meaning is: "Or like the likeness of those under a rain-cloud," so the word mithl (likeness) is omitted, the conjunction ('aṭf) indicating it, and the word dhawī (those possessed of) is omitted, the phrase yajʿalūna (they put) indicating it. What is meant is: like the likeness of a people whom the sky seized in this condition, and they suffered what they suffered from it. This is a comparison of things with things, except that the compared items (al-mushabbahāt) are not explicitly mentioned, as He did explicitly mention them in His saying: ﴿The blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the evildoer﴾ [Ghafir: 58]. And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nests, are jujubes and a withered date-stalk."

Rather, he brought it with its mention folded up, in the manner of metaphor (istiʿara, the use of a term for something else without stating the comparison). The sound view is that the two parables belong to the compound parables (al-tamthīlāt al-murakkaba, in which the whole picture is compared to a whole picture) and not the discrete ones (al-tamthīlāt al-mufarraqa, in which each element is compared separately), because each single element is given a part corresponding to its resemblance to what it is compared with. Its explanation: the Arabs take things singly, each separated from the others, so that one does not take this by the waistband of that and compare them with their counterparts, as Imru' al-Qays did. And they compare a state (kayfiyya) produced from a collection of things that have been joined and cohered until they became one thing, with another like it, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Jumuʿa: 5]. The meaning is to liken the state of the Jews in their ignorance of what they carried of the Torah to the state of the donkey in its ignorance of what it carries of books of wisdom, and the two states being equal for it, both carrying books of wisdom (p-٥٨) and carrying other burdens, and it perceives from that nothing but the fatigue and toil that pass over its two sides. And like His saying: ﴿And strike for them the likeness of the life of this world: like water which We sent down from the sky﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. The meaning is that the life of this world's splendour lasts briefly, as the greenery lasts briefly. This is the comparison of one state with another state. As for comparing individual things with individual things, where none is bound to another and they are not made into a single thing, that is not the case here. Likewise, when He described the hypocrites' falling into their error, and the bewilderment and astonishment in which they floundered, their bewilderment and the severity of the matter were likened to what one suffers whose fire has been extinguished after being kindled in the darkness of night, and likewise one whom the sky seized on a dark night with thunder and lightning and fear of thunderbolts. The second parable is more eloquent, because it is more indicative of extreme bewilderment and the severity of the matter; therefore it was placed last, since they ascend in such matters from the lighter to the more severe.

He connected one of the two parables to the other with ʾaw (or), because it is originally for the equivalence of two things or more [in doubt according to some, then it was borrowed for mere equivalence], as when you say: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning that they are equal in the fitness of being sat with. And His saying: ﴿And do not obey from among them a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], i.e., the sinner and the disbeliever are equal in the obligation of disobeying them. So here too the meaning is: the manner of the story of the hypocrites resembles the manner of these two stories, and the two stories are equal in that each one independently serves as a parable; so with whichever of them you liken it, you are correct, and if you liken it with both together, it is likewise.

The sayyib is the rain that pours (yaṣūb), i.e., descends and falls, and the cloud is also called ṣayyib. The word sayyib is indefinite because it is a kind of rain that is severe and terrifying, just as the fire was made indefinite in the first parable. The sama' (sky) here is this canopy. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is a restrained wave (mawj makfūf). The benefit of mentioning the sky, when the sayyib only comes from the sky, is that He brought the sky in the definite form, and this indicates that it is a cloud which has taken hold of the horizons of the sky, and He negated that it is from one sky, i.e., from one horizon among the rest of the horizons, because each of its horizons is a sky. So in the definiteness there is exaggeration, as in the indefiniteness of sayyib (p-٥٩) and its structure and form.

In this is evidence that the cloud descends from the sky, from which it takes its water. It was also said: it takes from the sea and rises up.

ẓulumāt (darknesses) is in the nominative, raised by the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-al-majrūr, "in which"), because the phrase has become strong by being a qualifier of sayyib, unlike if you began with "fīhi ẓulumāt" (in it are darknesses) directly; there is disagreement between al-Akhfash and Sibawayh on this.

al-raʿd (thunder) is the sound heard from the cloud due to the clashing of the cloud's bodies, or an angel driving the cloud. al-barq (lightning) is what gleams from the cloud, from baraqa al-shayʾu bariqan (the thing flashed), if it gleamed.

The pronoun in fīhi refers to the sayyib, so He made the sayyib a place for the darknesses. If by it the cloud is meant, its darkness is when it is black and covering, the two darknesses of its blackness and its covering, together with the darkness of night added to them. As for the darkness of the rain, it is the darkness of its density through the successive falling of drops, and the darkness of the shading of its cloud together with the darkness of night.

Making the sayyib a place for the thunder and lightning, on the understanding that the cloud is meant by it, is evident. Likewise if the rain is meant by it, since both are associated with it in general.

He did not make raʿd and barq plural, because both are verbal nouns (maṣdar) originally; one says: "The sky thundered (raʿdan) and flashed (barqan)." So the original status was preserved by leaving them unpluralized. These things are made indefinite because the intended meaning is kinds of them, as if it were said: "In it are intense darknesses, a crashing thunder, and a snatching lightning."

﴿They put their fingers into their ears﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of the sayyib, even though it is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿or they were napping﴾ [al-Araf: 4], because the omitted element remains in meaning even though its wording has dropped. There is no place (maḥall) for yajʿalūna because it is a resumptive (mustaʾnaf, new sentence), since when He mentioned the thunder and lightning in a way that signals severity and terror, it is as if someone said: "What is their state with the likes of that thunder?" So it was said: ﴿they put their fingers into their ears﴾. Then it is as if he said: "What is their state with the likes of that lightning?" So He said: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾ [al-Baqara: 20].

He mentioned the fingers and did not mention the finger-tips (anāmil), though the tips of the fingers are what are put into the ears, by way of extension (ittisāʿ), as in His saying: ﴿So cut off their hands﴾ [al-Maʾida: 38], where the intended meaning is up to the wrist. Also, mentioning the fingers carries an exaggeration that mentioning the finger-tips does not. He did not mention the particular finger with which the ear is plugged, because the index finger (sabbāba) is on the pattern faʿʿāla from al-sabb (cursing), so avoiding it was more fitting with the etiquette of the Qur'an. And He did not mention the misbaḥa (the counting finger/prayer-beads), because it is a newly introduced thing and not well known.

﴿From the thunderbolts﴾ is connected to yajʿalūna: i.e., because of the thunderbolts they put their fingers into their ears. The ṣāʿiqa (thunderbolt) is a crash of thunder with which a fiery shard descends. They said: it is struck out from the cloud when its bodies clash. It is a subtle, sharp fire that passes over nothing without consuming it, except that despite its sharpness it is quick to go out. It is related that it fell on a palm tree and burned about half of it, then went out. It is said: "The thunderbolt struck him (ṣaʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqa)" when it destroyed him so that he fell unconscious (faṣaʿiqa), i.e., died, either from the intensity of the sound or from the burning.

﴿Fear of death﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). Death (al-mawt): the corruption of the structure of a living being, or an accident which does not allow perception, opposed to life.

﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾: meaning that they cannot escape Him, just as the thing encompassed cannot escape the one who encompasses it. So it is a metaphor (majāz). This sentence is an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) with no place in the grammatical structure.

﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾. Al-khatf (snatching) means taking quickly. Kada (nearly) is used to indicate that an action is very close to happening. The position of yakhtifu (يَخْطِفُ) is accusative because it is the predicate (khabar) of kada.

﴿Whenever it lights up for them﴾. Kullama (كُلَّما, "whenever") is an adverb of time, and ma (ما) is a nakirah mawsufah (an indefinite noun qualified by a following clause). Its meaning is "time." The returning pronoun (al-ʾaʾid) is omitted, so the sense is: "every time it lit up for them in it." The word that governs it is its response clause, which is ﴿they walk in it﴾, meaning in its light. This is a third resumptive statement (istiʾnaf), as if it were an answer to someone who asks: "How do they act during the moments when the lightning flashes and when it fades?" This is an illustration (tamthil) of how severe the matter is for the hypocrites, comparable to its severity for the people of the downpour, and of their extreme bewilderment and ignorance about what they should do and what they should leave undone. When they encounter a flash of lightning, while fearing that it will snatch away their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few small steps. When it fades and its gleam dims, they remain standing.

Adaʾa (أضاءَ, "lit up") is transitive, meaning: whenever it illuminated for them a path and a way, they took it. The object is omitted. Or it is intransitive, meaning: whenever it shone for them, they walked in the place where its light fell. Al-mashy (المَشْيُ, "walking") is the general category of a particular movement. When it becomes more intense, it is saʿy (سَعْيٌ, "hurried walking"), and when it becomes even more intense, it is ʿadw (عَدْوٌ, "running").

﴿And when darkness falls upon them﴾. Adhlama (أظْلَمَ) is intransitive. The phrase mentions kullama with adaʾa and idhā with adhlama, because they are eager for the existence of that which their aim depends on, namely the possibility of walking. Whenever they encounter an opportunity from it, they seize it. This is not the case with stopping.

﴿they stand﴾, meaning they stop and remain firm in their place (p-61). From this comes qama al-ma' (قامَ الماءُ), meaning the water became still and solid.

﴿If God willed, He would have taken away their hearing﴾ with the crashing of thunder,

﴿and their sight﴾ with the flash of lightning. The object of shaʾa (شاءَ, "willed") is omitted because the response clause indicates it. The meaning is: if God willed to take away their hearing and their sight, He would have taken them away. This omission of the object after shaʾa is very common, and the author intends that they rarely express the object except in an unusual matter, as in the line of poetry:

*If I wished to weep blood, I would weep it over him, but the expanse of patience is wider.*
