And the words of the Exalted: ﴿If We had wished to take up a pastime﴾ [al-Anbiyaʾ 21:17], and ﴿If God had wished to take a son﴾ [al-Zumar 39:4].

﴿Indeed God is over all things Powerful﴾, meaning: indeed God is capable of everything.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 21:

When Allah enumerated the categories of the responsible (mukallafin) among the believers, the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and mentioned their attributes and states, and what each category is particularly characterized by, which makes them happy, makes them wretched, grants them favour, or casts them into ruin, He turned to them with direct address, which is of the type of iltifat (shift of grammatical person) mentioned earlier, and said: ﴿O people﴾. ʿAlqama said: whatever in the Qur'an says "O people" is addressed to the people of Makkah, and whatever says "O you who believe" is addressed to the people of Madinah. This is an address to the polytheists of Makkah. And "ya" (yā, the particle of calling) is a particle established for calling the distant, while ayyu and the hamza are for the near. Then it was used for calling one who is heedless and forgetful, even if he is near and close, treating him as if he were in the position of one who is far and remote. When the one who is near and present is called with it, that is for emphasis, indicating that the address which follows it is of very great concern. And the words of the supplicant, "O my Lord," while He is nearer to him than the jugular vein, are a belittling of himself by himself, and a distancing of himself from the places of nearness, a humbling of his own self, and an acknowledgement against himself of negligence, together with his extreme eagerness for the answering of his supplication. Ayyu (ayyu, "which/whoever"): a connective to the calling of what has the definite article "al-", just as "dhu" (possessor) and "alladhi" (who) are connectives to the description of generic nouns by means of sentences describing definites. It is an ambiguous noun (ism mubham) which requires something to remove its ambiguity, so it must be followed by a generic noun, or what takes its place, which it is described by, until the intended object of the call becomes clear. The element governed by "ya" is ayyu, and the element following it is its attribute (sifa), as in: "O Zayd the witty" (ya Zaydu al-zarif). Except that ayyu does not stand independently as Zayd does, so it is never separated from the attribute; and the particle of alerting (kalimat al-tanbih) is inserted between the attribute and the thing it describes, to emphasize the meaning of calling and as a substitute for what it deserves, namely the idafa (annexation). Calling in the Qur'an occurs frequently in this manner, because what Allah called His servants to, of His commands and prohibitions, His promise and threat, are great matters and weighty affairs, which require them to be alert to them and to incline their hearts towards them, while they are heedless of them. So it required that they be called with the most emphatic and most eloquent form: ﴿Worship your Lord﴾, that is, affirm His oneness. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: every act of worship (ʿibada) in the Qur'an is tawhid. ﴿who created you﴾ is a descriptive attribute (sifa) that clarifies and distinguishes, because they used to call the gods lords (arbab). Creation (khalq): bringing into existence what did not exist, according to a measure and proportion. According to the Mu'tazila: bringing a thing into existence according to a measure and proportion. This is based on their view that the non-existent is a thing (shay') for them, since "thing" is what may be known and spoken of, in their view; while for us it is a name for what exists. "Khalaqakum" with idgham (assimilation): Abu ʿAmr. ﴿and those before you﴾: He argued against them that He is their creator and the creator of those before them, because they used to acknowledge this. So it was said to them: If you acknowledge that He is your creator, then worship Him, and do not worship the idols. ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾: that is, worship in the hope that you will be mindful of Him and thereby be saved from the punishment. "La'alla" is for expectation and hope, but it is a hope from a Generous One, so it takes the place of His binding promise, whose fulfilment is certain. This is the view of Sibawayh. Qutrub said: it has the meaning of kay, that is, "in order that you may be God-fearing."

﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ﴾ أي: صَيَّرَ (ja'ala, "made"). ومَحِلُّ الَّذِي نَصْبٌ عَلى المَدْحِ (madh, "praise"), أوْ رَفْعٌ بِإضْمارِ هو (by supposing a hidden "huwa"). ﴿فِراشًا﴾ بِساطًا تَقْعُدُونَ عَلَيْها، وتَنامُونَ، وتَتَقَلَّبُونَ، وهو مَفْعُولٌ ثانٍ لِجَعَلَ. ولَيْسَ فِيهِ دَلِيلٌ عَلى أنَّ الأرْضَ مُسَطَّحَةٌ أوْ كُرِّيَّةٌ، إذِ الِافْتِراشُ مُمْكِنٌ عَلى التَقْدِيرَيْنِ. ﴿والسَماءَ بِناءً﴾ سَقْفًا، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وَجَعَلْنا (p-63) السَماءَ سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا﴾ [الأنبياء: 32]، وهو مَصْدَرٌ سُمِّي بِهِ المَبْنِيُّ. ﴿وَأنْـزَلَ مِنَ السَماءِ ماءً﴾ مَطَرًا ﴿فَأخْرَجَ بِهِ﴾ بِالماءِ. نَعَمْ، خُرُوجُ الثَمَراتِ بِقُدْرَتِهِ ومَشِيئَتِهِ وإيجادِهِ، ولَكِنَّ جَعْلَ الماءِ سَبَبًا في خُرُوجِها، كَماءِ الفَحْلِ في خَلْقِ الوَلَدِ، وهو قادِرٌ عَلى إنْشاءِ الكُلِّ بِلا سَبَبٍ، كَما أنْشَأ نُفُوسَ الأسْبابِ والمَوادِّ، ولَكِنَّ لَهُ في إنْشاءِ الأشْياءِ مَدْرَجًا لَها مِن حالٍ إلى حالٍ، وناقِلًا مِن مَرْتَبَةٍ إلى مَرْتَبَةٍ، حِكَمًا وعِبَرًا لِلنُّظّارِ بِعُيُونِ الِاسْتِبْصارِ. و"مِن" في ﴿مِنَ الثَمَراتِ﴾ لِلتَّبْعِيضِ، أوْ لِلْبَيانِ. ﴿رِزْقًا﴾ مَفْعُولٌ لَهُ إنْ كانَتْ "مِن" لِلتَّبْعِيضِ، ومَفْعُولٌ بِهِ لِأخْرَجَ إنْ كانَتْ لِلْبَيانِ. وإنَّما قِيلَ: الثَمَراتُ دُونَ الثَمَرِ والثِمارِ، وإنْ كانَ الثَمَرُ المُخْرَجُ بِماءِ السَماءِ كَثِيرًا، لِأنَّ المُرادَ جَماعَةُ الثَمَرَةِ، ولِأنَّ الجُمُوعَ يَتَعاوَرُ بَعْضُها مَوْقِعَ بَعْضٍ، لِالتِقائِها في الجَمْعِيَّةِ. ﴿لَكُمُ﴾ صِفَةٌ جارِيَةٌ عَلى الرِزْقِ إنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ العَيْنُ، وإنْ جُعِلَ اسْمًا لِلْمَعْنى فَهو مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ، كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: رِزْقًا إيّاكم. ﴿فَلا تَجْعَلُوا لِلَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾ هو مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِالأمْرِ، أيِ: اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكم فَلا تَجْعَلُوا لَهُ أنْدادًا، لِأنَّ أصْلَ العِبادَةِ وأساسَها التَوْحِيدُ، وأنْ لا يُجْعَلَ لَهُ نِدٌّ ولا شَرِيكٌ. ويَجُوزُ أنْ يَكُونَ الَّذِي رَفْعًا عَلى الِابْتِداءِ، وخَبَرُهُ ﴿فَلا تَجْعَلُوا﴾، ودُخُولُ الفاءِ لِأنَّ الكَلامَ يَتَضَمَّنُ الجَزاءَ، أيِ: الَّذِي حَفَّكم بِهَذِهِ الآياتِ العَظِيمَةِ، والدَلائِلِ النَيِّرَةِ الشاهِدَةِ بِالوَحْدانِيَّةِ، فَلا تَتَّخِذُوا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ. والنِدُّ: المَثَلُ، ولا يُقالُ إلّا لِلْمَثَلِ المُخالِفِ والمُنافِي. ومَعْنى قَوْلِهِمْ: لَيْسَ لِلَّهِ نِدٌّ ولا ضِدٌّ: نَفْيُ ما يَسُدُّ مَسَدَّهُ، ونَفْيُ ما يُنافِيهِ. ﴿وَأنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ أنَّها لا تَخْلُقُ شَيْئًا، ولا تَرْزُقُ، واللهُ الخالِقُ الرازِقُ. أوْ مَفْعُولُ تَعْلَمُونَ مَتْرُوكٌ، أيْ: وأنْتُمْ مِن أهْلِ العِلْمِ. وجَعْلُ الأصْنامِ لِلَّهِ أنْدادًا غايَةُ الجَهْلِ، والجُمْلَةُ حالٌ مِنَ الضَمِيرِ في ﴿فَلا تَجْعَلُوا﴾.

[p. 64] When He argued against them with that which establishes the oneness of God (tawhid) and refutes associating partners with Him (shirk), namely His creating them as living, capable beings, His creating the earth which is their place and dwelling, and His creating the sky, which is like a raised dome and a tent stretched over this resting place, and what else He, Mighty and Majestic, has made, such as the likeness of the marriage contract between the sperm and the womb through the sending down of water from the sky onto the earth, and the bringing forth through it from the earth's belly, as a provision for the children of Adam, things resembling offspring in the form of fruits: all of this is a proof that leads to tawhid and refutes shirk, because none of the created things is able to bring any of these into existence. He then followed this with that which is the proof for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and which confirms the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an. So He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down﴾, and so on. "Ma" (ما) is an indefinite, qualified noun, or it has the meaning of "alladhi" (the one which). ﴿upon Our servant﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). "Abd" (servant) is a name for a owned being of the rational kind. The "mamluk" (owned one) is an existing being who has been subjugated by taking possession.

It was also said: "nazzalna" (نَزَّلْنا, We sent down, with the intensive form) is used instead of "anzalna" (أَنْزَلْنا, We sent down), because what is meant by it is descent by way of gradualness and in installments (tanjim), and this is a metaphorical usage because of the context of the challenge (tahaddi). That is because they used to say: "If this were from Allah, it would not have come down in this way, in installments, surah after surah and verses following verses, according to the occurrences, and in the manner we see among the people of oratory and poetry, in which what is produced by them is found piece by piece, time after time, little by little. The composer of poetry does not release his collection of poems all at once, nor does the prose writer throw out his speeches in a single blow. So if Allah had sent it down, He would have sent it down all at once." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. So it was said: "If you doubt this, which has been sent down in this gradual manner, then ﴿produce a surah﴾, that is: then you bring forth one turn of its turns, and come forward with one single installment of its installments: a surah from the shortest of surahs. The "surah" is a section of the Qur'an, distinct and marked off, the least of which is three verses. As for its waw (و): if it is an original letter, then either it is named after the "sur" (سُور) of a city, which is its wall, because it is a section of the Qur'an that is bounded and enclosed on its own, like a walled town; or because it contains branches of knowledge and kinds of benefits, just as the wall of a city contains what is within it. Or it is named after "al-surah" (السُورَة) meaning rank or level, because the walls are like stations and ranks through which the reciter ascends, and it is itself also ordered in levels: long, medium and short; or because of the height of its structure and the greatness of its standing in the religion. If it is an altered form of a hamza, then it is because it is a piece and a section of the Qur'an, like "al-su'ra" (السُؤْرَة), which means the remainder of a thing. As for the benefit of dividing the Qur'an and cutting it into surahs, it is abundant. For this reason Allah, the Exalted, sent down the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and all that He revealed to His prophets arranged in surahs with headings, and the authors of every discipline divided their books into chapters adorned with headings. Among its benefits: when a genre encompasses types and includes various kinds, it is better than being one continuous exposition. Among them: when the reader finishes a surah or a chapter of the book and then begins another, it is more energizing for him and more inciting to study and acquire from it than if the book continued at its full length. For this reason the reciters divided the Qur'an into sevenths, parts, tenths, and fifths. Among them: when the memorizer masters a surah, he believes that he has taken from the Book of Allah a section that is independent in itself, with a beginning and an end, so what he has memorized becomes great in his eyes and is held in high esteem in his soul. From this is the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "When a man recited al-Baqara and Al 'Imran, he became great among us." For this reason reciting a complete surah in the prayer is more excellent. ﴿Of its like﴾ is connected to "surah" as a descriptive qualifier of it. The pronoun (in "mithlihi," its like) refers to "ma nazzalna," meaning: a surah existing of its like. That is: produce a surah of what has the same qualities in its extraordinary eloquence and its high rank in the beauty of composition. Or (the pronoun refers) to "Our servant," meaning: produce it from someone who is in his condition, in that he is unlettered, did not read the books, did not take from the scholars, and did not seek out any model or equivalent in that place. Returning the pronoun to the one who sent it down (the Qur'an) is preferable, because of Allah's saying: ﴿So produce a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38], ﴿So produce ten surahs like it﴾ [Hud: 13], ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like﴾ [al-Isra: 88]. Also, the discourse, with the pronoun returning to the one who sent it down, is more excellent in order, because the discussion is about the sent-down (the Qur'an), not about the one upon whom it was sent down, though the address is directed to him. The meaning is: "And if you doubt that the Qur'an has been sent down from Allah, then you produce fragments like it." The order would require, if the pronoun referred to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that it be said: "And if you doubt that Muhammad has been sent down to, [p. 67] then produce a Qur'an like it." Also, this interpretation fits His saying: ﴿And call your witnesses﴾, the plural of "shahid" (شَهِيد), meaning one present or one who gives testimony.

﴿Other than Allah﴾, that is: apart from Allah. It is connected to "your witnesses," meaning: call those whom you have taken as gods besides Allah, and whom you claimed would testify for you on the Day of Resurrection that you were upon the truth; or whoever will testify for you that it is like the Qur'an.

﴿If you are truthful﴾: that this is fabricated and that it is the speech of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. The answer to the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: if you are truthful in your claim, then you produce its like yourselves, and seek help from your gods in doing so.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 24:

﴿But if you do not, and you will never do, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. When He had guided them to the aspect by which they could recognize the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ, He said to them: If you do not oppose him, your incapacity becomes clear, and it becomes obligatory to affirm him, then believe, and fear the punishment prepared for those who deny and obstinately oppose. In this verse there are two proofs of the establishment of prophethood: the soundness of the challenge (*tahaddi*) being a miracle (*mu'jiz*), and the report that they will never do it, which is unseen knowledge that none knows but Allah. Since inability to counter-produce something (*mu'arada*) before reflection resembled a matter of doubt for them, because they relied on their eloquence and depended on their rhetorical skill, the discourse was framed in accordance with their own reckoning. Thus the particle *in* (if), which expresses doubt, was used instead of *idha* (when), which expresses certainty. The expression for producing it was made with the verb *fa'ala* (to do), because it is one of the acts, and the benefit of this is that it works as a metonymy (*kinaya*) which gives you brevity. For if he had not shifted from the word *ityan* (bringing) to the word *fi'l* (doing), it would have been lengthy to say: "If you do not bring a surah like it, and you will never bring a surah like it." There is no grammatical position (*mahall*) for His words ﴿and you will never do﴾, because it is a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tiraDiyya*). What makes this parenthesis good is that the conditional particle is for expressing hesitation, so He cut off the hesitation with His words ﴿and you will never do﴾. "Lan" and "la" do not differ in negating the future, except that "lan" carries emphasis. It is reported from al-Khalil that its origin is *la an*; according to al-Farra', it is *la*, whose alif was replaced with a nun. According to Sibawayh, it is a particle placed for emphasizing the negation of the future. It was known that this is a report of the unseen as it actually is, to the point that it became a miracle, because had they countered him with something, it would have become famous. How much more so, since those who attack him are greater in number than those who defend him?! And the condition for protection from the Fire is the absence of their producing a surah like it, because if they do not produce it and their incapacity to counter-produce becomes evident, the truthfulness of the Messenger becomes sound for them. And when his truthfulness became sound for them (p-67), then if they persist in obstinacy and refuse submission, they deserve the Fire. So it was said to them: If you have realized your incapacity, then abandon obstinacy. He placed ﴿fear the Fire﴾ in its place, because fearing the Fire is the cause of abandoning obstinacy, and this is from the category of metonymy, which is among the branches of eloquence. Its benefit is brevity (*ijaz*), which is among the stratagems of the Qur'an.

*Al-waqud* is that by which fire is kindled, meaning firewood. As for the verbal noun (*masdar*), it is with a *damma*, though *fath* has also come in it. The relative clause (*silat*) of *alladhi* and *allati* must be known to the addressee. It is possible that they had heard it from the People of the Book, or from the Messenger of Allah, or they had heard before this verse His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. The word "fire" came indefinite there and definite here, because that verse was revealed in Makkah, and then this verse was revealed in Madinah, pointing to what they had already recognized. The meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whose fuel is men and stones﴾ is that it is a fire distinguished from other fires in that it is kindled by men and stones, and these are stones of sulphur, so it is more intense in blazing, slower to die down, more foul in smell, and clings more closely to the body. Or the stones are the idols that were worshipped. He joined men with stones because they joined themselves with them in this world, when they worshipped them and made them rivals to Allah. A similar statement is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98], that is, its firewood. So He joined them with it, heated in the Fire of Hell, as an intensification of their torment.

﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, meaning it has been readied for them. In this there is evidence that the Fire is created, contrary to what Jahm says.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 25:

It is God's practice in His Book to mention encouragement alongside warning, to stir people toward acquiring what brings them near (to Him), and to restrain them from committing what destroys them. When He mentioned the disbelievers and their deeds, and threatened them with punishment, He followed this with mention of the believers and their deeds, and with the good news of them, in His saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (p. 68). The one commanded by His saying ﴿give good news﴾ is the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, or it is every person. The second view is the better one, because it indicates that the matter, owing to its greatness and the magnificence of its status, deserves to be announced by everyone who is able to announce it. The verse is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿So fear﴾. It is like when you say: "O Banu Tamim, beware the punishment for what you have committed, and give good news, O so-and-so, to Banu Asad of my kindness toward them." Alternatively, the clause describing the reward of the believers is conjoined to the clause describing the punishment of the disbelievers, like your saying: "Zayd is punished with shackles and oppression, and give good news to 'Amr of pardon and release."

Bishara (glad tidings) is informing someone of something that manifests the joy of the one informed. Hence the scholars [said]: if a man says to his slaves, "Whichever of you brings me the news of so-and-so's arrival is free," and they bring the news individually, the first of them is freed, because he is the one who showed his joy at the news, to the exclusion of the others. But if he said, "Inform me" instead of "Give me good news," they would all be freed, because they informed him. From the same root is bashra (the skin's outer surface), and tabashir al-subh (the first glimmers of dawn), which are the first appearances of its light.

As for ﴿So give them news of a painful punishment﴾ (Al 'Imran: 21), it is an inversion (in usage) found in speech intended as excessive mockery, increasing the anger of the one mocked, as a man says to his enemy: "Rejoice at the killing of your offspring and the plundering of your wealth."

Salihah (righteous) is like hasanah (good) in that it functions as a noun. Al-salihat (the righteous deeds) means everything that is upright among deeds, by the evidence of reason, the Book, and the Sunnah. The definite article (al-) in al-salihat is for the category (li-l-jins). This verse is a proof against those who make deeds part of faith (iman), because it conjoined the righteous deeds to faith, and the conjoined is other than that to which it is conjoined. It may not be said: "You (Mu'tazilites) say that it is possible for God to admit a believer to Paradise without righteous deeds, yet God gave good news of Paradise to whoever believes and does righteous deeds." That is because unconditional good news of Paradise is conditional on the conjunction of righteous deeds with faith. We do not grant the unconditional good news to the one guilty of a major sin; rather, we affirm good news qualified by the will of God: if He wills, He forgives him, and if He wills, He punishes him in proportion to his sins, and then He admits him to Paradise.

﴿That for them are gardens﴾: that is, "that for them" (an-na is the particle here). The position of an and what it governs is in the accusative (nasb) by the verb "give good news," according to Sibawayh, contrary to al-Khalil, and this is frequent in the Revelation. Jannah (garden) is an orchard of palm trees and dense trees. The root (j-n-n) revolves around the meaning of concealment, and from it come jinn (hidden beings), junun (madness), janin (fetus), jannah (garden), jann (a hidden one), and janan (heart/inner part). The abode of reward was called jannah because of the concealing foliage (janan) within it. Paradise is created, as in His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ (al-Baqarah: 35), contrary to some Mu'tazilites.

The meaning of pluralizing and indefinitizing "jannah" is that jannah is a name for the whole abode of reward, which contains many gardens, arranged in ranks according to the deeds of those who act, such that for each class among them there are gardens from those gardens.

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾: the clause is in the accusative position as a description (sifah) of "gardens." The meaning is: beneath their trees, as you see trees growing on the banks of flowing rivers. The rivers of Paradise flow without a trench, and the most delightful gardens are those whose trees give shade while the rivers flow through them in steady courses. Jary (flowing) is steady movement (iṭṭirad). Nahr (river) is a wide channel, larger than a jadwal (rivulet) and smaller than a sea. The Nile is called "the River of Egypt." The dominant usage is nahr, and the root's core meaning is breadth/spaciousness. Attributing the flowing to the rivers is metaphorical (majazi). The rivers are made definite because it is possible that their rivers (of the gardens) are intended; so the definite article (al-) substitutes for the definition by annexation (idafah), as in His saying: ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ (Maryam: 4). Or the article (al-) points to the rivers mentioned in His saying: ﴿therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾ (Muhammad: 15). Flowing water is the greatest of blessings and the supreme delight; therefore God linked the gardens with the mention of flowing rivers, and placed it before all their other attributes.

﴿Every time they are provided﴾: a second description of "gardens," or a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah). Because it was said, "For them are gardens," the listener's mind could not avoid wondering whether the fruits of those gardens resemble the fruits of the gardens of this world, or are other kinds not resembling these. So it was said that their fruits resemble the fruits of the gardens of this world, i.e., their kinds are the same kinds, although they differ to a degree known only to God.

﴿Whenever they are given from it a provision of fruit, they say, "This is what we were provided before"﴾: that is, every time they are provided from the gardens with any fruit whatsoever, whether apples, pomegranates, or otherwise, they say this. The first "min" (from) and the second are both for the starting point of the source (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), because the provision began from the gardens, and the provision from the gardens began from a fruit. A parallel is your saying: "So-and-so provided me," and it is said to you, "From where?" and you say, "From his orchard." Then it is said, "From which fruit did he provide you from his orchard?" and you say, "From pomegranates." The intended "fruit" is not one single apple or one solitary pomegranate; rather, it is a type of fruit.

﴿We were provided﴾: that is, "we were provided it," so the returning pronoun was deleted. ﴿Before﴾ (min qablu): that is, before this. When it is cut off from the annexation (i.e., when qablu lacks its complement), it is built on a fixed form (mabni, on damm). The meaning is: "This is like what we were provided before and its semblance," as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and they will be brought it, similar (mutashabihan)﴾. This is like your saying: "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifah," meaning that because of the strong resemblance, his essence is as if it were their essence.

The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to what is provided, in both this world and the Hereafter together, because His saying "This is what we were provided before" encompasses what they were provided in both abodes. The fruits of Paradise were like the fruits of this world, and were not other kinds, because a person is more at ease with what is familiar and more inclined to what is known. When he sees what he is not accustomed to, his nature recoils from it and his soul dislikes it. Also, when he witnesses what he previously knew, and sees in it a clear superiority and an evident difference, his wonder at it is greater and his astonishment more abundant. Their repeating this saying at every fruit they are provided is evidence of the extreme degree of the matter, and of the continuing state of manifest superiority, and that this great difference is what keeps their wonder alive at every moment.

Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the provision (rizq), just as "this" (hadha) points to it. The meaning is that what they are provided of the fruits of Paradise comes to them homogeneous in itself. As is related from al-Hasan: one of them is brought a dish, eats from it, then another is brought, and he says, "This is what we were brought before." The angel says, "Eat," for the color is one, but the taste differs.

And from him (al-Hasan) ﷺ (the Prophet, peace be upon him): "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, indeed a man of the people of Paradise reaches out to take a fruit to eat it, but it has not reached his mouth before God replaces it with another like it." So when they see it, and its appearance is the appearance of the first, they say this.

His saying ﴿and they will be brought it, similar﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumlah mu'taridah) for confirmation, like your saying: "So-and-so did well by so-and-so, and what a good thing he did, and he held an opinion, and it was correct." From the same usage is: ﴿And they made the honored of its people abased, and thus they do﴾ (al-Naml: 34).

﴿And for them therein are spouses﴾: azwaj (spouses) is the subject (mubtada'), and lahum (for them) is the predicate (khabar); fiha (therein) is an adverbial phrase (zarf) indicating settledness (li-l-istiqrar).

﴿Purified﴾: purified of bad morals, neither arrogant (tamihat) nor frivolous (marihat); or purified of what is specific to women, such as menstruation and irregular bleeding, and of what is not specific to them, such as urine, feces, and all filth and impurities. The adjective was not made plural like its noun, because both forms (mutahharah and mutahharat) are eloquent dialects. He did not say "tahirah" (pure), because mutahharah is more emphatic, since it can denote intensity; and it contains a hint that a purifier purified them, and that none does this but God, may He be exalted and majestic.

﴿And they therein are abiding forever﴾: al-khuld is lasting permanence that never ends. In it is the refutation of the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah, for they hold that Paradise and its people will perish. God is described as "the First and the Last," and the realization of the attribute of firstness is by His precedence over all creation; thus the realization of the attribute of lastness must be by His outlasting all created things, and this is realized only after the perishing of all, so it must be affirmed necessarily. Also, God is enduring, and His attributes are enduring; so if Paradise remained along with its people, resemblance would occur between the Creator and the created, and this is impossible.

We reply: the First, with respect to Him, is the one for whose existence there is no beginning, and the Last is the one for whom there is no end. With respect to us, the first is the individual who precedes, and the last is the individual who follows. His being described by both is to show the attribute of perfection and the negation of deficiency and cessation; and this applies to His transcendence above the possibility of origination and perishing, not to what they claimed. And how could resemblance occur in permanence, when He, may He be exalted, is enduring by His own essence, and His permanence is necessarily existent, while the permanence of creation is through Him, and it is possibly existent?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 26:

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book and cited them as an example, the Jews laughed and said: "What resembles this as speech of Allah?" So there was revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a gnat﴾. That is: He does not abstain from citing the gnat as an example in the manner of one who is ashamed to use it as a comparison because of its insignificance. The root of *ḥayāʾ* (shame, modesty) is a change and a breaking that comes over a person from fear of being blamed and censured for something. Such change, fear and censure are not permissible for the Eternal (*al-Qadīm*), but since abstaining (*al-tark*) is among its necessary consequences, it is expressed by it. It is also possible that this expression occurred in the speech of the disbelievers (p. 72), who said: "Is the Lord of Muhammad not ashamed to cite as an example the fly and the spider?" So [the verse] came in the manner of a response that matches the question and covers it fully (*al-muqābala wa-iṭbāq al-jawāb ʿalā al-suʾāl*), which is an elegant genre of their speech. The verb has two constructions: it is transitive directly and with a preposition. One says *istaḥyaytuhu* and *istaḥyaytu minhu*, and both are possible here. *Ḍarb al-mathal* means to make or fashion an example, from the expressions *ḍaraba al-laban* (he churned the milk) and *ḍaraba al-khātam* (he struck the seal). The *mā* here is *ibhāmiyya* (indefinite-intensifying): when it is attached to an indefinite noun, it makes that noun more vague and adds generality, as in your saying "Give me a book, any [book]," meaning: whatever book it may be. Or it is *ṣila lil-taʾkīd* (a particle for emphasis), like the one in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So, because of their breaking their covenant﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 155]. It is as if He said: "He is not ashamed to present an example at all." *Baʿūḍatan* is either an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*) to *mathalan*, or an object of *yaḍribu*; *mathalan* is either a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from the indefinite noun placed before it, or both are accusative as two objects, on the basis that *ḍaraba* here means *jaʿala* (made). Its derivation is from *al-baʿḍ*, which means cutting, like *al-baḍʿ* and *al-ʿaḍb*: one says *baʿaḍahu al-baʿūḍ* (the gnat bit him), and from this comes *baʿḍ al-shay'* (a part of a thing), because it is a piece of it. *Al-baʿūḍ* in its original form is an adjective on the pattern *faʿūl*, like *al-qatūʿ*, but it became a noun by predominance. ﴿So what is above it﴾ means: what exceeds it. It goes beyond it in the meaning in which it was used as an example, which is littleness and insignificance; or [it means] what is larger than it in size. It is as if He intended by this to answer what they found objectionable about citing the fly and the spider, since these two are larger than the gnat. It is not said: "How can [Allah] cite as an example something smaller than the gnat, which is the extreme of smallness?" Because the wing of the gnat is smaller than it and less by degrees; and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cited it as an example for this world. ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth﴾: the pronoun refers to the example, or to the act of citing [it]. *Al-ḥaqq* is what is established and cannot rightly be denied; one says *ḥaqqa al-amr* when it is confirmed and becomes binding.

﴿From their Lord﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*); the operator is the meaning of *al-ḥaqq*, and the one it refers to is the hidden pronoun within it. ﴿And as for those who disbelieve, they say: What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ One stops here, for if it were joined, what follows would become an adjective of it, and that is not the case. In their saying ﴿What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ there is contempt, as ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said about ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr (p. 73): "How strange is this son of ʿAmr!", belittling him. *Mathalan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*) or as a circumstantial phrase, like His words ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 73]. *Amma* is a particle that carries the meaning of a condition, and therefore its answer is introduced by *fa* (then). Its function in speech is to give emphasis: you say "Zayd is going"; but when you intend to emphasize it, and that he is certainly going, you say: "As for Zayd, he is going." Hence Sibawayh said in explaining it: "Whatever there may be of a thing, Zayd is going." This explanation indicates that it is for emphasis and that it has the meaning of a condition. In introducing both clauses with it, even though He did not say "those who believe know, and those who disbelieve say," there is a great praise of the affair of the believers, a forceful reckoning of their knowledge that it is the truth, a censure of the disbelievers for their neglect of their own portion, and a casting upon them of a foolish word. As for *māḏā* in this context, there are two possibilities: either *dhā* is a relative noun meaning "the one which," and *mā* is an interrogative, making two words; or *dhā* combined with *mā* is made into one interrogative noun, making one word. On the first, *mā* is nominative as the subject, and its predicate is *dhā* with its relative clause, meaning "what [did] He intend," and the returning pronoun is omitted; on the second, it is accusative in position as object of *arāda*, and the sense is "what thing did Allah intend?" *Al-irāda* is the verbal noun of *aradtu al-shay'*, when your self seeks it and your heart inclines to it. According to the theologians (*al-mutakallimūn*), it is a meaning that requires the specification of objects in one aspect rather than another. Allah, exalted is He, is described with will (*irāda*) in its literal sense according to Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). The Baghdadi Mu'tazila said that He, exalted is He, is not described with will in its literal sense. So when it is said "Allah intended such-and-such," if it is His own act, its meaning is that He did it, without being heedless or compelled to it; and if it is the act of another, its meaning is that He commanded it. ﴿He misguides many by it and guides many by it﴾ serves as an explanation and clarification of the two clauses introduced by *amma*: that the group who know it is the truth and the group of ignorant mockers of it are both described as numerous; that knowledge that it is true belongs to guidance, and ignorance of the goodness of its purpose belongs to misguidance. The people of guidance are many in themselves; they are described as few only in comparison with the people of misguidance; and because the few among the guided are many in reality, even if they are few in appearance.

*The generous are many in the lands, even if they are few,*
*just as others are few, even if they are many.*

*Al-iḍlāl* (misguiding) is the creation of the act of going astray in the servant, and *al-hidāya* (guidance) is the creation of the act of being guided (p. 74). This is the reality according to Ahl al-Sunna. The context of the verse is to show that what the ignorant disbelievers found objectionable and strange, namely that the most insignificant things should be used as examples, is not a matter for objection or astonishment. For citing an example is only resorted to because of what it brings of clarifying the meaning and bringing the imagined close to the observed. If the one represented is great, the representing thing is likewise great; if it is contemptible, the representing thing is likewise contemptible. Do you not see that since the truth is clear and manifest, it is represented by light and radiance, and since falsehood is the opposite of its attribute, it is represented by darkness? And since the state of the idols that the disbelievers made equals to Allah was nothing more contemptible or lowly than that, and therefore they liken the spider's house to them in weakness and frailty, and they were said to be less than the fly, and the gnat was cited for them, so whatever is below it is an example, he (the Prophet) did not find it objectionable or strange and did not say to the one citing: "Be ashamed of citing it with the gnat," because he is correct in his citation, right in his saying, leading the example according to the case it is struck for. Moreover, it shows that the believers, whose habit is fairness and considering matters with the eye of reason, when they hear this comparison, know that it is the truth; and that the disbelievers, whom ignorance has overcome over their intellects, when they hear it, act stubbornly, oppose, pass judgment that it is false, and meet it with denial; and that this is the cause of the guidance of the believers and the misguidance of the defiantly wicked. It is strange that they denied this, when people have always struck examples with animals, birds and small creatures of the earth. They say: "More gathering than the ant; bolder than the fly; more hearing than the tick; weaker than the butterfly; more eating than the weevil; weaker than the gnat; more precious than the marrow of the gnat." But the habit of one who is refuted and confounded is to accept, out of extreme bewilderment, the rejection of what is manifest and the denial of what is evident.

﴿And He does not misguide by it except the defiantly wicked﴾: *huwa* is the object of *yuḍillu* and is not in the accusative as an exception (*istithnāʾ*), because *yuḍillu* has not fully taken its object. *Al-fisq* is departing from the right course. In the Sharia, it is one who departs from the command by committing a major sin; and he is the one who stands between the two positions, that is, between the position of the believer and the position of the disbeliever according to the Mu'tazila. What refutes this will pass before you, if Allah wills.

(p. 75) ﴿Those who break the covenant of God﴾. *Al-naqd* (breaking) means annulling and undoing a structure. *Al-'ahd* (covenant) means a binding pledge. By "those who break the covenant of God" are meant the obstinate rabbis of the Jews (*ahbar al-yahud*), or their hypocrites, or the disbelievers in general. The "covenant of God" (*'ahd Allah*) is the proof concerning monotheism that He placed in their intellects, as if it were a command He enjoined upon them and bound them to. Or it is the covenant He took from them that if a messenger were sent to them, whom God would confirm through his miracles, they would believe him, follow him, and not conceal his mention. Or it is the covenant God took from them that they would not shed one another's blood, would not oppress one another, and would not sever their kinship ties. It has been said: God's covenant with His creation consists of three covenants. The first is the covenant He took from all the offspring of Adam, peace be upon him, that they would acknowledge His lordship, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and so on. The second is a covenant specific to the prophets, that they would convey the message and establish the religion, which is His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7]. The third is a covenant specific to the scholars, which is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187].

﴿From after its binding﴾. Its root is from *al-wathaqah* (being firm), which is the making of a thing firm. The pronoun refers to the covenant, namely that by which they had bound themselves to God's covenant through acceptance of it and their obligation of themselves to it. It is permissible that *mithaq* (binding) means *tawaththaqtuhu* (I bound myself to it), just as *mi'ad* (promise) means *wa'd* (promise). Or the pronoun refers to God, exalted is He, meaning: after His binding them to it. And *min* (from) denotes the starting point of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghayah*).

﴿And they sever what God has commanded to be joined﴾. This is their severing of kinship ties and their alliance with the believers. Or it is their severing of the connection and unity upon the truth between the prophets, through their believing in some of them and disbelieving in others. *Al-amr* (command) is the demand for an act through a specific utterance in the manner of superiority.

*Ma* here is either an indefinite qualified noun (*nakirah mawsufah*), or it has the meaning of *alladhi* (which). The phrase *an yuwassala* (that it be joined) is in the position of a substitute in the genitive (*badal*) for the pronoun *ha'* (it), meaning: they sever it from being joined; or it is in the nominative position, meaning: it is that it be joined.

﴿And they cause corruption on the earth﴾ by cutting off the way and hindering from faith.

﴿Those﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), ﴿they﴾ is a separating pronoun (*fasl*). The predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿the losers﴾, meaning: those who are defrauded, since they exchanged breaking for fulfilment, severing for joining, corruption for righteousness, and punishment for reward.

(p-76) ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ The meaning of the interrogative particle *hamza* (the *alif* of interrogation) in *kayfa* (how) is like its meaning in your saying: "Do you disbelieve in God when with you is that which turns you away from disbelief and calls you to faith?" It expresses denial (*inkar*) and wonder (*taʿajjub*). Its parallel is your saying: "Will you fly without wings?!" or "How will you fly without wings?!"

The *waw* in ﴿and you were dead﴾, meaning "as sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers," is for the circumstantial clause (*li-l-ḥal*, a clause describing the state of the subject), and the verb *qad* is implied. *Al-amwat* is the plural of *mayyit* (dead), like *al-aqwal* is the plural of *qawl* (saying). The term *mayyit* is also applied to one who originally lacks life, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a dead land﴾ [al-Furqan: 49].

﴿Then He gave you life﴾ in the wombs; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ when your appointed terms end; ﴿then He will give you life again﴾ for resurrection; ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning you will be brought back to the reckoning. Or it means: then He gives you life in your graves, then to Him you will be returned for the resurrection.

The first conjunction is with *fa'* (then, immediately), and the rest are with *thumma* (then, after an interval), because the first giving of life followed death without delay, whereas death came after life with an interval. The second life is likewise delayed after death if the meaning is the resurrection (*nushur*). If the meaning is the giving of life in the grave, then one acquires knowledge from it by its delay. The return to the reckoning is also delayed after the resurrection.

He denied that disbelief could coexist with the account He mentioned, because it contains clear signs which turn them away from disbelief, and because it contains great blessings whose due is that you give thanks and not disbelieve.

﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾, i.e., for your sake, and for your benefit in your worldly life and your religion. As for the first, it is evident. As for the second, it consists in contemplating it and the wonders it contains that point to a Creator who is All-Powerful, Wise and All-Knowing, and in the reminder of the Hereafter found in it, since its pleasures remind one of its reward and its hardships remind one of its punishment. Al-Karkhi, Abu Bakr al-Razi and the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school) used His saying ﴿He created for you﴾ as evidence that things which can be benefited from are, originally, created permissible (mubah, i.e., permitted by default). ﴿Jami'an (all)﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of ﴿ma (whatever)﴾. ﴿Thumma istawa ila al-sama' (Then He turned to the heaven)﴾. Al-istiwa' (lit. "straightening," the sense of "rising to" or "turning toward," a term for the act of turning or directing) means al-i'tidal (evenness, uprightness) and al-istiqamah (straightness), as one says, "istawa al-'ud," meaning it stood up and became straight. Then it was said: "istawa ilayhi" is like an arrow loosed, when one aims at it in a straight course without turning aside from anything. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾, meaning He turned and set His purpose toward creating the heavens after creating what is on the earth, without intending between that any other creation. By "al-sama' (the heaven)" is meant the directions of elevation, as if it were said: "Then He rose upward." The pronoun in ﴿fasawwahunna (and He completed them)﴾ is vague (mubham), and it is explained by ﴿seven heavens﴾, like their saying: "rubbahu rajulan (a man, indeed him)." It was also said: the pronoun refers to "al-sama'," and its wording is singular while its meaning is plural, because it has the sense of a genus. The meaning of their being made even (taswiyatuhunna) is making their creation balanced (ta'dil khalqihinna) and upright, and free of crookedness and fissures; or completing their creation. And "thumma (then)" here is to indicate the excellence of the creation of the heavens over the creation of the earth. This does not contradict His saying: ﴿And the earth, after that, He spread out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30], because the body of the earth was created before the creation of the heaven, whereas its spreading out (dahw) came later. It is reported from al-Hasan: God created the earth at the place of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) like the shape of a grinding stone (fihr), with smoke clinging to it. Then He raised up the smoke and created the heavens from it, and He held the fihr in its place and spread out the earth from it. This is His saying: ﴿Were the heavens and the earth joined together (ratqan)﴾ [al-Anbiya': 30], and ratq is adhesion (iltizaq). ﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾. Therefore He created them in a level, firm creation without disparity, along with creating what is in the earth according to the needs of its inhabitants and their benefits.

"Wa-huwa" and its counterparts are Medinan (readings) except Warsh. "Wa-huwa": Hisham, Abu 'Amr and 'Ali read it so that they treated the waw as if it were part of the word itself, so it became like 'adud (arm), and they say in 'adud, "'add" with sukun (silent vowel).

(p-77)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 30:

When God Most High created the earth, He settled the jinn in it, and He settled the angels in the heaven. The jinn caused corruption on the earth, so He sent to them a company of angels, who drove them out to the islands of the seas and the tops of the mountains. They remained in their places. He then commanded His Prophet, upon him be peace, to relate their story, so He said: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾. *Idh* (when) is in the accusative by an implied *udhkur* (mention). *Al-mala'ika* (the angels) is the plural of *malak*, like *al-shama'il* is the plural of *sham'al*, and the attaching of the *ta'* (taa marbuta) is for the feminine plural. ﴿Indi ja'ilun﴾ means: I am one who will make, from *ja'ala* which has two objects, and they are ﴿fi al-ardi khalifa﴾ (a successor on the earth). *Khalifa* is one who succeeds another; it is of the pattern *fa'ila* in the sense of *fa'ila* (active), and the *ha'* was added for emphasis. The meaning: a successor from among you (p-78), because they were the inhabitants of the earth, so He created Adam and his offspring in it. He did not say *khullaf* or *khulafa'*, because by *khalifa* is meant Adam, and by mentioning him He dispensed with mentioning his sons, just as you dispense with mentioning the ancestor of a tribe when you say: Mudar and Hashim. Or it is meant: one who will succeed you, or successors who will succeed you, so He used the singular for that reason. Or: a successor from Me, because Adam was the khalifa of God on His earth, and so is every prophet. God Most High said: ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor on the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. He informed them of this only so that they would ask that question and be answered with what they were answered, and thus they would know His wisdom in appointing them as successors before their existence; or so that He would teach His servants consultation in their affairs before undertaking them, although He, by His knowledge and perfect wisdom, is free of need for consultation. ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?﴾ This is an expression of wonder that He would appoint in place of the people of obedience the people of disobedience, when He is the Wise who does not act in ignorance. They knew this either by information from God Most High, or from the direction of the Preserved Tablet, or they measured one of the two weighty ones (jinn and humans) against the other.

﴿And shed blood﴾ means: pour it out. The *waw* in ﴿while we glorify﴾ is for the circumstantial (*hal*), as you say: Do you do good to so-and-so while I am more deserving of good from him?! ﴿with Your praise﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning: we glorify You while praising You and clothed in Your praise, like His saying, Most High: ﴿They entered with disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 61], meaning: they entered as disbelievers. ﴿And sanctify You﴾ means: and we purify ourselves for You. It was also said: *tasbih* (glorification) and *taqdis* (sanctification) mean: removing God far from evil, from *sabaha fi al-ard* and *qaddasa fiha*, when one goes off in the land and gets far away. ﴿He said: Indeed I know what you do not know﴾ means: I know, of the wisdom in that, what is hidden from you. That is: among them will be prophets, saints, and scholars. *Ma* is in the sense of *alladhi* (that which), and it is the object of *a'lamu*, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: *ma la ta'lamunahu*. *Inni* is read by the Hijazi reciters and Abu 'Amr.

﴿And He taught Adam﴾ is a non-Arabic name (ism a'jami). The most likely form of it is fa'al, like Azar (آزَر). Their derivation of Adam (آدَم) is from the surface of the earth (adim al-ardh), or from al-udmah (the brownness of complexion), just as they derive Ya'qub (يَعْقُوب) from al-aqab (heel), Idris (إدْرِيس) from al-dars (study), and Iblis (إبْلِيس) from al-iblas (despair). ﴿the names, all of them﴾, i.e., the names of the named things (asma' al-musammayat). The genitive complement is omitted because it is known and indicated by the mention of "names", since the name points to what it names. The lam (ال) is put in its place, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. It is not valid to estimate the phrase as "He taught Adam the named things (musammayat al-asma')", with the genitive omitted and the complement put in its place, because teaching was connected to the names, not to the named things, as in His saying: ﴿Tell Me the names of these﴾ and ﴿Tell them their names﴾, and He did not say: "Tell Me about these" and "Inform them about them." The meaning of His teaching him the names of the named things is that God, exalted is He, showed him the kinds He had created and taught him that the name of this is "horse" (faras), the name of this is "camel" (ba'ir), the name of this is such-and-such, and the name of this is such-and-such. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: He taught him the name of everything, even the bowl (qas'ah) and the ladle (mighrafah). ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾, i.e., He presented the named things. He used the masculine pronoun because among the named things are rational beings (al-'uqala'), so he gave them precedence. He asked them about the names although He knew their inability to give them, by way of rebuke (al-tabkit): ﴿so He said: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾, i.e., inform Me ﴿of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that I will appoint on earth those who cause corruption and shed blood. In this there is a refutation of them and an explanation that the scientific benefits (al-fawa'id al-'ilmiyyah) that are the roots of all benefits, which He has granted to the one He appoints, are what qualify them for the appointment.

﴿They said: Glory be to You﴾, (a declaration of Your transcendence, tanzih, meaning) that nothing should be hidden from You, or (a declaration that they should not) object to You in Your governance. The verse also indicates that knowledge of the names is superior to devoting oneself to worship, so how much more is knowledge of the Shari'ah?! Its position in the accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar). Its estimated form is: "I glorified God with glorification" (sabbahtu Allaha tasbihan).

﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾, and there is no mention of the knowledge of the names in it. The word "ما" (ma) is in the sense of "الَّذِي" (alladhi, "that which"), and "العِلْمُ" (al-'ilm, "knowledge") is in the sense of "المَعْلُومُ" (al-ma'lum, "that which is known"). That is: we have no known object except that which You have taught us. ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing﴾, who is not taught, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what You decree and ordain. The "الكاف" (al-kaf, the "ka" suffix) is the ism (subject) of "إنَّ" (inna), and "أنْتَ" (anta, "You") is the mubtada' (subject of the nominal sentence), and what follows it is its khabar (predicate), and the whole sentence is the khabar of inna. Or, "أنْتَ" (anta) is a fasl (separating pronoun), and the khabar is "العَلِيمُ" (al-'alim, "the All-Knowing"), and "الحَكِيمُ" (al-hakim, "the All-Wise") is a second khabar.

"He said, 'O Adam, inform them of their names.' And when he had informed them of their names, He said, 'Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?'" (Qur'an 2:33)

Adam taught them the names of all things, naming every thing by its name. ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth"﴾ — that is, I know what is hidden from you in them, (p-80) of what has been and what will be. ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾ — what you make apparent, ﴿and what you conceal﴾ — what you keep secret.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 34:**

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ That is: submit to him and acknowledge his superiority. From Ubayy ibn Ka'b and from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: that was a bowing, and it was not falling prostrate upon the chin. The majority hold that what was commanded was placing the face on the ground. The prostration was a greeting to Adam (peace be upon him) according to the sound view, for if it had been for Allah the Exalted, Iblis would not have refused it. Prostration as a greeting was permissible in earlier times, but it was abrogated (naskh, the cancelling of an earlier ruling by a later one) by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Salman when he wanted to prostrate to him: "It is not fitting for a created being to prostrate to anyone except Allah the Exalted."

﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ The exception is connected (istithna' muttasil, an exception of the same category as what precedes it), because he was among the angels. This was said by 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them all, and because the principle is that the exception is of the same kind as what it excepts from. For this reason He said: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. His saying: ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50] means: he became one of the jinn, like His saying: ﴿so he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud: 43]. It has also been said that the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same kind), because he was not among the angels but was of the jinn by the textual evidence. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. Also, he was created from fire, whereas the angels were created from light. Also, he refused, disobeyed and was arrogant, whereas the angels do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, nor are they arrogant toward His worship. Also, He said: ﴿Will you take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and the angels have no offspring. It is reported from al-Jahiz that the jinn and the angels are one genus: whoever is pure among them is an angel, whoever is corrupt is a devil (shaytan), and whoever is in between is a jinn.

﴿Refused (abá)﴾ he declined to do what he was commanded. ﴿And was arrogant (istakbara)﴾ he considered himself too great for it. ﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾ he became one of the disbelievers by his refusal, his arrogance and his rejection of the command, not by abandoning the act of obeying the command, because abandoning prostration does not take a person out of faith, and it is not disbelief according to the people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the majority Sunni orthodox position), in contrast to the Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij. Or it means: he was among the disbelievers in the knowledge of Allah, that is, it was in Allah's knowledge that he would disbelieve after his faith, not that he had been a disbeliever forever in Allah's knowledge. This is the question of the muwafah (the question of how a person's final state, at the end of life, determines their standing).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 35:

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell﴾ is an imperative from sakana al-dar, yaskunuha suknā, meaning he resided in the house (sakana, to dwell, to settle). It is also said: sakkana al-mutaharrik sukūnan (he made the moving thing still). ﴿You﴾ is an emphasis for the pronoun hidden in uskun, so that ﴿and your wife﴾ may validly be conjoined to it.

﴿The Garden﴾ is the Garden of Eternity that was promised to the God-fearing, by well-known transmission, and the alif-lam is for definition. The Mu'tazila said: it was a garden (bustan) in Yemen, because the Garden has no obligation (taklif) in it and no departure from it. We say: only one who enters it as a reward does not leave it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) entered it on the night of the Mi'raj, then left it, and the people of the Garden are obligated to know God and affirm His unity (tawhid).

﴿And eat from it﴾ means from its fruits, the object being elided (the genitive noun was omitted). ﴿Freely﴾ is an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning: eat freely, abundantly. ﴿Wherever you wish﴾: Abu 'Amr read shi'tuma and its like without a hamza. Hayth is for an indefinite place, meaning: any place in the Garden that you two wish.

﴿And do not approach this tree﴾, that is, the wheat (al-hintah); hence it was said: how could man not disobey, when his sustenance comes from the tree of disobedience? Or it was the vine (al-karmah), since it is the root of every trial; or it was the fig (al-tinah). ﴿So you will be﴾ is in the jussive mood by conjunction with "approach" (taqraba), or in the subjunctive as an answer to the prohibition. ﴿Among the wrongdoers﴾: among those who wronged themselves, or among those who harmed themselves.

﴿So the Shaytan caused them to slip from it﴾, i.e., from the tree. That is, the Shaytan induced them to commit the slip through it (the tree). Its precise meaning: the Shaytan caused their slip to proceed from it (the tree); or, "he caused them to slip from it" means he removed them from it (the Garden) and drove them away from it.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾: Hamzah (read it as). The slip of Adam was a mistake in interpretation, either by taking the prohibition as a matter of reprehensibility (tanzih) rather than prohibition (tahrim), or by taking the lam (in "al-shajarah", "the tree") as the definite article of a specific reference (al-'ahd), while God, exalted is He, may have intended the genus. This is evidence that the term "slip" (zallah) may be applied to the Prophets, peace be upon them, as the masters of Bukhara said, for it is a term for an action that occurs contrary to what is commanded without intent to oppose, like the slip of one walking in mud. The masters of Samarqand said: the term "slip" is not applied to their actions, just as the term "disobedience" (ma'siyah) is not applied; rather it is said: they did what was superior and left what was more excellent, and so they were rebuked for it.

﴿So He brought them out of what they were in﴾ of bliss and honour, or out of the Garden, if the pronoun in "from it" refers to the tree. He reached their slipping after it had been said to him: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ [al-Hijr: 34], because he was prevented from entering it in the manner of honour, as the angels entered it, not from entering it in the manner of temptation as a trial for Adam and Eve. It is narrated that he wished to enter, but the guardians prevented him, so he entered into the mouth of the serpent until it carried him in. It is also said that he stood at the gate and called out.

﴿And We said: Go down﴾. Hubut (descent) means coming down to the earth. The address is to Adam, Eve and Iblis; it is also said to include the serpent. The sound view is that it is addressed to Adam and Eve. What is meant is them and their descendants, for since they were the origin of mankind and its branches, they were treated as though they were all of mankind. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123]. ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾: what is meant by this is what people have of mutual oppression, hostility, and misleading one another. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the waw in "go down", i.e., go down as enemies to one another.

﴿And for you on the earth there is a dwelling place﴾: a place of settling or a place of residence.

﴿And enjoyment﴾ and provision of living ﴿for a time﴾: until the Day of Resurrection, or until death. Ibrahim ibn Adham said: that single meal brought us long sorrow.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 37:

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ That is, he received them by accepting them, consenting to them and acting upon them. Reading "Ādama" in the accusative and "kalimātun" in the nominative is attributed to Makki, on the basis that the words reached him, connected to him, and they were his saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. In this there is an admonition for their offspring, since they came to know the manner of the way to disown sins. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the most beloved speech to Allah, exalted is He, is what our father Adam said when he committed the sin: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: O my Lord, did You not create me with Your hand? He said: Yes. He said: O my Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit? Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath? Did You not settle me in Your Garden? And He, exalted is He, says: Yes, yes. He said: Then why did You expel me from the Garden? He said: Because of the ill-omen of your disobedience. He said: If I repent, will You return me to it? He said: Yes.

﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ That is, He turned to him with mercy and acceptance, and He suffices with mentioning the repentance of Adam (p-83) because Hawwa' was following him. Mention of women has indeed been omitted in most of the Qur'an and the Sunnah for this reason. ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance﴾, the one who accepts repentance much, ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His servants.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 38:

﴿We said: "Go down from it, all of you."﴾ "All of you" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: gathered together. He repeated the command to descend either for emphasis (ta'kid), or because the first descent was from the Garden to the heaven and the second from the heaven to the earth, or because of what was attached to it of the addition of His words: ﴿And if there comes to you from Me guidance﴾, i.e., a messenger I send to you, or a book I send down upon you. The evidence for this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾, which stand in opposition to His words: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance﴾, i.e., by accepting it and believing in it, ﴿there will be no fear upon them﴾ regarding the future, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ over what they left behind. The second conditional clause together with its response is the response to the first conditional clause, like your saying: "If you come to me, then if I am able, I will do good to you."

﴿Fa-lā khawf﴾ with a fatḥa throughout the whole Qur'an: Ya'qub (Ya'qub al-Ḥaḍrami, one of the ten readers).

And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, ﴿those﴾ is the mubtada' (the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the khabar (the predicate) is ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning its people and those deserving of it. The clause is in a position of raising (rafʿ) as the khabar of the mubtada', I mean: الَّذِينَ, ﴿who abide therein forever﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 40:

﴿يا بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ "O Children of Israel." He is Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and this is his epithet (laqab). Its meaning in their language is "the chosen one of Allah" or "the servant of Allah." So "Isra" is "the servant" or "the chosen one," and "Il" is "Allah" in Hebrew. It is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because of the presence of proper-noun status (ʿalamiyya) and foreignness (ʿujma).

﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَتِيَ الَّتِي أنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ "Remember My favour which I have bestowed upon you." He reminded them of the favour so that they would not neglect its gratitude and would obey its Giver. By it He meant what He bestowed upon their forefathers, among what He enumerated to them: deliverance from Pharaoh and his torment, and from drowning, and pardon for taking the calf and His accepting their repentance, and what He bestowed upon them by reaching the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), who was given good tidings of in the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿وَأوْفُوا﴾ "And fulfil," i.e., discharge it fully and completely. It is said: "Wafaytu lahu bil-ʿahd, fa-ana wafin bihi" (I fulfilled the covenant to him, so I am one who fulfils it), and "Awfaytu lahu bil-ʿahd, fa-ana muwfin bihi" (I fulfilled it for him, so I am one who fulfils it). The preferred form is "awfaytu," and the revelation came in this form.

﴿بِعَهْدِي﴾ "My covenant," i.e., what you covenanted with Me concerning faith in Me and obedience to Me, or concerning faith in the Prophet of Mercy and the inimitable Book.

﴿أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ﴾ "I will fulfil your covenant," i.e., what I covenanted with you concerning the goodly reward for your good deeds. The word "ʿahd" is attributed to both the one who is covenanted with and the one who covenants together. According to Qatada, these are: ﴿لَئِنْ أقَمْتُمُ﴾ "If you establish" and ﴿لأُكَفِّرَنَّ﴾ "I will surely remove" [al-Ma'ida: 12].

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: "Fulfil in the abode of My trial, upon the carpet of My service, by guarding My sanctity, [and] I will fulfil in the abode of My blessing, upon the carpet of My honour, with the joy of My vision."

﴿وَإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾ "And of Me alone be in awe." So do not break My covenant. It comes from your saying: "Zaydan rahibtuhu" (I feared Zayd). It is more emphatic in conveying exclusivity than ﴿إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. "Iyaya" is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by what follows it, its estimate being: "Fa-rhabu iyaya fa-rhabuni" (so fear Me, and fear Me), and the first was omitted because the second indicates it. It is not governed by His saying ﴿فارْهَبُونِ﴾ "fa-rhabuni" because that verb has already taken its object, which is the elided yaʾ, and the kasra of the nun is the indication of the yaʾ, just as it is not permissible to put Zayd in the accusative in: "Zaydan fa-idribhu," with "idrib" governing the one that is apparent.

"And believe in what I have sent down," meaning the Qur'an, "confirming" (muṣaddiqan), a emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl mu'akkid) from the omitted pronoun ha', as if it were said: "I sent it down confirming" — "what is with you," from the Torah. That is: in worship, in monotheism, in prophethood, and in the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

"And do not be the first to disbelieve in it," i.e., the first to disbelieve in it, or the first party or group to disbelieve in it, or: let not each one of you be the first disbeliever in it. This is an implicit rebuke, meaning that they should have been the first to believe in it, given their knowledge of it and of its description.

The pronoun in "bihi" (in it) refers to the Qur'an.

"And do not exchange" — and do not substitute — "My verses" by altering them and distorting them, "for a small price." Al-Ḥasan said: it is the world in its entirety. It was also said: it is the leadership that they held among their people, for they feared losing it if they followed the Messenger of God.

"And Me alone, so fear Me" (fakhāfūnī, fārhabūnī, fattaqūnī), with the yā' (ya') in both cases; and likewise every yā' that is omitted in the script: Ya'qub (Ya'qūb, i.e., the reader Ya'qub al-Hadrami).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 42:

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾. Labs (mixing, confusion) of the truth with falsehood is its khalt (mixing it together). If the bāʾ (ب) is ṣila (a redundant, connecting particle), like it in your saying: labistu al-shay' bi-al-shay' (I mixed the thing with the thing), meaning: khaltuhu bihi (I mixed it with it), then the meaning is: "And do not write in the Torah what is not from it, so that the revealed truth becomes mixed with the falsehood that you have written, until its truth and your falsehood cannot be distinguished." And if it is the bāʾ of istiʿana (instrumental bāʾ, indicating means), like the one in your saying: katabtu bi-al-qalam (I wrote with the pen), then the meaning is: "And do not make the truth confused and resembling your falsehood which you write."

﴿and conceal the truth﴾ is majzūm (in the jussive mood), included under the rule of the prohibition, meaning: "and do not conceal the truth." Or it is manṣūb (in the subjunctive mood) by the implied particle an (that), and the waw (و) carries the sense of joining, i.e., "do not combine between mixing the truth with falsehood and concealing the truth," like your saying: lā taʾkul al-samak wa-tashraba al-laban (do not eat the fish and drink the milk). These are two distinct matters, because mixing the truth with falsehood is what we mentioned of their books in the Torah, writing in it what is not from it. And their concealing the truth is that they would say: "We find in the Torah the description of Muhammad," or "the ruling of such-and-such."

﴿while you know﴾, in the state of your knowing that you are mixers and concealers, and this is more abhorrent for them, because ignorance of an abhorrent act may at times excuse the one who commits it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 43:

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾, i.e., the prayer and zakat of the Muslims. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, from among them, because the Jews have no bowing (ruku') in their prayer. That is: embrace Islam and act according to the practice of the people of Islam. It is also permissible that by "bowing" (ruku') is meant the prayer, just as a part is expressed by naming the whole, as the prayer is expressed by "prostration" (sujud). And it may be an command to pray along with those who pray, meaning: in congregation. That is: pray with those who pray, not alone.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 44:

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people⁠—﴾ The hamza here is for confirmation (taqrir) accompanied by rebuke and wonder at their state.

﴿Righteousness (al-birr)﴾ means abundance of good and what is recognized as good. From it comes "al-barr" (the broad, vast land), because of its vastness, and it encompasses every kind of good. From it also comes their saying: "You have spoken truly (sadaqta), and you have done well (barrata)." The rabbis (al-ahbar) used to command those among their relatives and others whom they advised privately to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), while they themselves did not follow him. It is also said: they used to command giving charity while not giving charity themselves, and when they brought the charities to distribute them, they would embezzle from them.

﴿And you forget yourselves⁠—﴾ and leave them aside from righteousness, like those who are forgotten.

﴿And you recite the Scripture⁠—﴾ this is a rebuke, meaning: you recite the Torah, in which is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), or in which is the warning against betrayal, abandoning righteousness, and saying one thing while doing another.

﴿Will you not then use your intellect?⁠—﴾ will you not perceive the ugliness of what you have undertaken, so that its ugliness would restrain you from committing it? This is a severe rebuke.

ØSeek help in your needs from God through patience and prayer (al-sabr wa'l-salah). That is, by combining the two, and by praying while being patient with the burdens of prayer, enduring its hardships, and what it requires of sincerity of heart, repelling satanic whisperings and passing thoughts of the soul, observing its etiquette, humility (khushu'), and keeping in mind the knowledge that one is standing before the Overpowering Lord of the heavens and the earth. Or: seek help against calamities and misfortunes through patience in bearing them, and by turning to prayer when they befall you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to turn to prayer whenever a matter distressed him. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) that when news of the death of his brother Qutham reached him while he was on a journey, he said "Inna li-llahi wa-inna ilayhi raji'un," prayed two rak'ahs, and then said: "Seek help through patience and prayer." It was also said: patience (al-sabr) means fasting, because it is a restraint from things that break the fast, and for this reason the month of Ramadan is called the month of patience. It was also said: prayer (al-salah) means supplication (du'a'), i.e., seek help against calamities through patience and turning to supplication and earnestly beseeching God to repel them. ﴿And indeed it﴾: the pronoun refers to prayer, or to seeking help.

﴿Is indeed a great burden﴾: difficult and heavy, from your saying "this matter weighed heavily upon me" (kabura 'alayya hadha al-amr). ﴿Except for the humble (al-khashi'in)﴾, because they anticipate what has been stored up for those who are patient with its hardships, so it becomes easy for them. Do you not see to his saying:

﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ means: they expect to meet His reward, to attain what is with Him, and they hope for it. He explained *yaẓunnūna* (يَظُنُّونَ) as *yatayaqqanūna* (يَتَيَقَّنُونَ), according to the reading of ʿAbd Allah, which has *yaʿlamūna* (يَعْلَمُونَ), meaning: they know that they must meet the recompense, so they act accordingly. As for one who has no certainty about the recompense and does not hope for the reward, [his worship] is pure hardship. *Al-khushūʿ* (humility) and *al-ikhbāt* (lowliness) mean humbling oneself (*al-taṭāmmuṭ*). As for *al-khuḍūʿ* (submission), it means gentleness and yielding. He explained *al-liqāʾ* (meeting) as seeing (*al-ruʾya*), and *mulāqū rabbihim* (meeting their Lord) as beholding Him without modality (*bi-lā kayf*). ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾: none other than Him has authority over their affairs in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 47:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. The repetition is for emphasis (al-takrir li'l-ta'kid).

﴿And that I preferred you﴾: "that I preferred you" (wa-anni faddaltukum) is in the accusative case, being coordinated (ʿatf) upon "My favour" (niʿmati). That is, remember My favour and My preferring you.

﴿over the worlds﴾: over the vast multitude (al-jamm al-ghafir) of people. It is said: "I saw a scholar (ʿalim) from among the people," and what is meant is abundance (al-kathrah).

(p-87) ﴿Be mindful of a Day﴾ — that is, the Day of Resurrection. It is the object of the verb (maf'ul bihi), not an adverb of time (zarf). ﴿On which no soul will avail another soul﴾ — a believing soul — ﴿against another soul﴾ — a disbelieving soul — ﴿anything﴾; that is, it will not discharge for it any of the obligations that had become binding upon it. "Shay'an" (anything) is either the object of the verb or a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: a little of the recompense.
