The clause is in the accusative position as a qualifier (sifah) of "yawman" (a Day), and its returning pronoun (al-'a'id) to the qualified noun is omitted; its estimated form is: "no soul will avail in it." ﴿Nor will any intercession be accepted from it﴾ — "wa-la tuqbalu" (and it will not be accepted) with the feminine ta' is read by Makki and Basri. The pronoun in "minha" (from it) refers to the believing soul; that is, no intercession will be accepted from it on behalf of the disbelieving soul. It has been said: the Jews used to claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them, so they were disappointed; this is like His saying: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:48]. The Mu'tazilah clung to this verse to deny intercession for the sinners, and this is rejected, because what is negated is the intercession of the disbelievers, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My intercession is for the people of the major sins from my community; whoever denies it will not attain it." ﴿Nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾ — that is, a ransom (fidyah), because it is equivalent to what is being ransomed (al-mufda).

﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ — they will not be aided. The plural is used because the indefinite "soul" (nafs) denotes many souls, and the masculine is used in consideration of the meaning of "servants" (al-'ibad) or "human beings" (al-anasi).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 49:

﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ The root of āl (family, people) is ahl (people), which is why its diminutive is uhayl; its hamza-less h was replaced by an alif. Its usage is restricted to people of high standing, such as kings and their likes, so one does not say āl al-iskāf (the family of the cobbler) or āl al-ḥajjām (the family of the cupper). Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is a proper name for the ruler of the 'Amalīq (Amalekites), like Qayṣar (Caesar) for the kingdom of the Romans and Kisrā (Khosrow) for the kingdom of the Persians.

﴿who afflicted you﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the people of Pharaoh, meaning: they inflicted upon you, from sāmahu khasfan, when he inflicted upon him injustice. Its origin is from sāma al-silʿah (he offered the goods), when he sought them, as if it means: they sought from you.

﴿a wretched torment﴾ And they desired you to it. Al-musāwamah in trade means bidding up or demanding. Sū' (wretched) is the second object of yasūmūnakum; it is a verbal noun of sī'a (to be bad). It is said: "I seek refuge in Allah from sū' al-khuluq and sū' al-fi'l," meaning their ugliness. The meaning of sū' al-ʿadhāb, and every torment is bad, is: its most severe and most dreadful.

﴿slaughtering your sons﴾ This is an explanation of His words ﴿who afflicted you﴾, and therefore the conjunction is omitted. ﴿And sparing your women﴾: they would leave your daughters alive for service. They did this to them because the soothsayers warned Pharaoh that a boy would be born who would end his kingdom by his means, just as they warned Nimrod, and the efforts of the two of them to guard against it did not avail them, and what Allah willed came to pass. ﴿And in that was a trial﴾: a test, if "that" refers to Pharaoh's deed, and a blessing, if it refers to the deliverance. ﴿from your Lord﴾ is an attribute of "trial". ﴿Great﴾ is a second attribute.

﴿And when We divided﴾ the sea: We separated its parts from one another until there came to be in it paths for you. It is also recited as (farraqnā), meaning "We separated." It is said *faraqa bayna al-shay'ayn* (he separated between two things) and *farraqa bayna al-ashyā'* (he separated between many things), because the paths were twelve, according to the number of the *asbāṭ* (the tribes descended from the sons of Jacob). ﴿The sea, with you﴾: they used to traverse it, and the water would part as they passed through it, so it is as if it parted with them. Or the meaning is: We parted it because of you. Or: We parted it while it was associated with you, and in that case the phrase is in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause).

It was narrated that the Children of Israel said to Mūsā, peace be upon him: "Where are our companions? We will not be content until we see them." So Allah revealed to him that he should strike the walls with his staff in such and such a way. He struck them with it, and openings (*kuwan*) appeared in them, so they saw one another and heard each other's speech.

﴿So We rescued you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on﴾ at that and witnessing it, and you had no doubt about it.

Nasafi said: The phrase ﴿and when We made an appointment with Moses﴾ is used because God Most High promised him revelation, and the promise was his coming to the appointed time at Mount Ṭūr. The verb "wa'adnā" (with the alif, from wā'ada) appears in the Qur'an with this form; "wa'adnā" (without the alif) wherever it occurs is the reading of Abū 'Amr, who was from Basra. This was when the Children of Israel entered Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, and they had no scripture to turn to. God promised Moses that He would send down the Torah to him, and He set for him an appointed time: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten days of Dhu al-Ḥijjah. He said ﴿forty nights﴾ because the months are reckoned by their nights (at their beginnings). "Arba'īna" (forty) is the second object (mafʿūl thānī, the second direct object) of "wā'adnā," not an adverb of time (ẓarf), because the meaning is not "We made an appointment with him during forty nights."

﴿Then you took the calf﴾, that is, as a god. The second object of "ittakhadhtum" (you took) is omitted. Its class of reading with clear articulation (iẓhār, pronouncing the consonants separately rather than assimilating them) is the reading of Makkī and Ḥafṣ.

﴿after him﴾, after his departure to Mount Ṭūr. ﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾, that is, by placing worship in other than its proper place. The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: you worshipped it while being wrongdoers.

Then We pardoned you after that, so that you might be grateful.

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾: We erased your sins from you. ﴿after that﴾: after your taking the calf (for worship). ﴿so that you might be grateful﴾: so that you would give thanks for the favour of pardoning you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 53:

﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾ meaning: the one that combines being a revealed Book and a Criterion (furqan) that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and this is the Torah. Its parallel is the saying: "I saw the rain-cloud and the lion," meaning: the man who combines generosity and courage. Or it means the Torah and the clear proof (burhan) that separates disbelief from faith, [namely] the staff, the hand, and other signs. Or it means the Law (shar') that separates the lawful from the unlawful. It has also been said: the Criterion is the splitting of the sea, or the victory that separated him from his enemy. ﴿So that you may be guided﴾ meaning: in order that you may be guided.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 54:

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾ (i.e., to those who worshipped the calf), ﴿"O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking the calf"﴾ (as a deity to be worshipped), ﴿"so turn in repentance to your Bari' (Creator)"﴾, who is He who created creation free from disparity (tafawut). In this there is a rebuke for what had come from them of abandoning the worship of the All-Knowing, All-Wise, who created them free from disparity, in favour of worshipping a cow, which is a proverb for dullness and stupidity.

﴿"So kill yourselves"﴾. It has been said: it is to be taken literally, and it is al-bakhʿ (the self-slaughter of the unrestrained kind). It has also been said: its meaning is that some of them killed others. And it has been said: he commanded those who had not worshipped the calf to kill the worshippers, and seventy thousand were killed. (p-90) ﴿"That"﴾ — the repentance and the killing — ﴿"is better for you with your Creator"﴾ than persisting in disobedience. ﴿"Then He turned to you in forgiveness; indeed He is the Oft-Returning (al-Tawwab), the Bountiful"﴾ in accepting repentance however much it multiplies, ﴿"the Most Merciful (al-Rahim)"﴾ who pardons the sin however great it is.

The first fa' (فاء) is for causation (al-tasbib), because wrongdoing is the cause of repentance. The second is for sequence (al-taʿqib), because the meaning is: resolve upon repentance, then kill yourselves, since God, exalted is He, made their repentance the killing of themselves. The third is linked to an elided condition, as if he had said: "If you do so, then He has turned to you in forgiveness."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 55:

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾ (ʿiyānan, "plainly, before the eyes"). Its placement (*intiṣābuhā*) is as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), just as *al-qurfuṣāʾ* (the squatting position) is put in the accusative by the verb of sitting. Or it is in the circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) of *narā* ("we see"), meaning: "those who see Him openly." ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized you﴾, that is, death. It is said: it was a fire that came from the sky and burned them.

It was narrated that the seventy men who were with Musa, peace be upon him, at the time of setting out for the mountain, said to him: "We did not worship the calf as these did, so show us Allah openly." Musa said: "I asked Him for that, and He refused me." They said: "You have seen Allah, the Exalted, so we will never believe you until we see Allah openly." Then Allah sent a thunderbolt upon them and it burned them.

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) relied on this verse to deny the possibility of seeing Allah, arguing that if seeing Him were permissible, they would not have been punished for asking for something whose existence is permissible. We say: they were punished only for their disbelief, because their saying, "You have seen Allah, so we will never believe you until we see Allah openly," was disbelief on their part. Also, they refused to believe in Musa after his miracle had appeared, until they saw their Lord openly, while belief in the prophets is obligatory once their miracles have appeared, and it is not permissible to demand signs from them. Furthermore, they did not ask in seeking guidance, but in obstinacy and stubbornness. ﴿And you were looking on﴾ at it when it descended.

﴿Then We raised you﴾: that is, "We gave you life" (aḥyaynākum). Its original meaning is al-ithāra (stirring up, arousing) ﴿after your death, so that you might give thanks﴾, that is, for the blessing of being raised after death.

(p-91) ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾: We made the clouds shade you. This was in the wilderness of wandering (al-tih). God subjected the clouds for them, moving with their movement, shading them from the sun. At night a pillar of fire would descend, and they traveled by its light. Their clothes did not get soiled, nor did they wear out. ﴿And We sent down to you the manna﴾: the turanjabin (a sweet exudation, sometimes glossed as honey-dew or manna). It would descend upon them like snow from the break of dawn until sunrise, a ṣāʿ (a measure of volume) for each person. ﴿And the quails﴾: God would send the south wind upon them, and it would gather the quails over them, and they are the summān (fat birds). So a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him. And We said to them: ﴿Eat of the good things﴾ — delicious things, or lawful things — ﴿that We have provided for you. And they did not wrong Us﴾, meaning: they wronged themselves by being ungrateful for these blessings. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾: "themselves" (anfusahum) is the object of "they were wronging," and it is the predicate (khabar) of kāna (was/were).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 58:

﴿And when We said﴾ to them, after they had come out of the wandering (al-tih), ﴿"Enter this town"﴾, i.e., Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or Ariha (Jericho). The word qarya (town) means a gathering place, derived from qaraytu (I gathered), because it gathers people. They were commanded to enter it after the wandering. ﴿"And eat from it"﴾, from the food and fruits of the town, ﴿"wherever you wish, in abundance"﴾, plentifully, ﴿"and enter the gate"﴾, the gate of the town, or the gate of the dome to which they used to make their way. They did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis during the lifetime of Musa (peace be upon him); rather, they entered the gate during his lifetime, and they entered Bayt al-Maqdis after him.

﴿"Prostrating"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is the plural of sajid (one who prostrates). They were commanded to prostrate upon reaching the gate, out of thankfulness to Allah the Exalted and humility before Him. ﴿"And say: hittah"﴾ is a form (fi'la) from al-hatt (lowering), like jilsa (a sitting). It is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: our request is hittah, or your command is hittah. The original form is the accusative (naṣb), and it has been recited that way, meaning "Lower our sins from us, a lowering." It was put in the nominative to convey the sense of firmness. It has also been said: our affair is hittah, meaning that we should settle down in this town and remain in it. It is reported from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) that it is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." And it is reported from ʿIkrima that it is "There is no god but Allah."

﴿"We will forgive you your wrongs"﴾, plural of khati'a (wrong), which is sin. (yaghfir) is the reading of Madani; (tughfar) is the reading of Shami.

﴿"And We will increase the good-doers"﴾, i.e., whoever among you was a good-doer, that word was a cause for increasing his reward, and whoever was a wrongdoer, it was for him a repentance and forgiveness. (p-92)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 59:

﴿So those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾. There is an ellipsis (*ḥadhf*) here. Its implied sense is: ﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾ for that which had been said to them ﴿a word other than that which had been said to them﴾. *Baddala* (بَدَّلَ) takes one object directly and another with the preposition *bi-* (بِ). The one with *bi-* is omitted, and the one without it is present. The meaning is: they put in place of *ḥiṭṭa* (ḥiṭṭa, "remit/forgive us"; a gloss: the word of repentance and seeking forgiveness) another word. They were commanded with a word whose meaning is repentance and seeking forgiveness, but they departed from it to a word whose meaning is not the meaning of what they were commanded, and they did not obey God's command. It is said that they said *ḥinṭa* (حِنْطَةً, "wheat") in place of *ḥiṭṭa*. It is also said that they said in Nabataean (*al-Nabatiyya*): *ḥaṭṭā samqāthā*, meaning "red wheat," mocking what had been said to them, and turning away from seeking what is with God to seeking what they desired of the worldly goods of this life.

﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment (*rijz*, رِجْزًا)﴾, meaning a torment. The repetition of ﴿those who did wrong﴾ serves to add condemnation of their conduct and to announce that the punishment was sent down upon them because of their wrongdoing. ﴿From the sky﴾ is a qualifier of *rijz*. ﴿Because they used to defiantly transgress﴾ means because of their transgression (*fisq*). It is related that there died of them in one hour from the plague twenty-four thousand, and it is said seventy thousand.

﴿And when Moses prayed for water for his people﴾. The position of إذ (idh, "when") is accusative, as if it were said: "And remember when he asked for water," that is, he sought that water be given to his people. ﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾. They were thirsty in the wilderness (al-tih), so Moses prayed for them to be given water, and it was said to him: "Strike the rock with your staff." The definite article in "the rock" is the lām of prior reference (lam al-'ahd), and it points to a specific, known rock. It is related that it was a Tur stone (hajar ṭūrī), which he carried with him. It was square, with four faces, and from each face three springs gushed forth, one for each tribe. They numbered six hundred thousand, and the width of the camp was twelve miles. Alternatively, the definite article is the lām of genus (lam al-jins), meaning: strike the thing that is called "rock." This reading is more evident as a proof and clearer as a demonstration of power. ﴿So there gushed forth﴾: the fa' (fa') is connected to an omitted element, meaning: he struck, and there gushed forth, that is, it flowed abundantly. Or, meaning: if you strike, then it has gushed forth. In this reading it is a fa' faṣīḥah (an eloquent fa', the fa' that expresses an implied conditional or omitted action), which occurs only in eloquent speech. ﴿From it, twelve springs﴾, according to the number of the tribes (asbaṭ). It is recited with the shin (in ﴿mashrabahum﴾) vowelled with kasra and with fatha; both are dialectal variants (lughatān). ʿAyanan (springs) is a tamyīz (specification of number). ﴿Each people knew their drinking place﴾: each tribe knew its own spring from which they drank. ﴿Eat﴾: and We said to them: eat of the manna and the quail. ﴿And drink﴾ of the water of the springs. ﴿From the provision of God﴾, that is, all of it is from what God has provided for you.

﴿And do not commit corruption in the earth﴾: do not cause corruption in it. ʿAth (al-ʿaythu) is the most severe corruption. ﴿Causing corruption﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl mu'akkidah), meaning: do not persist in corruption while you are in a state of corruption, because they were persistently engaged in it.

(p. 93)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 61:**

﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food."﴾ This refers to what they were provided with during the wandering (al-tih, the wandering in the wilderness) of manna (al-manna) and quail (al-salwa). They said ﴿one kind of food﴾ although there were two kinds of food, because by "one" they meant what does not change. If a man's table had several kinds of dishes, but he persisted in them every day without changing them, one would say: "So-and-so eats only one kind of food," and by "oneness" is meant the negation of change and variety. Or they meant that the two were one type, because both were from the food of people of luxury and comfort (al-taladhdhudh wa-al-tarafuh), whereas they were people of cultivation, so they meant what they were accustomed to of vegetables (al-buqul), grains (al-hubub), and other things.

﴿So call upon your Lord for us﴾: ask Him, and say to Him: bring forth for us. ﴿He will bring forth for us﴾: He will make manifest for us and produce. ﴿from what the earth produces: its herbs﴾: what the earth grows of greens (al-khudar), and what is meant by it is the good vegetables, such as mint (al-nan'a), chervil (al-karafs), leek (al-kurrath), and the like of what people eat.

﴿And its cucumbers﴾: meaning the cucumber (al-khiyar). ﴿And its garlic﴾: it is wheat (al-hintah) or garlic (al-thum), according to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-thumiha" (with the thaʾ).

﴿And its lentils and its onions.﴾ He said: ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower﴾: nearer in rank and lesser in value. Nearness (al-dunuw) and closeness (al-qurb) are expressions used for small quantity.

﴿for that which is better﴾: higher and more noble. ﴿Go down to a city (misran)﴾ of the cities, meaning: descend to it from the wilderness. The lands of the wilderness are what lies between Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and Qinnasrin, and it is twelve farsakhs (farsakh, a unit of distance, roughly three miles) by eight farsakhs. Or it is the Egypt of Pharaoh. He made it triptote (sarafahu, i.e. he gave it nunation) despite the presence of the two causes (for diptote status), namely the feminine ending and definiteness, because it is intended as a place-name (al-balad), or because its middle letter is quiescent like Nuh and Lut; and in both of them there is foreignness (al-ujmah) and definiteness.

﴿For you will have in it﴾: ﴿what you asked for﴾: that is, what you asked for will be in the cities, not in the wilderness.

﴿And they were struck with humiliation (al-dhillah) and poverty (al-maskanah)﴾: that is, abasement and want. The meaning is: humiliation was made to encompass them and enclose them, so they are within it as one who is under a dome (al-qubbah) is within it, or it was affixed to them until it clung to them like a sticky clay (darbata lazib), as clay is plastered onto a wall and adheres to it. So the Jews are debased, abased, people of poverty and want, either in reality, or by feigning lowliness and poverty for fear that the jizya (the poll tax) would be increased upon them. (ʿalayhumu al-dhillah) is read by Hamzah and Ali, and likewise every case where a quiescent yaʾ precedes the hāʾ; and (with the kasra on the hāʾ and the mim) by Abu ʿAmr; and with kasra on the hāʾ and damma on the mim by the others.

﴿And they returned with anger from Allah﴾: from your saying: "baʾa so-and-so with so-and-so," when it is due retaliation (haqiqiyyan), by which he is killed in return for him, due to their equality; that is, they became worthy of His anger. From al-Kisai: they returned (raja'u).

﴿That﴾: a reference to what preceded of the imposition of humiliation, want, and the bearing of anger. ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets﴾ with the hamza, read by Nafi', and likewise his school; meaning: that is due to their disbelief and their killing of the prophets. The Jews killed Shiʿya, Zakariyya, and Yahya, may the blessings of Allah be upon them. The word nabi (prophet) derives from naba' (news), because he informs about Allah the Exalted, and it is in the pattern fa'il in the sense of mufʿil; or in the sense of mufʿal; or from naba, meaning "to be elevated," and nubuwwah means an elevated place.

﴿Without right﴾: also in their view; for if they were just, they would not mention anything for which they deserve killing in their view. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yaqtulun" (they kill), meaning: they kill them while being in the wrong (mubtilin).

﴿That﴾: a repetition of the demonstrative. ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾: due to their committing various kinds of sins and their transgressing the limits of Allah in everything, together with their disbelief in the signs of Allah and their killing of the prophets. It has been said: it is their transgression on the Sabbath. It is also permissible that the demonstrative refers to disbelief and the killing of the prophets, on the basis that this is due to their disobedience and transgression, because they were immersed in these two and went to extremes until their hearts hardened, so they dared to deny the signs and kill the prophets. Or: that disbelief and killing together with what they disobeyed.

(p-94)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ with their tongues, without their hearts agreeing (muwata'a al-qulub), and they are the hypocrites (munafiqun). ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ (hadu): they became Jews (tahawwadu). It is said: hada yahudu and tahawwada, when one enters Judaism (al-yahudiyya), so he is "ha'id" (a Jew), and the plural is "hud." ﴿And the Christians (al-nasara)﴾: the plural of "nasran," like "nadman" and "nadama." It is said: a man is "nasran" and a woman is "nasrana." The yā' in "nasrani" is for emphasis (lil-mubalagha), like the one in "ahmari." They were named "nasara" because they helped (nasaru) the Messiah. ﴿And the Sabeans (al-sabi'in)﴾: those who leave one well-known religion for another, from "saba'a," when one leaves religion. They are a people who turned away from the religion of Judaism and Christianity and worshipped the angels. It was also said they recite the Psalms (al-Zabur).

﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ among these disbelievers, with sincere faith, ﴿and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward﴾, their recompense,

﴿with their Lord﴾ in the Hereafter, ﴿and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ The place of ﴿whoever believes﴾ is in the nominative (raf') if you make it a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿for them is their reward﴾, and in the accusative (nasb) if you make it a substitute (badal) for the noun of "inna" and what is conjoined to it. The predicate of "inna" in the first case is the whole sentence as it is; in the second case it is "fa-lahum." The fa' is because "man" implies the meaning of a condition (shart).

﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant﴾ by [your] accepting what is in the Tawrah (Torah), ﴿and raised the mountain above you﴾, i.e., the mountain, until you accepted and gave the covenant. This was because Musa (peace be upon him) came to them with the tablets, and they saw what was in them of burdens (āṣār) and arduous obligations. These were hard for them, and they refused to accept them. So Allah the Exalted commanded Jibril (peace be upon him), who uprooted the mountain from its base, lifted it, and held it over them like a canopy. Musa said to them: "Either you accept, or it will be dropped upon you." So they accepted. And We said to them: ﴿Take what We have given you﴾ of the Book, i.e., the Tawrah, ﴿with strength﴾, with earnestness and resolve,

﴿and remember what is in it﴾, preserve what is in the Book, study it, do not forget it, and do not neglect it,

﴿that you may be among the righteous﴾, [this being] a hope on your part that you may become people of taqwā (God-consciousness).

Then you turned away, meaning you turned away from the covenant and from fulfilling it, ﴿after that﴾, meaning after acceptance. ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾, by delaying the punishment from you, or by granting you success in repentance, ﴿you would surely have been among the losers﴾, those destroyed by the punishment. (p-96)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 65:**

﴿And certainly you have known﴾ — ʿarafttum (you recognized, you knew). It takes one object here. ﴿Those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ — al-sabt is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from sabatat al-yahud, meaning the Jews glorified the Day of Sabbath (Saturday). They transgressed in it, i.e., they went beyond what was prescribed for them regarding devoting themselves to worship and honouring it, and they occupied themselves with hunting. The reason is that God Most High had forbidden them to hunt on the Sabbath, then He tested them: no fish remained in the sea except that it put its snout out on the Sabbath day, and when it passed, they dispersed. So they dug pools beside the sea and ran channels to them, and the fish would enter them on the Sabbath, being safe from hunting. Then they would block their channels from the sea, and catch them on Sunday. That confinement in the pools was their transgression.

﴿So We said to them: Be﴾ — by Our creating you — ﴿apes, despised﴾ — khasi'in is the predicate of kana (khabar kana), meaning: be combining both apehood and abasement, which is humiliation and expulsion.

﴿So We made it﴾ meaning: the transformation (al-maskha), ﴿an example﴾, a lesson that deters whoever takes heed from it, i.e., prevents him ﴿for what was before it﴾, for what preceded it, ﴿and what was after it﴾, and what came after it of nations and apes, because their transformation was mentioned in the books of the earlier people, so they took heed from it, and those among the later ones who received word of it also took heed from it.

﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, those who forbade them from transgression from among the righteous of their people; or for every God-fearing person who heard of it.

﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾: meaning, "Remember when Moses said." It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "My favour" in His words: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40], as if He had said: "Remember that, and remember when Moses said." Likewise this applies to the past occasions, i.e., "Remember My favour, and remember the time of Our delivering you, and remember the time of Our parting (the sea) for you, and remember My favour, and remember the time when Moses asked his Lord for water for his people." The occasions that follow extend up to His words: ﴿And when his Lord tested Abraham﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

﴿Indeed, Allah commands you that﴾, i.e., "that" (anna) ﴿you slaughter a cow﴾. The commentators (mufassirun) said: the beginning of the story is placed later in the recitation (tilawa), and it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed concerning it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72]. This is because a wealthy man named ʿAmiyl was killed by his cousins so that they might inherit from him. They threw him at the gate of a city, then came demanding his blood-money (diyya). So Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it so that he would come to life and inform them of his killer.

﴿They said: "Do you take us in mockery?"﴾ That is, "Do you make us the object of mockery, or people of mockery, or mockery itself, due to excessive ridicule?" (huzuwan) is read with the zay and the hamza unpunctuated (sukun) by Hamzah; and with two dammas (ḍammatayn) and a waw by Hafs. The others read it with the tashdid (emphatic doubling) and the hamza.

﴿He said: "I seek refuge in Allah"﴾: al-ʿiyadh (seeking refuge) and al-liyadh (seeking shelter) come from one root.

﴿lest I be among the ignorant﴾: because mockery in such a matter belongs to the category of ignorance and foolishness. In it there is an indirect rebuke of them, i.e., "You are ignorant, since you attribute mockery to me."

[Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 68]

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is."﴾ This is a question about its condition and its attributes, because they were already acquainted with its essence (māhiyyah). For although *mā* (what) is used to ask about the genus, and *kayf* (how) about the attribute, *mā* may occupy the position of *kayf*. They were amazed at a dead cow, by part of which a dead man would be struck and then come to life, so they asked about the attributes of that cow, which was wondrous in its affair. Is *mā hiya* a predicate and subject (khabar and mubtada')?

﴿He said: "Indeed, He says it is a cow, neither old (fāriḍ)"﴾ meaning advanced in age. It was called *fāriḍ* because it had "fariḍa sinnahā," that is, it had cut its teeth and reached their end. *Fāriḍ* is in the nominative because it is an attribute of *baqarah* (cow).

﴿"nor a virgin (bikr)"﴾ meaning young. ﴿"ʿawān"﴾ is conjoined to it, meaning middle-aged, ﴿"between that"﴾ between the old and the young. He did not say *bayna dhayn*, even though *bayna* requires two or more things, because he intended "between this which has been mentioned." The pronoun may be treated like the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah) in this usage. Abu ʿUbaydah said: I said to Ruʾbah regarding his saying:

*Therein are streaks of black and white,*
*as if on its hide is the mottling of al-bahaq.*

"If you mean the streaks, say *kaʾannahā* (as if they), and if you mean the black and the white, say *kaʾannahumā* (as if they two)." He said: "I mean, *ka'anna dhāka* (as if that)."

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾ meaning, do what you are commanded to do, or in the sense of "do what you are commanded to do," or your command is in the sense of "what is commanded to you," naming the object (al-mafʿūl) by the verbal noun (al-maṣdar), like *ḍarb al-amīr* (the amir's striking, i.e., the one struck by the amir's order).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 69:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its color is."﴾ The position of "mā" (what) is in the nominative case (raf'), because its meaning is interrogative (istifham). Its estimated form is: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what kind of color it is." ﴿He said: "Indeed He says, it is a yellow cow, bright in its yellowness is its color."﴾ Al-Fuqu' (intense brightness): it is the utmost degree of yellowness and its purest form. It is said for emphasis: "aṣfar fāqi'" (intensely yellow), and it is an emphasis for "ṣafrā'" (yellow), not a predicate about the color. However, the color has been raised by it in the manner of the subject (fā'il), and there is no difference between your saying "ṣafrā' fāqi'a" (yellow, intensely so) and "ṣafrā' fāqi' lawnuhā" (yellow, its color intensely so). In mentioning the color there is the benefit of emphasis, because "lawn" (color) is a name for the appearance (hay'ah), and that is the yellowness. So it is as if it were said: "Its yellowness is of intense yellowness," and this is from your saying: "jadda jidduhu" (his effort was great).

﴿Gladdening the beholders﴾ because of its beauty. And surur (gladness) is a pleasure in the heart upon the attainment or anticipation of a benefit. From ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever wears yellow sandals, his anxiety decreases," based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Gladdening the beholders.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 70:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is."﴾ This is a repetition of the question about its condition and its description, and a further inquiry so that they may gain more clarity regarding its description. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had taken up any cow at all and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them. But they made it strict, so Allah made it strict upon them." Excessive questioning is ill-omened. ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused for us﴾: indeed, the cow described as yellow-black and bright yellow is many, so it became confused for us. ﴿And indeed we, if Allah wills, will be guided﴾ to the particular cow whose slaughter is intended, or to what was hidden from us concerning the matter of the killer. And ﴿if Allah wills﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the subject of "inna" and its predicate. And in the hadith: "If they had not made the exception, what was made clear to them would never have been made clear to them until the end of time," meaning: if they had not said "if Allah wills."

(p-99) ﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow neither broken to plough nor to water the tilth, sound, with no blemish on her.﴾ Hmm, let me render it properly.

﴿قالَ إنَّهُ يَقُولُ إنَّها بَقَرَةٌ لا ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ الأرْضَ﴾ "لا ذَلُولٌ" is an adjective of "بَقَرَةٌ" meaning "a cow that is not docile", i.e., she has not been trained for ploughing and turning up the earth. ﴿وَلا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ﴾ nor does she water the tilled land, nor is she one of the water-carrying camels by which the crops are irrigated. The first "لا" is a negation, and the second is an emphatic addition to reinforce the first, because the meaning is: "not docile, turning up the earth", i.e., overturning it for cultivation, "and watering the tilth." The two verbs are then attributes of "ذَلُولٌ", as if it were said: "not docile, [one that is] turning up and watering."

﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ﴾ free from defects and traces of labour. ﴿لا شِيَةَ فِيها﴾ there is no spot of any colour other than yellow on her hide; she is entirely yellow, even her horn and hoof. The word "شِيَة" is originally a verbal noun: "شّاهُ وشْيًا وشِيَةً" means he mixed another colour into its colour.

﴿قالُوا الآنَ جِئْتَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ i.e., you have brought the true description of the cow, and no difficulty remains concerning her. The reading of "جِيتَ" and its class without hamza is by Abu 'Amr.

﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾ so they obtained the cow combining all these attributes, and slaughtered her.

﴿وَما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ because of the high price of her, or for fear of exposure when the killer became known. It is narrated: "There was among the Children of Israel a righteous old man who had a calf. He brought it to a thicket and said: 'O Allah, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up.' He was dutiful to his parents. The cow grew, and she was among the finest and fattest of cows. They haggled with the orphan and his mother until they bought her for a hide filled with gold, and that cow was worth three dinars; they had sought the described cow for forty years."

This explanation is a form of restricting the absolute, so it is abrogation (naskh). Abrogation before the act is permissible, and likewise before the capacity to act, according to us, in contrast to the Mu'tazila.

﴿وَإذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا﴾ "And when you killed a soul." The verb is governed by an implied "remember" (بِتَقْدِيرِ: واذْكُرُوا), i.e. "and remember when you killed a soul." The address is in the plural because the killing was committed by a group (الجَماعَةُ) among them.

﴿فادّارَأْتُمْ فِيها﴾ "...then you disputed concerning it," meaning you differed and quarrelled about its matter, because each of the disputants repels (يَدْرَأُ) the other, that is, pushes him away. Or the meaning is "you pushed the blame onto one another" (تَدافَعْتُمْ): each of you cast the killing of it onto another, so the one to whom it was cast repels the one who cast it. Or, because the act of casting (الطَرْح) is itself a form of repelling. The original form is تَدارَأْتُمْ. To lighten it, they changed the ta' into dal so that it would be of the same kind as the dal that is the first radical of the root (فاءُ الكَلِمَةِ), making idgham (assimilation of doubled letters) possible. Then they made the dal quiescent (ساكِنًا), since a condition of idgham is that the first of the two letters be quiescent. The connective hamza (هَمْزَةُ الوَصْلِ) was added, because it is not possible to begin with a quiescent letter without a hamza. Abu 'Amr read it as (فادّاراتُمْ) without a hamza.

﴿واللهُ مُخْرِجٌ ما كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ﴾ "And Allah will surely bring forth what you were concealing." That is, He will certainly make manifest what you had hidden of the matter of the killing, and He will not leave it concealed. The active participle مُخْرِجٌ is used to narrate (حِكايَةً) what was future at the time of the disputing. This sentence is a parenthetical interjection (اعْتِراضٌ) between the conjoined verb and the verb it is conjoined to, namely "ادّارَأْتُمْ" and what precedes it.

﴿So We said﴾ The pronoun in ﴿strike him﴾ refers to the soul (nafs), and the masculine form is used because it is interpreted as "the person" (al-shakhs) or "the human being" (al-insan). Alternatively, it refers to the slain man, based on what the context indicates.

﴿what you were concealing﴾ ﴿with part of it﴾: with part of the cow. This is its tongue, or its right thigh, or its tailbone (ʿajb). The meaning is: they struck him and he came to life, and this is omitted because of the indication of the words ﴿Thus does God bring the dead to life﴾. It is narrated that when they struck him, he rose by God's permission and said: "So-and-so and so-and-so killed me," naming his two cousins. Then he fell dead again. The two were seized and executed, and no murderer inherited after that.

The words ﴿Thus does God bring the dead to life﴾ may either be an address to the deniers in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, or an address to those who witnessed the slain man's coming back to life, meaning: and We said to them, "Thus will God bring the dead to life on the Day of Resurrection." ﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ is evidence that He is capable of everything. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, that you may act according to the dictate of your intellects, which is that whoever is able to bring one soul back to life is able to bring all of them back to life, since there is no exclusivity.

The wisdom in slaughtering the cow and striking the body with a part of it, although He was able to revive him without an intermediary, is: to indicate the goodness of making an act of devotion (qurbah) precede the request; and to teach His servants to avoid rigidity in matters, to hasten to comply with God's commands without inquiring excessively, asking many questions, and other such things. It has been said: they were commanded to slaughter a cow rather than any other animal because it was the most excellent of their offerings, and because of their worship of the calf; God wished to lower their idol in their eyes. It would have been more fitting to mention the slain man and the striking with part of the cow before the command to slaughter it, and to say: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾, then ﴿We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with part of it﴾. But He, exalted is He, related the story of the Children of Israel only to enumerate the crimes committed by them and to rebuke them for these. These two narratives, although connected, each stand on their own with a kind of rebuke: the first is to rebuke them for mockery and for neglecting to hasten to comply, and what follows from that. The second is to rebuke them for killing a forbidden soul and what followed from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man because, had it been arranged the other way, it would have become a single story, and the intended purpose of the double rebuke would have been lost. And a subtle point is observed: after the second story is begun as a fresh narrative, it is connected to the first by the pronoun referring to the cow, not by its explicit name in the words ﴿strike him with part of it﴾, so that it is known that they are two stories as regards the rebuke, and a single story by the pronoun referring back to the cow. It has also been said: this story points out that whoever wishes to revive his heart through witnessing should cause his self to die through various kinds of striving.

وَمَعْنى ﴿ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾ اسْتِبْعادُ القَسْوَةِ ﴿مِن بَعْدِ﴾ ما ذَكَرَ مِمّا يُوجِبُ لِينَ القُلُوبِ ورَقَّتَها

The meaning of ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾ is an expression of astonishment at the hardness, ﴿after﴾ what was mentioned that calls for the softening and tenderness of hearts. Describing the hearts as hard is a metaphor for their being barren of reflection (i'tibar) and admonition (ittiʿaz), ﴿after that﴾. ﴿That﴾ refers either to the raising of the murdered man to life, or to all the signs mentioned earlier.

﴿فَهِيَ كالحِجارَةِ﴾ فَهي في قَسْوَتِها مِثْلُ الحِجارَةِ

﴿They are like stones﴾: in their hardness they are like stones.

﴿أوْ أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً﴾ مِنها. وأشَدُّ: مَعْطُوفٌ عَلى الكافِ، تَقْدِيرُهُ: أوْ مِثْلُ أشَدِّ قَسْوَةٍ، فَحُذِفَ المُضافُ، وأُقِيمَ المُضافُ إلَيْهِ مَقامَهُ، أوْ هي في أنْفُسِها أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً، يَعْنِي: أنَّ مَن عَرَفَ حالَها شَبَّهَها بِالحِجارَةِ، أوْ بِجَوْهَرٍ أقْسى مِنها، وهو الحَدِيدُ مَثَلًا، أوْ مَن عَرَفَها شَبَّهَها بِالحِجارَةِ، أوْ قالَ: هي أقْسى مِنَ الحِجارَةِ،

﴿Or harder in hardness﴾ than them. The word ashadd (harder) is coordinated with the kaf (like) in ﴿like﴾; its implied sense is: "or like the hardest of hardness," in which the governing noun was omitted and the noun after it was put in its place. Or the meaning is: they themselves are harder in hardness. That is, whoever knew their condition would liken them to stones, or to a substance harder than them, such as iron for example; or whoever knew them would liken them to stones, or would say: they are harder than stones.

(p-102) وَإنَّما لَمْ يَقُلْ أقْسى لِكَوْنِهِ أبْيَنَ وأدَلَّ عَلى فَرْطِ القَسْوَةِ، وتُرِكَ ضَمِيرُ المُفَضَّلِ عَلَيْهِ لِعَدَمِ الإلْباسِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: زَيْدٌ كَرِيمٌ، وعَمْرٌو أكْرَمُ،

He did not say ﴿aqsa﴾ (harder) because ashadd is clearer and more indicative of excessive hardness. The object of comparison was left out because there is no ambiguity, as in your saying: "Zayd is generous, and ʿAmr is more generous."

﴿وَإنَّ مِنَ الحِجارَةِ﴾ بَيانٌ لِزِيادَةِ قَسْوَةِ قُلُوبِهِمْ عَلى الحِجارَةِ ﴿لَما يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنهُ الأنْهارُ﴾ "ما" بِمَعْنى: الَّذِي، في مَوْضِعِ النَصْبِ، وهو اسْمُ إنَّ، واللامُ لِلتَّوْكِيدِ، والتَفَجُّرُ: التَفَتُّحُ بِالسَعَةِ والكَثْرَةِ.

﴿And indeed among stones﴾ is an explanation of the excess of their hearts' hardness over stones: ﴿there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾. The word ma (that which) here means "those which", in the accusative position, and it is the noun of inna; the lam is for emphasis. Tafajjur (gushing) means opening up with abundance and plenty.

﴿وَإنَّ مِنها لَما يَشَّقَّقُ﴾ أصْلُهُ: يَتَشَقَّقُ، وبِهِ قَرَأ الأعْمَشُ، فَقُلِبَتِ التاءُ شَيْئًا، وأُدْغِمَتْ ﴿فَيَخْرُجُ مِنهُ الماءُ﴾ يَعْنِي: أنَّ مِنَ الحِجارَةِ ما فِيهِ خُرُوقٌ واسِعَةٌ يَتَدَفَّقُ مِنها الماءُ الكَثِيرُ، ومِنها: ما يَنْشَقُّ انْشِقاقًا بِالطُولِ، أوْ بِالعَرْضِ فَيَنْبُعُ مِنهُ الماءُ أيْضًا، وقُلُوبُهم لا تَنْدى،

﴿And indeed among them is that which splits open﴾: its original form is yatashaqqaq (with the tāʾ), and it was read this way by al-Aʿmash. The tāʾ was changed into shīn and then assimilated (idghām), giving yashsháqqu. ﴿So water comes out from it﴾: that is, among stones there are those with wide openings from which abundant water pours forth; and among them are those that split lengthwise or widthwise, so that water also springs from them, while their hearts do not soften.

﴿وَإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ﴾ يَتَرَدّى مِن أعْلى الجَبَلِ ﴿مِن خَشْيَةِ اللهِ﴾ قِيلَ: هو مَجازٌ عَنِ انْقِيادِها لِأمْرِ اللهِ، وأنَّها لا تَمْتَنِعُ عَلى ما يُرِيدُ فِيها، وقُلُوبُ هَؤُلاءِ لا تَنْقادُ ولا تَفْعَلُ ما أُمِرَتْ بِهِ، وقِيلَ: المُرادُ بِهِ: حَقِيقَةُ الخَشْيَةِ عَلى مَعْنى: أنَّهُ يَخْلُقُ فِيها الحَياةَ والتَمْيِيزَ، ولَيْسَ شَرْطُ خَلْقِ الحَياةِ. والتَمْيِيزِ في الجِسْمِ أنْ يَكُونَ عَلى بِنْيَةٍ مَخْصُوصَةٍ عِنْدَ أهْلِ السُنَّةِ، وعَلى هَذا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿لَوْ أنْـزَلْنا هَذا القُرْآنَ عَلى جَبَلٍ﴾ الآيَةُ [الحَشْرُ: ٢١] يَعْنِي: وقُلُوبُهم لا تَخْشى.

﴿And indeed among them is that which casts itself down﴾ (yahbiṭu), i.e., falls from the top of the mountain, ﴿out of fear of God﴾. It was said: this is a metaphor for their submission to God's command and that they do not resist what He wills concerning them, whereas the hearts of these people do not submit nor do what they are commanded. It was also said: what is meant is the literal meaning of fear, in the sense that He creates life and discernment in them; and the condition for creating life and discernment in a body, according to the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah, the orthodox majority), is not that it be in a particular structure. On this basis is His saying: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain...﴾ (59:21), meaning: and their hearts do not fear.

﴿وَما اللهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ وبِالياءِ، مَكِّيٌّ. وهو وعِيدٌ.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾. With the yāʾ (ya'malūna, "they do"), it is read by Makkī (Ibn Kathīr). It is a warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 75:

﴿Do you hope﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers.

﴿that they will believe you﴾ That they would believe for the sake of your call (da'wah), and respond to you, as in His saying: ﴿Lot believed in him﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26], meaning: the Jews.

﴿And there was a group of them﴾ a company among those who passed before them, ﴿who heard the words of Allah﴾ i.e., the Torah,

﴿then they distorted it﴾ as they distorted the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning (rajm),

﴿after they had understood it﴾ after they had comprehended it and retained it with their intellects,

﴿and they knew﴾ that they were liars and fabricators. The meaning is: if these people disbelieved and distorted, then they have a precedent in that.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 76:**

﴿When they meet those who believe⦆ That is, the hypocrites, or the Jews, ﴿those who believe﴾, that is, (p-103) the sincere ones among the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿they say﴾, that is, the hypocrites,

﴿"We believe"﴾ that you are upon the truth, and that Muhammad is the Messenger whose coming was foretold,

﴿But when they are alone, some of them with others﴾, those who did not become hypocrites with those who did become hypocrites, ﴿they say﴾, reproaching them:

﴿"Do you tell them what God has disclosed to you"﴾, that is, do you inform the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) of what God has made clear to you in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, that is, so that they may argue against you with what your Lord has revealed in His Book. They treated their argument with it, and their saying "It is in your Book thus," as an argument before God, just as you say "It is in the Book of God Most High thus" and "It is thus before God," with one meaning. It has also been said that this is by elision of a noun: before the Book of your Lord. It has also been said that the meaning is "so that they may dispute with you and contend with you about it, with what you have told them, before your Lord on the Day of Resurrection," where they will say, "You disbelieved after you had come to know its truth." ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾, that this is a proof against you, since you acknowledge it and then do not follow it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 77:

﴿Do they not know that Allah knows﴾ all of ﴿what they conceal and what they reveal﴾. And among that is their concealing of disbelief and their displaying of faith.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 78:

﴿And among them﴾ (i.e., among the Jews) ﴿are unlettered folk﴾ who do not know how to read the books, so they cannot study the Torah and verify what is in it. ﴿They know not the Book﴾, namely the Torah, ﴿except wishful fancies﴾, meaning except what they hold of their own wishes (amani), and that God will pardon them, have mercy on them, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days (Qur'an 2:80), or except for various lies they heard from their scholars and so accepted by way of taqlid (blind imitation). From this is the saying of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not wished (tamanna) since I embraced Islam, except for what they recite," from the verse of the poet:

Tamanna kitab Allah awwal layla * wa akhiruha la fi himam al-maqadir

(He wished for the Book of God at the beginning of the night, and its end was not in the death decreed by fate.)

That is: these people do not know the true reality of what was revealed; rather they only recite things they took from their rabbis. The exception (istithna') is disjunctive (munqati').

﴿And they are not﴾ ﴿except conjecturing﴾, meaning they do not understand what is in it, so they deny your prophethood on the basis of conjecture. He mentioned first the scholars who obstinately distorted the text while knowing the truth, and then the common folk who imitated them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 79:

﴿So woe﴾ In the hadith: "Woe (Wayl) is a valley in Hell." ﴿to those who write the Book﴾ distorted (muharraf) ﴿with their own hands﴾, from their own selves, without it being revealed. The mention of "hands" is for emphasis (ta'kid), and it is of the figurative usage of emphasis (majaz al-ta'kid). ﴿Then they say: "This is from Allah," to exchange it for a small price﴾, a meager gain. ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn﴾, from bribery (al-risha).

﴿And they say: The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days.﴾ Forty days, equal to the number of days they spent worshipping the calf. It is also reported from Mujahid (may Allah be pleased with him) that they used to say: "The lifespan of this world is seven thousand years, and we will be punished only one day for every thousand years."

﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ That is: Has He promised you that He will punish you only for this amount of time?

﴿Then Allah will not break His covenant.﴾ This phrase is connected (muta'alliq) to an omitted element (mahdhuf), whose implied meaning is: "If you have taken a covenant with Allah, then Allah will not break His covenant."

﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ The particle "أمْ" (am) may be either equivalential (mu'adilah, linking two alternatives in a question), meaning: "Do you say about Allah what you know, or do you say about Him what you do not know?" Or it may be disjunctive (munqati'ah, introducing a new question and meaning "rather"), meaning: "Rather, do you say about Allah what you do not know?!"

﴿Bala﴾ (Yes, indeed) is an affirmation of what follows the negation, namely: ﴿"The Fire will not touch us"﴾. That is: Yes, you will be touched by it forever, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿"They will abide therein forever"﴾.

﴿"Whoever earns an evil deed"﴾ — shirk (associating partners with Allah), according to Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and others, may Allah be pleased with them — ﴿"and his sin encompasses him"﴾, and blocks off the paths of salvation for him, by his dying upon his shirk. As for one who dies a believer, the greatest of acts of obedience, which is faith, accompanies him, so sin does not encompass him, and the text does not apply to him. By this interpretation, the argument of the Mu'tazila and the Khawarij is refuted. It has also been said: it has overpowered him, as an enemy overpowers, and he was not freed from it by repentance. (Khatiyatuhu) is Madani [a reading].

﴿"Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 83:

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾. Al-Mithaq: the covenant, confirmed to the utmost degree of confirmation.

﴿You shall worship none but Allah﴾. This is an informative statement carrying the meaning of a prohibition, just as you say: "You go to so-and-so and tell him such-and-such," meaning a command. It is more emphatic than an explicit command or prohibition, because it is as if one has hastened to comply and desist, and the statement reports on that. It is supported by the reading of Ubayy: (لا تَعْبُدُوا, "do not worship"). And His saying: ﴿And say﴾, where "say" is implied. (لا يَعْبُدُونَ, "they shall not worship") is the reading of Makki, Hamza and Ali, because "Children of Israel" is an apparent noun, and all apparent nouns are third person. Its meaning is: that they should not worship; then, when "an" (that) was elided, the verb was put in the nominative.

﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾. That is: and be good, so that the coordination of the command, which is His saying ﴿And say﴾, is consistent with it.

﴿And to the near relatives﴾, of kinship,

﴿and the orphans﴾, plural of yatim (orphan), who is one whose father died before reaching puberty, until puberty, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no orphanhood after reaching maturity."

﴿And the needy﴾, plural of miskin (needy), who is one whom need has made to dwell (in the dust, i.e., destitute).

﴿And speak to people good words﴾: a speech that is good in itself due to its excessive goodness.

(p-106) (ḥasanan, "good") is the reading of Hamza and Ali.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat; then you turned away﴾ from the covenant and rejected it.

﴿Except a few of you﴾. It was said: they are those among them who embraced Islam.

﴿And you are withdrawers﴾: you are a people whose habit is turning away, and turning away from covenants.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 84:

﴿And when We took your covenant: You shall not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes﴾ Meaning: none of you shall do this to another. He made the other person like one's own self when they are connected by lineage (aslan) or by religion (dinan). It was also said: whoever kills another, it is as though he has killed himself, because he will be retaliated against for it.

﴿Then you acknowledged﴾ the covenant, and you confessed against yourselves its binding obligation,

﴿and you were witnesses﴾ to it, just as you say: so-and-so acknowledges against himself such-and-such, and is a witness against it. Or, ﴿and you were witnesses﴾ today, O assembly of Jews, to the acknowledgment of your forefathers of this covenant.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 85:

﴿Then you are these people﴾ This is an expression of astonishment at what was attributed to them of killing, expulsion and transgression, after the covenant had been taken from them, and after their acknowledgment and their testimony. "Antum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "haa'ulaa'" means "alladhina" (those who).

﴿You kill yourselves﴾ is the relative clause (silah) of "haa'ulaa'", and "haa'ulaa'" together with its relative clause is the predicate (khabar) of "antum".

﴿And you expel a group of you from their homes﴾ not observing the covenant of God.

﴿You support against them﴾ With the lightened form (tukhaffifun), Kufan (the reading of the Kufans) reads it, meaning: you cooperate. With the doubled form (tazzahirun, with tashdid), the others read it. Whoever reads it lightened has dropped one of the two taa'. Then it is said: it is the second one, because the heaviness is carried by it; and it is said: the first. Whoever doubles it changes the second taa' into a za' and assimilates it (idgham).

﴿With sin and transgression﴾ with disobedience and wrongdoing.

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ ("usara tufduhum"): Abu 'Amr reads it so. ("Usra tufadūhum"): Makki and Shami. ("Usra tafduhum"): Hamzah. ("Usara tufadūhum"): 'Ali. "Fada" and "fadaa" have the same meaning, and "usara" is a state (hal) construction; it is the plural of "asir" (captive), and likewise "usra".

﴿And it is forbidden to you﴾ The pronoun refers to the matter (ash-shan), or it is an ambiguous pronoun whose explanation is: ﴿their expulsion﴾ (p-107) ﴿Do you then believe in part of the Book﴾ by ransoming the captives ﴿and disbelieve in part﴾ by fighting and expulsion. Al-Suddi said: God took from them four covenants: abandoning killing, abandoning expulsion, abandoning support (against others), and ransoming the captive. They turned away from everything they were commanded except the ransoming.

﴿So what is the recompense of those who do that﴾ It refers to believing in part and disbelieving in part. ﴿among you, except disgrace﴾ ignominy and humiliation ﴿in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾, which is the punishment in which there is neither rest nor relief; or it means a punishment more severe than the punishment of this world.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ With the "ya" (yaʿmalūna) read by Makki, Nafi', and Abu Bakr.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 86:**

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter.﴾ They chose it over the Hereafter with the choice of one who buys. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.﴾ No one will help them by repelling it from them.

﴿And We certainly gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. He gave it to him all at once.

﴿And We followed up after him with the messengers﴾. It is said *qaffāhu* (he followed him), when one pursues him from the *qafā* (back of the neck), like *dhanabuhu* (his tail) from *al-dhanab* (the tail). And *qaffāhu bihi* means he made him follow it. The meaning is: And We sent, following in his footsteps, many messengers. They are Yusha' (Joshua), Shamwil (Samuel), Sham'un (Simeon), Dawud (David), Sulayman (Solomon), Sha'ya (Isaiah), Armiya (Jeremiah), Uzayr (Ezra), Hizqil (Ezekiel), Ilyas (Elijah), al-Yasa' (Elisha), Yunus (Jonah), Zakariyya (Zechariah), Yahya (John), and others.

﴿And We gave Isa, son of Maryam, the clear proofs﴾. It is in the sense of *al-khādim* (the servant). The *wazn* (morphological pattern) of Maryam, according to the grammarians, is *maf'al*, because *fa'il* (the pattern *fa'īl*) is not attested among the patterns. *Al-bayyināt* (the clear proofs) are the manifest miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and informing of unseen matters.

﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾. That is, *al-ṭahāra* (purity). The reading with *sukūn* (silent vowel) wherever it occurs is that of Makki, meaning "with the holy spirit," as one says *Hātim al-Jūd* (Hatim of generosity). He described it as holy for specification and honour, or it refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), because he brings that by which hearts live. That is because he (Allah) raised him (Isa) to the heavens when the Jews intended to kill him. Or it refers to the Injil, as He said in the Qur'an: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. Or it refers to the Greatest Name of Allah, by mentioning which he used to revive the dead.

﴿Is it then that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls do not desire﴾, i.e., what you love, ﴿you grew arrogant﴾, i.e., you considered yourselves too great to accept him? ﴿So a party you denied﴾, like Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both), ﴿and a party you killed﴾, like Zakariyya and Yahya (peace be upon them both).

He did not say "you killed" (*qataltum*) for the sake of matching the endings (*fawāṣil*), or because the intended meaning is: and a party you are going to kill afterwards, since you were circling around the killing of Muhammad ﷺ, were it not that I protect him from you. For this reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him. The meaning is: And We certainly gave the prophets of the Children of Israel what We gave them; so whenever a messenger from among them came to you with the truth, you were arrogant towards believing in him. The interrogative *hamza* of rebuke and wonder at their affair has been placed between the *fā'* (then) and what it is connected to.

(p-108)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 88:

﴿And they say: "Our hearts are uncovered."﴾ It is the plural of aghlaf (ghulf, "wrapped/sheathed"), meaning: it is a natural creation covered with coverings through which what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought cannot reach them, and they do not comprehend it. It is a metaphor taken from the aghlaf, the one who has not been circumcised.

﴿Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief.﴾ Thus Allah rejected that their hearts were created in such a state, because they were created upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and the capacity to accept the truth. Rather, He drove them away because of their disbelief and their deviation.

﴿So little is it that they believe.﴾ "Faqaliylan" is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "So they believe with a little faith." The "ma" is extra (mazidah), and it refers to their belief in some of the Book. It has also been said: "al-qillah" here means "al-'adam" (nonexistence). It has also been said: "ghulf" is a lightened form of "ghuluf," and it has been read that way, being the plural of "ghilaf" (covering), meaning: "Our hearts are containers for knowledge, so we are content with what we have from others; or they are containers for knowledge, so if what you brought were true, it would have preceded us to it."

(p-109) ﴿And when there came to them﴾, i.e., the Jews:

﴿a Book from Allah﴾, i.e., the Qur'an.

﴿confirming what is with them﴾ from their Book, not contradicting it.

﴿And they had been, before,﴾ meaning: before the Qur'an,

﴿seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾: they would seek victory against the polytheists when they fought them, saying, "O Allah, give us victory through the Prophet who will be sent at the end of time, whose description we find in the Torah," and they would say to their polytheist enemies, "The time of a prophet has drawn near who will come confirming what we have said, and we will kill you along with him the killing of ʿAd and Iram."

﴿But when there came to them what they recognised﴾: "mā" is a relative pronoun, meaning what they recognised, and it is the subject of "jāʾa" (came),

﴿they disbelieved in it﴾ out of rebellion (baghy), envy, and greed for leadership. ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾: i.e., upon them, the apparent noun being placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that the curse befell them because of their disbelief. The lām is for specificity (al-ʿahd) or for genus (al-jins), and they entered into it with an initial entry (dukhūlan awwaliyyan). The response (jawāb) of the first "lammā" is omitted, and it is something like: "they denied it," or "they rejected it," or "kafarū" is the response of both the first and the second, because what they require is one and the same.

90. The *ma* in ﴿بِئْسَما﴾ is an indefinite noun (*ma nakirah*) described by the following clause, explaining the subject of *bi'sa* (an expression of disapproval). The meaning is: "Evil is the thing..."

﴿اشْتَرَوْا بِهِ أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ means they sold it. The object of the blame is ﴿أنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِما أنْـزَلَ اللهُ﴾, that is, the Qur'an.

﴿بَغْيًا﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning out of envy and in pursuit of what was not theirs. It gives the reason for ﴿اشْتَرَوْا﴾. The phrase ﴿أنْ يُنَـزِّلَ اللهُ﴾ is read as "because God sends down" or "in that God sends down." The meaning is that they envied him because God sends down ﴿مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾, which is the revelation, ﴿عَلى مَن يَشاءُ مِن عِبادِهِ﴾, who is Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿فَباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ عَلى غَضَبٍ﴾ means they became deserving of one wrath after another. They did so because they disbelieved in the true Prophet and transgressed against him. Alternatively, they disbelieved in Muhammad after Jesus, peace be upon them both, or after their saying, ﴿عُزَيْرٌ ابْنُ اللهِ﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], and their saying, ﴿يَدُ اللهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and other such things.

﴿وَلِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ مُهِينٌ﴾ means a humiliating punishment.

(بِيسَما): Abu 'Amr read it without hamza, and the same applies to words of its pattern. (يُنْزِلُ) with the lightened form (*al-takhfif*, reading ﴿يُنْزِلُ﴾ rather than ﴿يُنَـزِّلُ﴾) is the reading of al-Makki and al-Basri.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 91:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ — to these Jews — ﴿"Believe in what Allah has sent down,"﴾ meaning: the Qur'an. Or it is unrestricted, encompassing every Book.

﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us,"﴾ that is, the Torah.

﴿and they disbelieve in what is beyond it,﴾ that is: they say this, while in fact they disbelieve in what lies beyond the Torah.

﴿while it is the truth, confirming what is with them﴾ — not contradicting it. In this there is a refutation of their statement, for if they disbelieve in what agrees with the Torah, then they have disbelieved in the Torah itself. And "confirming" (muṣaddiqan) is a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl muʾakkidah).

﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah﴾ — that is, why did you kill — so the future tense is placed in the position of the past, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿before, if you were believers﴾ — that is, before Muhammad ﷺ. It is a rebuke against them for killing the prophets while claiming to believe in the Torah, and the Torah does not permit the killing of prophets. It has been said: they killed three hundred prophets in a single day in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

﴿And certainly Moses came to you with the clear signs﴾ — with the nine signs. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and 'Ali assimilated the dal (الدال) into the jim (الجيم) wherever it occurred (idgham).

﴿Then you took the calf﴾ as a god ﴿after him﴾, after Moses (peace be upon him) went up to the Tur (Mount Sinai).

﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: you worshipped the calf while you were placing worship in other than its proper place; or it is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ), meaning: and you were a people whose habit was wrongdoing.

﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised the Mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you with strength."﴾ He repeated the mention of raising the Mount because of an added matter attached to it that was not part of the first mention. ﴿And listen﴾ to what you were commanded in the Torah. ﴿They said, "We hear"﴾ your word, ﴿"and we disobey"﴾ your command. His words correspond to their answer in that he said to them, "Listen," and their listening should have been listening of acceptance and obedience, (p-111) but they said, "We hear," without listening in obedience. ﴿And the calf was made to sink into their hearts﴾, meaning its love and eagerness to worship it permeated them, just as dye permeates cloth. His words ﴿into their hearts﴾ explain the place of the sinking in, and the omitted element (muḍāf) is "love," which is removed. ﴿Because of their disbelief﴾, meaning because of their disbelief and their belief in anthropomorphism (tashbih, ascribing likeness to God).

﴿Say: "Evil is what your faith commands you, if you are believers."﴾ "Your faith" refers to their belief in the Torah, because there is nothing in the Torah about worshipping the calf. Attributing the command to their faith is mockery (tahakkum), and so is attributing faith to them. ﴿If you are believers﴾ casts doubt on their faith and undermines the soundness of their claim to it.

Say: "If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively" — that is, Paradise.

"With Allah" (ʿinda Allāh) is a circumstantial adverbial phrase (ẓarf), and "for you" (lakum) is the predicate of kāna (the predicate of kāna, "was/is").

"Exclusively" (khāliṣatan) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) relating to "the Last Abode," meaning: pure for you, with no one else among others having a right in it. That is, if your claim holds true: "None shall enter Paradise except those who are Jews" [al-Baqarah: 111], "to the exclusion of other people" — here "people" (al-nās) is generic (li-l-jins) — "then wish for death, if you are truthful" in what you say. For whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise longs for it, in order to be free of the abode that is full of defects, just as it is reported from the Ten Promised Paradise (al-ʿAshara al-Mubashshirūn) that each one of them used to love death and yearn for it.

Surah al-Baqarah, verse 95, in al-Nasafi's Madarik al-Tanzil:

﴿And they will never wish for it, ever﴾ This is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning: they will never wish for it as long as they live. ﴿Because of what their hands have put forward﴾ because of what they had previously committed of disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ), the distortion of the Book of Allah, and other things. This is one of the miracles (mu'jizat), because it is a report of the unseen, and it happened as he had reported it, like His saying: ﴿And you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. Had they wished for it, that would have been transmitted just as other events were transmitted.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ a warning to them.

(p-112)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 96:

﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people﴾. The object of "wajada" (found) is "hum" (them) and "aḥraṣa" (most eager).

﴿for life﴾. The indefiniteness (tanwin, here the indefinite noun ḥayāh) indicates that what is meant is a particular life, namely a long-extended life. That is why the reading with it is more forceful than the reading of Ubayy: (ʿalā al-ḥayāh) [with the definite article].

﴿And of those who associated partners [with God]﴾. This is understood according to meaning, because the meaning of "most eager of people" is: most eager of [all] people. Indeed, those who associated partners are included under "people", but they are singled out for mention because their eagerness is intense, just as Jibril and Mika'il are singled out for mention although they are included under the angels. Or it is intended: "and more eager than those who associated partners," and it is omitted because "most eager of people" points to it. In this there is a great rebuke, because those who associated partners do not believe in an afterlife and know only the worldly life, so their eagerness for it is not surprising, since it is their paradise. When one who has a Book, and who acknowledges recompense, increases in eagerness, he is deserving of the greatest rebuke. Their eagerness increased beyond those who associated partners because they knew that they were destined for the Fire, given their knowledge of their own state, whereas the polytheists do not know this. His saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ is an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, in the manner of a resumptive (istiʾnaf) statement. It has been said: by "those who associated partners" he meant the Magians, because they used to say to their kings: "Live a thousand Nayruz (festivals)." And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is the saying of the non-Arabs: "Zi hazar sal" (live a thousand years). It has also been said: ﴿And of those who associated partners﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, meaning: "and among them are people, each one of whom wishes...", with the qualified noun omitted. And ﴿those who associated partners﴾ on this view refers to the Jews, because they said: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah.

﴿And it will not remove him from the punishment that he be given life.﴾ The pronoun refers to "one of them", and his saying ﴿that he be given life﴾ is the subject (fāʿil) of "muzaḥziḥihi" (removing him), meaning: and none of them is one whose long life will remove him from the Fire. It is permissible for "huwa" (it/he) to be an unspecified pronoun (mubham), with ﴿an yuʿammar﴾ (that he be given life) clarifying it. Zaḥzaḥah means distancing and withdrawing. In "Jamiʿ al-ʿUlum" and elsewhere it is said: ﴿law yuʿammar﴾ (if he be given life) has the sense of ﴿an yuʿammar﴾ (that he be given life). So "law" here stands in place of "an", and "an" together with the verb is in the sense of a verbal noun (maṣdar), which is the object of "yawaddu" (wishes), meaning: each one of them wishes for the lengthening of a thousand years. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, meaning: of the deeds of these disbelievers, so He will recompense them for it. With the letter "ta" (ya-taʿmalūna as ta-), it is read by Yaʿqub.

(p-113)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 97:

﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ (with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the ra, without hamza, is the reading of Makki). With a fatha on the ra and the jim and a hamza, prolonged (mushba'an), is the reading of the Kufans other than Hafs. With a kasra on the ra and the jim without hamza is the reading of the others. The diptote form (man' al-sarf) is due to definiteness (al-ta'rif) and foreignness (al-'ujma). Its meaning is "servant of Allah," because Jabr is "the servant" in Syriac (al-Suryaniyya), and Il is the name of Allah. It is narrated that Ibn Suriya, one of the rabbis of the Jews, disputed with the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about the one who descends to him with the revelation. He said: "Jibril." He said: "That is our enemy. Had it been other than him, we would have believed in you. He has been hostile to us many times, and the most severe of them is that he brought down to our Prophet that Bayt al-Maqdis would be destroyed by Bukhtunassar. So we sent someone to kill him, and he met him in Babil as a poor boy, and Jibril repelled him and said: 'If your Lord commanded him to destroy you, he will not give him power over you; and if it was not He, then for what sin are you killing him?!'" ﴿For indeed, he revealed it﴾, that is, Jibril revealed the Qur'an. This kind of pronominal reference, I mean referring to something whose mention has not preceded, carries grandeur, since it is made, because of its extreme fame, as if it indicates itself, and it dispenses with its explicit name by mentioning some of its attributes.

﴿upon your heart﴾, that is, his preserving it for you. The heart is singled out because it is the locus of memorization, as in His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down, upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193-194]. The proper form of speech would have been "upon my heart," but it came in the mode of quoting the words of Allah as He spoke them. The phrase "for indeed, he revealed it" may stand as the answer to the condition (jaza' li-l-shart), because its implied sense is: if anyone among the People of the Book is hostile to Jibril, there is no justification for enmity toward him, since he revealed a Book confirming what lies before it of the scriptures. Had they been fair, they would have loved him and thanked him for his favor in revealing to them what benefits them and corrects what was revealed to them. It is also said that the answer to the condition is omitted, its implied sense being: whoever is an enemy to Jibril, let him die of rage, for indeed he revealed the revelation upon your heart ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, by His command, ﴿confirming what lies before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾. This is a refutation of the Jews when they said that Jibril descends with war and severity, so it was said: rather, he descends also with guidance and good tidings. (p-114)

﴿By the permission of Allah﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun of the subject in "nazala," meaning: permitted by Him. "Confirming" is a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "nazzalahu," and likewise "guidance and good tidings," meaning: guiding and bringing good tidings.

The Batiniyya said: The Qur'an did not descend upon the Messenger of Allah in these letters which we recite; rather it is an inspiration that descended upon his heart, except that Muhammad ﷺ expressed it in Arabic, with these letters which we recite. So the Qur'an is that inner meaning, not these wordings, based on His saying: ﴿He revealed it upon your heart﴾. But we say: this is corrupt, because Allah the Exalted made it miraculous through its wondrous composition, when He said: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], and said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2]. This belongs to the discipline of speculative reasoning (al-nazar).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 98:

﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mikal﴾: Basri and Hafs (read it as Mīkāl), and (Mīkā'īl) with the hamza elided, like Mīkā'il, is Madani. (Mīkā'īl) with the long vowel and a fully pronounced hamza with a kasra, is the reading of the others. The two angels were singled out for mention because of their excellence, as if they were of a different kind, since difference in attribute is treated as if it were difference in essence. ﴿Then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾: that is, to them. The apparent noun was used so as to show that Allah only opposed them because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels is disbelief, just as enmity toward the prophets is, and whoever opposes them, Allah opposes him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 99:

﴿And We have indeed sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ [That is] the rebellious among the disbelievers. The article (al-lam) here is for the genus (li-l-jins), and it is best that it refers to the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab).
