From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Ibn Suriya said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You have brought us nothing that we recognize, and no sign has been sent down to you that we would follow you in." So this was revealed.

The waw in ﴿Awa-kullama﴾ is for coordinating with something omitted, whose implied sense is: "Did they disbelieve in the clear signs?"

﴿Awa-kullama ʿāhadū ʿahdan nabadhahu﴾ — "Whenever they made a covenant, a party of them threw it away," meaning he broke it and discarded it. He said ﴿a party of them﴾ because some of them did not break it.

﴿Bal aktharuhum lā yu'minūn﴾ — "Rather, most of them do not believe" in the Torah, and they have nothing to do with religion (p-115), so they do not regard breaking covenants as a sin, nor do they care about it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 101:

﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from God﴾ — Muhammad (ﷺ) — ﴿confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Book threw away﴾ — i.e., the Torah — and ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ are the Jews.

﴿the Book of God﴾ means the Torah, because by their disbelief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who confirms what was with them, they were disbelievers in it and casters of it away. Or, "the Book of God" is the Qur'an, which they threw away after it had become binding upon them to receive it with acceptance.

﴿behind their backs﴾ is a parable for their abandonment of it and their turning away from it. It is depicted by what is cast behind the back, signifying their disregard for it and their scant attention to it.

﴿as if they did not know﴾ that it is the Book of God.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 102:

﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ That is: the Jews discarded the Book of God and followed the books of magic and sorcery which the devils used to read ﴿during the reign of Solomon﴾, that is, in the time of his kingdom and during his era. The reason was that the devils used to eavesdrop, then they would add to what they had heard lies which they fabricated, and they would convey them to the soothsayers (kahana). They recorded these in books which they would read and teach to the people. This spread during the time of Solomon, peace be upon him, to the point that they said: "The jinn know the unseen," and they would say: "This is the knowledge of Solomon, and Solomon's kingdom was only established by this knowledge, and by it he subjugated the jinn, the humans, and the wind."

﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve﴾ This is a refutation of the devils and a rejection of what they had slandered Solomon with, namely the belief in magic and the practice of it.

﴿But the devils﴾ are the ones who ﴿disbelieved﴾ by using magic and recording it. ("Wa-lakin" with the light pronunciation, "al-shayatin" with the nominative: Ibn Amir (al-Shami), Hamzah and Ali.)

﴿teaching people magic﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they disbelieved while teaching people magic, intending by it to mislead them and lead them astray.

﴿And [they followed] what was sent down to the two angels﴾ The majority hold that "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and it is in the accusative as a conjunction with "al-sihr," meaning: and they teach them what was sent down to the two angels; or it is conjoined with ﴿ma tatlu﴾, meaning: and they followed what was sent down to the two angels ﴿at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾ (p-116), two named angels, and they are an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to the two angels. What was sent down to them was the knowledge of magic as a trial from God for people. Whoever among them learned it and acted upon it became a disbeliever, if it contained the denial of what is obligatory in the condition of faith. Whoever avoided it, or learned it not in order to act upon it but to guard against it and so as not to be deceived by it, was a believer. Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The claim that magic is disbelief absolutely is an error; rather, its reality must be investigated. If it contains the denial of what is obligatory in the condition of faith, then it is disbelief; otherwise it is not. Then, magic which is disbelief is punished by death for men but not for women; and that which is not disbelief but involves the destruction of a soul carries the ruling of highway robbers, and in it men and women are equal, and repentance is accepted if one repents. Whoever says that repentance is not accepted has erred, for the repentance of Pharaoh's sorcerers was accepted. It was said: "sent down" means cast into their hearts together with a prohibition against acting upon it. It was said: they are two angels whom the angels chose so that desire would be placed in them when they reproached the children of Adam; they used to judge on earth and ascend at night, and they fell in love with Zuhrah, who led them to drink wine, and they committed fornication; a man saw them and they killed him, so they chose the punishment of this world over the punishment of the Hereafter, and they are punished upside down in a well at Babylon. It was called Babylon because of the confusion (tabalbul) of tongues there.

﴿And they do not teach anyone﴾ and the two angels do not teach anyone ﴿until they say﴾ until they warn him, advise him, and say to him: ﴿"We are only a trial"﴾ a test and examination from God.

﴿So do not disbelieve﴾ by learning it and knowing it in a way that would amount to disbelief.

﴿Then they learn from both of them﴾ The "fa" is conjoined with his saying: ﴿teaching people magic﴾, meaning: they teach them and then they learn from the magic and the disbelief indicated by His saying ﴿they disbelieved﴾ and ﴿teaching people magic﴾. Or it is conjoined with an implied element, the sense being: then they come and then they learn, and the pronoun refers to what is indicated by "anyone" (min ahad), meaning: then people learn from the two angels.

﴿That by which they cause division between a man and his wife﴾ meaning: the knowledge of magic which is a cause of separation between spouses, by God creating discord and disagreement between them as a trial from Him. Magic has a real existence according to the People of the Sunnah, may God increase them, while according to the Mu'tazilah it is imagination and deception.

﴿But they cannot harm anyone thereby﴾ by the magic ﴿except by God's permission﴾ by His knowledge and His will,

﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾ in the Hereafter. In this is evidence that it is obligatory to avoid it, like learning philosophy which leads to misguidance.

﴿And they certainly knew﴾ that is, the Jews.

﴿that whoever purchases it﴾ that is, whoever exchanges what the devils recite for the Book of God ﴿has no share in the Hereafter﴾ no portion,

﴿and wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾ they sold them. He only negated knowledge from them by His saying ﴿if they had known﴾ while affirming it for them by His saying ﴿and they certainly knew﴾, by way of emphatic oath, because its meaning is: if they had acted upon their knowledge. He made them, when they did not act upon it, as though they did not know.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 103:

﴿And if they had believed﴾ in the Messenger of Allah and the Qur'an, ﴿and feared Allah﴾, abandoning what they were upon of casting aside the Book of Allah and following the books of the devils, ﴿a reward from Allah would have been better, if they had known﴾ that the reward of Allah is better than what they are in, and they had known it, but He made them ignorant because they abandoned acting upon knowledge. The meaning is: they would have been rewarded from Allah with what is better. The nominal sentence was preferred over the verbal one in the apodosis of "law" (lau), because of what it conveys of the permanence and stability of the reward. He did not say "the reward of Allah is better," because the meaning is: some of the reward would be better for them. It has also been said: "law" here carries the sense of wishing, as if it were said: "Would that they had believed," and then he began: ﴿a reward from Allah is better﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 104:

﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen.﴾ The Muslims used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he imparted to them some knowledge: "Ra'ina, O Messenger of Allah!" That is: "Be attentive to us and wait for us until we understand it and memorize it." The Jews had a word they used to revile one another with (p-118), in Hebrew or Syriac, and it was: "Ra'ina." So when they heard the believers' saying "Ra'ina," they seized upon it and addressed the Messenger with it, meaning by it that insult. So the believers were forbidden from it, and they were commanded to say what has the same meaning, which is ﴿Unzurna﴾, from "nazara," meaning: when he waited for him.

﴿And listen﴾: and listen well to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) speaks to you and the questions he puts to you, with attentive ears and present minds, so that you will not need to ask him to repeat and to request consideration. Or: and listen with a listening of acceptance and obedience, and let your listening not be like the listening of the Jews, when they said: "We hear and we disobey."

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾: and for the Jews who reviled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ﴿is a painful punishment﴾: painful, causing pain.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 105:

﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish that any good be sent down upon you﴾. Read with the lightened form (yunazzala, "to be sent down," with the verbal noun pattern not doubled) by Ibn Kathir (Makki) and Abu 'Amr.

﴿from your Lord﴾. The first "min" (from) is for explanation (li-l-bayan), because "those who disbelieve" is a genus under which there are two types: the People of the Book and the polytheists. The second "min" is extra (mazidah), for the sake of encompassing all good (li-istighraq al-khayr). The third "min" indicates the starting point of the act (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). "Good" (khayr) here means revelation, and likewise mercy (al-rahmah).

﴿But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾. This means: they think that they themselves are more deserving of having revelation sent to them, so they envy you, and they do not wish that any revelation be sent down upon you; but Allah singles out for prophethood whom He wills.

﴿And Allah is the Lord of great bounty﴾. In this there is an indication that bestowing prophethood is among the great bounties.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 106:

When they criticized abrogation (naskh) and said: "Do you not see that Muhammad orders his companions to do one thing, then forbids them from it, orders them to do its opposite, says one thing today and retracts it tomorrow?" then this was revealed: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or the like of it.﴾ The linguistic meaning of naskh (abrogation) is substitution (tabdil). Its technical meaning (shari'ah) is the clarification of the end of a legal ruling (hukm shar'i) that was absolute, whose continuance had become fixed in our minds through the means of delay. Thus it is a substitution with respect to us, and a pure clarification with respect to the Lawgiver (sahib al-shar'), and in it is a response to the notion of change of mind (bada') claimed by its deniers, namely the Jews. Its locus (mahall) is a ruling that is capable of existence and non-existence in itself, to which nothing has attached that contradicts abrogation, such as a time limit (tawqit) or perpetuity (ta'bid), whether established by explicit text (nass) or by implication (dalalah). Its condition (shart) is the ability to form conviction in the heart according to us, not the ability to act, contrary to the Mu'tazilah. Abrogation is permissible only through the Book and the Sunnah, whether they are alike or different. It is permissible to abrogate the recitation and the ruling, the ruling without the recitation, the recitation without the ruling, and to abrogate a attribute by a ruling, such as an addition to the text, which according to us is abrogation, contrary to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Causing to forget (al-insa') is that one removes its memorization from the hearts. Or (nansa'ha) is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr, meaning: We postpone it, from nasa'tu, meaning: I postponed.

﴿We bring one better than it﴾ meaning: We bring a verse better than it for the servants, that is, a verse whose practice yields more reward.

﴿Or the like of it﴾ in that, since there is no superiority of some verses over others.

﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ meaning: capable; so He is able to do what is better and what is its like.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 107:

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ So He governs your affairs and manages them, and He is most knowing of what He obligates you to worship through (ʿibadah), of abrogating (naskh) and abrogated (mansukh) rulings.

﴿And you have not, besides Allah, any protector (walī)﴾ who takes charge of your affairs.

﴿Nor any helper (naṣīr)﴾ a supporter who would prevent you from the punishment.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 108:**

﴿Am turidūna﴾ "Am" is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and its implied sense is: "Do you desire...?"

﴿an tas'alū rasūlakum kamā su'ila Mūsā min qablu﴾ It is narrated that the Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, make Safa gold for us, and widen the land of Makkah for us." So they were forbidden to propose signs to him, as the people of Musa (Moses) proposed to him when they said: ﴿Make for us a god⁠﻿ as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138].

﴿Wa man yatabaddal al-kufra bil-iman﴾ Whoever abandons trust in the revealed signs, doubts them, and proposes others instead.

﴿Faqad dalla sawa' al-sabil﴾ He has strayed from its direct course (qasduhu) and its middle path (wasituhu).

(p-120)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 109:

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish that they could turn you back﴾ to (literally: that they would turn you back) ﴿from your faith into disbelief﴾. ﴿Kafiran﴾ (disbelievers) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from "kum" (you), meaning: they would turn you away from your religion while you are disbelievers. It was revealed when the Jews said to the Muslims after the Battle of Uhud: "Do you not see what has befallen you? Had you been upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better for you,"

﴿ḥasadan﴾ (out of envy) is a maf‘ūl lahu (object of purpose), meaning: out of envy, which is grief at the good enjoyed by others.

﴿min ʿindi anfusihim﴾ (from their own selves) is connected to "wadda" (wish), meaning: they wish this from their own selves and from the prompting of their desires, not from religious conviction or inclination toward the truth, because they wished that.

﴿min baʿdi mā tabayyana lahumu al-ḥaqq﴾ (after the truth has become clear to them) means: after their knowledge that you are upon the truth. Or it means: "ḥasadan" (out of envy), that is, intense envy, arising from the very core of their souls. ﴿Fa-ʿfū wa-iṣfaḥū﴾ (so pardon and overlook): adopt toward them the way of pardon and forgiveness for what comes from them of ignorance and hostility.

﴿Ḥattā yaʾtiya Allāhu bi-amrihi﴾ (until Allah brings His command): that is, with fighting.

﴿Inna Allāha ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr﴾ (indeed Allah is over all things capable): He is able to take vengeance upon them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 110:

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah.﴾ (That is) from a good deed: prayer, or charity, or other than these. ﴿You will find it with Allah﴾: you will find its reward with Him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾: so the work of no worker is lost with Him.

The pronoun in ﴿They say: none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ refers to the People of the Book, from among the Jews and the Christians. That is: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews (hud)," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except those who are Christians (nasara)." He combined the two statements, relying on the listener to assign each statement to its own group, and to be safe from confusion, given the known hostility between the two groups and each one's misleading of the other. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]? (p-121)

Hud is the plural of ha'id (one who repents), like ta'idh and ‘uudh. He made the verb kana ("was") singular to agree with the word man ("whoever"), and made the predicate plural to agree with its meaning. ﴿Those are their wishful fancies﴾: by this is indicated the wishful fancies mentioned earlier, namely their wish that no good from their Lord should descend upon the believers, their wish to turn them back into disbelievers, and their wish that no one other than themselves enter Paradise. That is: those false wishes are their wishful fancies. The word umniyyah (wishful fancy) is of the pattern uf‘ūlah, derived from tamanni (wishing), like udhūkah (a laughing-stock).

﴿Say: bring your proof﴾: that is, produce your argument for your exclusive claim to entering Paradise. Hat (bring) has the same meaning as haa (come here), with the sense of "present yourselves." It is connected to their saying, ﴿none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, and ﴿those are their wishful fancies﴾ is a parenthetical clause. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in your claim.

Yes ("بلى") is an affirmation of what they denied, namely that anyone other than themselves would enter the Garden.

"Whoever submits his face to Allah" (﴿مَن أسْلَمَ وجْهَهُ لِلَّهِ﴾): whoever sincerely devotes himself to Him, associating no other with Him.

"and he is a doer of good" (﴿وَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ﴾): one who believes in the Qur'an (مُصَدِّقٌ بِالقُرْآنِ). "Then he will have his reward" (﴿فَلَهُ أجْرُهُ﴾): this is the response (جَوابُ) to "whoever submits" (﴿مَن أسْلَمَ﴾). It is an independent sentence (كَلامٌ مُبْتَدَأٌ) that contains the meaning of a conditional (مُتَضَمِّنٌ لِمَعْنى الشَرْطِ). And "Yes" (﴿بَلى﴾) is a rejection of their statement: "Only those who are Jews or Christians will enter the Garden," and "Whoever is not of their group will not enter it" (﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِ ولا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ is the continuation of that rejection).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 113:

﴿And the Jews say: "The Christians are not based on anything," and the Christians say: "The Jews are not based on anything,"﴾ i.e., on anything that is sound and has any value. The waw in ﴿while they recite the Book﴾ is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and "the Book" is used generically (li-l-jins), meaning: they say this while their condition is that they are people of knowledge and of recitation of the books, and it is the right of one who carries the Torah and the Gospel and believes in it not to disbelieve in what remains, because each of the two Books confirms the other.

﴿Likewise﴾, like that statement you have heard, ﴿said those who have no knowledge, the like of their words﴾, i.e., the ignorant who have neither knowledge nor a Book, such as the idol-worshippers and the deniers (al-mu'attilah), who said to the adherents of every religion: "You are not based on anything." This is a great rebuke to them, since they have placed themselves, despite their knowledge, in the same category as those who have no knowledge.

(p-122) ﴿So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, i.e., between the Jews and the Christians, by apportioning to each party among them the punishment appropriate to it.

The Qur'an, verse 2:114:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein?﴾ The position of "man" (*man*) is nominative as a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and it is interrogative, while "aẓlamu" (more unjust) is its *khabar* (predicate). The meaning is: which person is more unjust? "An yudhkara" (that His name be mentioned) is the second object of *mana'a* (to prevent), because you say *mana'tuhu kadhā* (I prevented him from such-and-such). A similar usage is found in ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs﴾ [al-Isra: 59] and ﴿And nothing prevented people from believing﴾ [al-Isra: 94]. It is also permissible for the preposition to be omitted with *an*, meaning "from *an yudhkara*," and for *an* to be parsed as a *mafʿūl lahu* (object of purpose), meaning: he prevented them out of aversion to His name being mentioned. This is a general ruling applying to the category of the mosques of Allah, and that one who prevents them from the remembrance of Allah is exceedingly unjust. The cause (of its revelation) was the Christians' throwing of filth into Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and their preventing people from praying in it, or the polytheists' preventing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from entering al-Masjid al-Haram in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. The phrase "the mosques of Allah" (plural) was used, although the prohibition concerned one mosque, namely Bayt al-Maqdis or al-Masjid al-Haram, because the ruling was revealed in general terms, even though its cause was specific, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], whereas the one about whom it was revealed was al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. ﴿And strove for their ruin﴾ by cutting off the remembrance (of Allah). The word "man" is intended in a general sense, just as the mosques of Allah are intended in a general sense. ﴿Those﴾ who prevent them ﴿it was not for them to enter them﴾, that is, it was not fitting for them to enter the mosques of Allah ﴿except in fear﴾. "Khā'ifīn" (in fear) is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) referring to the pronoun in "yadkhulūhā" (enter them), meaning: in a state of awe and trembling of the heart, out of fear of the believers striking them, let alone seizing it, taking possession of it, and preventing the believers from it. The meaning is: the truth was only this, were it not for the oppression and insolence of the disbelievers. It was also said: "mā kāna lahum" (it was not for them) refers to the judgment of Allah, meaning that Allah has decreed and recorded in the Preserved Tablet that He will support the believers and strengthen them, so that they will not enter it except in fear.

It is narrated that no Christian would enter Bayt al-Maqdis except in disguise, out of fear of being killed. Qatadah said: No Christian would be found in Bayt al-Maqdis without being severely beaten. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proclaimed: 'Let no polytheist perform the pilgrimage after this year.'" (p-123) It was also said: its meaning is the prohibition of enabling them to enter, and of allowing them free access to it, as in His saying: ﴿And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾: killing and captivity for the combatant (*ḥarbī*), and humiliation through the imposition of the poll-tax (*jizyah*) on the protected non-Muslim (*dhimmī*). ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾, that is, the Fire.

The Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿To Allah belong the east and the west.﴾ That is: the lands of the east and the west, all of them, belong to Him; He is their Owner and their Governor. ﴿Wherever﴾ (fa-ayna, "wherever") is a conditional particle (shart).

﴿you turn﴾ (tuwallū) is in the jussive mood as the object of the conditional, meaning: wherever you perform the turning, that is, the turning of your faces toward the qiblah. This is shown by the words of the Exalted: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144]. The response (jawab) is: ﴿then there is the Face of Allah﴾, that is, His direction, which He commanded and approved. The meaning is: when you are prevented from praying in the Sacred Mosque or in Bayt al-Maqdis, the earth has been made a place of prostration (masjid) for you, so pray in whatever spot of its places you wish and perform the turning there, for turning toward the qiblah is possible in every place. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾: that is, He is vast in mercy, desiring ease for His servants, and He is All-Knowing of their interests. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning the prayer of the traveler on his mount, wherever it turns. It was also said: the qiblah was obscured for a people, so they prayed in various directions, and when morning came they realized their error and were excused. This is a proof against al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning the case where one prays with his back to the qiblah. It was also said: ﴿wherever you turn﴾ is for remembrance (dhikr) and supplication (du'a').

﴿They say: God has taken a son.﴾ He means those who said: "The Messiah is the son of God," and "'Uzayr is the son of God." (قالُوا) is a Shāmī (the reading of the Syrian school of Qur'anic recitation). The affirmation of the *wāw* (و) is in view of its being a story conjoined to what precedes it, and its omission is in view of its being the resumption of a different story.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence (*tanzīh*, declaring Him free of such attributes) above that, and a removing of Him far from it. ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning He is their Creator and Owner, and among them are the Messiah and 'Uzayr, and begetting is incompatible with ownership.

﴿All are obedient to Him﴾: *qānitūn* means submissive, none of them refusing His bringing into being or His decree. The nunation (*tanwīn*) in (كُلٌّ) is a substitute (*'iwaḍ*) for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: all that is in (p-124) the heavens and the earth, or all of those whom they made a son for God. ﴿Obedient to Him﴾ means: obeying, worshipping, acknowledging His lordship, and denying what they attributed to them. The word (ما), which is used for other than rational beings (*ghayr ulī al-'ilm*), is used here together with His saying ﴿obedient﴾, like His saying: ﴿Glory be to what subjected this to us﴾.

﴿Badi'u al-samawati wa-l-ard﴾ (the Originator of the heavens and the earth). That is, He is their inventor and originator, not according to any previous pattern. Anyone who does something that has not been done before is said to have "abda'ta" (you have innovated). For this reason, whoever opposes the Sunnah and the Jama'ah (the Prophetic way and the consensus of the community) is called "mubtadi'" (an innovator), because he introduces into the religion of Islam what the Companions (al-Sahaba) and the Successors (al-Tabi'un) did not do, may God be pleased with them. ﴿Wa-idha qada amran﴾ (And when He decrees a matter): that is, He judges or determines it.

﴿Fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun﴾ (Then He only says to it, "Be," and it is). The word "kun" here is from "kana al-tamma" (the complete form of "to be", meaning "to come into existence" and not requiring a predicate). That is, "ihduth fa-yahduth" (come into being, and it comes into being). This is a metaphor for the speed of bringing into existence and an illustration. There is no actual speech there. The meaning is that whatever He has decreed of affairs and willed to exist comes into being and enters existence without any refusal or hesitation, just as an obedient subordinate who is commanded and carries out the command does not delay, does not refuse, and shows no reluctance. By this, He emphasises the improbability of begetting (offspring), because whoever has this attribute in terms of power has attributes that are different from the attributes of bodies, so how can procreation be imagined there?

The correct reading of "fa-yakunu" is with a "damma" (nominative), which is the reading of the majority of reciters, either as a new sentence (istinaf), meaning "so He is (the one who) brings it into being", or as a conjunction with "yaqulu". Ibn 'Amir read it with a "fatha" (accusative) according to the wording of "kun", because it is a command, and the response to a command introduced by "fa" is in the accusative. We have said that "kun" is not truly a command, since there is no difference between saying "wa-idha qada amran fa-innama yakunuhu fa-yakun" and saying "fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun". If that is so, there is no point in the accusative. This is because, if it were a command, it would either be addressed to something that already exists, and what exists is not addressed with "kun", or to something that does not exist, and what does not exist is not addressed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 118:

﴿And those who do not know said﴾ — from among the polytheists or from among the People of the Book. He denied them knowledge because they did not act upon it. ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾ — why does He not speak to us as He speaks to the angels, and as He spoke to Musa — out of their arrogance and insolence.

﴿Or a sign come to us?﴾ — out of denial, that what came to them should not be among the signs of Allah, and out of contempt for them.

﴿Thus said those before them, the like of their saying. Their hearts are alike.﴾ — that is, the hearts of these people and of those before them are alike in blindness.

﴿We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾ — that is, for a people who are fair-minded and thus become certain that they are signs which must be acknowledged, submitted to, and sufficed by, in place of anything else.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 119:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news﴾ to the believers of reward, ﴿and a warner﴾ to the disbelievers of punishment. ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ That is: We will not ask you about them, [i.e.,] what is the matter with them that they did not believe after you had conveyed [the message] and exerted your utmost effort in calling them [to faith]? The phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal), like "as a bringer of good news" and "as a warner" and "with the truth," meaning: "and not being questioned," or it is a new (resumed) sentence. The reading of Nafi' is (﴿وَلا تَسْأَلْ﴾), in the prohibitive mood. Its meaning is to magnify the punishment into which the disbelievers have fallen, just as you say, "How is so-and-so?" asking about someone who is in a calamity, and it is said to you, "Do not ask about him." It has also been said: God forbade His Prophet from asking about the states of the disbelievers when he said: "Would that I knew what my two parents did?"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 2, verse 120:

﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion.﴾ It is as if they said: "They will never be pleased with you, even if you exert every effort in seeking our approval, until you follow our *millah* (religious community and creed)." This was out of their despair (*iqnat*) regarding the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entering their religion, Islam. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related their statement. ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾ which He has approved for His servants ﴿is the [true] guidance﴾, meaning Islam. It is all of guidance; there is no guidance beyond it. And what you call them to follow is not guidance; it is only desire (*hawa*). Do you not see His saying: ﴿And if you followed their desires﴾, meaning their statements, which are desires and innovations (*bida'*),

﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, meaning: from the knowledge that Allah's religion is Islam, or from the religion whose truth is known (p-١٢٦) through clear proofs and manifest arguments, ﴿you would have from Allah﴾, meaning from the punishment of Allah, ﴿no protector or helper﴾, meaning no supporter (*nasir*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 121:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿We have given them the Book﴾ is its relative clause (silah). They are the believers among the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), and the Book is the Torah and the Gospel; or they are the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Book is the Qur'an.

﴿Who recite it﴾ is a descriptive circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) of "them", because they were not reciting it at the time it was given to them. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar): ﴿with its due recitation﴾, meaning they read it with its proper reading, in measured recitation (tartil), correct articulation of the letters, reflection (tadabbur), and contemplation (tafakkur); or they act upon it and believe in what it contains, and they do not alter what is in it concerning the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Those﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿they believe in it﴾, and this sentence is the predicate of "those to whom". It is also permissible for ﴿who recite it﴾ to be the predicate, and the sentence then serves as another predicate. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾, in that they have exchanged guidance for misguidance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 122:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾ i.e., I bestowed it upon you, ﴿and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ and My preferring you over the worlds of your own time.

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will any ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped﴾. "Hum" (هُمْ) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is "yunsarun" (they will be helped). The four clauses are a qualifier (wasf) of "yawman" (a Day), meaning: fear a Day on which no soul will be recompensed, no ransom will be accepted from it, no intercession will benefit it, and they will not be helped therein. The repetition of these two verses is due to the repeated sins of the Children of Israel, and He concluded the story of the Children of Israel with what He began it with.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 124:

﴿And [remember] when﴾ means: remember when ﴿Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words﴾; He tested him with commands and prohibitions. Testing (ikhtibar) from us is for the manifestation of what we did not know, and from God it is for the manifestation of what is already known. The outcome of testing is the manifestation of the hidden matter in both the witnessed and the unseen realms, and for this reason it is permissible to attribute it to God (p-127) Exalted is He. It has been said: God's testing of His servant is a metaphor for enabling him to test one of two matters, as though He examines him regarding what he does, so that He may recompense him according to that. Abu Hanifa (may God be pleased with him) read: "Ibrahim, his Lord" with the ﻿ibrahim﻿ in the nominative (raf'), and this is also the reading of Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with both of them), meaning: he called upon Him with words of supplication, acting as one who tests, [asking] whether He would answer him in them or not. ﴿So he fulfilled them﴾ means: he performed them with their due right and discharged them in the best manner, without neglect or laxity. A similar expression is: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]. Its meaning in the reading of Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) is: He gave him what he asked, not diminishing anything from it. On this view, the "words" are what Abraham asked his Lord in His saying: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126],

﴿and make us submissive to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128], ﴿and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129],

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 127]. According to the well-known reading, the "words" are five on the head: parting the hair, trimming the moustache, the siwak (tooth-cleaning stick), rinsing the mouth, and sniffing water into the nose. And five on the body: circumcision, clipping the nails, plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, and istinja' (cleansing after relieving oneself). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with both of them) that they are thirty portions of the sacred laws: ten in Bara'ah, ﴿the repentant﴾ verse [al-Tawbah: 112]; ten in al-Ahzab, ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ verse [al-Ahzab: 35]; and ten in al-Mu'minun and al-Ma'arij up to His saying "they guard" [al-Mu'minun: 9 and al-Ma'arij: 34]. It has also been said: they are the rites of Hajj.

﴿He said: Indeed, I will make you a leader (imam) for the people﴾. Imam is the name of one who is followed, i.e., they take you as their model in their religion. ﴿He said: And from my descendants﴾ means: and make from my descendants a leader to be followed. The "dhurriyyah" of a man are his children, males and females alike in this. It is of the form fi'iyyah from dhara' (to create), meaning creation, and the hamzah was changed into a yā'. ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ — with the yā' sukūn, read by Hamzah and Hafs. That is: leadership does not attain to the wrongdoers among your offspring, i.e., the people of disbelief. He informed that leadership of the Muslims does not hold for the people of disbelief, and that among his offspring there are both believers and disbelievers. God Exalted said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac; and among their descendants are the good-doer and the one who wrongs himself clearly﴾ [al-Saffat: 113]. The muhsin (good-doer) is the believer, and the zalim (wrongdoer) is the disbeliever. The Mu'tazilah said: This is evidence that the sinner (fasiq) is not fit for leadership. They said: How is it permissible to appoint a wrongdoer as imam, when the imam exists only to restrain wrongdoers? If one who is a wrongdoer in himself is appointed, then the well-known proverb applies: "Whoever entrusts the wolf with the flock has wronged it." But we say: what is meant by the wrongdoer here is the disbeliever, since he is the absolute wrongdoer. It has been said: he asked that his son be a prophet as he was, and he was informed that a wrongdoer cannot be a prophet.

﴿And when We made the House﴾ — that is, the Ka'bah. It is the name that predominates for it, like "the star" for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). ﴿a place of return for the people﴾ — a resort and a place to which they return. Pilgrims and visitors (al-'ummar) disperse from it, then return to it again. ﴿and a sanctuary﴾ — a place of security, for the wrongdoer (al-jani) takes refuge in it and is not touched until he leaves. This is evidence for us regarding one who seeks refuge in the Haram (the sacred precinct).

﴿And take, from the Station of Abraham, a place of prayer﴾ — and We said: take from it a place of prayer in which you pray. It is narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he took the hand of 'Umar and said: "This is the Station of Abraham." 'Umar said: "Should we not take it as a place of prayer?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have not been commanded with that." Before the sun had set, it was revealed. It has been said: "muṣallā" means a place of supplication (mad'an). The Station of Abraham is the stone upon which is (p-129) the trace of his two feet. It has also been said: the entire Haram is the Station of Abraham.

"Wa-ittakhadhū" (وَاتَّخَذُوا) is read in the past tense by Shami (Ibn 'Amir) and Nafi', coordinated with "ja'alnā" (جَعَلْنا), meaning: and the people took, from the place of Abraham that was marked by him, because of his concern for it and the settling of his descendants beside it, a qiblah toward which they pray.

﴿And We charged Abraham and Ishmael﴾ — We commanded them ﴿that purify My House﴾ — with the vowel on the yā' (يَاء) pronounced with a fatḥah (فَتْحَة), as read by Madani and Hafs. That is: "that you purify," or: "purify!" The meaning: purify it from the idols, the impurities, and all the abominations.

﴿for those who circle it﴾ — those who go around it. ﴿and those who cleave to it﴾ — the residents who remain beside it, who stay and do not depart, or those in seclusion (al-mu'takifin). It has been said: ﴿for those who circle it﴾ means those who travel to it from the lands, ﴿and those who cleave to it﴾ means those who reside there from the people of Makkah, ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾ — those who pray, being the plurals of rāki' (one who bows) and sājid (one who prostrates).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 126:**

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this⟩ — that is, make this land, or this place, ﴿a secure land﴾ — possessing security, like "a pleasing life" (ʿīshatun rāḍiyah), or "secure" in the sense of making secure those who are in it, as when you say: "a sleeping night." So "this" is the first object (maf'ūl awwal), "a land" is the second object (maf'ūl thānī), and "secure" is an attribute (ṣifah) of it. ﴿And provide its people with fruits﴾ — because there were no fruits for them. Then the following was substituted: ﴿those of them who believe in God and the Last Day﴾ from "its people," as a substitution of part for the whole (badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull); that is: "And provide the believers among its people only with fruits," for he analogized provision to leadership (imāmah), so He restricted provision to the believers. ﴿He said﴾ — God, Exalted, answering him: ﴿"And as for him who disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little while"⟩ — that is: "And I will provide for him who disbelieves," ﴿then I will compel him﴾ — I will force him ﴿to the torment of the Fire. And wretched is the destination﴾ — the place of return to which he comes, namely the Fire. The object of the blame is therefore omitted.

(Note: "fa-umatti'uhu" with the verb read by Ibn ʿĀmir in the Syrian reading, as stated in the text.)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 127:

﴿And when Abraham was raising﴾: a narration of a past situation. ﴿The foundations﴾: the plural of qa'idah (foundation), which is the base and root of what is above it. It is a predominantly used adjective, and its meaning is "that which is firm." "Raising the foundations" means building upon them, because when a building is erected on them, they are moved from the state of lowness to the state of height, and they become long after being short.

﴿of the House﴾: the House of Allah, which is the Ka'bah. (p-130) ﴿And Isma'il﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) with Ibrahim. Ibrahim was building, and Isma'il was handing him the stones. ﴿Our Lord﴾: that is, they both say, "Our Lord." This verb is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) made it explicit in his recitation, and its meaning is: they raise it, saying, "Our Lord." ﴿Accept from us﴾: we draw near to You by building this House. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing﴾ of our supplication, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of our inner thoughts and our intentions. And in the indefiniteness of "the foundations" followed by their specification after the indefiniteness, there is an exaltation of the status of what is specified.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 128:

﴿Our Lord, and make us submitting (muslimayn) to You﴾: (meaning) devoting our faces (akhlisayn) to You, derived from His saying: ﴿He submitted his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112]. Or (it means) submitting humbly (mustaslimayn). It is said: aslama lahu, and istaslama, when one yields and submits. The meaning is: increase us in sincerity and in submission to You. ﴿And from our offspring﴾: make from our offspring ﴿a community submitting to You﴾. Min (from) is partitive, or (refers) to the prophets. It has been said that by "community" is meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). They two specifically asked on behalf of their offspring because they are more deserving of compassion, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Guard yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. ﴿And show us our rites﴾: it is transitive from ra'a, in the sense of "saw" or "knew." For this reason it does not exceed two objects, meaning: make us see, or make us know, our acts of worship in the Hajj. The singular of manasik is mansak, with a fatha or kasra on the sin, and it means the place of worship; for this reason the worshipper is called nasik. (Wa-arna) is from Makki, who analogised it to fakhdh in fakhidh (i.e., the vowel pattern of the verb is treated like that of similar forms). Abu 'Amr pronounces the kasra with a slight rounding (ishmam).

﴿And accept our repentance﴾: (forgive) what shortcomings have proceeded from us, or (ask) that they make their offspring repent. ﴿Indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 129:

﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾ among the Muslim community, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾ from among themselves. So God sent Muhammad (ﷺ) among them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, peace and blessings be upon him: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, the glad tidings of Jesus, and the vision of my mother." That is: Aminah saw that a light came out from her that filled Mecca.

﴿He recites to them Your verses﴾ he reads to them and conveys to them what You reveal to him of the proofs of Your oneness (p-131) and the truthfulness of Your prophets and messengers.

﴿And teaches them the Book﴾ the Qur'an,

﴿and the wisdom﴾ the Sunnah (the prophetic practice), and the understanding of the Qur'an,

﴿and purifies them﴾ and cleanses them from polytheism and all other impurities. ﴿Indeed, You are the Mighty﴾ the Victorious, who is not overcome, ﴿the Wise﴾ in what You have bestowed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 130:

﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Ibrahim﴾ is an interrogative used in the sense of denial and rejection, meaning that it is inconceivable that among sensible people there could be anyone who turns away from the clear truth, which is the creed (millah) of Ibrahim. The millah (creed) means the sunnah (way) and the tariqah (path). This is related from al-Zajjaj. ﴿Except one who﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in yarghabu (turns away). The substitution is valid because the phrase man yarghabu is non-affirmative, as in your saying: "Has anyone come to you except Zayd?!" The meaning is: "None turns away from the creed of Ibrahim except one who ﴿has made a fool of himself﴾," that is, who was ignorant of himself, meaning he did not reflect upon himself. So safiha ("to be foolish") is placed in the position of jahila ("to be ignorant") and is construed with the same complement as it. Or its meaning is: "he was foolish regarding himself," so fi ("in") has been omitted, just as min ("from") is omitted in His saying: ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], meaning "from his people," and 'ala ("upon") in His saying: ﴿And do not determine the tie of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235], meaning "upon the tie of marriage." Both possibilities are related from al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification), but this is weak because it is definite. ﴿And We certainly chose him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ is a clarification of the error of the opinion of one who turns away from his creed, because whoever combined the honour of both abodes, no one is more worthy of desiring his way than he.

﴿When﴾ is an adverb of time (ẓarf, "adverb of time") governed by ﴿We chose him﴾, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said: "Remember that time, so that you know that he was the chosen, righteous one, from whose religion (millah) none turns away, [the religion] of one like him."

﴿His Lord said to him: "Submit"﴾: that is, humble yourself (adhʿin), or obey (aṭiʿ), or devote your religion to God (akhliṣ dīnaka lillāh). ﴿He said: "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾: that is, "I have devoted myself," or "I have yielded."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 132:

﴿And enjoined﴾ (wa-awsā) is the reading of Madani and Shami (readers).

﴿Therewith﴾: with the millah (religious community/creed), or with the kalimah (word/declaration), which is ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. ﴿Ibrahim enjoined upon his sons, and Ya'qub (as well)﴾: the latter is conjoined to Ibrahim and falls under his ruling, and the meaning is: Ya'qub also enjoined therewith upon his sons, ﴿O my sons﴾ (p-132), with the verb of saying implied, ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾, i.e., He has given you the religion which is the choicest of religions, and it is the religion of Islam, and He has enabled you to adopt it.

﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾: so let your death not occur except in a state in which you are steadfast upon Islam. The prohibition is, in reality, against being in a condition other than the state of Islam when they die, like your saying: "Do not pray except while you are humbly attentive (khashi'), " where you are not forbidding him from prayer, but rather from abandoning humble attentiveness in his prayer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 133:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub (Jacob)?﴾ "Am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the meaning of the interrogative hamzah in it is denial (inkar). "Shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of "shahid," in the sense of "hadir" (present), i.e., you were not present with Ya'qub, peace be upon him, when death came to him, meaning when he was at the point of death. The address is to the believers, in the sense: you did not witness that, and knowledge of it reached you only through revelation. Or it is conjunctive (muttasilah), and something omitted is presumed before it, and the address is to the Jews, because they used to say: No prophet died except upon Judaism. It is as if it were said: Do you attribute Judaism to the prophets? Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?! ﴿When he said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first "idh," and the governing element in both is "shuhada'," or it is an adverbial phrase of time (zarf) governed by "hadara" (approached).

﴿To his sons: What will you worship after me?﴾ "Ma" is an interrogative in the accusative position governed by "ta'budun" (you worship), meaning: what thing do you worship? "Ma" is general to everything, or it is a question about the attribute of the worshipped, as you say: "Ma Zayd turid, afaqihun am tabib?" (What is Zayd, do you mean a jurist or a physician?). ﴿After me﴾ means after my death. ﴿They said: We worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾ the mention of "God" is repeated so that it is not conjoined to the pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition. ﴿Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾ is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to "your fathers." Isma'il is counted among his fathers, though he was his paternal uncle, because the paternal uncle is a father. Peace be upon him said concerning al-Abbas: "This is the remainder of my fathers." ﴿One God﴾ is a substitute for "the God of your fathers," like His saying: ﴿By the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 15-16]; or it is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), meaning: we intend by the God of your fathers one God.

﴿And to Him we are submitting﴾ (p-133) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "na'budu," or a clause conjoined to "na'budu," or a parenthetical emphatic clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah mu'akkidah).

"That" is a reference to the community mentioned, namely Abraham, Jacob and their offspring, the monotheists. "A community that has passed away," meaning it has gone. "For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned." That is: no one benefits from the earning of another, whether earlier or later. Just as those people benefit only from what they themselves earned, so too you benefit only from what you yourselves earn. This is said because of their boasting in their forefathers. "And you will not be questioned about what they used to do," meaning you will not be held accountable for their misdeeds.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 135:

﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, [and] you will be guided."﴾ That is: the Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." ﴿You will be guided﴾ is in the jussive (jazm) because it is the answer (jawab) to the imperative.

﴿Say: "Rather, [we follow] the religion (millah) of Ibrahim"﴾: rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim. ﴿Hanifan﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the genitive noun that is annexed (al-mudaf ilayhi), as in your saying: "I saw the face of Hind standing." The hanif (ḥanīf, one who turns away from every false religion toward the religion of truth) is the one who inclines away from every false religion toward the religion of truth.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists (mushrikin)﴾: this is an indirect allusion (ta'ridh) to the People of the Book and others, because each of them claims to follow the religion of Ibrahim, while they are upon polytheism.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 136:

﴿Say﴾ This is an address to the believers, or to the disbelievers; meaning: say it so that you may be upon the truth, otherwise you are upon falsehood.

﴿We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾ i.e., the Qur'an.

﴿and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes (al-asbat)﴾ The sibt (sibt, "grandson") is the descendant (al-hafid, "grandson/grandchild"). Al-Hasan and al-Husayn were the two grandsons (sibtayn) of the Messenger of God ﷺ. And al-asbat are the descendants (hafadah) of Jacob, the offspring of his twelve sons. The verb anzala ("sent down") is construed with ilā and with ʿalā; therefore it occurs here with ilā, and in Āl ʿImrān with ʿalā.

﴿and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ i.e., we do not believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. And "aḥad" ("any one") carries the sense of a group (jamāʿa), which is why "bayn" ("between") is permitted to govern it.

﴿and to Him we are submitting (muslimūn)﴾ sincerely devoted to God.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 137:

﴿فَإنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ ما آمَنتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾ ("If they believe in the like of what you believe in, then they have been guided.") The apparent meaning of the verse is problematic, because it implies that God has a like (*mithl*), and He is exalted above that. It has therefore been said: the *bāʾ* (الباء, "in") is extra (*zāʾidah*), "like" (مِثْل) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and its implied sense is: "If they believe a belief like your belief," and the pronoun in *bihi* refers to God, exalted and majestic. The addition of the *bāʾ* is not uncommon; God, exalted, says: ﴿Those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like﴾ [Yunus: 27], and the implied sense is: "the recompense of an evil deed is one like it," as in His words in another verse: ﴿And the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

It has also been said: "like" (*mithl*) is an addition (*ziyādah*), meaning: "If they believe in what you believe in." This is supported by the recitation (*qirāʾah*, a variant reading of the Qur'an) of Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: (*bi-mā āmantum bihi*), and *mā* (ما) here means *alladhī* (الَّذِي, "that which"), as evidenced by the recitation of Ubayy: (*bi-alladhī āmantum bihi*).

It has also been said: the *bāʾ* (الباء) is for instrumentality (*al-istiʿānah*), as in your saying: "I wrote with the pen," meaning: "If they enter into faith with a testimony like your testimony by which you believe," ﴿but if they turn away﴾ from what you say to them, and do not act justly; or, "if they turn away from the testimony and from entering into faith by it" ﴿then they are only in opposition﴾, meaning: they are only in dissension and enmity, and they are not seeking the truth in anything. ﴿So God will suffice you against them﴾: this is a guarantee from God that He will make His Messenger prevail over them. He has indeed fulfilled His promise, by killing some of them and expelling some. The meaning of the *sīn* (السين, "so" / future marker) is that this is certain to happen, though it may be delayed for a time. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of what they utter, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of what they conceal of envy and rancor, and He will requite them for it; so this is a warning to them. Or it is a promise to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning: He hears what you invoke with, He knows your intention and what you desire of making the religion of truth manifest, He responds to you, and He brings you to your aim.

ṣibghat Allāh (the dye of God): the religion of God. It is a emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu’akkid) in the accusative, governed by His saying: ﴿We believe in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. It is of the form fi‘lah from ṣabagha, like jilsah from jalasa, and denotes the state in which dyeing takes place. The meaning is: the purification of God, because faith purifies souls. The background is that the Christians used to immerse their children in yellow water, which they called the ma‘mudiyyah (baptism), and they would say: it is a purification for them. When one of them did this to his child, he would say: Now he has truly become a Christian. So the Muslims were commanded to say to them: We believe in God, and God has dyed us (ṣabaghanā Allāh) with His dye, the faith, and we have not been dyed with your dye. The word ṣibghah was used for the sake of mushākalah (correspondence of wording), like your saying to one who plants trees: Plant as so-and-so plants, meaning: a man who cultivates vineyards.

﴿And who is better than God in dye?﴾ This is a tamyīz (specification): that is, there is no dye better than His dye. He means: the religion, or the purification.

﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "āmannā bi-Llāh" (we believe in God). This conjunction indicates that His saying ﴿the dye of God﴾ falls within the object of ﴿Say: We believe﴾, that is: say this and this,

﴿and we are worshippers of Him﴾. It also refutes the view of those who claimed that ṣibghat Allāh is a substitute (badal) for "millat Ibrāhīm" (the religion of Abraham), or an accusative by way of incitement (ighrā’) meaning "upon you is the dye of God", because this involves breaking up the structure and removing the speech from its coherence. Its being in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun is what Sībawayh mentioned, and "the saying is what Ḥadhām said".

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 139:

﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning Allah﴾, that is: Do you argue with us about the affair of Allah, and about His choosing the Prophet from among the Arabs rather than you? And you say: "If Allah had sent down [revelation] upon anyone, He would have sent it down upon us"? And you consider yourselves more deserving of prophethood than us? ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: we all share in being His servants, He is our Lord and your Lord, and He bestows His mercy and honour upon whomever He wills of His servants. ﴿And for us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾: meaning that deeds are the foundation of the matter, and just as you have deeds, so we have deeds likewise.

﴿And we are sincerely devoted to Him﴾: that is, we are monotheists of Him, we make Him sincerely ours through faith, while you associate others with Him. The one who is sincere (mukhlis) is more worthy of honour and more deserving of prophethood than anyone else.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 140:

﴿Or do you say﴾ With the ta' (taqulūna, "you say"): Shami and Kufi readers, except Abu Bakr. In this reading, "am" (or) is an equivalent to the hamza in "Do you dispute with us" (atuhājjūnanā), meaning: which of the two matters do you undertake, disputing about the judgment of God, or claiming Jewishness and Christianity for the prophets? Or it is disconnected (munqati'a), i.e. "Rather, do you say?" The others read it with the ya' (yaqūlūna, "they say"). According to this reading, the hamza can only be disconnected.

﴿Indeed Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians﴾ Then He commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say, asking a question and refuting them with His words: ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾ meaning: God testified for them to the religion of Islam in His words: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a upright monotheist (hanif), a Muslim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ That is: he concealed God's testimony which he possesses, that He bore witness to it, and it is God's testimony to Abraham's hanifiyya (upright monotheism). The meaning: there is no one more unjust than the People of the Book, because they concealed this testimony while knowing it; or, if we concealed this testimony, no one would be more unjust than us, so we will not conceal it. Within this there is an allusion to their concealing God's testimony to Muhammad ﷺ regarding prophethood in their books and his other testimonies. The "min" (from) in His words ﴿from God﴾ is like it in your saying: "This is a testimony from me for so-and-so," when you testify on his behalf, in that it is a description of it.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ of denying the Messengers and concealing the testimony.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 141:

﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earned. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ It is repeated for emphasis (ta'kid), or because what is meant by the first is the Prophets, peace be upon them, and what is meant by the second is the forefathers of the Jews and the Christians.

The foolish among the people will say: ﴿What has turned them away from their qibla, which they used to face?﴾ The foolish (al-sufaha') are the light-minded, for the root meaning of safah (folly) is lightness. They are the Jews, because they disliked turning toward the Kaaba and because they did not accept abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another). Or they are the hypocrites, because of their eagerness to slander and mock. Or they are the polytheists, because of their saying: "He has turned away from the qibla of his fathers, and then returned to it; by God, he will return to their religion."

The benefit of reporting their statement before it occurs is to prepare the soul, since being taken by surprise by something disliked is harder to bear, and preparing a reply before it is needed is more decisive against the opponent. It is said: "The archer sharpens his arrow [before the shot]."

﴿Say: Unto God belong the East and the West.﴾ That is, the lands of the East and the West, and the whole earth, belong to Him.

﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ of its people ﴿to a straight path﴾, a level road. That is, He guides whom He wills to the qibla of truth, which is the Kaaba, the one He commanded us to face (p-137). Or, all places belong to God, so He commands facing wherever He wills: at times toward the Kaaba, and at other times toward Bayt al-Maqdis. There is no objection to Him, because He alone is the Owner.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 143:**

﴿And thus We made you﴾: Like that wondrous making, We made you. The *kaf* (ك) is for comparison (*tashbih*). *Dhā* (ذا) is in the genitive case after the *kaf*. The *lam* (ل) is to distinguish between pointing to what is near and pointing to what is far. The *kaf* (ك) is for address and has no place in terms of *i'rab* (grammatical case-inflection).

﴿A community of the middle﴾: best (*khiyaran*). It is said that the best is called *wasat* (middle) because the extremities are quickly subject to defect, whereas the middles are protected. That is, just as We made your *qiblah* the best of *qiblahs*, We made you the best of nations. The reason for the making is: so that you may know, through reflection on the proofs set up for you and the Book sent down to you, that He, exalted is He, has never been stingy toward anyone nor been unjust. Rather, He made the ways clear and sent the messengers, who conveyed and gave sincere counsel. But those who disbelieved were driven by wretchedness to follow their desires and to turn away from the signs. Thus you will bear witness to this against your contemporaries and against those before you and after you.

Or [*wasat* means] *just* (*'udulan*), because the middle is a balance between the extremes, not closer to one of them than to the other. That is: just as We made your *qiblah* intermediate between the east and the west, We made you a middle community between excess and deficiency. For you did not commit the excess of the Christians, who ascribed divinity to the Messiah, nor did you commit the deficiency of the Jews, who accused Mary of fornication and described Jesus as a child of fornication.

﴿That you may be witnesses﴾: *shuhada'* is not declined (*ghayr munsarif*) because of the feminine *alif* (ألف التأنيث) in it. ﴿over the people﴾: the complement (*silah*) of *shuhada'*. ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) upon ﴿that you may be﴾. It is narrated that on the Day of Resurrection the nations will deny that the prophets conveyed the message. God will then demand of the prophets proof that they conveyed it—and He knows best—so the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and will bear witness. The nations will say: "How do you know?" They will say: "We know it through God's report in His Book, which speaks through the tongue of His truthful Prophet." Then Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the condition of his community, and he will vouch for them and testify to their uprightness.

Testimony may be without direct observation, as in testimony by hearsay concerning well-known matters. Since the witness is like a watcher (*raqib*), the preposition denoting elevation (*isti'la'*) was used, as in His saying: ﴿You were the watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117].

It is said: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ in this world, regarding matters that are not valid except by the testimony of upright, good people (p-138), ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾: he will vouch for you and will know of your uprightness.

Shaykh Abu Mansur, may God have mercy on him, used this verse to argue that *ijma'* (scholarly consensus) is a proof, because God described this community as upright (*'adl*), and the upright one is the one who deserves to give testimony and whose testimony is accepted. So when they agree upon something and testify to it, it becomes obligatory to accept it.

The complement of the testimony was placed later at the beginning and moved forward at the end, because what is intended at the first is establishing their testimony over the nations, and at the end, their being singled out by the Messenger being a witness over them.

﴿And We did not make the qiblah that you were upon﴾: that is, ﴿And We did not make the qiblah﴾, the direction, ﴿that you were upon﴾, which is the Ka'bah. So *allati kunta 'alayha* (the one you were upon) is not an adjective of *qiblah*; rather it is the second object of *ja'ala* (made).

It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to pray in Mecca toward the Ka'bah, then after the Hijrah he was commanded to pray toward the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), to win over the Jews, and then he was turned back to the Ka'bah. [In this there is evidence for the permissibility of abrogating the *sunnah* by the Qur'an, contrary to what al-Shafi'i says, because facing Bayt al-Maqdis was established by a non-recited revelation (*wahy ghayr matluww*), and it was abrogated by the Qur'an.]

﴿Except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾: that is, ﴿And We did not make the qiblah﴾ which you love to face, the direction ﴿that you were upon﴾ initially in Mecca, except as a trial for people and a test, so that We might know the one who is steadfast in Islam and truthful in it from the one who is on the edge, who turns back ﴿on his heels﴾, out of his restlessness, returning and apostatizing from Islam when the *qiblah* is changed.

Shaykh Abu Mansur, may God have mercy on him, said: The meaning of His saying ﴿that We might know﴾ is: that We might know, as existing or as already present, what We had already known would occur and come into existence. God, exalted is He, has known from eternity everything He willed to exist, that it would exist at the time He willed its existence. He is not described as knowing from eternity that a thing is existent and present, because it did not exist in eternity, so how could He know it as existent? When it becomes existent, it enters under His eternal knowledge, and so it becomes known to Him as existent and present. The change is in the known, not in the knowledge.

Or it is to distinguish the follower from the one who recoils, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾ [al-Anfal: 37]. So knowledge was placed in the position of distinguishing, because distinction occurs through knowledge of it. Or it means that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers would know. The attribution of their knowledge to Himself is because they are His elite (*khawass*). Or it is a manner of gentle address to one who does not know, like your saying to someone who denies that gold melts: "Let us throw it into the fire, that we may know whether it melts?"

﴿And indeed it was [the change] a great matter﴾: that is, the change, or the making, or the *qiblah*. *In* here is the lightened form (*mukhaffafah*) of *inna*. ﴿a great matter﴾: that is, heavy and burdensome. It is the predicate of *kana* (was), and the *lam* is the distinguishing *lam* (*lam al-farqa*).

﴿Except upon those whom God guided﴾: that is, those whom God guided. The returning pronoun has been omitted, that is: except upon those steadfast and truthful in following the Messenger. ﴿And God would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾: that is, your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. He called prayer *iman* (faith), because its obligation is upon the people of faith, its acceptance is from the people of faith, and its performance in congregation is a sign of faith. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned toward the Ka'bah, they said: "What about those of our brothers who died before the change?" So this was revealed. Then He gave the reason for that, saying: ﴿Indeed God is, toward the people, Most Kind﴾: it is hamzated and prolonged (*mahmuz mushbi'*), in the Hijazi and Syrian readings, and in that of Hafs (*ra'uf*); the others read it as *Ra'uf* on the pattern of *fa'ul*. Both are for intensification (*mubalagha*).

﴿Merciful﴾: He does not waste their rewards. *Ra'fah* (tenderness) is stronger than *rahmah* (mercy), and He combined both, as in ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Fatihah: 3].

﴿قَدْ نَرى تَقَلُّبَ وجْهِكَ في السَماءِ﴾ [We see the turning of your face toward the sky.] That is, the restlessness of your face and the shifting of your gaze toward the direction of the sky. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to hope from his Lord that He would turn him toward the Ka'bah, in agreement with Ibrahim (Abraham), in opposition to the Jews, and because it would more effectively draw the Arabs to faith, since it was their source of pride, their place of visitation, and their place of circumambulation.

﴿فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ﴾ [So We will surely turn you] means: We will surely give you, and We will surely enable you to face it, from your saying "wallaytu-hu kadhā" (I made him take such-and-such a direction), when you make him face it, with the ya' (ي) being for him (i.e., the object). Or it means: We will surely make you face its direction, rather than the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House in Jerusalem).

﴿قِبْلَةً تَرْضاها﴾ [a qiblah (direction of prayer) that you will be pleased with] means: that you love and incline toward, for your sound purposes which you harbored, and which accorded with God's will and His wisdom.

﴿فَوَلِّ وجْهَكَ شَطْرَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ [So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque], that is: toward it. The word "shatra" (شَطْرَ) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), meaning: make the turning of the face be in the direction of the Mosque, that is, in its direction and its facing, because facing the exact point of the qiblah is difficult for one who is far away. The mention of "al-Masjid al-Haram" (the Sacred Mosque) rather than the Ka'bah is evidence that what is obligatory is observing the direction, not the exact spot. It is narrated that "he (ﷺ) came to Medina and prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months, then he was turned toward the Ka'bah."

﴿وَحَيْثُ ما كُنْتُمْ﴾ [And wherever you are] from the earth, and you intend the prayer, ﴿فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكم شَطْرَهُ﴾ [turn your faces toward it]. ﴿وإنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ لَيَعْلَمُونَ أنَّهُ الحَقُّ﴾ [And indeed those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth], that is: the turning toward the Ka'bah is the truth, because it was in the good tidings of their prophets concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he would pray toward the two qiblahs.

﴿مِن رَبِّهِمْ وما اللهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا يَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [from their Lord. And God is not unaware of what they do]. With the ya' (يَعْمَلُونَ, "they do" in the masculine third person, i.e., "عَمّا يَعْمَلُونَ" with ي), it is the recitation of Makki, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', and 'Asim; with the ta' (تَعْمَلُونَ, second person), it is the recitation of the others. The first is a warning to the disbelievers of punishment for their denial and refusal, and the second is a promise to the believers of reward for their acceptance and compliance.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 145:**

﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Scripture every sign﴾: he means their stubborn ones (*dhawi al-'inad*), ﴿every sign﴾, a conclusive proof that facing the Ka'ba is the truth, ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾. Their refusal to follow you is not due to a doubt (*shubha*) that you could remove by presenting an argument. It is rather due to wilful obstinacy (*mukabara*) and stubbornness ('*inad*), even though they know, from what is in their books, the description of you that you are upon the truth. The answer to the omitted oath has taken the place of the answer to the conditional clause.

﴿And you are not a follower of their qibla﴾: this is a cutting off of their hopes, since they had been in turmoil about this matter and said: "If he remained upon our qibla, we would hope that he is the one we are awaiting," and they hoped for his return to their qibla. The qibla is mentioned in the singular, although they have two qiblas, the Jews having a qibla and the Christians a qibla, because they are united in falsehood.

﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾: meaning, despite their agreement in opposing you, they disagree concerning the matter of the qibla, and their agreement is not to be hoped for, just as their agreement with you is not to be hoped for. The Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians face the rising of the sun.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: that is, after the clarity of the proof and the full awareness that the qibla is the Ka'ba and that the religion of Allah is (p-141) Islam. ﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾: among those who commit gross wrongdoing. In this there is gentleness toward the listeners, an incitement to steadfastness upon the truth, and a warning to whoever abandons the evidence after it has been made clear and follows his desire. It has been said: the address is outwardly to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is his community. The pause on ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ is obligatory (*lazima al-waqf*), for if it were connected, it would become [a different meaning].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 146:

﴿The ones to whom We gave the Book﴾ is a description (ṣifah) of "the wrongdoers" (al-ẓālimīn), and it is the subject (mubtada'), while the predicate (khabar) is ﴿they recognize it﴾, that is: Muhammad (ﷺ); or the Qur'an; or the change of the qiblah. The first is the most apparent, due to His saying: ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾. ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: "I know him better than I know my own son." ʿUmar said to him: "And why?" He said: "Because I do not doubt that Muhammad is a Prophet, whereas as for my son, perhaps his mother betrayed her husband." So ʿUmar kissed his head. ﴿And indeed a party of them﴾, that is: those who did not embrace Islam.

﴿Surely they conceal the truth﴾ out of envy and obstinacy, ﴿while they know﴾ that Allah the Exalted has made it clear in their Book.

The Truth (al-Haqq) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is: "from your Lord." The lam in "al-Haqq" is for genus (lam al-jins), meaning: the truth is from God and not from anyone else. That is, what is established as coming from God is the truth, like what you (ﷺ) are upon; and what is not established as coming from God, like what the People of the Book hold, is falsehood (al-batil). Alternatively, the lam is for a specific reference (lam al-'ahd), pointing to the truth upon which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stands. Or it is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: "It is the truth," and "from your Lord" is a second predicate after the first, or a circumstantial clause (hal). "So do not be among those who doubt" (al-mumtarin), the ones who are uncertain that it is from your Lord.

﴿And for each﴾ of the followers of the different religions ﴿there is a direction﴾, a qibla (direction of prayer). It is also read as ﴿wijhatun﴾ with the vowel changed. ﴿He﴾: the pronoun refers to ﴿each﴾. ﴿Who turns toward it﴾: the pronoun refers to the direction, meaning that He turns it toward them as a direction. One of the two objects of the verb has been omitted. Alternatively, ﴿He﴾ refers to God, meaning God turns them toward it. ﴿Mawlaha﴾ (with the vowel on the lam changed to a fatha, "the one who turns it") is the reading of Shami (the Syrian reader), meaning: He is the master of that direction, who has taken charge of it. The meaning is: for every community there is a direction toward which it turns, both you and others. ﴿So race﴾ you, ﴿to the good deeds﴾, so race ahead of others to them in the matter of the qibla and other matters (p-142). ﴿Wherever you are﴾, you and your enemies, ﴿God will bring you all together﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and He will separate the one who is right from the one who is wrong.
