Or: ﴿for each of you﴾, O community of Muhammad, ﴿there is a direction﴾, a direction toward which you pray, whether southward, northward, eastward, or westward. So face the most excellent of the directions, which is the one directly facing the Ka'ba, even if they differ. ﴿Wherever you are﴾ from the different directions, ﴿God will bring you all together﴾ and gather you, and will make your prayer as though it were toward a single direction, and as though you were praying in the presence of the Sacred Mosque. ﴿Indeed God is over all things Powerful﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾ from whatever land you leave on a journey, ﴿turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ when you pray. ﴿And indeed it﴾, and indeed this commanded matter, ﴿is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. With the ya' (yā'), Abu 'Amr [reads ya'malūna, "they do"].

And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. This repetition serves to emphasize and reinforce the matter of the qibla, because abrogation (naskh) is one of the places where doubt and confusion arise. So He repeated it to them so that they would be firm. Moreover, each of the two statements was tied to something that the other was not tied to, so their benefits differed. ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning: God, exalted is His mention, has already informed you of how to answer the objection about the qibla by what He stated in His words: ﴿For every one there is a direction toward which he turns﴾. ﴿So that people will have no argument﴾, that is, the Jews, ﴿against you﴾, regarding the contradiction with what is in the Torah concerning the change of the qibla. He applied the term "argument" to the words of the obstinate, because they present them in the manner of an argument. ﴿Except those who have wronged among them﴾ is an exception from "people", meaning: so that no one among the Jews will have an argument, except the obstinate among them, who say: "He did not abandon our qibla for the Ka'bah except out of inclination toward the religion of his people and love for his land, and if he were upon the truth he would have adhered to the qibla of the prophets, peace be upon them." Or its meaning is: so that the Arabs will have no argument or objection against you for abandoning the turning toward the Ka'bah, which is the qibla of Ibrahim and Isma'il, the fathers of the Arabs. ﴿Except those who have wronged among them﴾, namely the people of Makkah, when they say: "It has become apparent to him, so he has returned to the qibla of his fathers, and he is about to return to their religion." (p-143) Then he resumed, alerting with His words: ﴿So do not fear them﴾, that is, do not fear their disparagement of your qibla, for they will not harm you. ﴿But fear Me﴾, so do not oppose My command. ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, that is, it informed you so that there would be no argument against you, and so that I may complete My favor upon you by My guiding you to the Ka'bah. ﴿And that you may be guided﴾, and so that you may be guided to the qibla of Ibrahim.

The kaf in ﴿كَما أرْسَلْنا فِيكُمْ﴾ ("as We sent among you") may be connected to what precedes it, meaning: "and that I may complete My favour upon you in the Hereafter through reward, just as I completed it upon you in this world by sending a Messenger." Or it may be connected to what follows it, meaning: "just as I mentioned you by sending a Messenger, so remember Me through obedience and I will remember you through reward." According to this second view, one stops at ﴿تَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("you may be guided"), whereas according to the first view one does not stop there.

﴿رَسُولا مِنكُمْ﴾ ("a Messenger from among you") — from among the Arabs — ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("who recites to you") — reads to you — ﴿آياتِنا﴾ ("Our verses") — the Qur'an,

﴿وَيُزَكِّيكم ويُعَلِّمُكُمُ الكِتابَ﴾ ("and purifies you and teaches you the Book") — the Qur'an — ﴿والحِكْمَةَ﴾ ("and the Wisdom") — the Sunnah and the fiqh (jurisprudence) — ﴿وَيُعَلِّمُكم ما لَمْ تَكُونُوا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("and teaches you what you did not know") — that which there is no way to know except through revelation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 152:

﴿So remember Me﴾ with the excuse (al-ma'dhira), ﴿I will remember you﴾ with forgiveness (al-maghfira), or with praise (al-thana') and giving (al-'ata'), or with asking (al-su'al) and bestowal (al-nawal), or with repentance (al-tawba) and the pardoning of sin ('afw al-hawba), or with sincerity (al-ikhlas) and deliverance (al-khalas), or with intimate conversation (al-munajat) or salvation (al-najat).

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ for the favours I have bestowed upon you, ﴿and do not deny Me﴾, that is, do not reject My blessings.

O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.

Patience (ṣabr): by it every virtue is attained. And prayer (ṣalāh): for it forbids every vice. Indeed, Allah is with the patient: with help and support.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 154:

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah﴾ It was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen men. ﴿They are dead﴾ i.e., they are dead,

﴿Rather, they are alive﴾ i.e., they are alive. ﴿But you do not perceive﴾ i.e., you do not know that, because the life of the martyr is not known through the senses. From al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him): The martyrs are alive with Allah; their provisions are presented to their spirits, so joy and delight reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the spirits of the family of Pharaoh morning and evening, so pain reaches them. From Mujahid: they are provided with fruit of Paradise, and they find its fragrance, though they are not in it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 155:**

﴿And We will surely test you﴾: "And We will surely afflict you with that, an affliction resembling the action of one who tests your conditions, (to see) whether you will be patient in the obedience in which you are, or not?" ﴿with something﴾: "with a little of each one of these trials and a portion of it." He used the diminutive so that it would be known that every affliction that befalls a person, however great, has above it what is less than it, and so that He would show them that His mercy is with them in every state. He informed them of the occurrence of the trial before it occurred, so that they would prepare their souls for it,

﴿of fear﴾: fear of the enemy or of Allah; ﴿and hunger﴾: that is, famine, or the fasting of the month of Ramadan; ﴿and loss of wealth﴾: by the death of livestock, or by zakat. It is a conjunction with "something," or with "fear," meaning: "and a portion of the loss of wealth."

﴿and lives﴾: by killing and death, or by sickness and grey hair; ﴿and fruits﴾: the fruits of the crops, or the death of children, because the child is the fruit of the heart. ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾: those who are patient through these trials, or "those who say 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' (To Allah we belong and to Him we shall return) at the time of trials," because the saying of "inna lillahi" is submission and acceptance. In a hadith: "Whoever says 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un' at the time of calamity, Allah will recompense his calamity, grant him a better outcome, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with." And the lamp of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out, and he said: "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un." It was asked: "Is it a calamity?" He said: "Yes, everything that harms the believer is a calamity." The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone from whom good tidings may come.

﴿Alladhina﴾ (those who) is in the accusative (naṣb) as a qualifier (ṣifah) of ﴿al-ṣabirin﴾ (the patient). There is no pause (waqf) on it. Rather, one pauses on ﴿raji'un﴾ (returning). Whoever begins with ﴿alladhina﴾ and makes the predicate (khabar) ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (those), pauses on ﴿al-ṣabirin﴾, not on ﴿raji'un﴾. The first view is preferred, because ﴿alladhina﴾ and what follows it are an explanation (bayān) of ﴿al-sabr﴾ (patience).

﴿When a calamity befalls them﴾: "makrūh" (disliked) is an active participle from "aṣābathu shiddah," meaning it reached him (laḥiqathu). There is no pause on "muṣībah" (calamity), because ﴿they say﴾ is the response (jawāb) of ﴿idhā﴾ (when), and ﴿idhā﴾ with its response is the relative clause (ṣilah) of ﴿alladhina﴾. ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah﴾ is an acknowledgment of His dominion (mulk), and ﴿indeed to Him we return﴾ is an acknowledgment against ourselves of destruction (halak).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 157:

﴿Those are the ones upon whom there are blessings (ṣalawāt) from their Lord, and mercy﴾. Ṣalāh (prayer, in the sense of compassion and tenderness; the root meaning is ḥunū, inclination, and taʿaṭṭuf, kindly solicitude) is placed in the position of raʾfah (tenderness), and the two are combined with mercy, as in His saying: ﴿tenderness and mercy﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 27], and ﴿Compassionate, Merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117]. The meaning is: upon them is tenderness after tenderness, and mercy after mercy. ﴿And those are the ones who are guided﴾ to the path of what is right, since they said "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return" and submitted to the command of Allah. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "What an excellent pair, and what an excellent addition", that is: the ṣalawāt and the mercy, and the guidance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 158:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾ are two landmarks for the two hills,

﴿are among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah﴾: among the markers of His rites (manasik) and acts of worship (mutaʿabbadat). It is the plural of sha'ira (sing.), which means a sign.

﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House﴾ intends the Ka'bah.

﴿or performs the 'umrah﴾ visits the Ka'bah. Thus hajj (ḥajj, lit. intention) means intending, and i'timar (ʿumrah, lit. visiting) means visiting; then both came to be applied specifically to intending and visiting the House for the two well-known rites. In meaning they are like the star and the house in terms of concrete entities.

﴿there is no blame upon him﴾, i.e., no sin upon him ﴿in going around between them﴾, i.e., yataṭawwaf (he goes around), where the tā' is assimilated into the ṭā' (fa-adgham al-tā' fī al-ṭā'). The root meaning of ṭawf is walking around something, and what is meant here is the sa'y (running/walking back and forth) between them. It is said that on al-Safa there was an idol called Isaf and on al-Marwah one called Na'ilah, and they were two idols. It is narrated that they were a man and a woman who committed fornication inside the Ka'bah, so they were transformed into two stones, which were placed upon the two hills as a lesson. When a long time passed, they were worshipped besides Allah. The people of the Jahiliyyah, whenever they performed sa'y, would touch them. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked going around between them because of the practice of the Jahiliyyah, so He lifted the blame from them by His saying: ﴿there is no blame﴾. This is evidence that it is not a pillar (rukn) of Hajj, as Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah Most High have mercy on them both, said.

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, i.e., by going around between them. This too indicates that it is not a pillar. (Wa-man yaṭṭawwaʿ), Hamzah and ʿAli (read it), i.e., yatatawwaʿ, where the tā' is assimilated into the ṭā'.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Grateful, All-Knowing﴾: He rewards the little with much, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of things, whether small or great.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ what We sent down, from among the *ahbar* (rabbis) of the Jews, ﴿of the clear proofs﴾, meaning the signs bearing witness to the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and the guidance﴾, meaning the guidance to Islam through his (ﷺ) attributes, ﴿after We made it clear﴾, meaning We explained it, ﴿for the people in the Book﴾, meaning in the Tawrah (Torah), where We left no point of ambiguity, yet they deliberately went to that clear statement and concealed it.

﴿Those are cursed by Allah, and cursed by those who curse﴾, those who are able to curse, namely the angels and the believers from both the two weighty ones (*thaqalan*, i.e. humans and jinn).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 160:

﴿Except those who repent﴾ from concealing (the truth) and abandoning faith, ﴿and make amends﴾ for what they had corrupted of their conditions, and make up for what they had neglected of their duties,

﴿and make clear﴾ and manifest what they had concealed,

﴿Then I shall accept their repentance﴾, that is, I shall accept their repentance,

﴿For I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 161:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ means: those who died from among these concealers (al-kātimīn) and did not repent. ﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of the people, all together.﴾ He mentioned their being cursed while they were alive, then He cursed them after they had died. By "the people" is meant the believers, or the believers and the disbelievers together, since some of them curse others on the Day of Resurrection. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [al-A'raf: 38].

﴿Khalidina﴾ (abiding eternally) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to "hum" in "ʿalayhim."

﴿fīhā﴾ refers to the curse (al-laʿna), or to the Fire (al-nār). The pronoun has been left unstated (uḍmirat) to magnify its status and to instill awe (tahwīl).

﴿Lā yukhaffafu ʿanhumu al-ʿadhābu wa lā hum yunẓarūn﴾ — from al-inẓār (granting respite): that is, they will not be given respite; or, they will not be awaited so that they may make excuse; or, He will not look upon them with a look of mercy. (p-147)

"And your God is One God" — singular in His divinity, with no partner in it, and it is not valid that anyone other than Him be called a god. "There is no god but He" — an affirmation of the oneness by negating anything other than Him and affirming Him. The position of "Huwa" (He) is in the nominative case, because it is a substitute (badal) for the position of "lā ilāha" (there is no god). The accusative is not permissible here, because the substitute indicates that the emphasis (i'timad) is on the second, and the meaning of the verse is upon that, whereas the accusative would indicate that the emphasis is on the first. As for "al-Raḥmānu al-Raḥīm" (the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate) in the nominative: that is, the Bestower (al-Mawlā) of all blessings, both their roots and their branches, and there is nothing other than Him with this attribute; so whatever else there is, either it is a blessing, or it is one upon whom a blessing is bestowed. It is nominative because it is the predicate of an inchoative (khabar mubtada'), or in apposition (badal) to "Huwa," not as an adjective (wasf), because a pronoun cannot be described.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 164:

When the polytheists marvelled at the One God (ilah wahid) and demanded a sign for this, there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day﴾, in colour, length and shortness, and their succession in going and coming,

﴿and the ship that runs in the sea with that which benefits people﴾ — with what benefits them of what it carries in it, or with the benefit of people. The "min" in ﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky﴾ is for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah).

﴿of water﴾ — rain. The "min" is for specification of kind (li-bayan al-jins), because what descends from the sky is rain and other than it. Then it is conjoined (ʿataffa) to "anzala" (sent down): ﴿and He gives life thereby﴾ — by the water — ﴿to the earth after its death﴾ — its dryness. Then it is conjoined to "fa-ahya" (and gave life):

﴿and He scattered﴾ — and dispersed —

﴿therein﴾ — in the earth —

﴿every kind of creature﴾ — which is everything that crawls (yadibb). ﴿And the variation of the winds﴾ — the wind, according to Hamzah and ʿAli. That is: their turning in their directions, the eastern, the western, the southern and the northern, and in their states, hot and cold, violent and gentle, barren and fertile (lawaqih). It has been said: at times with mercy, and at other times with punishment.

﴿and the clouds made subservient﴾ — made docile and compliant to the will of Allah the Exalted, so that it rains wherever He wills — ﴿between the sky and the earth﴾ — in the air — ﴿are indeed signs for a people who understand﴾ — who look with the eyes of their intellects (p-148) and take heed, reflecting upon these things as proofs of the power of their Originator, the wisdom of their Creator, and the oneness of their Maker. And in a hadith: "Woe to him who recites this verse and then passes over it (famajja bi-ha)," meaning: he did not reflect upon it and did not take heed from it.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 165:**

﴿And among mankind﴾, i.e., despite this clear proof, there are among mankind those who take, besides God, ﴿rivals (andad)﴾, i.e., equals, from among the idols, ﴿who love them﴾, i.e., they venerate them and submit to them with the veneration of one who is loved, ﴿as they love God﴾, i.e., as the veneration of God and submission to Him. That is, they love the idols as they love God, meaning they equate between the idols and God in their love, because they used to acknowledge God and draw near to Him. It was also said: they love them as the believers love God.

﴿But those who believe are more intense in love for God﴾ than the polytheists are for their gods, because they never turn away from Him to other than Him in any circumstance, whereas the polytheists turn away from their rivals to God in times of hardship, so they seek refuge in Him and submit to Him. ﴿And if only they could see﴾: (ترى, "see") is read by Nafi' and Shami, addressing the Messenger, or every addressee. I.e., if you saw that, you would see a great matter. ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ refers to those who take rivals. ﴿When they see the punishment﴾: (يُرَوْن, "they are shown") is the reading of Shami.

﴿That power belongs entirely to God﴾: (أنّ, "that") here is a circumstantial clause (حال, ḥāl). ﴿And that God is severe in punishment﴾, i.e., His punishment is severe. That is, if those who committed the great wrong of polytheism knew that all power, over reward and punishment and everything else, belongs to God Most High and not to their rivals, and if they knew the severity of His punishment for wrongdoers when they witness the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, there would arise in them regret and anguish beyond description. The answer (جواب, jawāb) has been omitted, because (لو, "if only") when it appears in what is desired or feared is rarely followed by an answer, so that the heart may go every way in its imagining. Even when the past tense follows it, and likewise (إذ, "when"), which is placed to indicate the past, they are used here with the future, because God's report about the future, given its certain truth, is like the past.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 166:

﴿Idh tabarra'a﴾ with the dhal assimilated into the ta' wherever it occurs (tashdid, idgham), a reading of the Iraqi (Kufan) readers other than ʿĀṣim. (p-149) It is a substitute (badal) for ﴿Idh yarawna al-ʿadhāb﴾ (when they see the punishment). ﴿Alladhīna ittubiʿū﴾ means: those who were followed (al-mutabaʿūn), and they are the leaders (al-ru'asāʾ).

﴿Min alladhīna ittabaʿū﴾ (from those who followed): from among the followers (min al-atbāʿ). ﴿Wa-raʾaw al-ʿadhāb﴾: the waw here is for the circumstantial (li-l-ḥāl), meaning: they disown them at the time of seeing the punishment. ﴿Wa-taqaṭṭaʿat﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon tabarra'a. ﴿Bihim al-asbāb﴾: the ties (al-wuṣul) that were between them, from agreement upon one religion, and from kinship (al-ansāb), and mutual affections (al-maḥabb).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 167:

﴿And those who followed said﴾: that is, the followers (al-atba').

﴿If only we had a return﴾: a return to the world (al-dunya), ﴿so that we might disown﴾: the verb is in the subjunctive (nasb) as an answer to the wish (jawab al-tamanni), because law (lau) here carries the meaning of wishing. The meaning is: "Would that we had a return, so that we might disown

﴿them, as they have disowned us﴾ now. ﴿Thus﴾: like that dreadful showing (al-ira' al-fazi'). ﴿Thus does Allah show them their deeds﴾: that is, their worship of idols. ﴿As regrets for them﴾: as remorse (nadamat). The word (hasarat) is the third object (maf'ul thalith) of yuriHim (He shows them). Its meaning is that their deeds will be turned into regrets for them, so they will see nothing but regrets in place of their deeds. ﴿And they will not come out of the Fire﴾: rather, they will remain in it forever.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 168:

It was revealed concerning those who forbade for themselves the baḥā'ir (she-camels whose ears were slit, deemed sacred) and similar things: ﴿O people, eat﴾ — an command of permission — ﴿of what is in the earth﴾, where "min" (mina) is partitive (li-l-tab'īḍ), because not everything in the earth is edible; ﴿lawful﴾ (ḥalālan) is the object of "eat," or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of what is in the earth; ﴿good﴾ (ṭayyiban) means pure, free of any doubt (shubha); ﴿and do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ — his paths to which he invites you. It is read with the vowel on the "ṭā'" (ṭ) silent (sukūn) by Abū ʿAmr (except ʿAyyāsh), Nāfiʿ, Ḥamza and Abū Bakr. The khuṭwa (step) originally means the distance between the two feet of a walker. It is said: "He followed his steps" when he imitated him and followed his practice.

﴿Indeed he is to you a manifest enemy﴾, whose enmity is clear and beyond concealment. The verb abāna is both transitive and intransitive. This verse is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], i.e., Satan, because he is in truth an enemy to people (p-150), and their protector outwardly, for he shows them loyalty outwardly, adorns their deeds for them, and intends by that their destruction inwardly.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 169:

﴿Indeed, he only commands you﴾ is an explanation of the obligation to refrain from following him and of the manifestness of his enmity; that is, he never commands you to do anything good, but he only commands you to ﴿evil﴾, that is, to what is ugly,

﴿and immorality﴾, and what exceeds the limit in ugliness among great matters. It has also been said: evil (sū') is that which has no limit (ḥadd) in it, and immorality (faḥshā') is that which has a limit (ḥadd) in it.

﴿And that you say﴾ is in the genitive position by coordination with ﴿evil﴾, that is: and that you say (bi-an taqūlū).

﴿about Allah what you do not know﴾ refers to your saying: "This is lawful, and this is unlawful," without knowledge. It also includes everything that is attributed to God Most High which is not permissible for Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 170:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾ The pronoun (refers) to the people, and the address was turned away from them by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). It was said: they are the polytheists. And it was said: a group of the Jews, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to faith and to following the Qur'an.

﴿They say, "Rather, we follow what we found﴾ (wajadna) ﴿our fathers upon﴾ — for they were better than us and more knowledgeable" — so Allah refuted them with His words: ﴿Even though their fathers﴾ — the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), and the hamza carries the meaning of rebuke and wonder. Its meaning: Would they follow them even if their fathers ﴿did not understand anything﴾ of the religion ﴿nor were they guided﴾ to what is right?

Then He set forth for them a parable, saying: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve﴾. The noun that is governed is omitted, meaning: ﴿And the likeness﴾ of the caller of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ ﴿is like that of one who shouts (yanti) to﴾, i.e., cries out (yaṣīḥu). What is meant by ﴿that which hears nothing but a call and a cry﴾ is the cattle. The meaning is: the likeness of their caller to faith, in that they hear from the call nothing but the sound of the tone and the echo of the voice, without giving heed (ilqa' adhhān) and without insight (istibṣār), is like the likeness of one who shouts at cattle, which hear nothing but the call and cry of the one who shouts, which is a vocalising to them and a driving of them away, and they understand nothing else of it as intelligent people would understand. Al-na'iq (ya'iq, shouting) means vocalising. It is said: "nasaqa al-mu'adhdhin" (the muezzin cried out), and "na'aqa al-ra'i bil-ḍa'n" (the shepherd called out to the sheep). Al-nida' is that which is heard, while al-du'a' may or may not be heard.

﴿Deaf﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are deaf.

﴿Dumb﴾ is a second predicate; ﴿blind﴾ [in respect of the truth] is a third predicate.

﴿So they do not understand﴾ the admonition.

Then he explained that what the polytheists had forbidden is lawful, so he said: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you with﴾ — of its delicious things, or of its lawful things —

﴿and give thanks to Allah﴾ who provided them for you, ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾ — if it is correct that you single Him out for worship and acknowledge that He is the Giver of blessings.

Then he clarified what is forbidden, saying: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾, which is everything whose soul has departed from it without slaughter (dhakah) of what is slaughtered. The word ﴿only﴾ (innama) serves to affirm what is mentioned and negate what is other than it, meaning: He has forbidden you nothing but carrion ﴿and blood﴾, meaning flowing blood, due to His saying elsewhere: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. Both kinds of carrion and both kinds of blood have been made lawful by the hadith: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts, and liver and spleen." ﴿And the flesh of swine﴾, meaning swine in all its parts; the flesh was singled out because it is the primary object of eating.

﴿And that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾, meaning what was slaughtered for idols, so that other than the name of Allah was pronounced over it. The original meaning of ihlal is raising the voice, that is, one raises the voice with it for the idol, and this is the saying of the people of ignorance: "In the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza."

﴿Whoever is compelled﴾, meaning forced by necessity, with the nun kasra, read by Basri, Hamza and 'Asim, due to the meeting of two sukun letters, namely the nun and the dad. Others read it with a damma, due to the damma on the ta'.

﴿Neither desiring﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he eats without being one who desires (bagh) out of pleasure and appetite.

﴿Nor transgressing﴾ meaning exceeding the measure of need. The saying of one who said: "neither desiring against the imam nor transgressing on a forbidden journey" is weak, because a journey of obedience does not permit it without necessity, and detention in a settled place permits it without travel; and because his rebellion does not take him out of faith, so he does not deserve to be deprived. The one who is compelled is permitted only the amount by which sustenance is secured and life is preserved, not what achieves satiety, because the permission granted by necessity is measured by the amount that removes the necessity. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ in eating. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of major sins, so how could he be held accountable for eating carrion under necessity? ﴿Merciful﴾, in that He granted the concession.

It was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews, and their altering the description of the Prophet ﷺ, and their taking a bribe for that.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾ concerning the description of Muhammad ﷺ, ﴿and purchase with it a small price﴾ — i.e., a substitute (ʿiwaḍan), or something having a price.

﴿They eat not into their bellies﴾ except the full contents of their bellies. One says: "So-and-so ate in his belly," and "he ate in part of his belly."

﴿except the Fire﴾ because when one eats what is associated with the Fire, since it is a punishment for him, it is as though he ate the Fire. And from this is their saying: "So-and-so ate blood," when he consumed the blood-money (diyah), which is a substitute for it. The poet said:

"They eat every night a saddle-cover (ikāf)"

i.e., the price of a saddle-cover; he called it a saddle-cover because it is associated with it by being its price. ﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ speech that would gladden them; rather, in a manner like His saying: ﴿Remain in it, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108]. ﴿Nor will He purify them﴾ nor cleanse them from the filth of their sins, or He will not praise them. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ — painful. The three clauses are conjoined to the predicate of "inna," so "inna" has four predicates in the form of clauses.

Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. By concealing the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿How patient are they in the Fire!﴾ That is, what made them so patient in the Fire? What made them so patient in a deed that leads to the Fire? This is an interrogative (istifham) whose meaning is rebuke (tawbikh).

(p-153)

﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth﴾. That is: that punishment is because Allah sent down the Books that He sent down with the truth. ﴿And indeed those who differed﴾, that is, the People of the Book.

﴿Concerning the Book﴾: the definite article here, الكِتابِ (al-Kitab), is for the category (li-l-jins), meaning the books of Allah. So some of them said that some of it is true and some of it is false.

﴿Are in extreme dissension﴾, meaning opposition, ﴿far﴾ from the truth. Or their disbelief in that is because Allah sent down the Qur'an with the truth, as they know, and indeed those who differed concerning it are in far-reaching dissension from guidance.

**"It is not righteousness that you turn your faces"** means: it is not righteousness that you turn your faces **"toward the east and the west."** The address is to the People of the Book, because the qiblah of the Christians was the east of Bayt al-Maqdis, and the qiblah of the Jews was its west. Each of the two groups claimed that righteousness lies in facing its own qiblah, so He refuted them by saying that righteousness is not in what you are upon, because that has been abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation). **"But righteousness is"** the righteousness **"of one who believes in Allah,"** or "the one who is [truly] righteous is one who believes." Both views involve an omitted noun (*al-mudaf*), and the first is the better. *Al-birr* (righteousness) is a name for good and for every pleasing act. It has been said: the Muslims and the People of the Book engaged deeply in the matter of the qiblah, so it was said: the great righteousness that you must not be distracted by, away from the other kinds of righteousness, is not the matter of the qiblah; rather, the righteousness that must be given attention is the righteousness of one who believes and carries out these deeds.

(*Laysa al-birra*) is read with the accusative, as the predicate of *laysa*, and its subject is (*an tuwallū*). Hamzah and Hafs read it so. (*Wa-lakinna al-birru*) is read by Nafi' and al-Shami. It is reported from al-Mubarrad: "If I were one of those who recite the Qur'an, I would recite *wa-lakinna al-birru*." It has also been read as *wa-lakinna al-barra* (with the accusative and the word *al-barr*, one who is righteous).

**"And the Last Day"**, that is, the Day of Resurrection.

**"And the angels, and the Book"**, that is, the category of Allah's books, or the Qur'an.

**"And the prophets. And he gives wealth, despite loving it"**, that is, despite his love for Allah, or his love for wealth, or his love for giving; the meaning is that he gives it while his soul is content to give it. **"To relatives"**, that is, the kin. He mentioned them first because they have the greatest claim. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your charity to the poor is charity, and to your kin it is charity and a bond of kinship." **"And orphans."** What is meant is the poor among the relatives and the orphans; it was stated in general because there is no ambiguity.

**"And the needy"**: *al-miskīn* is one who constantly relies on people, because he has nothing, like *al-sikkīr* for one who is constantly drunk.

**"And the wayfarer"**: the traveler who has been cut off. This is a collective noun, though it is singular in form. He was called "son of the road" because he is constantly on it, or it refers to the guest.

**"And those who ask"**, that is, those who seek food. **"And for the captives"**, that is, to help those under contract for manumission (*al-mukātabīn*) until they free their necks, or for the release of prisoners.

**"And establishes the prayer"**, the obligatory prayer. **"And gives the zakat"**, the obligatory alms. It has been said: this is an emphasis of the first; and it has been said: what is meant by the first is voluntary charities and acts of kindness.

**"And those who fulfill"** is a conjunction with **"those who believe"**: **"their covenant when they make a covenant"**, whether with Allah or with people. **"And the patient"** is in the accusative, as a praise and specification, to show the excellence of patience in hardship and in places of battle over all other deeds.

**"In misfortune"**, poverty and hardship; **"and in adversity"**, sickness and disability; **"and in the time of battle"**, at the time of fighting.

**"Those are the ones who are true"**, that is, the people of this description are the ones who are truthful in religion. **"And those are the God-fearing."**

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 178:

It is related that "there was enmity in the Jahiliyya between two of the tribes of the Arabs, and one of them had superiority over the other. So they swore that they would kill the free man among you for the slave, the male for the female, and two for one. Then they brought their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when Allah brought Islam, and there was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, prescribed﴾." That is: ordained,

﴿for you is retaliation (al-qisas)﴾, which is an expression for equality. Its root is from qassa athrahu (he followed his trace), and iqtassahu (he pursued him). From this comes al-qass (the narrator), because he follows the traces and reports. ﴿In the matter of the slain﴾, the plural of qatil (slain). The meaning: He has ordained for you the consideration of equivalence and parity among the slain.

﴿The free for the free﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning: the free man is seized or killed for the free man. ﴿And the slave for the slave, and the female for the female.﴾ Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the free man is not to be killed for the slave, on account of this text. But according to us, retaliation applies between the free man and the slave, by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], just as it applies between the male and the female; and by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Muslims' blood is equal (tatakafa'u dima'uhum)"; and because superiority is not considered regarding souls, as evidence that if a group kills one person, they are all killed for him; and because restricting the ruling to one type does not negate it from another type, rather the ruling remains suspended pending another text, and such a text has come, as we have shown. ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother in anything, then follow up with fairness and pay him with good conduct.﴾ They said: al-'afw (pardon) is the opposite of punishment. It is said: 'afawtu 'an fulan (I pardoned so-and-so) when you overlook him and refrain from punishing him. It is transitive with 'an to the offender and to the offence,

﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 52], ﴿and He pardons evil deeds﴾ [al-Shura: 25]. When both occur together, it is transitive to the first with al-lam, so you say: 'afawtu lahu 'an dhanbihi (I pardoned him for his sin). From this is the hadith: "I have pardoned you regarding the charity of horses and slaves." Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿whoever is pardoned﴾ means: whoever is left the killing in exchange for blood-money. Al-Azhari said: al-'afw in the language means excess, and from it: ﴿and they ask you what they should spend; say: the excess﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. It is said: 'afawtu lifulan bimal (I gave excess to so-and-so with wealth) when you grant him generously and give him, and 'afawtu lahu 'amma li 'alayhi (I released him from what he owed me) when you leave it. The meaning of the verse according to the majority: whoever is granted some pardon from the side of his brother, the verb being attributed to the verbal noun as in: "he was journeyed with Zayd for part of the journey." The brother: the guardian of the slain, and he is mentioned by the term brotherhood to incite him to compassion, because of the kinship and Islam between them. "Man" is the killer who is pardoned for his offence, and the second object is omitted as being understood; it was said: it is set in place of 'an. The pronoun in "lahu" and "akhihi" refers to "man", and in "ilayhi" refers to the brother, or to the follower indicated by it.

﴿Then following (ittiba')﴾, because the meaning is: let the claimant follow the killer (ﷺ) with fairness, by demanding of him in a gracious manner, and let the killer pay the due, that is, the blood-price in place of the blood, paying with good conduct, without delaying or defrauding him. It was said "some of the pardon" so that it is known that if he pardons part of the blood, or some of the heirs pardon him, the pardon is complete and retaliation falls away. Whoever interprets "ufiya" as "turuka" (left) makes "shay'" the direct object, and likewise whoever interprets it as "u'tiya" (given). That is: if something from his brother's property, that is the killer, is given to the guardian by way of settlement, let him take it fairly without harshness, and let the killer pay it to him without procrastination. The raising of ﴿ittiba'﴾ is because it is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: so what is required is ittiba'.

﴿That﴾ refers to the aforementioned ruling of pardon and taking blood-money.

﴿is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy.﴾ For in the Torah there was only killing, and in the Gospel only pardon without compensation; and for us retaliation, pardon, and taking property by way of settlement have been permitted, as an expansion and facilitation. The verse indicates that the perpetrator of a major sin remains a believer, because he is described with faith after the killing has occurred, and because the brotherhood established by faith persists, and because he deserves the lightening and mercy.

﴿Then whoever transgresses after that﴾ the lightening, so exceeds what was prescribed for him, by killing someone other than the killer, or killing after taking the blood-money.

﴿For him is a painful punishment﴾: a kind of punishment of severe pain in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And in retaliation (qisas) there is life for you﴾. This is an eloquent expression, because of the strangeness in it: retaliation is killing and the destruction of life, yet life has been made the container (zarf) of it. In the definiteness of "retaliation" and the indefiniteness of "life" there is clear eloquence, since the meaning is: "And for you, in this category of ruling, which is specification (ikhtisas), there is great life, because it prevents you from what they used to do, namely killing a group for one person whenever they had the power. So retaliation was life, and what a life!" Or [life here is] a kind of life, namely the life that results from restraint from killing, because when the killer knows of retaliation, and he intends to kill, he remembers the retaliation and is restrained, so his intended victim is spared from being killed, and this is from qawd (retaliation). Thus the legislation of retaliation was the cause of the life of two souls. ﴿O people of understanding (ya ulil-albab)﴾: O those possessing intellect (al-'aql). ﴿That you may be righteous (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾: that you may guard against killing, out of fear of retaliation.

Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil* (Commentary), on Surah 2, verse 180:

﴿Prescribed﴾ (furiḍa, "was made obligatory") ﴿for you, when death approaches one of you﴾, i.e., when it draws near to him and its signs appear, ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, meaning abundant wealth. This is in line with what is related from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): that a freedman of his wished to make a bequest (waṣiyya), and he had seven hundred (dirhams), but ʿAlī prevented him and said: "Allah the Exalted says: ﴿if he leaves behind good﴾, and good is abundant wealth, and you have no wealth."

The subject of ﴿كُتِبَ﴾ (kutiba, "was prescribed") is ﴿the bequest to parents and relatives﴾. It was obligatory for the heir at the beginning of Islam, but it was abrogated (naskh, "replacement of a ruling by a later one") by the verses of inheritance, as we have explained in *Sharh al-Manar*. It has also been said that it is not abrogated, because it was revealed concerning one who is not an heir due to disbelief, since they had only recently embraced Islam: a man would become Muslim while his parents and close relatives did not, and Islam cuts off inheritance between them. Therefore a bequest was legislated among them as a fulfilment of the right of kinship, as a recommended act. On this view, by ﴿كُتِبَ﴾ is not meant "was made obligatory."

﴿with fairness﴾ (bil-maʿrūf), i.e., with justice, which is that one does not bequeath to the rich while leaving the poor, and does not exceed one-third. ﴿A duty﴾ (ḥaqqan) is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), meaning: this is a right, truly a right. ﴿Upon the God-fearing﴾, i.e., upon those who guard themselves against shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 181:

﴿Then whoever alters it﴾: whoever changes the bequest from its proper form, if it was in accordance with the Sharia, from among the executors and the witnesses, ﴿after he has heard it﴾: i.e., the bequest. ﴿Its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾: the sin of alteration rests only upon those who alter it, and not upon others besides them, from among the testator and the beneficiary, because the two of them are innocent of injustice (ḥayf). ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of the testator's words, ﴿Knowing﴾ of the wrongdoing of the one who alters.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 182:

﴿Then whoever fears﴾ knows (ʿalima). This is common in their speech: they say, "I fear (akhāfu) that the sky will send down rain," and they mean the predominant assumption that takes the place of certain knowledge (al-ẓann al-ghālib al-jārī majrā al-ʿilm). ﴿From a testator﴾ (muwaṣṣin), with the doubled ṣād, is the reading of Kufan transmitters other than Ḥafṣ.

﴿Injustice (janafan)﴾ means deviation from the truth through error in the bequest.

﴿Or sin (ithman)﴾ means deliberately so as to wrong [the heirs]. ﴿And makes peace between them﴾ between those to whom the bequest is made, namely: the young children (al-wildān) and the close relatives (al-aqrabūn), by bringing them into line with the path of the Sharʿ.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ at that time, because altering it is a change from falsehood to truth. [The verse] mentioned the one who alters it with falsehood, then the one who alters it with truth, so that it would be known that every alteration of this kind does not incur sin. (p-158) It has also been said: this applies while the testator is still alive, that is: whoever is present at his bequest and sees it contrary to the Sharʿ, forbids him from that and steers him toward what is right, then there is no sin upon this testator for what he said at first. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you (kutiba): that is, it has been made obligatory (furiḍa) for you, al-ṣiyām (fasting). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of ṣāma, and what is meant is the fasting of the month of Ramaḍān.

As it was prescribed (kamā kutiba): that is, a prescription like the one that was prescribed, so it is an adjective (ṣifa) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf), upon those before you, upon the prophets and the nations from the time of Ādam (peace be upon him) until your era. Thus it is an ancient worship. The comparison is in terms of the fact that each one of them had days of fasting; that is, you are commanded to fast on certain days, just as those before you were commanded. "So that you may become God-fearing" (la'allakum tattaqūn): by fasting you may guard against sins, because fasting weakens the self (aẓlaf li-nafsih) and restrains it (arda' lahā) more than engaging in evil (muwāqa'at al-sū'). Or, "so that you may be counted among the God-fearing" (tantaẓimūn fī zumrat al-muttaqīn), since fasting is their emblem (shi'ār).

The accusative of ﴿ayyāman﴾ (days) is governed by "al-ṣiyām" (fasting), meaning: "It has been prescribed for you" (kutiba ʿalaykum) that you fast ﴿for a number of days﴾, specified by a known count, i.e., a few. Its underlying principle is that a small amount of wealth is measured by number, not a large amount. ﴿So whoever among you is sick﴾, fearing that fasting would increase the illness, ﴿or is on a journey﴾, or is one who is riding on a journey, ﴿then (the obligation is) a number﴾. Fa-ʿiddatun, its (implied) predicate is ʿiddatun, meaning: he breaks the fast, so upon him is the fasting of the number of days he broke. The word ʿiddah here means "the counted (ma'dūd)," i.e., he is commanded to fast a number of counted days in their place ﴿from other days﴾, apart from the days of his illness and journey. The word ﴿ukhar﴾ (other) is not declined, because of its descriptive function and because it is deflected from "al" (the definite article), since the original rule for fuʿlā used as an adjective is that it is used in the plural with "al," like al-kubrā and al-kubar, and al-ṣughrā and al-ṣughar.

﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾, that is, for those who are able to fast and have no excuse if they break the fast.

﴿A ransom: feeding a poor person﴾: half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or a full ṣāʿ of something else. Thus "ṭaʿām" (food) is an apposition to "fidyah" (fidyat ṭaʿām masākīn), according to the reader Madani and Ibn Dhakwān. This was at the beginning of Islam: fasting was obligatory for them, but they were not accustomed to it, so it was hard on them, and He permitted them to break the fast and pay the ransom. Then the option was abrogated (naskh) by His saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. For this reason He repeated His saying: ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey﴾, because it had been mentioned together with the abrogated ruling, it was mentioned again with the abrogating ruling, to indicate that this ruling remains in force. It is also said that the meaning is: ﴿they are not able to do it﴾, so the negative particle lā is understood (implied) to match the reading of Ḥafṣa, and according to this, the verse is not abrogated. ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, by giving more than the amount of the ransom, ﴿it is better for him﴾. So the voluntary act or the good is better for him. (Yaṭṭawwaʿ) with the meaning of (yataṭawwaʿ) is the reading of Ḥamzah and ʿAlī.

﴿And that you fast﴾, O you who are able, ﴿is better for you﴾ than the ransom and voluntary good. This applies at the beginning. It is also said: fasting during a journey or illness is better for you, because it is more difficult for you.

﴿If you know﴾: a conditional clause whose answer is omitted.

**"The month of Ramadan"** is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is: **"in which the Qur'an was sent down."** That is, its revelation began in it. This took place on the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr). Or the Qur'an was sent down concerning it, and this is His, the Exalted, saying: **"Fasting has been prescribed for you."** The phrase is either a substitution (badal) for "al-siyam" (fasting), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is the month.

Ramadan is a verbal noun (masdar) of ramada, meaning to be scorched by the ramda' (hot sand). The word "month" (al-shahr) was added to it and it became a proper name (alam). It is diptote (ghayr munsarif) because of its definiteness (ta'rif) and the alif and nun. They named it so because of the scorching of hunger they endured in it and their suffering of its intensity. They also named the months after the seasons in which they fell, and this month coincided with the days of the scorching heat (ramd al-harr).

If you ask: what is the meaning of what came in the hadith, "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward," regarding the naming applying to both the annexed term and the term it is annexed to together? I say: it is of the type of omission (hadhf) for the sake of avoiding confusion. (The Qur'an) is written without a hamza, and it is Meccan.

**"As guidance for mankind and as clear proofs of guidance and the criterion"** is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal). That is: He sent it down while it is guidance for mankind toward the truth, and it is clear, manifest signs that guide to the truth and distinguish between the truth and falsehood (p-160). He mentioned first that it is guidance, then mentioned that it consists of clear proofs from among what God guided by. It distinguishes between truth and falsehood through His revelation and His heavenly books, which guide and separate guidance from misguidance.

**"So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it."** Whoever was present (shahid), that is, resident and present in the month and not a traveler, let him fast in it and not break the fast. "The month" is in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf), and likewise the pronoun in "li-yasumhu" (let him fast it). It cannot be a direct object (maf'ul bihi), because both the resident and the traveler are witnesses of the month.

**"And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days."** "A number" (fa-'iddatun) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, meaning: then upon him is a number, that is, the fasting of a number [of days].

**"God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you"** in that He permitted breaking the fast due to travel and illness. Whoever obligates breaking the fast on the sick and the traveler, such that if they fast they must repeat it, has deviated from the requirement of this.

**"And that you complete the number"**, the number of what you broke, by making up (qada') when the illness and the journey have ended. So the verb of purpose is omitted, indicated by what was previously estimated: "so that you may know and so that you may complete the number."

**"And that you magnify God for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful."** He legislated this, meaning the whole of what He mentioned: the command for the resident to fast the month, the command for the one granted the concession to observe the number of days he broke, and the concession permitting breaking the fast. Thus His saying "so that you may complete" is the reason for the command to observe the number; "so that you may magnify" is the reason for what was known of the manner of making up and of discharging the obligation of breaking the fast; and "perhaps you will be grateful" is the reason for the concession. This is a kind of subtle, elegant turn of expression (laff latif al-maslak). The verb "takbir" (magnifying) is followed by "'ala" because it implies the meaning of praise, as if it were said: that you magnify God, that is, that you glorify Him, praising Him for having guided you to it. (Wa-li-tukammilu) with doubling of the letter (tashdid) is by Abu Bakr.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 186:

When "a Bedouin Arab said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Is our Lord near, that we may confide in Him, or far, that we should call out to Him?' Then there was revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾" — (a statement of) knowledge and a response, to exclude (Allah) from nearness in terms of place (p-161). ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ — (al-Da'i, da'ani; i.e., the reading of "al-da'i" and "da'ani") in both states (of pausing and continuing). Sahl and Ya'qub read it with the yā' in both cases; Abu 'Amr and Nafi' agreed with them, except Qalun in continuous recitation (wasl). Others read it without the yā' in both cases. Then, the answering of supplication is a true promise from Allah, with no breach in it. However, answering the invocation differs from the granting of need. The answering of the invocation is that the servant says, "O Lord," and Allah says, "Here I am, My servant." This is a promised matter that exists for every believer. The granting of need is the giving of what is desired, and this may happen immediately, may happen after a period, may happen in the Hereafter, and the choice for him may lie in something other than it. ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ — when you call them to faith and obedience, just as I respond to them when they call upon Me for their needs. ﴿And let them believe in Me﴾ — the lam in it is for command. ﴿That they may be guided﴾ — so that they may be upon hope of attaining rectitude (rushd), which is the opposite of error (ghayy).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 2, verse 187:

It was the custom that when a man reached the evening, eating, drinking, and intercourse were lawful for him until he prayed the late night prayer (al-'isha'), or went to sleep. But if he had prayed it or gone to sleep without having broken his fast, then food, drink, and women became unlawful for him until the following night. Then 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, had intercourse with his wife after the late night prayer. When he performed the ritual bath (ghusl), he began to weep and blame himself. So he came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of what he had done. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You were not deserving of that." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to approach your wives (for intercourse)﴾. That is, *al-rafath* (the intercourse). The verb is governed by *ila* (to) because it includes the meaning of *al-ifda'* (reaching/going unto). He referred to it with the word *al-rafath*, which indicates the sense of ugliness, and did not say *al-ifda'* ("reaching"), out of disapproval of what had occurred from them before the permission was given, just as He called it "betrayal of themselves" (*ikhtiyan*). Since a man and a woman embrace, and each one wraps the other in his embrace, it was compared to the garment that envelops, through the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾. It was also said: *libas* means a covering (*sitr*) against what is forbidden. The phrase ﴿They are a garment for you﴾ is a resumed statement (*isti'naf*), serving as an explanation of the cause of the permission: when there is between you and them this kind of close contact and intimacy, your patience with them diminishes and abstaining from them becomes difficult for you, so He granted you a concession regarding their physical contact. ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾, wronging them by intercourse and depriving them of their share of good. *Al-ikhtiyan* is derived from *al-khiyana* (betrayal), like *al-iktisab* from *al-kasb* (earning); it carries an added sense of intensity. ﴿So He turned to you﴾ when you repented of what you had committed of the forbidden, ﴿and pardoned you﴾ for what you had done before the concession.

﴿So now, have intercourse with them﴾, that is, have sexual relations with them during the nights of fasting. This is a command of permission. Intercourse was called *mubashara* (physical contact) because the two skins (*bashara*) touch.

﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾, that is, seek what Allah has apportioned for you and recorded in the Preserved Tablet, namely offspring through intercourse. In other words, do not engage in intercourse merely to satisfy desire, but to pursue that for which Allah instituted marriage, namely procreation. Alternatively, ﴿seek﴾ means the place which Allah has ordained for you and made lawful, rather than the forbidden place which He has not ordained for you.

﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾. The "white thread" is the first thing that appears of the dawn, the streak spreading across the horizon like a stretched thread, ﴿from the black thread﴾, which is the darkness of the night extending. They are likened to two threads, white and black, because of their extension.

﴿of the dawn﴾ clarifies that the white thread is of the dawn and not of anything else. He suffices with this for explaining the black thread, because clarifying one of them is clarifying the other. Alternatively, *min* ("of") is partitive, because it is a part of the dawn and its beginning. His saying ﴿of the dawn﴾ removes it from the category of metaphor (*isti'ara*) and makes it an intensive simile (*tashbih baligh*). Just as your saying "I saw a lion" is a metaphor, but if you add "from so-and-so," it returns to being a simile.

It is narrated from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "I took two cords, one white and one black, and placed them under my pillow. I looked at them, but the white did not become distinct to me from the black." So I informed the Prophet ﷺ of that, and he said: "You have a broad nape" (that is, simple of heart, because this is one of the things used to indicate a man's dullness and lack of understanding), "That is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night."

In His saying ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, that is, abstain from these things. This contains evidence for: the permissibility of making the intention (*niyya*) for the fast of Ramadan during the day; the permissibility of delaying the ghusl until dawn for one who is in a state of major impurity (*janaba*); the prohibition of continuous fasting (*wisal*), i.e., fasting without eating between days; the obligation of expiation (*kaffara*) for eating and drinking (deliberately during the fast); and that being in a state of *janaba* does not invalidate the fast.

﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are staying in the mosques﴾, that is, while you are performing i'tikaf (retreat) in them. He clarified that intercourse is lawful during the nights of Ramadan, but not for one in a state of i'tikaf. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*). This contains evidence that i'tikaf is valid only in a mosque, and that it is not restricted to any particular mosque over another.

﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾, that is, the rulings that have been mentioned, His prescribed boundaries. ﴿So do not approach them﴾ by violating or altering them.

﴿Thus Allah makes His signs clear to mankind﴾, that is, His laws, ﴿so that they may become God-fearing﴾, that is, avoid what is forbidden.

﴿And do not consume one another's property﴾ meaning: let none of you consume the property of another ﴿unjustly﴾, by a means that Allah has not permitted and has not legislated. ﴿And do not bring it down to the rulers﴾, that is, do not bring it forward (to them). The verb ﴿تُدْلُوا﴾ (tudlū) is in the jussive (majzūm, the grammatical mood marking a verb after a prohibition), so it falls under the scope of the prohibition. The meaning is: do not hand over the matter of the property and the adjudication concerning it to the rulers,

﴿so that you may consume﴾ through litigation ﴿a portion﴾, a part, ﴿of people's property sinfully﴾, by giving false testimony, or by false oaths, or by reconciliation while knowing that the one in whose favour the judgment is given is a wrongdoer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the two disputants: "Indeed I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes before me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than the other, so I judge for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I give him something of his brother's right, let him not take it, for what I give him is a piece of fire." So they both wept, and each of them said: "My right belongs to my companion."

It has also been said: ﴿and bring it down﴾ means to offer some of it to corrupt rulers by way of bribery (rashwa). It is said: adlā dalwahu (أدْلى دَلْوَهُ), meaning he lowered his bucket into the well to draw water. ﴿While you know﴾ that you are upon falsehood. Committing disobedience while knowing its ugliness is more ugly, and its doer is more deserving of reproach.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 189:

"Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), what is the matter with the crescent (*hilal*) that it appears thin like a thread, then grows until it becomes full and complete, and then keeps waning until it returns as it first appeared, unlike the sun, which remains in one state?' So there was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons.﴾" *Al-ahilla* is the plural of *hilal*, and it was so named because people raise their voices (*ruf' al-aswat*) when they see it.

﴿Say: They are signs marking times for people and for the Hajj.﴾ That is, they are markers by which people set the times of their planting, their trade, the settlement of their debts, their fasting and breaking of the fast, the waiting period (*'iddah*) of their wives, the days of their menstruation, the duration of their pregnancy, and other matters, and markers for the Hajj by which its time is known. Some of the Ansar, when they entered the state of ihram, would not enter any garden wall, house, or tent through its door. If a man was of the settled people (*ahl al-mudar*), he would make a breach (*naqb*) in the back of his house through which he entered and exited; and if he was of the nomadic people (*ahl al-wabar*), he would leave from behind the tent. So there was revealed: ﴿And it is not righteousness to enter houses from their backs.﴾ That is, righteousness does not lie in your scrupulousness about entering through the door.

There is no disagreement over the *raf'* (nominative case) of *al-birr* here, because the verse there (in the previous discussion) admits both readings as explained, so both *raf'* and *nasb* were permissible there; but this verse admits only one reading, which is *raf'*, since the *ba'* (preposition) enters only upon the predicate of *laysa* (the negative verb).

﴿But righteousness is [the righteousness] of one who fears (*ittaqa*)﴾ what Allah has forbidden. *Al-buyut* (houses), its transmission is Madani, Basri and Hafs, and this is the original form, like *ka'b* and *ku'ub*. Whoever reads the *ba'* with kasra (*al-birr* as *bi'r*) does so because of the *ya'* after it, but the *ya'* requires moving from kasra to damma. It is as if it was said to them, when they asked about the new moons and about the wisdom in their waning and fullness: It is known that everything Allah the Exalted does is nothing but wisdom, so leave off asking about it, and consider one single practice of yours that is not righteousness at all while you think it is righteousness. This is the connection of this verse with what precedes it. It may also be that this is by way of digression (*istitrad*) from what was mentioned, that they are markers of the Hajj, because this was among their practices in the Hajj. It may also be that this is an illustration of the inversion (*ta'kis*) in their questioning, and that their case in it is like that of one who leaves the door of the house and enters from its back. The meaning is: righteousness, and what you ought to be upon, is not that you invert your questions; rather, righteousness is the righteousness of one who fears Allah regarding that and avoids it, and does not dare to do the like of it (p-165).

﴿And come to houses by their doors﴾ and undertake matters from their proper directions, in which they must be undertaken, and do not invert them. Or the intended meaning is: the obligation to believe that all of Allah the Exalted's actions are wisdom and rightness, without any stirring of doubt or objection of uncertainty about that, so that one does not ask about it, because asking implies accusing oneself of entertaining doubt. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you.

﴿That perhaps you may prosper﴾ so that you may attain the everlasting bliss.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿وَقاتِلُوا في سَبِيلِ اللهِ﴾ "And fight in the way of Allah." Fighting in the way of Allah is jihad (striving) to raise high the word of Allah and to strengthen the religion.

﴿الَّذِينَ يُقاتِلُونَكُمْ﴾ "Those who fight you." That is, those who engage you in actual fighting, not those who refrain from fighting you (al-muhajizin). On this view the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿وَقاتِلُوا المُشْرِكِينَ كافَّةً﴾ "And fight the polytheists all together" [al-Tawbah: 36]. It was also said: this is the first verse revealed about fighting, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would fight those who fought him and refrain from those who refrained. Or, "those who fight you" refers to those who take up fighting against you, excluding those who are not of the fighting class, such as the old men, the children, the monks, and the women. Or it refers to all the disbelievers, because they intend to fight the Muslims, so they are in the status of fighters.

﴿وَلا تَعْتَدُوا﴾ "And do not transgress." This means: in starting the fighting, or by fighting those you have been forbidden to fight, such as women, old men and the like, or by mutilation.

﴿إنَّ اللهَ لا يُحِبُّ المُعْتَدِينَ﴾ "Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 191:

﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾: wherever you find them, (thaqif means) finding them in a manner of seizing and overpowering. ﴿And expel them from wherever they expelled you﴾: i.e., from Makkah. Allah the Exalted promised them the conquest of Makkah through this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indeed did this to those among them who had not embraced Islam on the Day of the Conquest. ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾: i.e., their associating partners with Allah is greater than the killing that befalls them at your hands. It was also said: fitnah is the punishment of the Hereafter. And it was said: fitnah is the trial and affliction that befalls a person, by which he is tormented, which is harder for him than being killed. It was said to a wise man: "What is worse than death?" He replied: "That in which death is wished for." Thus he made expulsion from one's homeland among the trials in which death is wished for. ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾ (p-166): i.e., do not begin fighting them in the Sanctuary until they begin. According to us, "the Sacred Mosque" refers to the whole Sanctuary (al-Haram).

﴿But if they fight you, then kill them﴾ in the Sanctuary. According to us, they are to be killed in the sacred months except when they start fighting with us; then we kill them. Although the apparent meaning of His words ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾ permits killing in all places, the Sanctuary is specified by His words ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you therein﴾, except when they initiate hostilities. So (it is reported) in "Sharh al-Ta'wilat." ﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ is a subject and predicate: "Do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you..." Hamzah and Ali read "qatalukum" (they kill you) without the alif (qataluukum → qatalukum in this reading).

Note on the passage: the translation must follow the Arabic text exactly. Here it is.

﴿And if they desist﴾ from polytheism and fighting, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what has passed of their transgression.

﴿Merciful﴾ in accepting their repentance and their faith.

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ are translated, and technical terms glossed on first use.

﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ — shirk (associating partners with God). "Kāna" here is a complete (tāmmah) verb, meaning "exists" or "occurs." "Ḥattā" is taken to mean "so that" (kay) or "until" (ilā an). ﴿And religion is for Allah﴾ — sincere, with nothing of Satan in it, i.e., nothing is worshipped besides Him. ﴿But if they desist, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾ — if they refrain from disbelief, then do not fight them, for there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers, and they will no longer be wrongdoers. Or: do not wrong anyone except the wrongdoers who do not desist. He called the recompense of the wrongdoers "wrongdoing" by way of mushākalah (correspondence of expression), as in His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194].

The Mushrikun fought them at the Hudaybiyya in the sacred month, which was Dhu al-Qa'da. It was said to them when they set out for the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the making-up 'umra), and they disliked fighting, and that was in Dhu al-Qa'da: ﴿The sacred month﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿for the sacred month﴾, meaning: this month is in exchange for that month, and its violation is met with its violation, i.e., you violate its sanctity against them just as they violated its sanctity against you. ﴿And for sacred things there is retaliation﴾, meaning: every sanctity in which retaliation applies—whoever violates a sanctity, whatever sanctity it may be, is retaliated against by having his sanctities violated in return. So when they violated the sanctity of your month, do likewise to them, and do not hesitate. He emphasized this with His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. Here "man" (whoever) is conditional; the "ba'" (with/in the manner of) is not superfluous, and the implied sense is: with a punishment equivalent [to the offence]. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding their transgression. Or the "ba'" is superfluous, and its implied sense is: a transgression like their transgression.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ while you are seeking victory over those who transgress against you, so do not transgress beyond what is lawful for you. ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾ by giving them victory.

﴿And spend in the way of God﴾: give charity seeking God's pleasure (*tuṣaddiqū fī riḍā Allāh*). It is general, covering both jihad and other things.

﴿And do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾: that is, your selves. The *bāʼ* (in *bi-aydīkum*) is extra (*zāʼida*, grammatically redundant). Or the meaning is: do not kill yourselves with your hands, as one says, "So-and-so destroyed himself with his own hand," when he causes his own ruin. The meaning is a prohibition against abandoning spending in the way of God, because that is a cause of ruin; or against extravagance in spending, to the point of impoverishing oneself and neglecting one's dependents; or against exposing oneself to danger; or against abandoning the raid, which strengthens the enemy. *Al-tahlukah* (destruction), *al-halāk* (perishing) and *al-hulk* (ruin) are one and the same.

﴿And do good﴾: think well of God regarding His replacing what is spent (*fī al-ikhlāf*). ﴿Indeed God loves the good-doers﴾: toward the needy.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 2, verse 196:**

﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾. Perform them complete, with their conditions (sharaʾit) and obligatory acts (faraʾid), seeking the Face of Allah, Exalted, without delay or deficiency. It has also been said: "completion" (al-itmam) occurs after one has begun. This indicates that whoever begins them is obligated to complete them. We hold accordingly that ʿUmrah becomes binding by beginning it. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, has no proof from this verse for the obligation of ʿUmrah, because He commanded its completion, and one may be commanded to complete an obligatory act or a voluntary one. Or "completing them" means: that you enter into ihram for both from your household's dwelling-place (duwayrat ahlika), or that you make a separate journey for each of them, or that you spend on them only what is lawful, or that you do not engage in trade alongside them.

﴿But if you are prevented﴾. It is said: "Ahsara fulan" (someone was prevented) when a matter has hindered him, whether through fear, illness, or inability. "Hussira" means: when an enemy has detained him from proceeding. According to us, ihsar (being prevented) is established by any obstruction, whether from an enemy, illness, or other causes, based on the apparent wording of the text. There has come in a hadith: "Whoever is broken or lamed has (become permitted to) exit the state of ihram," meaning: it is permissible for him to exit ihram, "and upon him is Hajj in the following year." According to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, ihsar applies only to an enemy. The apparent wording of the text indicates that (p-168) ihsar also applies to ʿUmrah, because it is mentioned immediately after the two.

﴿then what is available of the offering (hady)﴾. Fa-ma tayassara minhu. It is said: "yasura al-amr" and "istaysara", just as it is said "saʿuba" and "istaṣʿaba" (both meaning "it became easy/difficult"). Al-hady is the plural of hadiyyah. The meaning is: if you are prevented from proceeding to the House while you are in ihram for Hajj or ʿUmrah, then upon you, when you wish to exit the state of ihram, is what is available of the offering: a camel, a cow, or a sheep. Fa-ma is in the nominative case by way of the subject (mubtada'), meaning: "upon you is what is available"; or it is in the accusative, meaning: "offer what is available."

﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. The address is to those who have been prevented: do not exit ihram by shaving the head until you know that the offering which you have sent to the Haram has reached its place (mahill), that is, its place where it must be slaughtered, and this is the Haram. This is an argument for us, that the blood-offering for ihsar is not slaughtered except in the Haram, against al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, since according to him it is permissible outside the Haram.

﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: whoever among you has an illness that compels him to shave.

﴿or has an affliction of the head﴾: such as lice, or a wound.

﴿then there is a ransom﴾: upon him, if he shaves, is a ransom (fidyah)

﴿of fasting﴾: three days;

﴿or charity﴾: to six needy persons, half a ṣaʿ of wheat for each needy person;

﴿or a sacrifice﴾: a sheep. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar), or the plural of nasikah.

﴿When you are secure﴾ from ihsar, that is, when you are not prevented, and you are in a state of safety and ease: ﴿then whoever enjoys (tamatta'a)﴾, that is, benefits, ﴿through ʿUmrah until Hajj﴾. His enjoyment of ʿUmrah until the time of Hajj is his benefiting from drawing near to Allah through it before benefiting from drawing near through Hajj. It has also been said: when he exits from his ʿUmrah, he benefits by permitting what had been forbidden to him until he enters ihram for Hajj.

﴿then what is available of the offering﴾: this is the offering of tamattuʿ (tamattuʿ offering), which is a sacrifice from which one may eat, and which is slaughtered on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr).

﴿But whoever does not find﴾ the offering,

﴿then a fast of three days during Hajj﴾: upon him is fasting three days during the time of Hajj, which is its months, between the two ihrams: the ihram of ʿUmrah and the ihram of Hajj.

﴿and seven when you return﴾: when you depart and have finished the acts of Hajj. ﴿That is ten complete﴾: in their substituting for the offering, or in reward. Or the purpose is to remove ambiguity, so that the conjunction "wa" is not understood to mean permission, as in "sit with al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin." Do you not see that if he sat with both of them, or with one of them, he would have complied?

﴿That﴾ refers to tamattuʿ, since according to us there is no tamattuʿ or qiran for the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram. According to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, it refers to the ruling, which is the obligation of the offering or the fast, and he did not obligate anything upon them (p-169).

﴿For one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾: they are the people of the miqat-stations, and whoever is short of them up to Makkah.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in what He has commanded you and forbidden you, in Hajj and otherwise. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ toward whoever does not fear Him.

﴿The Hajj﴾, i.e., the time of the Hajj, as in your saying, "The cold is two months."

﴿The months are well-known﴾, known to the people, so that they are not confused about them. They are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. The benefit of specifying the Hajj by these months is that none of the acts of Hajj is valid outside them. The same applies to the ihram (the state of ritual consecration), according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. According to us (the Hanafis), although the ihram is valid if entered outside these months, it is disliked. The word "months" is in the plural form (ashhur) for the sake of the majority of the third, or because the plural form of a noun is applied to what is beyond one, as evidenced by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Your hearts have inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], where the dual is addressed in the plural.

﴿Whoever imposes upon himself the Hajj in them﴾, i.e., whoever obligates himself to it by entering the state of ihram, ﴿in these months﴾. ﴿There shall be no rafath﴾, which is sexual intercourse, or mention of it in the presence of women, or obscene speech.

﴿Nor fusuq﴾, which is sins, or cursing, due to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Cursing a believer is fusuq." Or it is insulting one another with nicknames, due to the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How evil is the name of wickedness after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

﴿Nor quarrelling during the Hajj﴾, nor disputing with companions, servants, or hired camel-drivers. The command to avoid these things, although they must be avoided at all times, is because they are more repugnant during the Hajj, just as wearing silk during prayer and beautifying the recitation of the Qur'an (are disliked).
