The negation here means that their existence is obligatory to be absent, and that they are deserving of not existing. Abu 'Amr and Makki recited (the first two) with a raised vowel (raf'), understanding them in the sense of a prohibition, as if it were said: "Let there be no rafath and no fusuq." The third (word) they recited with a fatha (nasb), in the sense of a statement of the absence of quarrelling, as if it were said: "There is no doubt and no disagreement in the Hajj."

Then He urged what is good immediately after forbidding what is evil, and that they should use good speech in place of ugly speech, righteousness and piety in place of wickedness, and agreement, good character, and good manners in place of quarrelling, by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾. Know that He is aware of it and will reward you for it. This also refutes the view of those who denied His knowledge of particulars. (It was said that) the people of Yemen did not take provisions, saying: "We are reliant upon Allah (mutawakkilun)," and so they became a burden upon the people. So this was revealed concerning them: ﴿And take provisions﴾, i.e., take provisions, and beware of begging from people, pestering them, and burdening them.

﴿Indeed, the best provision is piety﴾, i.e., abstaining from pestering and burdening the people. Or: take provisions for the Hereafter by refraining from what is forbidden, for the best provision is abstaining from it. ﴿And fear Me﴾, and fear My punishment. It is like the words: "Call upon Me" (ud'uni).

﴿O people of understanding﴾, O possessors of intellects. The meaning is that the requirement of intellect is the fear of Allah, and whoever among the intelligent does not fear Him, it is as if he has no intellect.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 198:

It was revealed concerning a people who claimed that there is no pilgrimage for a camel-driver or a merchant, and they said: "These are the ones who go (al-dāhhāj), not the pilgrims (al-hājj)."

﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek﴾ in seeking during the seasons of the Hajj ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾: a gift and favour, which is gain and profit through trade and hiring out (of animals).

﴿So when you pour forth﴾ means you press on in great numbers, from the pouring (ifāḍah) of water, which is pouring it out abundantly. Its original form is "afaḍtum anfusakum" (you poured yourselves forth), and the object is omitted. ﴿from ʿArafāt﴾ is a proper name for the standing-place, named after a plural like Adhri‘āt. It is declined (ṣurifat) because the tā' in it is not a feminine marker; rather, it together with the alif before it is the sign of the feminine plural. It was so named because it was described to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and when he saw it he recognised it (ʿarafahā). It is also said: Adam and Eve met there and recognised one another (fa-taʿārafā). In this there is evidence for the obligation of standing at ʿArafah, because the pouring forth is not possible except after it.

﴿Then remember Allah﴾ with the talbiyah, the tahlil, the takbir, praise, and supplications, or with the Maghrib and ʿIshā' prayers ﴿at the Sacred Landmark﴾, which is Quzah, the mountain on which the imam stands and on which there is the fire (al-mīqadah). Al-mashʿar means the landmark, because it is the landmark of worship, and it is described as "sacred" because of its sanctity. It is also said that al-mashʿar al-ḥarām is Muzdalifah. Muzdalifah was also called Jamʿ because Adam, peace be upon him, gathered there with Eve (ijtamaʿa) and drew near to her (izdalafa ilayhā), meaning he came close to her; or because the two prayers are combined there; or because people draw near (yazdalifūn) to Allah the Exalted, meaning they seek nearness through standing there.

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾: "mā" is either a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah) or a restrictive particle (kāffah). That is: remember Him with a good remembrance, as He has guided you with good guidance; or remember Him as He has taught you how to remember Him, and do not deviate from it. ﴿And indeed you were before it﴾, before the guidance, ﴿among the astray﴾, the ignorant, not knowing how to remember Him and worship Him. Inna here is the lightened form of the heavy inna, and the lām is the lām of distinction (lām al-fāriqah).

**Then pass on from where the people pass on.** That is, let your passing on be ﴿from where the people pass on﴾, and do not be from Muzdalifah (a place between 'Arafat and Mina, also called Jam'). They said: this is a command to the Quraysh to pass on from 'Arafat to Jam' (Muzdalifah). They used to stand at Jam' while the rest of the people stood at 'Arafat, and they would say: "We are the residents (quttan) of His Sacred Precinct, so we do not leave it." It was also said: the passing on from 'Arafat is what is mentioned, so it means the passing on from Jam' to Mina. On this view, the "people" means the Hums (the Quraysh and those who followed their religious practices, who claimed special sanctity and did not leave the Sacred Precinct), and the address is to the believers.

﴿And seek forgiveness from God﴾ for your opposition in the standing place and the like of that from your pre-Islamic ignorance (jahiliyyah), or for your shortcomings in the rites of the Hajj. ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward you.

When you have completed your rites (﴿فَإذا قَضَيْتُمْ مَناسِكَكُمْ﴾)": that is, when you have finished the acts of worship (ʿibādāt) that you were commanded to perform in the ḥajj (the pilgrimage to Makkah), and have departed.

﴿فاذْكُرُوا اللهَ كَذِكْرِكم آباءَكُمْ﴾: "remember God as you remember your fathers." That is, remember God with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers. The meaning is: remember God abundantly and with great effort, just as you do in remembering your fathers, their glories, and their days. When they had completed their rites, they would stand between the mosque at Minā and the mountain, enumerating the virtues of their fathers and recounting the noble deeds of their days.

﴿أوْ أشَدَّ ذِكْرًا﴾: "or with a greater remembrance," that is, more. It is in the genitive position as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with [what the word "remembrance" was added to] in His saying ﴿كَذِكْرِكُمْ﴾ ("as your remembrance"), just as you say: "like the remembrance of Quraysh of their fathers, or of a people greater than them in remembrance." And ﴿ذِكْرًا﴾ is a specifier (tamyīz).

﴿فَمِنَ الناسِ مَن يَقُولُ﴾: "Among the people is one who says": among those who attend the ḥajj is one who asks God for the worldly portions, so he says: ﴿رَبَّنا آتِنا في الدُنْيا﴾, "Our Lord, give us in this world." The phrase "give us" means: let our coming (itynānā), that is, our being given, be in this world specifically, meaning: status and wealth.

﴿وَما لَهُ في الآخِرَةِ مِن خَلاقٍ﴾: "and he has no portion (khalāq) in the Hereafter," that is, no share, because his aim is confined to this world due to his disbelief in the Hereafter. The meaning is: be abundant in the remembrance of God and in supplicating to Him, for people are of two kinds: one of little means, who through the remembrance of God seeks only the goals of this world, and one of abundance, who seeks the good of both abodes. So be among the abundant ones, that is, among those of whom it was said:

﴿And among them﴾ (i.e., among those who attend the Hajj [the pilgrimage to Makkah]) ﴿are those who say: "Our Lord, give us good in this world"﴾: blessing and well-being, or knowledge and worship.

﴿And good in the Hereafter﴾: pardon and forgiveness, or wealth and Paradise, or the praise of creation and the pleasure of the Truth, or faith and security, or sincerity and deliverance, or the Sunnah and Paradise, or contentment and intercession, or a righteous wife and the wide-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn), or living in happiness and being raised from the graves with glad tidings.

﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾: guard us from the punishment of Hell, or from the punishment of the Fire, which is the bad wife.

(p-173)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 202:

﴿Those﴾ i.e., those who supplicate for the two good things (al-hasanatayn). ﴿For them there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ That is, of the same kind as what they earned of good deeds, namely the reward, which is the good benefits. Or, it means "because of what they earned." Or, he called supplication "earning" because it is among the deeds, and deeds are described as being earned. It is also permissible that ﴿those﴾ refers to both groups, and that each group has a share of the same kind as what they earned.

﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ He is about to establish the Resurrection and call His servants to account, so hasten to repeat the remembrance (of Allah) and to seek the Hereafter. Or, He described Himself with swiftness in reckoning creatures despite their great number and the abundance of their deeds, to show the perfection of His power and the obligation to beware of Him. It is related that He will reckon all creatures in the time it takes to milk a sheep, and it is related that it will be in the time of a blink of an eye.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 203:

﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days﴾ — these are the days of al-tashriq (the days after the Eid sacrifice, 11th to 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah). Remembering Allah during them is the takbir after the prescribed prayers and at the jamarat (the pillars at Mina).

﴿Whoever hastens﴾ — whoever hastens in leaving (al-nafr), or seeks to hasten the departure. Ta'ajjala and ista'jala come intransitively, as equivalents of 'ajjala, as in one says ta'ajjala fi al-amr and ista'jala; and transitively, as in one says ta'ajjala li al-dhahab and ista'jalahu. The intransitive sense fits better with His words: ﴿and whoever delays﴾ ﴿within two days﴾ of these three days, so that he does not remain until he throws on the third day, and is content with throwing at the pillars on two of these three days ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning he is not sinful by this hastening. ﴿And whoever delays﴾ until he throws on the third day ﴿there is no sin upon him for whoever fears Allah﴾ — from hunting, or from obscenity and wickedness. That is, he has the choice between hastening and delaying, even though delaying is better; a choice may occur between the permissible and the more excellent, just as the traveller was given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast, although fasting is better. It is also said: the people of the Jahiliyyah were of two groups: some considered the one who hastened to be sinful, and others considered the one who delayed to be sinful, so the Qur'an came down negating sin from both.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all matters ﴿and know that you will be gathered to Him﴾ when He raises you from the graves.

(p-174)

Al-Akhnas ibn Shariq was sweet-tongued. Whenever he met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would soften his speech to him, claim that he loved him, and claim that he was a Muslim, saying: "Allah knows that I am truthful." So there was revealed concerning him: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech pleases you﴾, that is, it delights you and becomes great in your heart. "Al-'ajib" (the marvellous) is something that is held in great esteem by the soul.

﴿In the life of this world﴾. "Fi" (in) is connected to "al-qawl" (the speech), meaning: what he says pleases you concerning the matter of this world, because by his claim of love he seeks the share of this world and does not intend by it the Hereafter. Or it is connected to "yu'jibuka" (pleases you), meaning: his sweet speech pleases you in this world, not in the Hereafter, because of the stammering and incoherence that will overtake him at the standing place (of judgement).

﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾, that is: he swears and says, "Allah is witness to what is in my heart of love for you and of Islam."

﴿Yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾, i.e. the most fierce in contention and enmity toward the Muslims. "Al-khisam" means mutual contention. The construction here is in the sense of "fi" (in): the superlative "af'al" is annexed to what is part of it, as you say, "Zayd is the best of the people", and a person cannot be part of an event; so the meaning is: "most stubborn in contention." Or "al-khisam" is the plural of "khasm" (adversary), like "sa'b" and "si'ab", and the sense is: "he is the most contentious of adversaries in contention."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 205:

﴿And when he turns away﴾ from you, and goes off after gentle speech and sweet discourse,

﴿he strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾, as he did with Thaqif. There was a dispute between him and them, so he attacked them by night, destroyed their livestock, and burned their crops.

﴿therein, and destroys the crops and the offspring﴾. That is, the crops and the animals. Or, if he is a ruler, he does what the rulers of evil do of corruption in the land, by destroying the crops and the offspring. It is also said: he spreads injustice until, because of the evil of his injustice, Allah withholds the rain, so the crops perish and the offspring too. ﴿And Allah does not love corruption.﴾

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 206:**

﴿And when it is said to him﴾ — to al-Akhnas — ﴿"Fear Allah"﴾ — regarding corruption and destruction — ﴿pride takes him to sin﴾: arrogance and the zeal of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) carry him to the sin which he forbids others from, and compel him to commit it. Or the bāʾ (ب in bi-l-ithm) indicates cause, meaning: pride takes him because of the sin that is in (p-175) his heart, which is disbelief. ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾, i.e., it suffices as his punishment. ﴿And what an evil resting-place﴾, i.e., the bed (al-firāsh) is Hell.

Revealed concerning Suhayb when the polytheists wanted to force him to abandon Islam, and they had killed a group of people who were with him. So he bought his own soul (nafsahu) from them with his wealth, and came to Madinah. Or it was revealed concerning whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, until he is killed. ﴿And among people is one who sells his soul﴾, selling it ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, in that He rewards them for that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 208:

﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace (al-silm) completely﴾ With the letter sīn vowelled with a fatḥa (al-silm), it is read by the Ḥijāzī (reciters) and ʿAlī. It means submission (al-istislām) and obedience (al-ṭāʿa), i.e., submit to God and obey Him; or it means Islam (al-Islām). The address is to the People of the Book (ahl al-kitāb), because they believed in their prophet and their scripture; or it is to the hypocrites (munāfiqūn), because they believed with their tongues.

﴿kāffatan﴾ No one among you should withdraw his hand from His obedience. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the pronoun in "udkhulū" (enter), meaning "all of you together"; or from "al-silm," because it is feminine in gender (yu'annathu). It is as if they were commanded to enter into all the acts of obedience, or into all the branches and all the laws of Islam. And kāffa is from kaff (restraint), as if they were restrained from anyone among them going out by their being united. ﴿And do not follow the steps (khuṭuwāt) of Satan﴾, i.e., his whisperings (wasāwis). ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, i.e., manifest in enmity.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 209:

﴿Then if you slip﴾ means you turn away from entering into peace (al-silm),

﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾. That is, the evident arguments and the manifest signs that you were called to enter into are the truth. ﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty﴾, dominant, nothing prevents Him from punishing you,

﴿Wise﴾, He does not punish except with right. It is related that a reciter recited (Ghafur Rahim) [Forgiving, Merciful], and a Bedouin who had not studied the Qur'an heard him and rejected it, saying: "This is not the word of Allah, for the Wise does not mention forgiveness at the time of slipping and disobedience, because that would be an incitement to it."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 210:

﴿Are they waiting﴾: i.e., what are they waiting for?

﴿except that Allah should come to them﴾: i.e., the command of Allah and His punishment, as in His saying: ﴿Or that the command of your Lord should come﴾ [al-Nahl: 33], and ﴿Then Our punishment came upon it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]. Or the thing brought is omitted, meaning: that Allah should come to them with His punishment, the sign of which is His saying: ﴿Know that Allah is Mighty﴾. ﴿In canopies﴾: plural of ﴿zullah﴾ (canopy), which is that which shades you, ﴿of the clouds﴾: the clouds. This is for magnification of the matter, since clouds are a sign of mercy; so when punishment descends from them, the matter is more grievous and more terrifying. ﴿And the angels﴾: i.e., and the angels who have been appointed to punish them will come. Or the intended meaning is: their presence on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And the matter is decided﴾: i.e., the matter of their destruction is complete and finished.

﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾: i.e., He has given the servants control over some matters, and all matters return to Him on the Day of Resurrection. (*Tur'jau al-umur*, "matters are returned," wherever it occurs) is read by Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami), Hamzah, and 'Ali (with the verb in the form *turja'u*, as recited by these readers).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 211:**

﴿Ask﴾. Its original form is *isal* (ask!), with the hamza's vowel (fatha) transferred to the sin after the hamza was dropped. The hamza of connection (*hamzat al-wasl*) was then dispensed with, so it became *sal*. It is an imperative addressed either to the Messenger or to everyone. It is a question of reproach (*su'al taqri'*), like the way the disbelievers will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Children of Israel, how many clear signs have We given them?﴾ Through the hands of their prophets, namely their miracles. Or it means a sign in the Scriptures testifying to the truth of the religion of Islam. *Kam* here is either interrogative or declarative (*khabariyyah*).

﴿And whoever substitutes the blessing of God﴾. This means His signs, which are the greatest blessing from God, because they are the means of guidance and of salvation from misguidance. Their substitution of them is that God manifested them so that they would be means of their guidance, but they made them means of their misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿So it added uncleanness to their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125]. Or it means they distorted the verses of the Scriptures that indicate the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿after it has come to them﴾, that is, after they had recognised it and it had been confirmed to them, because if one does not recognise it, it is as though it were absent from him. ﴿Indeed God is severe in retribution﴾ toward whoever deserves it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 212:

﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world.﴾ The one who adorns is Satan. He made the world appealing to them and beautified it in their eyes with his whisperings, and made it beloved to them, so they desire nothing other than it. Or it is God Most High who adorns it, by creating desires within them. Also, because all created beings come from Him. This is supported by the reading of one who recited: ﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world.﴾

﴿And they mock those who believe.﴾ They used to mock the poor believers, such as Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ammar, Suhayb, and their like. That is: they desire nothing but the world, and they mock those who have no share in it, or those who seek something other than it.

﴿But those who are mindful of God⁠﻿ [i.e., who guarded themselves] against polytheism, and they are these poor people.

﴿Will be above them on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Because they are in a lofty Garden, while they are in the abyss of Hell.

﴿And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning.﴾ Without restriction. That is: He expands [provision] for whom He wills to expand it upon, as He expanded it upon Qarun and others. This expansion upon you is from God for a wisdom, which is to draw you on gradually through favor. Had it been an honor, the believers would have been more worthy of it than you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 213:

﴿Mankind were one community﴾, agreed upon the religion of Islam from Adam to Noah, peace be upon them both; or they were Noah and those who were with him in the ark. Then they differed, ﴿so God sent the prophets﴾. The omission of this is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿to judge between people concerning that over which they differed﴾. And the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "Mankind were one community, then they differed" (كانَ الناسُ أُمَّةً واحِدَةً فاخْتَلَفُوا). And His words, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind were not but one community, then they differed﴾ [Yunus: 19]. Or: mankind were one community of disbelievers, so God sent the prophets, and they differed concerning them. The first is the more apparent (al-awjah).

﴿Bearers of good tidings﴾ of reward for the believers, ﴿and warners﴾ of punishment for the disbelievers; these two are circumstantial clauses (hal).

﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾, meaning: with each one of them, his book, ﴿with the truth﴾, by clarifying the truth,

﴿that it might judge﴾ (God, or the Book, or the Prophet to whom it was revealed)

﴿between people concerning that over which they differed﴾, in the religion of Islam, over which they differed after agreeing,

﴿And none differed concerning it﴾ regarding the truth ﴿except those who were given it﴾, i.e., the Book revealed to remove difference; meaning, they increased in difference after the Book was sent down to them ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾ confirming its truthfulness, ﴿out of envy among themselves﴾, an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., out of jealousy among themselves, and injustice due to their greed for this world and their lack of fairness. ﴿So God guided those who believed to the truth over which they had differed﴾, meaning: God guided those who believed to the truth about which those who differed had differed,

﴿by the truth﴾ is an explanation of what they differed over, ﴿by His permission﴾, by His knowledge, ﴿and God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

﴿Am ḥasibtum﴾ (Did you think?). *Am* here is *munqaṭi'a* (disjunctive, introducing a new question), not *muttaṣila* (connective, linking to a preceding question). Its condition is that a hamza of interrogation (*hamzat al-istifhām*) precedes it, as in your saying: *a-'indaka Zaydun am 'Amrun?* (Is Zayd with you, or 'Amr?), meaning: which of the two is with you? The answer is: Zayd, if Zayd is with him, or 'Amr, if 'Amr is with him. As for the disjunctive *am*, it occurs after an interrogation and after a declarative statement, and it has the meaning of *bal* (rather) together with the hamza. The implied sense is: "Rather, did you think?" The hamza in it is for confirmation (*taqrīr*) and for denying and deeming unlikely the thinking (*inkār al-ḥusbān wa-istib'ādihi*). When He mentioned what the nations had done of disagreement regarding the prophets after the clear proofs had come, encouraging the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers to steadfastness and patience alongside those who disagreed with him among the polytheists and the People of the Book, and their denial of His signs and their enmity towards him, He said to them, in the manner of *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person), which is more eloquent: ﴿Did you think﴾ ﴿that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not come to you?﴾ That is: "and it has not come to you." In *lammā* there is the meaning of expectation (*tawaqquʿ*), that is: the arrival of that is expected and awaited.

﴿Mathalu alladhīna khalaw﴾ (The example of those who passed away): *khalaw* means *maḍaw* (passed on). That is: their condition, which is an example of hardship, ﴿from before you﴾, of the prophets and the believers. ﴿Massathumu﴾ (touched them) is an explanation of the example, and it is a resumption (*istiʾnāf*), as if a speaker said: "How was that example?" So it was said: ﴿massathumu al-basāʾ﴾ (adversity touched them), that is, *al-bu's* (misery).

﴿Wal-ḍarrāʾ﴾ (and hardship): sickness and hunger.

﴿Wa-zulzilū﴾ (and they were shaken): they were moved and agitated by various kinds of afflictions, and they were driven out with a severe driving out, resembling an earthquake (*zalzala*).

﴿Ḥattā yaqūla al-rasūlu wal-ladhīna āmanū maʿahu﴾ (until the Messenger and those who believed with him said): up to the limit at which the Messenger and those believers with him said: ﴿matā naṣru Allāh﴾ (when is the help of God?). That is: their impatience reached such a point, and they had no patience left, until they said that. Its meaning is: a request for help and a wish for it, and a prolonging of the time of hardship.

﴿Alā inna naṣra Allāhi qarīb﴾ (Surely the help of God is near): it was said to them, as a response to them, granting their request for immediate help. (*Yaqūlu*) with the *raf'* (nominative vowel) is read by Nāfi', as a narration of a past state, like your saying: "The camels drank until the camel came dragging its belly." The others read it with the *naṣb* (accusative vowel) by implying *an* (that), and the meaning is the future, because *an* marks it.

When Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man and had considerable wealth, said: "What should we spend from our wealth, and where should we place it?", there was revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend, it is for parents and near relatives and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer﴾. Thus His saying ﴿whatever good you spend﴾ included an explanation of what they spend, namely every good thing, and the speech was built upon what is more important, which is the explanation of the recipients (al-masraf), because expenditure is not counted as valid unless it is placed in its proper place. According to al-Hasan, it refers to voluntary charity (al-tatawwu'). ﴿And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, so He will reward for it.

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: He made the jihad against the disbelievers obligatory upon you. ﴿And it is hateful to you﴾: from *al-karahah* (aversion). He placed the verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of the adjective for emphasis, as in the words of the poet:

"For it is only advance and retreat"

As if the thing itself were aversion, because of their extreme aversion to it. Or it is *fu'l* in the sense of *maf'ul*, like *khubz* in the sense of *makhbuz* (bread meaning baked), i.e., "and it is disliked by you."

﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾: you dislike the raid, yet in it is one of the two good outcomes: either victory and spoils, or martyrdom and Paradise.

﴿And perhaps you love a thing﴾, which is sitting out of the raid, ﴿while it is evil for you﴾, because of the humiliation, poverty, and deprivation of spoils and reward that it entails.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what is good for you, ﴿and you do not know﴾ that. So hasten to what He commands you, even if it is hard upon you.

(p-180)

Revealed concerning an expedition (sariyya) which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent out. They fought the polytheists, and the crescent of Rajab had appeared while they did not know it. Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made the sacred month lawful, a month in which the fearful are safe."

﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ That is: the disbelievers or the Muslims ask you about fighting in the sacred month. ﴿Fighting in it﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, substitution of inclusion) from "the month." It has also been read as "ʿan qitalin fihi" (about fighting in it), with the governing verb repeated (taktir al-ʿamil), like His saying: ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 75]. ﴿Say: fighting in it is a great [sin]﴾ That is: a great sin.

﴿Fighting﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and ﴿great﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The beginning of a sentence with an indefinite noun (ibtida' bil-nakira) is permitted because it has been qualified by "in it" (fihi). Most of the opinions hold that this ruling is abrogated (mansukha) by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

﴿And barring from the way of Allah﴾ That is: the polytheists prevented the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions from the House in the year of al-Hudaybiya. It is a subject (mubtada').

﴿And disbelief in Him﴾ That is: in Allah; it is coordinated (ʿatf) with it. ﴿And the Sacred Mosque﴾ is coordinated with "the way of Allah," meaning: barring from the way of Allah and from the Sacred Mosque. al-Farra' claimed that it is coordinated with the pronoun in "bihi" (in Him), meaning: disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque. However, according to the Basrans it is not permitted to coordinate upon a pronoun in the genitive case except by repeating the preposition. So you do not say "marartu bihi wa Zayd" (I passed by him and Zayd), but you say "wa bi-Zayd" (and by Zayd). Had it been coordinated upon the pronoun here, it would have been said: "wa kufrun bihi wa bil-masjid al-haram."

﴿And expelling its people﴾ That is: the people of the Sacred Mosque, who are the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers; it is coordinated upon it, likewise, [being an object of] ﴿barring﴾, ﴿from it﴾, from the Sacred Mosque. The predicate of the three nouns is ﴿greater in the sight of Allah﴾, that is: greater than what the expedition did of fighting in the sacred month by way of error and acting on assumption.

﴿And persecution﴾ means expulsion, or polytheism.

﴿Is greater than killing﴾ in the sacred month. Or: the disbelievers' torturing of the Muslims is more abominable than the killing of these Muslims in the sacred month.

﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾ That is: to disbelief. This is a report (ikhbar) of the continuance of the disbelievers' enmity toward the Muslims, and that they will not desist from it until they turn them back from their religion. The meaning of "hatta" here is causation (ta'lil), like your saying: "So-and-so worships Allah until he enters Paradise," meaning: they fight you so that they may turn you back. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if they are able﴾ is an expression of remoteness regarding their ability, like your saying to your enemy: "If you overpower me, then do not spare me," while you are confident that he will not overpower you.

﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ That is: whoever returns from his religion to their religion.

﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ That is: dies in apostasy (riddah). ﴿Those—their deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾ because of what escapes them through apostasy of what belongs to the Muslims in this world, such as the fruits of Islam, and in the Hereafter, such as the reward and the good final return. ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide eternally.﴾ By this al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) argued that apostasy does not void the deed unless one dies upon it. We say: He has tied the voiding (habat) to the apostasy itself by His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5]. The principle with us is that the absolute (mutlaq) is not to be carried over to the qualified (muqayyad), while with him it is carried over; so this is built upon that.

When the raiding party (*al-sariyya*, a detachment sent out on a military expedition) said: "Will we have the reward of those who strive in the way of Allah?", there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated﴾, who left Makkah and their kinsfolk,

﴿and strove in the way of Allah﴾ against the polytheists. There is no pause (*waqf*, a place where one may stop when reciting) at this point, because ﴿those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*, the complement that completes the sentence after *inna*) of *inna*. It was said: "Whoever hopes, seeks; and whoever fears, flees." ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The Qur'an was revealed about wine in four verses. The first was revealed in Mecca: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palm and the grapes you take intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. So the Muslims drank it, and it was permissible for them. Then "Umar and a group of the Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling about wine, for it takes away the intellect and strips away wealth.' So ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ was revealed. Some people drank it and others abstained. Then 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf invited a group, and they drank and became intoxicated. One of them led the prayer and recited: "Say, O disbelievers, I worship what you worship," so ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] was revealed. After that, very few drank it. Then 'Utban ibn Malik invited a group, and when they became intoxicated they quarrelled and struck one another. 'Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a complete explanation regarding wine." So ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾ down to His words ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90–91] was revealed. 'Umar said: "We have desisted, O Lord."

It is also related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "If a drop fell into a well and a minaret were built on its place, I would not call the adhan from it. If it fell into the sea and it dried up and grass grew in it, I would not graze it."

Khamr (wine, a term defined as the technical term for intoxicant): that which has fermented, become strong, and thrown up foam, from the juice of grapes. It is named khamr from the verbal noun of "khamarahu," meaning he covered it, because it covers the intellect.

Maysir (gambling): qimar, a verbal noun from "yasara," like al-maw'id from its verb. One says "yasartuhu" meaning "I gambled with him." Its derivation is from yusr (ease), because it is taking a man's wealth with ease and facility, without toil or hardship, or from yasar (wealth), as if it strips him of his wealth.

The description of maysir: they had ten arrows (qidah). Seven of them had markings: the fadhdh, which has one share; the tawam, which has two; the raqib, which has three; the hils, which has four; the nafis, which has five; the musbil, which has six; and the mu'alla, which has seven. Three had no share: the manih, the safih, and the wagh. They placed the arrows in a bag, gave it to a trustworthy person, who shook it, and then drew arrows one by one in the name of a man. If the arrow drawn for him was one of those with shares, he took the share marked on that arrow. If the arrow drawn was one of those without a share, he received nothing and was made to pay the price of the whole slaughtered camel. They would give those shares to the poor and not eat from them, and they took pride in this, and they blamed anyone who did not take part in it.

Within the ruling on maysir are all kinds of gambling, such as backgammon (nard), chess (shatranj), and others. The meaning is: they ask you about what is involved in engaging in them, as shown by ﴿Say: in both is great sin﴾, through quarrelling, mutual abuse, obscene speech and falsehood.

(Kathir) is read by Hamzah and 'Ali.

﴿And benefits for people﴾ through trade in wine, and the pleasure of drinking it; and in gambling, through the support of the poor, or gaining wealth without toil.

﴿But their sin﴾ and the punishment for sin in engaging in them

﴿is greater than their benefit﴾ because drinkers and gamblers commit sins in them in many ways.

﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus (al-'afw)﴾ i.e., the excess, meaning: spend what exceeds the need. At the beginning of Islam, giving away the surplus was obligatory. If a man was a farmer, he kept a year's sustenance and gave away the surplus; if he was a craftsman, he kept his day's sustenance and gave away the surplus. Then it was abrogated (naskh, the technical term for a later ruling cancelling an earlier one) by the verse of zakat.

(al-'afw) is read by Abu 'Amr. Whoever puts it in the accusative makes ﴿madha﴾ one word in the accusative position governed by ﴿yunfiquna﴾, the sense being: "Say: they spend the surplus." Whoever puts it in the nominative makes "ma" the subject, and its predicate "dha" with its relative clause, so "dha" means "alladhi" (which), and ﴿yunfiquna﴾ is its relative clause: "What is it that they spend?" Then the answer came as "al-'afw," meaning: it is the surplus. The i'rab (grammatical inflection) of the answer is like the i'rab of the question, so that the answer corresponds to the question.

﴿Thus﴾: the kaf is in the position of accusative as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an explanation like this explanation.

﴿Allah makes the signs clear to you, so that you may reflect﴾.

**﴿in the worldly life﴾**, meaning: concerning the affairs of this world **﴿and the Hereafter﴾**. The phrase "in" (fi) is connected to "you may reflect" (tatafakkarun), meaning: you may reflect on what pertains to the two abodes, so that you take what is more beneficial for you. Or: you may reflect on the two abodes, so that you prefer the more lasting of them and the one with more benefits. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "He makes clear" (yubayyin), meaning: He makes the signs clear to you concerning the affairs of the two abodes and what pertains to them, **﴿so that you may reflect﴾**.

"When the verse ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [al-Nisa': 10] was revealed, they withdrew from the orphans, abandoned mixing with them, and looking after their property. They mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is best﴾ was revealed." That is, dealing with them in a way that sets their affairs right, both for them and for their property, is better than keeping away from them.

**﴿And if you mix with them﴾**, and associate with them, and do not keep away from them,

**﴿then they are your brothers﴾**, they are your brothers in religion, and it is among the right of a brother that he mixes with his brother.

**﴿And Allah knows the corrupter﴾** of their property **﴿from the reformer﴾** of it, so He will reward each according to his dealings. So beware of Him, and do not seek anything other than setting things right.

**﴿And if Allah had willed﴾** to cause you hardship (p-١٨٤) **﴿He would have burdened you﴾**, that is, He would have driven you to *al-'anat*, which is hardship, and would have put you in distress, and so He would not have permitted you to mix with them.

**﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾**, Overpowering, able to cause His servants hardship and distress, **﴿Wise﴾**, who does not impose on them except what is within their capacity and their strength.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 221:

When Marthad [ibn Abi Marthad] asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about marrying ʿInaq, who was a polytheist, ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ was revealed. That is, do not marry them. It is said: *nakaha* means he married, and *ankaha* ghayrahu means he gave him in marriage (he married him off).

﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheistic woman, even though she may please you.﴾ That is, even if the situation is that the polytheistic woman pleases you and you love her. ﴿And do not marry [your women to] polytheistic men﴾ and do not give them your Muslim women in marriage. This is how al-Zajjaj stated it. But the author of Jami' al-Ulum said: one of the two objects has been omitted, and the intended meaning is: do not marry them [i.e., your women] to polytheistic men.

﴿until they believe. And a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he may please you.﴾ Then He explained the reason for this, saying: ﴿Those﴾, which refers to the polytheistic women and the polytheistic men, ﴿invite to the Fire﴾, that is, to disbelief, which is the deed of the people of the Fire. Therefore it is their due that they should not be taken as allies, nor should marriage ties be made with them. ﴿But Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness﴾, that is, the friends of Allah, who are the believers, invite to Paradise and forgiveness and to whatever leads to them. They are the ones whose friendship and marriage ties must be upheld. ﴿by His permission﴾, that is, by His knowledge, or by His command,

﴿and He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember﴾, that is, that they may take heed.

The Arabs would not eat with a menstruating woman (*ḥā'iḍ*), nor drink with her, nor live in the same house with her, like the practice of the Jews and the Magians. Abu al-Dahdah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about that and said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should we deal with women when they menstruate?" So there was revealed: ﴿And they ask you about menstruation.﴾ (p-185) It is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*); one says *ḥāḍat ḥayḍan*, like your saying *jāa majīʾan*. ﴿Say: It is an injury.﴾ That is, menstruation is something filthy that harms whoever approaches it.

﴿So keep away from women during menstruation.﴾ That is, avoid them, meaning avoid having intercourse with them. It was said that the Christians used to have intercourse with them, paying no heed to menstruation, while the Jews used to keep away from them in everything, so God commanded a moderate course between the two matters. Then, according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on them both, one avoids what the wrapper (*al-izār*) covers. Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that only avoiding the genital area (*al-farj*) is obligatory. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: one avoids the place of blood (*shiʿār al-dam*), and the rest is permitted to him.

﴿And do not approach them﴾ while having intercourse with them; or, do not approach having intercourse with them.

﴿Until they are purified﴾ with the doubled *ṭāʾ* (*yaṭṭahhurna*) is read by the Kufans other than Ḥafṣ. That is, they bathe. Its original form is *yataṭahharna*; the *tāʾ* was assimilated into the *ṭāʾ* because their points of articulation are close. Others read *yaṭhurna* (*yaṭhurna*), meaning their bleeding stops. The two readings are like two verses, so we act upon both. We said that he may approach her during the majority of the menstrual period after the blood has stopped, even if she has not bathed, acting upon the light reading. In a shorter period than that, he does not approach her until she bathes, or until the time of prayer passes over her, acting upon the doubled reading. Taking it this way is better than the reverse, because in that case it would be necessary to abandon acting on one of them, for a known reason. According to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him: he does not approach her until she is pure and has purified herself. His proof is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they have purified themselves, come to them﴾, meaning have intercourse with them, thus combining the two. ﴿From where Allah has commanded you﴾ means from the place of approach that Allah has commanded you and made lawful for you, which is the front passage (*al-qubul*).

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who repent often﴾ from committing what they were forbidden, or those who return often to Allah, the Exalted; and even if they slip, they return. Love is due to their knowing the greatness of Allah's pardon, since they do not despair.

﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾ with water, or those who keep themselves clean from the backsides of women, or from intercourse during menstruation, or from indecencies.

The Jews used to say: when a man has intercourse with his wife from behind (while she is bent over, "bārika"), the child will be born squint-eyed (aḥwal). So God revealed: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, meaning: places of tilling for you. This is a metaphor: they (the women) were likened to fields (maḥārīth), by way of comparison with the drops of seed (nuṭaf) that are deposited in their wombs, from which offspring comes, likening them to seeds, and the child to the plant. The words ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ came as an explanation and clarification of His words ﴿So go in unto them from where God has commanded you﴾, that is: the place of entry that God has commanded you to use is the place of tilth, not the place of filth (farth), as an alert that the primary aim in intercourse is seeking offspring, not the satisfaction of desire. So do not approach them except from the place of entry to which this aim has been attached.

﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾: have intercourse with them whenever you wish or however you wish, whether while they are bent over, lying on their backs, or lying on their sides, provided that the place of entry is one, namely the place of tilth. This is an analogy: that is, approach them as you approach your lands that you wish to till from whatever direction you like, with no direction forbidden to you over another. His words ﴿It is a harm, so keep away from women﴾, ﴿from where God has commanded you﴾, and ﴿So go to your tilth however you wish﴾ are among the subtle allusions and the admirable indirect expressions, so every Muslim should adopt good manners with them and make an effort to use the like of them in conversation and in writing.

﴿And advance for yourselves﴾: what must be advanced of righteous deeds, and what is contrary to what you have been forbidden; or it is seeking offspring, or saying the basmala at intercourse.

﴿And fear God﴾: do not dare to commit the prohibited things.

﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾: you will return to Him, so prepare yourselves for meeting Him. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ of reward, O Muhammad.

The reason why ﴿They ask you﴾ came three times without a conjunction (waw), and then three times with a waw, is that their questioning about those first events was as if it occurred in separate circumstances, so no conjunction particle was used, since each of the questions was an independent question; and they asked about the other events at one time, so the particle of conjunction (ḥarf al-jam‘) was used for that.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 224:**

﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths.﴾ The *ʿurḍa* (عُرْضَةُ) is of the form *fuʿla* (فُعْلَةٌ) in the sense of a passive object, like *qabḍa* (handful). It is the name for what you place across something, such as a stick of wood laid across a vessel, so that it stands in its way and becomes a barrier and a prevention from it. One says: "So-and-so is an *ʿurḍa* against good," meaning he stands as an obstacle to good. A man would swear not to do some good, such as maintaining family ties (*ṣilat al-raḥim*), reconciling people who are at odds, doing kindness to someone, or worship. Then he would say: "I fear Allah that I might break my oath," and so he would abandon the righteousness he intended by his oath. So it was said to them: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ (p-187), that is: a barrier against what you have sworn to. The thing sworn to is called an oath (*yamīn*) because it is bound up with the oath, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else to be better than it, let him expiate for his oath."

As for His saying: ﴿that you be righteous and God-fearing and make peace among people﴾, it is an *ʿaṭf bayān* (explicative apposition) to *aymānikum* (your oaths), meaning: concerning the matters sworn to, which are: righteousness, piety, and reconciling people. The *lām* (in *li-aymānikum*) is connected to the verb, meaning: "And do not make Allah a barrier for your oaths." It is also permissible for the *lām* to be causal (*lil-taʿlīl*), and *an tabarrū* (that you be righteous) to be connected either to the verb or to *ʿurḍa*, meaning: "And do not make Allah, by reason of your oaths, an obstacle, so that you would be righteous." ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of your oaths, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your intentions.

﴿لا يُؤاخِذُكُمُ اللهُ بِاللَغْوِ في أيْمانِكُمْ﴾ [God will not hold you accountable for the idle (*laghw*) in your oaths]. *Al-laghw* is what falls away and is not regarded as valid, whether in speech or otherwise. *Laghw al-yamin* (idle oath) is the oath that is not regarded as valid, namely when one swears to something he believes to be as he has sworn, while the matter is otherwise. The meaning is: He will not punish you for the idle oaths that any of you utters. According to al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him), it is what runs on one's tongue without intent to swear, such as "No, by God" and "Yes, by God."

﴿وَلَكِنْ يُؤاخِذُكُمْ﴾ But He will punish you ﴿بِما كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾ for what your hearts have earned, that is, for the sin of deliberately intending to lie in an oath, namely swearing to something one knows to be contrary to what he says. This is the *yamin al-ghamus* (deliberate false oath). Al-Shafi'i relied on this text to establish the obligation of *kaffara* (expiation) for the *ghamus*, because the earning of the heart is resolve and intention. The punishment (*mu'akhadha*) is not specified here, but it is specified in al-Ma'ida, so the specification there is a specification here. We say: the punishment here is unrestricted, and it is in the abode of recompense, whereas the punishment there is restricted to the abode of trial, so it is not valid to apply the one to the other. ﴿واللهُ غَفُورٌ حَلِيمٌ﴾ And God is All-Forgiving, All-Forbearing, in that He did not punish you for the idle oaths in your oaths.

(p-١٨٨)

For those who swear off (يُؤْلُونَ) from their wives — yu'lūna: they swear (an oath). This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. "From their wives" (مِن نِسائِهِمْ) is connected to the prepositional phrase, meaning: "for those who..." — just as you say, "You have from me support, and you have from me assistance," meaning: for those who swear off from their wives.

"A waiting period of four months" (تَرَبُّصُ أرْبَعَةِ أشْهُرٍ): it is established for those who swear off that there is a waiting of four months. It is not connected to "yu'lūna," because āla (to swear off) takes the preposition ʿalā: one says, "Fulan swore off (āla ʿalā) his wife," and the saying of someone who says, "Fulan swore off (āla min) his wife," is an error he imagined from this verse. But you may say that it takes min because this oath contains the meaning of distance, so it is as if it were said: they keep away from their wives, swearing off.

"Then if they return" (فَإنْ فاءُوا) within the months — according to the reading of ʿAbd Allah: (فَإنْ فاءُوا فِيهِنَّ), i.e., they return to intercourse, turning away from persistence by abandoning it.

"Then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful" (فَإنَّ اللهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ), in that He legislated the expiation (al-kaffārah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 227:

﴿And if they are resolved upon divorce﴾, by not returning (to their wives), then wait until the period (of four months) passes. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of their oath of abstention (īlāʾ), ﴿Knowing﴾ of their intention. This is a warning against their persistence and their failure to return (fayʾah).

According to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, its meaning is: ﴿And if they return﴾ ﴿and if they are resolved﴾ after the period has passed, because the fāʾ (of ﴿fa-in﴾) denotes sequence (taʿqīb). We say: His words ﴿And if they return﴾ ﴿and if they are resolved﴾ are an elaboration (tafṣīl) of His words ﴿for those who take an oath against their wives﴾, and an elaboration follows what it elaborates, as you say: "I am your guest (nazīl) for this month; if I please you, I will stay with you until its end, and if not, I will not stay except for a short while until I move on."

﴿Wal-muṭallaqāt﴾ (And the divorced women): he means those who have been consummated with, and who have menstrual cycles (dhawāt al-aqrā').

﴿Yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna﴾ (let them wait by themselves): this is a khabar (a declarative statement) that carries the meaning of an amr (a command). The original sentence was: "wal-tatarabbaṣi al-muṭallaqāt" (let the divorced women wait). Expressing the command in the form of a declarative statement is an emphasis on the command, and an indication that it is something that must be received with haste in carrying it out. It is as if they have already complied with the command to wait, so the statement reports it as existing. A similar case is the common supplication "raḥimaka Allāh" (may God have mercy on you), which is expressed in the form of a declarative statement out of confidence in being answered, as if the mercy had already occurred, so it reports on it. Its construction as a nominal sentence (mubtada') also adds further emphasis, because the nominal sentence indicates permanence and stability, unlike the verbal sentence. Mentioning "anfus" (selves) stirs them up to wait and adds further incitement, because women's souls are inclined toward men. So they are commanded to restrain their souls, overcome their desires, and compel themselves to wait.

﴿Thalāthata qurū'﴾ (three menstrual periods): the plural of qur' or qar', which means menstruation (ḥayḍ), according to his (ﷺ) saying: "Leave off prayer during your days of menstruation (aqrā'ik)." And his saying: "The divorce of a slave woman is two pronouncements, and her waiting period is two menstruations." He did not say "two purities." And God's saying: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Ṭalāq: 4]. Here He placed months in the position of menstruation, not of purities. Also, the purpose of the waiting period is to establish that the womb is clear, and it is menstruation, not purity, by which the womb is cleared. That is why the clearing of a slave woman is by one menstruation. Furthermore, if it were a purity, as al-Shāfi'ī said, the waiting period would be completed by two purities and part of the third, so the count would fall short of three. For if he divorced her at the end of a purity, that part is counted from the waiting period according to him, but if he divorced her at the end of a menstruation, that part is not counted from the waiting period according to us. The word "thalāth" (three) is a specific term for a particular number and does not apply to anything less than it. It is said: "aqrat al-mar'ah" when the woman menstruated, and "imra'ah muqri'" (a woman who menstruates). The accusative of "thalātha" is either because it is an object (maf'ūl bihi), meaning: they wait for the passing of three menstrual periods, or because it is an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning: they wait for the duration of three menstrual periods. The specifier (mumayyiz) came in the plural of abundance (jam' al-kathrah) rather than the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah), which is "aqrā'," because both share the sense of plurality, which is a broadening of usage. Perhaps "qurū'" was more commonly used as the plural of "qar'" than "aqrā'," so it was preferred over it, treating the rarely used form as if it were not used at all.

﴿Wa-lā yaḥillu lahunna an yaktumna mā khalaqa Allāh fī arḥāmihinna﴾ (And it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs): this refers to the child, or to the blood of menstruation, or to both. This applies when a woman wants to separate from her husband, so she conceals her pregnancy, so that he does not wait until she gives birth before divorcing her, and so that he does not feel compassion for the child and thereby abandon the divorce. Or she conceals her menstruation and says, while she is menstruating: "I have become pure," in haste for the divorce. ﴿If you truly believe in God and the Last Day﴾: this magnifies their action, because whoever believes in God and His punishment does not dare to commit such a grave matter.

﴿Wa-bu'ūluhunna﴾ (And their husbands): "al-bu'ūl" is the plural of "ba'l" (husband), and the "tā'" is attached to indicate the feminine form of the plural.

﴿Aḥaqqu bi-raddihinna﴾ (have more right to take them back): that is, their husbands are more entitled to their return (raj'ah). In this there is evidence that a revocable divorce (ṭalāq raj'ī) does not prohibit sexual intercourse, since He called him a husband after the divorce. ﴿In that﴾: during the period of that waiting. The meaning is that if the man wants to take her back, and the woman refuses, it is obligatory to prefer his word over hers, and he has more right than she does, not that she has a right to the return.

﴿If they desire﴾ by the return ﴿reconciliation﴾ between them and themselves, and kindness toward them, and they do not intend to harm them.

﴿And they (women) have rights similar to those they have (over men)﴾: it is obligatory for them, from the rights upon men, to receive the dower, maintenance, good companionship, and abstention from harm, similar to what is due to the men ﴿over them﴾ in command and prohibition,

﴿according to what is reasonable﴾: in the manner that is not rejected by the Sharī'ah and the customs of people. So neither spouse should burden the other with what is not his or her due. The meaning of "similarity" is the similarity of an obligation to an obligation in being a good deed, not in the kind of action. So it is not obligatory for him, if she washes his clothes or bakes for him, to do the same, but he should reciprocate with what is fitting for men. ﴿And men have a degree over them﴾: an increase in right, and a superiority through their responsibility for her affairs, even though they share in pleasure and enjoyment, and through maintenance, and through ownership by marriage.

﴿And God is Mighty﴾: His affairs cannot be questioned,

﴿Wise﴾: He commands only what is correct and good.

﴿The divorce is twice﴾. Al-talaq (divorce) here carries the sense of al-tatliq (the act of pronouncing divorce), like al-salam in the sense of al-taslim. That is, the lawful divorce is one pronouncement after another, separated, not gathered together and sent all at once. The "twice" does not mean the dual number but repetition, as in His saying: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning one glance after another, not two glances. This is evidence for us that gathering two or three pronouncements together in one tuhr (purity period) is a bid'ah (innovation, something introduced into the religion without basis), because God Most High commanded us to separate them. Although the form of the verse is a report, its meaning is a command. Otherwise it would lead to a contradiction in the report of God Most High, since divorce in the manner of gathering does sometimes occur. It is said that a woman of the Ansar said: "My husband said, 'I will not stop divorcing you and then taking you back,'" so the verse ﴿The divorce is twice﴾ was revealed, meaning the revocable divorce is twice, because there is no return (raj'ah) after the third.

﴿Then retain in good fellowship﴾, by taking back. (p-191) The meaning: it is obligatory upon you to retain in good fellowship, ﴿or release with kindness﴾, by not taking her back until she becomes separated by the 'iddah (waiting period). It is said: by divorcing her a third time in the third purity period. It was revealed concerning Jamila and her husband Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas. She hated him, while he loved her, and he had given her a garden. She sought khul' (divorce by compensation) from him in exchange for it, and this was the first khul' in Islam. ﴿And it is not lawful for you﴾, O husbands or rulers, because they are the ones who command the taking and giving when the matter is brought before them, so they are as if they were the ones taking and giving,

﴿to take back anything of what you have given them﴾, of the dowries you have given them, ﴿unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of God﴾, unless the spouses know that they will fail to observe the limits of God in what is required of them as marital obligations, because of the disobedience (nushuz) of the woman and her bad conduct,

﴿But if you fear﴾, O rulers, and it is permissible that the beginning of the address be to the husbands and its end to the judges, ﴿that they will not keep within the limits of God, then there is no blame upon them both﴾, meaning there is no blame upon the man for what he takes, nor upon her for what she gives,

﴿concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾, meaning by which she ransoms her own self and obtains khul' by giving up what she was given of the dowry. (Unless both fear) — Hamza reads it in the passive voice, and (that they will not keep) is a substitution (badal) for the alif of the pronoun, which is badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), like: "Zayd was feared, his abandoning the observance of the limits of God." ﴿These are the limits of God﴾, meaning what He has set as limits concerning marriage, oaths, ila' (vow of abstinence from wives), divorce, khul', and other matters.

﴿So do not transgress them﴾, do not go beyond them by opposing them. ﴿And whoever transgresses the limits of God, those are the wrongdoers﴾, those who harm themselves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 230:

﴿Then if he divorces her⦆ a third time after the two. If you say: "Khul' (divorce for consideration, the wife's release by payment) is a divorce according to us, and likewise according to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, in one opinion, so this would be a fourth pronouncement," I say: khul' is a divorce with a consideration, so it counts as a third pronouncement, and this verse explains that (the previous statement). That is, if he divorces her the third time with a consideration, then the ruling of tahlil (the rule that the woman becomes lawful again to her former husband) is as stated. ﴿Then she is not lawful to him thereafter⦆, that is, after the third pronouncement, ﴿until she marries a husband other than him⦆, until another man marries her. The verb nikah (marriage) is ascribed to the woman just as it is ascribed to the man, as with tazawwuj (to marry). In this there is evidence that the marriage contract is concluded by the woman's own expression. The requirement of consummation is established by the hadith of al-'Usaylah (the hadith about the wife's tasting of the second husband's sweetness), as is known in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence). The legal reasoning behind it is that, since he had proceeded to separation and no way remained for regret, she is not lawful to him except by the entry of a stallion (a man) upon her, so that he refrains from repeating it. ﴿Then if he divorces her⦆, the second husband, after intercourse, ﴿there is no blame upon them both⦆, upon the first husband and upon her, ﴿that they return to one another⦆, that each of them return to the other by marriage.

﴿If they both think that they will keep the limits of God⦆: if in their assumption they will uphold the rights of marriage. He did not say "if they know that they will uphold," because certainty is hidden from them, and none knows it except God. ﴿And these are the limits of God, which He makes clear⦆, and with the letter nun (reading "nubayyinuha," "We make clear," in the first person plural), it is the preferred reading, ﴿for a people who know⦆, who understand what He has made clear to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 231:

﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term (ajal)﴾ meaning: the end of their ʿidda (waiting period), and they are close to its completion. The word ajal applies to the whole span of a period and also to its last part. It is said of a person's lifespan: ajal, and of the death by which it ends: ajal.

﴿Then either retain them honorably or release them honorably﴾ meaning: either he takes her back without intending harm by the return, or he leaves her until her ʿidda ends and she becomes separated from him without harm.

﴿And do not retain them to their harm﴾ is a direct object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: intending to harm them. A man would divorce a woman and leave her until her ʿidda was nearly over, then take her back, not out of need, but in order to prolong the waiting period over her. This is retaining her to harm her.

﴿So that you may transgress﴾ meaning: so that you may wrong them, or so that you may force them into seeking ransom (iftidā).

﴿And whoever does that﴾ meaning: retaining them for harm,

﴿has wronged himself﴾ by exposing himself to the punishment of Allah.

﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest﴾ meaning: be earnest in acting upon them, practising what is in them, and observe them with proper observance; otherwise you would have taken them in jest. It is said of one who is not earnest in a matter: "You are merely a player and a mocker."

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ (p-193) through Islam and through the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and what He has sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom﴾ of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and He mentioned them in contrast with gratitude and fulfilling their right, ﴿He admonishes you with it﴾ with what He has sent down to you, and this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), ﴿and fear Allah﴾ regarding what He has tested you with, ﴿and know that Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ of remembrance, of guarding oneself, of taking admonition, and other matters, and this is the most eloquent of promise and warning.

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾, i.e., their waiting period ('idda) has ended. The context of the two statements indicates that the two instances of "reaching" are different, because marriage follows it here, and that happens after the waiting period, whereas in the first there is return (raj'a), and that happens during the waiting period. ﴿Do not prevent them﴾, i.e., do not hinder them. ʿAḍl means prevention and restriction. ﴿From marrying﴾ ﴿their husbands﴾, those whom they desire and who are suitable for them. This contains an indication that marriage is concluded by the expression of the women. The address is to the husbands who prevent their wives, unjustly, after the waiting period has ended, and do not leave them free to marry whichever husbands they wish. They were called "husbands" by the name of what they would become. Or the address is to the guardians regarding preventing the women from returning to their husbands, who had been their husbands; they were called "husbands" in consideration of what they had been. It was revealed concerning Maʿqil ibn Yasar when he prevented his sister from returning to her first husband. Or the address is to people in general, i.e., there should be no prevention among you, because if it occurs among them while the parties are content, they are in the status of those who prevent.

﴿When they agree among themselves﴾, when the suitors and the women agree ﴿in a reasonable manner﴾, with what is good in religion and decency of conditions, or with a bridal payment (mahr) equal to that of peers and a suitable match (kafāʾa), because when either of these is absent, the guardians may object. The address in ﴿that﴾ is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to each individual. ﴿By which is admonished whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾, for admonition only succeeds with them. ﴿That﴾, i.e., abandoning prevention and harm, ﴿is purer and more wholesome for you﴾, i.e., for you, from the filth of sins; or "purer and more wholesome" means more excellent and better. ﴿Allah knows﴾ what purity and cleanness there is in that, ﴿and you do not know﴾ it.

(p-194)

﴿Wal-wālidātu yurḍi'na awlādahunna﴾ (﴿And the mothers shall breastfeed their children﴾) is a informative statement (khabar) with the meaning of a emphatic command, like ﴿yatarabbaṣna﴾ (﴿they shall wait﴾). This command is either a recommendation (nadb), or an obligation (wujūb) when the child will accept only his mother's breast, or no wet-nurse (ẓi'r) can be found for him, or the father is unable to hire one, or the intended mothers are divorced women. The obligation of maintenance (nafaqah) and clothing (kiswah) is because of the breastfeeding. ﴿Ḥawlayni﴾ is an adverb of time (ẓarf). ﴿Kāmilayni﴾ means complete. This is an emphasis, because it is something one is lenient about: you say, "I stayed with so-and-so for two years," and you did not complete them. ﴿Liman arāda an yutimma al-raḍā'ah﴾ (﴿for whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding﴾) is a clarification of the person to whom the ruling is addressed, i.e., this ruling is for whoever wishes to complete the breastfeeding. The summary is that the father is obligated to have his child breastfed, not the mother, and he must hire a wet-nurse for him, unless the mother volunteers to breastfeed him. She is encouraged to do so, but is not compelled to it, and it is not permissible to hire the mother as long as she is a wife or in her waiting period ('iddah).

﴿Wa-ʿalā al-mawlūdi lahū﴾ (﴿and upon the one to whom the child is born﴾): the pronoun (hā') refers back to the lām in the sense of alladhī (the one who). The estimate is: "and upon the one to whom a child is born, who is the father." The word ﴿lahu﴾ is in a position of nominative (raf') by way of agency (fā'iliyyah), like ﴿ʿalayhim﴾ in ﴿al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim﴾ [al-Fatiḥah: 7]. It was said "upon the one to whom the child is born" rather than "upon the father," so that it would be known that the mothers gave birth to them for them, since children belong to the fathers and lineage is traced to them, not to the women. Therefore, it is incumbent upon them to provide for the women and clothe them when they breastfeed their children, like wet-nurses. Do you not see that He mentioned him by the name of "father" where this meaning is not intended? This is His saying: ﴿wa-ḫshawā yawman lā yajzī wālidun ʿan waladihi wa-lā mawlūdun huwa jāzin ʿan wālidihi shay'ā﴾ [Luqmān: 33] (﴿And fear a day when no father will avail his son, nor will a son avail his father at all﴾).

﴿Rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna bil-ma'rūf﴾ (﴿Their provision and their clothing according to what is customary﴾) means without extravagance and without stinginess. Its explanation is what follows it, which is that neither of them burdens the other with what is beyond his capacity, and that neither of them harms the other. ﴿Lā tukallafu nafsun illā wus'ahā﴾ (﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾): ﴿wus'ahā﴾ means its ability, or its capacity to bear. Taklīf (burdening) is imposing what is difficult to bear. The accusative of ﴿wus'ahā﴾ is as a second object of ﴿tukallafu﴾, not as an exception, and ﴿illā﴾ came between the two objects.

﴿Lā tuḍārra﴾ (﴿shall not be harmed﴾): Makkī and Baṣrī read it with a nominative (raf') by way of informative statement (ikhbār), and its meaning is prohibition (nahy). It may be read in the active voice or the passive voice, and the original may be tuḍārri with a kasra on the rāʾ, or tuḍārra with a fatḥa on it. The rest of the readers (read it as) ﴿lā tuḍārra﴾ as a prohibition. The original is tuḍārirhu: the first rāʾ was made quiescent (sukūn) and it was assimilated (idghām) into the second after it was made quiescent. Then the two quiescent letters met, so the second was given a fatḥah because of the meeting of the two quiescent letters.

﴿Wālidatun bi-waladihā﴾ (﴿a mother [shall not be harmed] because of her child﴾) means: a mother shall not be harmed by her husband because of her child, by his scolding her over it and demanding from her what is not just of provision and clothing, and by distracting his heart from neglecting the matter of the child, and by saying, after the child has become accustomed to her: "Look for a wet-nurse for him," and what is similar to that. ﴿Wa-lā mawlūdun lahū bi-waladihi﴾ (﴿nor a father because of his child﴾) means: nor shall the father harm his wife because of his child, by withholding from her anything that is obligatory upon him of her provision and clothing, or by taking the child from her while she wishes to breastfeed him.

When it is in the passive voice (mabnī lil-mafʿūl), it is a prohibition against harm reaching her from the side of the husband, and against harm reaching the husband from her side because of the child.

Or ﴿tuḍārra﴾ means ﴿taḍurru﴾ (to harm), and the bāʾ is part of its complement. That is: a mother shall not harm her child, so she does not mistreat his nourishment and care, and she does not hand him over to the father after he has become accustomed to her, and the father shall not harm him by snatching him from her hand, or by falling short in her rights, so she falls short in the rights of the child. It was said "with her child" and "with his child" because, when the woman was forbidden from causing harm, the child was attributed to her to win her compassion for him, and likewise for the father.

﴿Wa-ʿalā al-wārith﴾ (﴿And upon the heir﴾) is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon His saying: ﴿wa-ʿalā al-mawlūdi lahū rizquhunna wa-kiswatuhunna﴾. What lies between them is an explanation of al-maʿrūf, an interjection (muʿtariḍ) between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. That is: and upon the heir of the child, when the father is absent, ﴿mith'lu dhālika﴾ (﴿the like of that﴾), i.e., the like of what was upon his father during his life of provision and clothing. This was disputed: according to Ibn Abī Laylā, it is everyone who inherits from him. According to us, it is whoever is a close relative (dhū raḥim) within the prohibited degrees (muḥarram) of him, due to the reading of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): ﴿wa-ʿalā al-wārithi dhī al-raḥimi al-muḥarrami mith'lu dhālika﴾. According to al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah have mercy on him), there is no maintenance except for the children.

﴿Fa-in arādā﴾ (﴿Then if they both desire﴾), meaning: the two parents, ﴿fiṣālan﴾ (﴿weaning﴾), i.e., a weaning proceeding ﴿ʿan tarāḍin minhumā wa-tashāwur﴾ (﴿from mutual consent between them both and consultation﴾), ﴿fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā﴾ (﴿then there is no blame upon them both﴾) in that, whether they exceed the two years or fall short of them. This is an expansion (tawsiʿah) after a limit (taḥdīd). Tashāwur (consultation) is the extraction of an opinion, from shirtu al-ʿasal (I extracted the honey), when you extract it. He mentioned it so that the mutual consent would be based on reflection, so that it would not harm the suckling infant. So glory be to the One who disciplined the adult and did not neglect the infant. He required their agreement, because the father has lineage and guardianship, and the mother has compassion and care.

﴿Wa-in aradtum an tastarḍiʿū awlādakum﴾ (﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children﴾), i.e., for your children, according to al-Zajjāj. It was also said: istarḍaʿa is transitive from arḍaʿa. It is said: "the woman breastfed the child" (arḍaʿat al-mar'ah al-ṣabiyya), and "I had her breastfeed the child for me" (istarḍaʿtuhā al-ṣabiyya), transitive to two objects, i.e., that you seek wet-nurses (al-marāḍiʿ) for your children, so one of the two objects is omitted, meaning other than the mother when she refuses or is unable. ﴿Fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum idhā sallamtum﴾ (﴿then there is no blame upon you when you hand over﴾) to the wet-nurses ﴿mā ātaytum﴾ (﴿what you give﴾), i.e., what you intend to give of wages (ujrah). (Ātaytum) is Makkī, from atā ilayhi iḥsānan (he did good to him) when he did it, and from it His saying: ﴿kāna waʿduhu ma'tiyyā﴾ [Maryam: 61], i.e., fulfilled. Handing over (taslīm) is recommended (nadb), not a condition for permissibility. ﴿Bil-maʿrūf﴾ (﴿according to what is customary﴾) is connected to sallamtum, i.e., you hand over the wage to the wet-nurses with good will and joy.

﴿Wa-ttaqū Allāha wa-iʿlamū anna Allāha bimā taʿmalūna baṣīr﴾ (﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾): your deeds are not hidden from Him, so He will reward you for them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 234:

﴿Those of you who die﴾. It is said: *tawaffaytu al-shay'* and *istawfaytuhu*, when you take a thing in full and complete. That is, their lives are taken in full (*tustawfā arwāḥuhum*). ﴿And leave behind﴾ and abandon ﴿wives who shall wait, keeping themselves﴾. That is, the wives of those of you who die shall wait, meaning they shall observe the *'iddah* (the waiting period). Or its meaning is: they shall wait after them, keeping themselves, and *ba'dahum* ("after them") was omitted because it is known. It was necessary to supply it, because a returning pronoun must refer back to the subject (*mubtada'*) in the clause that serves as the predicate (*khabar*). The verb *yatawaffawna* is in the *mufaddal* form, that is, *yastawfūna ājālahum* ("they take their full terms").

﴿Four months and ten﴾, that is, and ten nights. The days are included along with them. The masculine form is not used for it, out of regard for the days. You say *ṣumtu 'ashran* ("I fasted ten"), and if you used the masculine you would depart from their speech.

﴿When they have reached their term﴾, that is, when their *'iddah* has ended. ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, O leaders and rulers, ﴿for what they do with themselves﴾, such as presenting themselves to suitors, ﴿in a proper manner﴾, in the way that the Shari'ah does not disapprove. ﴿And God is All-Aware of what you do﴾, knowing the inner secrets.

(p-197)

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at in proposing to women﴾. Khitba (خِطْبَة, proposal of marriage) means istinkah (اسْتِنْكاح, seeking to marry her). Ta'rid (تَعْرِيض, allusion) is that you say to her: "Indeed you are beautiful," or "righteous," or "I have a purpose of marrying," and similar speech that implies one wishes to marry her, so that she may hold herself back for him if she is inclined to him, without stating the marriage explicitly. So one does not say, "I think I should marry you." The difference between kinaya (كِنايَة, indirect expression by substitution) and ta'rid is that kinaya is mentioning a thing by other than its proper term, while ta'rid is mentioning a thing by which you indicate another thing you did not mention. This is like a needy person saying to one from whom he needs something: "I came to greet you, and to look upon your noble face." Hence they said:

"And let my greeting to you be enough as a claim."

So it is the inclining of speech toward a purpose that points to the purpose. ﴿Or what you conceal within yourselves﴾, or what you hide and harbor in your hearts, so that you do not mention it with your tongues, neither by allusion nor by explicit statement.

﴿Allah knows that you will mention them﴾ without doubt, and that you will not refrain from speaking of your desire for them. So mention them. ﴿But do not make a promise to them in secret﴾, meaning intercourse, because it is among the things kept secret. That is: do not say, during the waiting period: "I am able to do this deed."

﴿Except that you say a fair saying﴾, which is that you allude and do not state explicitly.
