Here "illa" (إلا, except) is connected to "la tuwa'idu-hunna" (لا تُواعِدُوهُنَّ, do not promise them): that is, do not make any promise at all, except a promise that is known and not objectionable. ﴿And do not determine the knot of marriage﴾, from 'azama al-amr (عَزَمَ الأمْر, he resolved the matter) and 'azama 'alayhi (عَزَمَ عَلَيْهِ, he resolved upon it). The mention of 'azm (عَزْم, resolve) is for emphasis in forbidding the contracting of marriage, because resolve to an act precedes it, so when one is forbidden from the resolve, one is more forbidden from the act. Its meaning: do not resolve to conclude the contract of the marriage knot, or do not cut off the marriage knot, because the true meaning of 'azm is cutting. From this is the hadith: "There is no fast for one who does not resolve the fast from the night." It is also narrated: "For one who does not make the fast a firm intention (lam yubayyit al-siyam)." That is: do not resolve upon the knot of marriage ﴿until the prescribed term reaches its end﴾, until her 'idda (عِدَّة, waiting period) ends. The 'idda was called a kitab (كِتاب, a written term) because it was enjoined by the Book; that is, until the waiting that is prescribed for her reaches its appointed end, meaning its limit.

﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls﴾ of resolve upon what is not permitted, ﴿so beware of Him﴾, and do not resolve upon it. ﴿And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾, who does not hasten to punish you.

And it was revealed concerning one who divorces his wife when he has not yet specified a bridal gift (mahr) for her and has not consummated the marriage: ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, meaning there is no liability upon you for the obligation to pay a mahr.

﴿If you divorce women﴾ is a conditional clause (shart). Its response is indicated by ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, and the full sense is: if you divorce women, then there is no blame upon you ﴿so long as you have not touched them﴾, meaning so long as you have not had intercourse with them. The word "ma" here is conditional (shartiyyah), meaning: if you have not touched them. Hamzah and ʿAli read "tamāssūhunna" (with the alif) wherever it occurs, because the action is between two parties. ﴿Or you have specified for them an obligation﴾ means: unless you specify for them an obligation, or until you specify it. The fixing of an obligation (farīḍah) is the naming of the mahr. This is because a divorced woman who has not been touched is entitled to half of the named mahr if a mahr was named for her. If no mahr was named for her, then she is not entitled to half of the mahr of equivalent (mahr al-mithl); rather, a provision (mutʿah) becomes obligatory. ﴿And provide for them﴾ is coordinated with a verb omitted from the text, its implied sense being: so divorce them, and provide for them. The mutʿah is a shirt, a wrap-cloth, and a head-covering.

﴿For the affluent﴾ is the one who has means, ﴿according to his capacity﴾, meaning his amount which he is able to bear. (Qadaruhu) in both places is read by the Kufans other than Abu Bakr, and these are two dialects. ﴿And for the straitened﴾ is the one whose circumstances are constrained. The proof that "blame" means liability for the mahr is His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them﴾ up to His saying ﴿then half of what you have specified﴾; so His saying ﴿then half of what you have specified﴾ is an affirmation of the blame that was negated there. ﴿According to his capacity﴾. In our school, the mutʿah is obligatory only for this case, and it is recommended for the rest of the divorced women. ﴿A provision﴾ is an emphatic restatement of "provide for them", meaning: providing. ﴿According to what is reasonable﴾ means in the manner that is good in the Shariʿah and in custom. ﴿As a duty﴾ is a qualifier of "a provision", meaning: a provision that is obligatory upon them; or it means: the right of that is a right.

﴿Upon the good-doers﴾ means upon the Muslims, or upon those who act kindly toward the divorced women by providing for them. He called them "good-doers" before the act, like His saying ﷺ: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, his spoils belong to him." This kindness is not the voluntary giving of what is not obligatory upon him, since this provision is obligatory. (p-١٩٩)

Then He explained the ruling concerning the woman for whom a dower had been specified, in the case of divorce before consummation. He said: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them﴾ — "an" together with the verb, interpreted as a verbal noun (maṣdar), is in the genitive position, meaning: "before your touching them."

﴿And you have already specified for them an obligation﴾ — in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) — ﴿a dower (farīḍah)﴾, i.e., a dower, ﴿then half of what you have specified, unless they forgive﴾ — he means the divorced women — "an" together with the verb is in the accusative position as an exception, as if it were said: "Then for you is half of what you have specified at all times, except the time of their forgoing it from you of the dower." The difference between "al-rijāl yaʿfūna" (the men forgive) and "al-nisāʾ yaʿfūna" (the women forgive) is that the wāw in the first is their pronoun and the nūn is the sign of the nominative, while the wāw in the second is the lām of the verb and the nūn is their pronoun; and the verb is indeclinable, so the governing agent has no effect on its form.

﴿Or [unless] he forgoes﴾ — coordinated with its place (maḥall) — ﴿the one in whose hand is the tie of marriage﴾, which is the husband. So ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, explained it, and this is the view of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Shurayḥ, Mujāhid, Abū Ḥanīfah, and al-Shāfiʿī in his new opinion (al-jadīd), may Allah be pleased with them all. This is because divorce is in his hand, so the continuation of the contract is in his hand. The meaning is: the obligation under the Law is half, unless she waives the whole, or he gives the whole as a favour. According to Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī in his old opinion (al-qadīm), it is the guardian (walī). We reply: he does not have the authority to make a gift of the minor's right, so how is it permissible to interpret it as referring to him?

﴿And that you forgo﴾ — a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿nearer to piety﴾ — and the address is to the husbands and wives by way of predominance (taghlīb), as mentioned by al-Zajjāj. That is: the husband's forgoing by giving the full dower is better for him, and the wife's forgoing by waiving all of it is better for her. Or the address is to the husbands alone.

﴿And do not forget graciousness﴾ — preference (tafḍīl) — ﴿among yourselves﴾, i.e., do not forget that some of you should show grace to one another. ﴿Indeed Allah, of what you do, is All-Seeing﴾, so He will reward you for your graciousness.

[p. 200] **﴿Guard over the prayers﴾**: be constant in them, observing their appointed times, their pillars (arkan), and their conditions (shara'it).

**﴿And the middle prayer﴾**: between the prayers. That is, the most excellent one. From their saying of the most excellent thing: "the middle" (al-awsat). It was singled out and joined to "the prayers" because of its distinction. It is the 'Asr prayer according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars hold this view, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of the Confederates: "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr. May God fill their houses with fire." He (ﷺ) also said: "It is the prayer that Solomon was preoccupied with until it was hidden behind the veil." In the codex (mushaf, written copy of the Qur'an) of Hafsa, the reading is: "and the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr." It is also because it lies between the night prayers and the day prayers. He gave it distinction because of the preoccupation of people with their trade and livelihood at its time. It has been said that it is the Dhuhr prayer, because it is in the middle of the day; or the Fajr prayer, because it lies between the day prayers and the night prayers; or the Maghrib prayer, because it lies between the four-rak'a and two-rak'a prayers, and because it lies between two quiet prayers and two loud prayers; or the 'Isha' prayer, because it lies between two odd-numbered prayers (witr). Or it is unspecified, like the Night of Power, so that they will guard all of them.

**﴿And stand before God﴾** in prayer **﴿in devotion﴾**: a circumstantial state (hal), meaning obedient and humble, or remembering God in your standing. Qunut means that you mention God while standing, or that you prolong the standing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 239:

﴿Then if you fear﴾ that is, if there is fear for you from an enemy or something else,

﴿on foot﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: pray on foot. It is the plural of rājil (one on foot), like qā'im and qiyām (standing).

﴿or riding﴾ singly, by gesture (bi-īmā'), and in this case facing the qibla is dropped.

﴿Then when you are secure﴾ that is, when your fear has gone, ﴿remember God﴾ — pray the prayer of security — ﴿as He taught you﴾ that is, a remembrance like that which He taught you ﴿what you did not know﴾ of the prayer of security.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 240:

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind—let them bequeath for their wives a provision for a year without their being turned out.﴾ With the accusative (bi-l-nasb, wa-siyyatan), it is read by Ibn ʿĀmir (al-Shāmī), Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ; meaning: "fa-l-yūṣū wasiyyatan" (let them make a bequest), from al-Zajjāj. Others read it in the nominative (bi-l-raf‘), meaning: "fa-ʿalayhim wasiyyatun" (so for them there is a bequest). ﴿Matāʿan﴾ is in the accusative by the verbal noun "al-wasiyyah," since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar); or its implied form is: "matticūhunna matāʿan" (provide for them a provision).

﴿Ilā al-ḥawl﴾ (until the year) is an attributive modifier of matāʿan. ﴿Ghayra ikhrāj﴾ (without being turned out) is an emphatic verbal noun, as in your saying: "hādhā al-qawl ghayru mā taqūl" (this statement is other than what you say); or it is a substitute (badal) for matāʿan. The meaning is: the right of those who die leaving wives is that they should make a bequest before they are at the point of death, that their wives should enjoy (provision) after them for a full year, meaning that they are to be maintained from his estate, and they are not to be turned out of their dwellings. This was prescribed at the beginning of Islam, then it was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind…﴾ up to His saying: ﴿four months and ten days﴾. The abrogating verse precedes it in recitation (tilāwah) but comes later in revelation (nuzūl), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The foolish among the people will say…﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] together with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

﴿Fa-in kharajna﴾ (But if they leave) after the year, ﴿fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fī mā faʿalna fī anfusihinna﴾ (there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves), of adornment and presenting themselves to suitors.

﴿Min maʿrūf﴾ (of what is proper), that which is not forbidden by the Law. ﴿Wa-llāhu ʿazīzun ḥakīm﴾ (And God is Mighty, Wise) in what He decrees.

﴿For divorced women is a provision﴾ That is: the maintenance (nafaqah) for the waiting period (ʿiddah, the prescribed period a woman must observe before remarrying after divorce or widowhood).

﴿according to what is reasonable, as a right﴾ "حَقًّا" is in the accusative (naṣb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a verbal noun in the accusative that emphasizes or specifies the verb).

﴿upon the God-fearing﴾

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, that you may understand.﴾ It is in the place of nominative case (raf'), because it is the predicate (khabar) of la'alla (perhaps/that). If by it is meant the provision (mut'ah), then what is meant is other than the divorced woman mentioned, and it is by way of recommendation (nadb).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 243:

﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is an affirmation addressed to whoever has heard their story from the People of the Book and the reports of the earlier generations, and an expression of wonder at their condition. It is permissible that it be addressed to one who neither saw nor heard it, because this statement has taken the form of a proverb in the sense of expressing wonder.

﴿Of those who went out from their homes﴾ from a town. It is said it was Wasit, where the plague (ṭāʿūn) broke out among them, so they fled, and God caused them to die, then brought them back to life through the supplication of Ḥizqīl (peace be upon him). It is also said they were a people of the Children of Israel whom their king called to jihad, so they fled for fear of death, and God caused them to die for eight days, then brought them back to life. ﴿And they were thousands﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it contains evidence for the large number of thousands, since ʾulūf is a plural of abundance (jamʿ kathra), and it is the plural of alf (thousand), not ʾālif.

﴿Fear of death﴾ is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). ﴿So God said to them, "Die"﴾ meaning: God caused them to die. It was phrased in this manner to indicate that they died as one man's death, by the command and will of God, and that is a death outside the usual custom. In it is an encouragement to the Muslims to engage in jihad, and that if death is unavoidable and there is no escape from it, it is more fitting that it be in the way of God.

﴿Then He brought them back to life﴾ so that they might take heed and know that there is no escape from the judgment and decree of God. It is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to a deleted verb whose estimate is: "So they died, then He brought them back to life." Or, since the meaning of His words ﴿So God said to them, "Die"﴾ is "so He caused them to die," the conjunction to it carries the meaning of ﴿Indeed, God is bounteous to mankind﴾, in that He shows them what they may take heed from, just as He showed those, and just as He showed you by relating their account. Or, He is bounteous to mankind in that He brought those back to life so that they might take heed and thereby prosper. Had He willed, He would have left them dead until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿But most people do not give thanks﴾ for that.

The evidence that he related this story as an incitement to jihad is what follows it of the command to fight in the way of Allah, namely His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾. So He urged to jihad after informing that fleeing from death does not avail. This address is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), or to those whom He brought to life. ﴿And know that Allah is All-Hearing﴾, He hears what those who stay behind and those who go forth say.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what they conceal.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 245:**

﴿مَن﴾ is an interrogative (*istifham*) in the position of the nominative by inception (*raf' bil-ibtida'*), and ﴿ذا﴾ is its predicate (*khabar*). ﴿الَّذِي﴾ is either a qualifier (*na't*) of ﴿ذا﴾ or a substitute (*badal*) for it.

﴿يُقْرِضُ اللهَ﴾ is the relative clause (*silah*) of ﴿الَّذِي﴾. What is spent in the way of Allah is called a loan (*qard*), because a loan is what is given out in exchange for a like return later. It is named thus because the lender cuts it (*yaqta'uhu*) from his wealth and hands it over to the borrower. *Al-qard* means cutting, and from the same root come *al-miqrad* (scissors), *qarḍ al-fa'r* (a mouse's gnawing), and *al-inqirad* (extinction). By this, He alerts them that it is not lost in His presence, and that He will certainly repay them for it.

﴿قَرْضًا حَسَنًا﴾: with a good heart, from good wealth. The intended meaning is spending in jihad, because when He commanded fighting in (p-٢٠٣) the way of Allah, which requires wealth, He urged them to give charity so that the means of jihad might be made ready.

﴿فَيُضاعِفَهُ لَهُ﴾: with the *nasb* (accusative) reading, ʿĀṣim (reads it so), as an answer to the interrogative; with the *raf'* (nominative) reading, Abū ʿAmr, Nāfiʿ, Ḥamzah and ʿAlī, as a coordination (*'atf*) upon ﴿يُقْرِضُ﴾, or it is a new independent clause (*mustaʾnaf*), meaning: "so He doubles it." (﴿فَيُضَعِّفَهُ﴾) is Shāmī's reading; (﴿فَيَضُعِّفُهُ﴾) is Makkī's reading.

﴿أضْعافًا﴾ is in the position of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). ﴿كَثِيرَةً﴾: none knows its true extent (*kunh*) except Allah. It is said that one becomes seven hundred.

﴿واللهُ يَقْبِضُ ويَبْسُطُ﴾: He restricts provision for His servants and expands it for them. So do not be stingy toward Him with what He has expanded for you; He will not replace your constriction with abundance. ﴿ويَبْصُطُ﴾ (with ṣād) is the reading of Ḥijāzī, ʿĀṣim and ʿAlī.

﴿وَإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾: then He will recompense you for what you have sent forward.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 246:

﴿Have you not considered the chiefs﴾ (al-mala'), i.e. the notables, because they fill hearts with awe and eyes with reverence.

﴿of the Children of Israel﴾. "Min" here is for partitive (tab'id, indicating a part).

﴿after Musa﴾, i.e. after his death. "Min" here is for the beginning of the extent (ibtida' al-ghaya, indicating the starting point of a time).

﴿when they said﴾, at the time they said ﴿to a prophet of theirs﴾, who was Shamun, or Yushu', or Ashmuwil.

﴿"Appoint for us a king﴾, raise up for us an amir to fight alongside us, whose opinion we will follow in directing the war, and to whose command we will submit.

﴿"that we may fight﴾: with the nun and with the jazm (apocopate) as an answer to the imperative, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, which is the complement (silah) of nuqatil. ﴿He said﴾, the Prophet: ﴿"Is it likely that﴾ ('asaytum, with kasra, wherever it occurs, is narrated by Nafi'), ...

﴿if fighting is prescribed for you﴾: a conditional clause separating the subject of 'asa from its predicate, which is ﴿"that you will not fight"﴾. The meaning is: "Is it likely that you will not fight?", i.e. "Is the matter as I expect, that you will not fight and will be cowardly?" He introduced "hal" as an interrogative about what he expected, and he intended by the interrogation the affirmation (taqrir), confirming that what he expected is indeed the case and that his expectation is correct.

﴿They said: "And why should we not fight in the way of Allah﴾, what reason do we have to abandon fighting, and what purpose would we have in it?

﴿when we have been driven out from our homes and our children﴾: the waw in "wa-qad" is for the circumstantial (hal). That is because the people of Jalut used to dwell between Egypt and Palestine, and they had captured four hundred and forty of the sons of their kings. They mean: when the matter has reached this extent with us, then jihad is inevitable.

﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them﴾, i.e. they were granted their request.

﴿they turned away﴾, they turned away from it ﴿except a few of them﴾, and they were three hundred and thirteen, according to the number of the people of Badr.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: a warning to them for their wrongdoing in abandoning jihad.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 247:

﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed Allah has raised up Talut (Saul) for you as king.﴾ It is a non-Arabic name, like Jalut (Goliath) and Dawud (David). It is not declined (diptotic) because of definiteness and foreignness.

﴿A king﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). ﴿They said: How can he have kingship over us?⁠﴾ That is: how? and from where? This is a denial of his being made king over them, and a deeming him unlikely.

﴿While we have more right to kingship than he does﴾ The wāw is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl). ﴿And he has not been given abundance of wealth⁠﴾ That is: how can he be made king over us, when the situation is that he does not deserve to be made king, because there exists one who has more right to kingship, and he is poor, while a king must have wealth by which he is supported. They only said this because prophethood was in the tribe of Levi son of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), and kingship in the tribe of Judah, whereas he was from the tribe of Benjamin, and he was a poor water-carrier or tanner. It is narrated that their prophet supplicated Allah when they asked him for a king, and he brought a staff by which the one who would be made king over them was measured, and none measured up to it except Talut.

﴿He said: Indeed Allah has chosen him over you⁠﴾ The ṭā' in iṣṭafāhu is a substitute for the tā' because of the quiescent ṣād, that is: He chose him over you, and He knows the interests better than you, and there is no objection to His judgment. Then he mentioned two interests more beneficial than what they mentioned of lineage and wealth, namely: extensive knowledge and physical stature, so he said: ﴿And has increased him broadly⁠﴾ is the second object.

﴿In knowledge and stature⁠﴾ They said: he was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel in war and religious matters of his time, and taller than every person by his head and shoulders. And al-baṣṭah (breadth) is abundance and extension. A king must necessarily be among the people of knowledge, for the ignorant is humiliated, despised, and not benefited by; and he must be large of body, for that is greater in souls and more awe-inspiring in hearts.

﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills⁠﴾ That is: kingship belongs to Him without dispute, and He gives it to whomever He wills to give it, and that is not by inheritance.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing⁠﴾ That is: abounding in bounty and giving, He grants abundance to the one who has no abundance of wealth, and enriches him after poverty.

﴿All-Knowing⁠﴾ of whom He chooses for kingship. Thereupon they asked their prophet for a sign of Allah's choosing Talut.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 248:

﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the ark will come to you⦄ That is: the chest of the Torah (tabut al-Tawrat). Whenever Musa (peace be upon him) went to fight, he would put it forward, and the hearts of the Children of Israel would be calmed, so they would not flee.

﴿In it is tranquility (sakinah) from your Lord⦄ Stillness and assurance.

﴿And a remnant (baqiyyah)⦄ These are the fragments of the tablets, the staff of Musa, his garments, some of the Torah, the sandals of Musa, and the turban of Harun (peace be upon them both).

﴿Of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind⦄ That is: of what Musa and Harun left behind. The word "family" (al) is inserted to magnify their status.

﴿Carried by the angels⦄ Meaning: the ark. Allah had raised it after Musa, and the angels descended carrying it while the people were looking at it. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). Likewise ﴿in it is tranquility⦄ and ﴿from your Lord⦄ are descriptive qualifiers of sakinah, and ﴿of what he left behind⦄ is a descriptive qualifier of baqiyyah.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers⦄ Indeed, in the return of the ark to you is a clear indication that Allah has made Talut king over you, if you are people who affirm the truth.

﴿فَلَمّا فَصَلَ طالُوتُ﴾ *When Talut set out* with ﴿بِالجُنُودِ﴾ *the troops*, leaving his land to fight the enemy. The phrase ﴿بِالجُنُودِ﴾ is in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), meaning: "mixed among the troops." They numbered eighty thousand. It was the height of summer, and they asked that God cause a river to flow for them. ﴿قالَ إنَّ اللهَ مُبْتَلِيكُمْ﴾ *He said: Indeed God will test you*, that is, He will try you, dealing with you as one who tests.

﴿بِنَهَرٍ﴾ *with a river*, which is the river of Palestine, so that the one truly committed to jihad would be distinguished from the one who makes excuses.

﴿فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنهُ﴾ *Whoever drinks from it* ﴿كَرِيمًا﴾ *karīman*, ﴿فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾ *is not of me*, that is, is not among my followers (p-206) and partisans. ﴿وَمَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ﴾ *And whoever does not taste it*, that is, does not partake of it. The verb *ṭaʿima* (to taste) with a thing means to take a taste of it.

﴿فَإنَّهُ مِنِّي﴾ is read with the *yāʾ* vowelled with a fatḥa (*fa-innahu minnī*, with a short "a" on the yāʾ) by Madani and Abu ʿAmr. The exception (*istithnāʾ*) is made from His saying ﴿فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾. The second clause is, in its legal effect, placed after the exception, but it has been placed first for emphasis (*ʿināya*).

﴿غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾ *a handful with his hand*. The reading *ghurfatan* (with fatḥa) by the Hijazi readers and Abu ʿAmr is in the sense of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), while with a ḍamma (*ghurfatun*) it is in the sense of the thing scooped (*maʿrūf*). The meaning is: a permission to scoop up a handful with the hand, rather than drinking directly with the mouth (*karʿ*). The proof of this is His saying ﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنهُ﴾, that is, they drank directly from it (*fa-kaʿarū*).

﴿إلا قَلِيلا مِنهُمْ﴾ *except a few of them*, and they were three hundred and thirteen men.

﴿فَلَمّا جاوَزَهُ﴾ *When he crossed it*, that is, the river.

﴿هُوَ﴾ *he*, Talut, ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ *and those who believed with him*, that is, the few.

﴿قالُوا لا طاقَةَ لَنا اليَوْمَ﴾ *They said: We have no power today* ﴿بِجالُوتَ﴾ *against Jalut*, that is, we have no strength. Jalut was a tyrant of the Amalekites, from the descendants of ʿImlīq ibn ʿĀd. In his helmet (*bayḍa*) there were three hundred *ritl* of iron.

﴿وَجُنُودِهِ قالَ الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أنَّهم مُلاقُو اللهِ﴾ *and his troops. Those who were certain that they would meet God said*, that is, were certain of martyrdom. It has been said that the pronoun in "they said" (*qālū*) refers to the majority who had abandoned him, and that ﴿الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ﴾ *those who were certain* are the few who remained steadfast with him. It is narrated that the handful of water was enough for a man to drink with his equipment, and that those who drank from the river directly had their lips blackened and were overcome by thirst.

﴿كَمْ مِن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ﴾ *How many a small company*: *kam* here is declarative (*khabariyya*, "many a"), and its position is nominative as the subject of the inchoative (*mubtadaʾ*).

﴿غَلَبَتْ﴾ *has overcome*, which is its predicate (*khabar*), ﴿فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإذْنِ اللهِ﴾ *a large company by God's permission*, that is, by His help. ﴿واللهُ مَعَ الصابِرِينَ﴾ *And God is with the steadfast*, through victory.

﴿وَلَمّا بَرَزُوا لِجالُوتَ وجُنُودِهِ﴾ [And when they came out against Jalut (Goliath) and his troops]: they went out to fight them. ﴿قالُوا رَبَّنا أفْرِغْ﴾ [They said: "Our Lord, pour out"]: i.e., pour down (اصْبُبْ).

﴿عَلَيْنا صَبْرًا﴾ [upon us patience]: in the fighting. ﴿وَثَبِّتْ أقْدامَنا﴾ [and make our feet firm]: by strengthening our hearts, and by casting terror into the breasts of our enemy.

﴿وانْصُرْنا عَلى القَوْمِ الكافِرِينَ﴾ [and help us against the disbelieving people]: aid us against them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 251:

﴿So they routed them﴾ i.e., Talut and the believers routed Jalut and his troops ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, by His decree. ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. Iyshi, the father of Dawud, was in the army of Talut together with six of his sons, and Dawud was the seventh of them. He was young and was tending the sheep. Allah revealed to their prophet that it was Dawud who would kill Jalut, so he asked for him from his father, and he came. On his way he passed three stones, each of which called on him to carry it, saying to him: "Indeed, you will kill Jalut with us." So he carried them in his shepherd's pouch and threw them at Jalut, and he killed him. Talut married him to his daughter, then envied him and intended to kill him, and then he died repentant.

﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾ in the eastern and western parts of the sacred land, and the Children of Israel had never gathered under a king before Dawud. ﴿And wisdom﴾, and prophethood. ﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾, of the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and other things.

﴿And had Allah not repelled some people﴾: this is the direct object (maf'ul bihi), ﴿by others﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "people". (Difa'): it is a verbal noun (masdar) of "dafa'a" or "dafa'a" (dafa'a/dafa'a), read as a Madani reading.

﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾: i.e., had Allah, exalted is He, not repelled some people by others and restrained their corruption through them, the corrupters would have prevailed and the earth would have been corrupted, and its benefits of tillage and procreation would have been nullified. Or: had Allah, exalted is He, not granted victory to the Muslims over the disbelievers, the earth would have been corrupted by the dominance of the disbelievers, the killing of the righteous, the ruin of lands, and the torment of servants.

﴿But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds﴾ by removing corruption from them. This is evidence for the Mu'tazila on the question of what is best (al-aslah).

﴿تِلْكَ﴾ is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿آياتُ اللهِ﴾. That is, ﴿آياتُ اللهِ﴾ means the stories that He related, from the account of thousands who left their homes, and of their death and their being brought back to life, and of the granting of kingship to Talut and his prevailing over the tyrants at the hand of a boy.

﴿نَتْلُوها﴾ is a *haal* (circumstantial accusative) of "آيات اللهِ", and the word governing it is the meaning of the demonstrative ("those"). Alternatively, "آيات اللهِ" is a *badal* (apposition) of "تِلْكَ", and ﴿نَتْلُوها﴾ is the predicate. ﴿عَلَيْكَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ means "with certainty, which the People of the Book have no doubt about, because it is so in their books."

﴿وَإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ means that you inform of these matters without having been known to read a book or to have heard them from its people.

(p-٢٠٨)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 253:**

﴿Those are the messengers﴾ refers to the group of messengers whose stories are mentioned in this surah, from Adam to Dawud, or to those whose knowledge was established with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾ through distinctions beyond the messengership, since they are equal in it, just as believers are. They are equal in the attribute of faith and differ in acts of obedience after faith. Then He clarified this by saying: ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾, meaning Allah spoke to him. The returning pronoun was omitted from the relative clause. The meaning is: among them is the one whom Allah preferred by speaking to him without an intermediary, and this is Musa (peace be upon him).

﴿And raised some of them﴾: the first object.

﴿in degrees﴾: the second object, meaning "by degrees" or "to degrees." The meaning is: among them is the one whom He elevated above the rest of the prophets, so that after their differing in merit, he was superior to them by many degrees. This is Muhammad (ﷺ), because he is the one preferred over them by being sent to all mankind, and because he was given what none of them was given: numerous signs, reaching a thousand or more, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, for it is the miracle that remains for all time. In this vagueness there is exaltation and a statement that he is the knowledge that is not confused for anyone and the distinguished one who is not obscured. It has also been said that it refers to Muhammad, Ibrahim, and others among the messengers of firm resolve (Ulul-'azm).

﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs﴾, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and other things.

﴿and We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾: We strengthened him with Jibril, or with the Injil.

﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought﴾: meaning, they would not have differed, for that is its cause.

﴿those who came after them﴾: after the messengers.

﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾: the manifest miracles.

﴿But they differed﴾ by My will. Then He explained the difference, saying: ﴿some of them believed and some of them disbelieved﴾ by My will. Allah says: the affairs of My messengers were run in this manner, meaning that obedience of all their community was never gathered for any one of them, neither during his life nor after his death, but rather they differed concerning him: ﴿some of them believed and some of them disbelieved﴾. ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another﴾: He repeated it for emphasis, meaning: if I had willed that they not fight, they would not have fought, since nothing takes place in My dominion except what accords with My will. This refutes the claim of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), for He informed that if He had willed that they not fight, they would not have fought, whereas they say: He willed that they not fight, yet they fought. (p-٢٠٩)

﴿But Allah does what He wills﴾: He affirmed will for Himself, as is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 254:

﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you﴾ in jihad in the way of Allah, or it is general for every obligatory charity.

﴿before there comes a Day in which is no trade﴾ i.e., before there comes a Day in which you will not be able to make up for what you missed of spending, because there is no trade in it through which you could buy what you spend.

﴿nor friendship﴾ so that your friends might grant you leniency concerning it,

﴿nor intercession﴾ i.e., for the disbelievers. As for the believers, they have intercession, or [it is] except by His permission.

﴿And the disbelievers – they are the wrongdoers﴾ who wrong themselves by their neglect of advancing [good deeds] for the day of their need; or, the disbelievers in this Day are the wrongdoers. (﴿There is no trade in it, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾) is read by Makki and Basri.

**Allah, there is no god except Him** (﴿اللهُ لا إلَهَ إلا هُوَ﴾): not with His name or His predicate. The words "there is no god except Him" are in the place of nominative (*raf'*) as the predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of the subject, *mubtada'*), and the subject is Allah.

**The Living** (﴿الحَيُّ﴾): the everlasting, the one who remains, for whom there is no way to perish.

**The Self-Subsisting** (﴿القَيُّومُ﴾): the one who is always standing in managing and preserving creation.

**Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him** (﴿لا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ﴾): *sinah* is drowsiness, which is the lethargy that precedes sleep.

**Nor sleep** (﴿وَلا نَوْمٌ﴾): from al-Mufaddal: *sinah* is heaviness in the head, *nu'as* is in the eye, and *nawm* is in the heart. This is an emphasis on *al-Qayyum*, because whoever is subject to these cannot be *Qayyum*. Allah revealed to Moses, peace be upon him: "Say to these people: I hold the heavens and the earth by My power. If slumber or sleep were to overtake Me, they would both cease to exist."

**To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth** (﴿لَهُ ما في السَماواتِ وما في الأرْضِ﴾): in sovereignty (*mulkan*) and in ownership (*milkan*).

**Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission** (﴿مَن ذا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِنْدَهُ إلا بِإذْنِهِ﴾): no one may intercede with Him except by His permission. This explains His dominion and His majesty, and that no one can even speak on the Day of Resurrection unless he is permitted to speak. It also refutes the claim of the disbelievers that the idols intercede for them.

**He knows what is before them and what is behind them** (﴿يَعْلَمُ ما بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وما خَلْفَهُمْ﴾): what was before them and what will be after them. The pronoun refers to what is in the heavens and the earth, because among them are rational beings (*al-'uqala'*).

**And they encompass nothing of His knowledge** (﴿وَلا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَيْءٍ مِن عِلْمِهِ﴾): nothing of what He knows (*ma'lumihi*). It is said in supplication: "O Allah, forgive Your knowledge of us," meaning Your known (*ma'lumuka*).

**Except what He wills** (﴿إلا بِما شاءَ﴾): except what He knows.

**His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth** (﴿وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَماواتِ والأرْضَ﴾): that is, His knowledge. From this comes *al-kurrasah* (notebook), because it contains knowledge, and *al-karasi* (scholars). Knowledge was called *kursi* by naming it after its place, which is the seat of the scholar. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. Or His dominion, named after its place, which is the seat of dominion. Or His throne (*'arsh*); this is related from al-Hasan. Or it is a throne (*sarir*) below the Throne (*'arsh*). In a hadith: "The seven heavens within the Kursi are no more than a ring thrown into a desert, and the superiority of the Throne over the Kursi is like the superiority of the desert over that ring." Or His power, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and it does not burden Him﴾, meaning it does not weigh on Him or cause Him difficulty.

**And their preservation does not tire Him** (﴿حِفْظُهُما﴾): the preservation of the heavens and the earth. **And He is the Most High** (﴿وَهُوَ العَلِيُّ﴾) in His kingdom and authority, **the Most Great** (﴿العَظِيمُ﴾) in His might and majesty. Or **al-'Aliyy** is the one exalted above attributes that do not befit Him, and **al-'Azim** is the one characterized by the attributes that befit Him. These two together comprise the perfection of monotheism (*tawhid*).

The sentences in the Verse of the Throne are arranged without a conjunction (*harf 'atf*), because they came in the manner of explanation (*bayan*). The first is an explanation of His standing in managing creation and His being the guardian over it, not heedless of it. The second is that He owns what He manages. The third is for the greatness of His affair. The fourth is for His encompassing of the conditions of creation. The fifth is for the vastness of His knowledge and its connection to all known things, or for His majesty and the greatness of His station.

This verse was given preference, so much so that what has been reported about its virtue has been reported. Among it is what is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, nothing will prevent him from entering Paradise except death, and none will persist in it except a truthful one (*siddiq*) or a worshipper. And whoever recites it when he takes his bed, Allah will grant him security for himself, his neighbor, his neighbor's neighbor, and the houses around him." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The master of mankind is Adam, and the master of the Arabs is Muhammad, without boasting. The master of the Persians is Salman, the master of the Romans is Suhayb, the master of the Abyssinians is Bilal, the master of mountains is Mount Tur, the master of days is Friday, the master of speech is the Qur'an, the master of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah, and the master of al-Baqarah is the Verse of the Throne." And he said: "This verse is not recited in a house except that the devils abandon it for thirty days, and no sorcerer or sorceress enters it for forty nights." And he said: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne at his sleep, a angel will be sent to him to guard him until morning." And he said: "Whoever recites these two verses in the evening will be protected by them until morning, and if he recites them in the morning he will be protected by them until evening: the Verse of the Throne and the beginning of Ha Mim (al-Mu'min) up to ﴿to Him is the final return﴾," because they contain the oneness of Allah, His glorification, His exaltation, and His supreme attributes. Nothing mentioned is greater than the Lord of Might, so whatever is a remembrance of Him is more excellent than all other remembrances. From this it is known that the most noble of the sciences is the science of monotheism (*'ilm al-tawhid*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 256:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ That is: there is no forcing into the true religion, which is the religion of Islam. It was also said: it is a report in the sense of a prohibition. It is narrated that "a man from the Ansar had two sons who had become Christians, and his father clung to them and said: 'By Allah, I will not leave you until you become Muslims.' They refused, so they took their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Ansari said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall part of me enter the Fire while I am looking on?!' So this was revealed, and he let them go." Ibn Mas'ud and a group said: this was at the beginning, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the command to fight. ﴿The right course has become distinct from error.﴾ Faith has been distinguished from disbelief by clear proofs. ﴿So whoever disbelieves in false deities (taghut)﴾ — by Satan, or by idols.

﴿And believes in Allah has grasped﴾ — held fast to — ﴿the most trustworthy handhold﴾. That is: the support and the thing one clings to.

﴿The most trustworthy (al-wuthqa)﴾ is the feminine form of al-awthaq, that is, the strongest of a firm rope, sound and dependable.

﴿There is no breaking of it﴾: there is no severing of the handhold. This is an illustration of what is known through reflection and inference by means of what is observed and perceived, so that the listener imagines it as though he were looking at it with his own eye, and thus his belief is firmly established. The meaning: he has tied for himself a firm bond of religion that no doubt can undo. ﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾ of his affirmation, ﴿Knowing﴾ of his belief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 257:

﴿Allah is the Protector (*walī*) of those who believe﴾: they wanted to believe, meaning: their helper and the one who manages their affairs.

﴿He brings them out of the darkness﴾: from the darknesses of disbelief (*kufr*) and misguidance. The word for "darknesses" (*ẓulumāt*) is in the plural because they are of different kinds.

﴿into the light﴾: into faith and guidance. The word for "light" (*nūr*) is in the singular because faith is one.

﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾: this is the subject (*mubtada'*) of the sentence, and the sentence is ﴿their protectors are the *ṭāghūt*﴾, where *awliyā'uhum al-ṭāghūt* is the predicate (*khabar*). The predicate continues: ﴿they bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾. The verb here is in the plural (*yukhrijūnahum*) because *al-ṭāghūt* carries the sense of a plural, meaning: those who firmly resolved upon disbelief and set their affairs in the opposite direction. Alternatively, Allah is the Protector of the believers; He brings them out of doubt (*shubha*) in religion, if it befalls them, by guiding them to what resolves it and enabling them to resolve it, until they come out of it into the light of certainty (*yaqīn*). And those who disbelieve have as their protectors the devils (*shayāṭīn*), who bring them out of the light of the clear proofs (*bayyināt*) which becomes manifest to them, into the darknesses of doubt and uncertainty.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾.

Then He (Allah) marvelled at His Prophet ﷺ and consoled him with the disputation of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with Nimrod, who claimed lordship, through His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord?﴾ by opposing the lordship of his Lord. The pronoun in "rabbihi" (his Lord) refers either to Ibrahim or to the one who argued, so He is the Lord of both of them. ﴿That Allah had given him dominion﴾, meaning, because Allah had given him dominion. That is, the granting of dominion made him insolent and gave him arrogance, so he argued on that account. This is evidence against the Mu'tazilah concerning al-aslah (what is most beneficial for the servant). Or it means: he argued at the time that Allah had given him dominion.

﴿When Ibrahim said﴾ is in the accusative governed by "hajja" (argued), or it is a substitute for "an atahu" (that He had given him) if it is taken to mean "the time."

﴿Ibrahim said: My Lord﴾ — "rabbi" (My Lord) is read by Hamzah with a different vocalisation of the final vowel. (The reading "rabbi" here is recorded for Hamzah.)

﴿Who gives life and causes death﴾ — it is as if he said to him: "Who is your Lord?" He said: (p-213) "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death." ﴿He said﴾: Nimrod said: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾, meaning: I pardon from killing, and I kill. The accursed one was silenced by this in the debate, so Ibrahim (peace be upon him) added what does not admit of confusion for the weak-minded, when ﴿Ibrahim said﴾ (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾. This is not a shift from one proof to another, as some have claimed, because the first proof was binding; but when the accursed one opposed the proof of giving life by freeing one man and killing another, he was addressed in a way that cannot be opposed. They were people of astrology. The movement of the stars from west to east was known to them, and the eastward movement perceived by us is forced, like the water moving the ant on the millstone in a direction other than the ant's own movement. So he said: My Lord moves the sun by compulsion against its own motion; if you are a lord, then move it by its own motion, for that is easier.

﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾: he was bewildered and dumbfounded.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, He does not grant them success. It was said: Nimrod did not say, "Then let your Lord bring the sun from the west," because Allah the Exalted turned him away from it. It was also said: he used to claim lordship for himself and did not acknowledge lordship in anyone else. The meaning of his saying ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ is that the one to whom giving life and causing death is attributed is I, and no one else. The verse indicates the permissibility of speaking in the science of kalam (theology) and of debating in it, because He said: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord?﴾ and argument takes place between two parties, which shows that Ibrahim also argued with him. Had it not been permissible, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) would not have engaged in it, since the prophets (peace be upon them) are protected from committing what is forbidden; and because we are commanded to call the disbelievers to faith in Allah and His oneness, and when we call them to that they must necessarily ask for proof of it, and this cannot happen except after debate. Thus in "Sharh al-Ta'wilat."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 259:

﴿Or like the one who passed by﴾. Its meaning: "Or have you not seen the likeness of the one who..." The phrase was elided because ﴿Have you not seen﴾ indicates it, since both expressions are phrases of wonder. Alternatively, it is governed by meaning rather than wording, and its supposed full form is: "Have you seen one like the one who argued with Abraham, or like the one who passed by?" The author of al-Kashshaf (*al-Kashshaf*) said: the kaf (ك) in it is *za'idah* (extra, non-operative), and the ﴿the one who﴾ is conjoined with his statement ﴿to the one who argued﴾. Al-Hasan reported that the passer-by was a disbeliever in resurrection, since he is grouped together with Nimrod in one string, and because of the expression of disbelief ﴿How can He give life﴾. The majority view is that he was Uzayr, who wished to witness the reviving of the dead in order to increase his insight, as Abraham, peace be upon him, had requested. And ﴿How can He give life﴾ is an admission of inability to know the manner of giving life and an expression of magnifying the power of the one who gives life.

﴿upon a town﴾: it is Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), where Bukhtanasr (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it. Or it is the town from which thousands went forth.

﴿and it was fallen down upon its roofs﴾: collapsed together with its roofs; or the roofs fell and then the walls fell upon them. *'Arsh* (عرش) means anything raised high.

﴿He said, "How can God give it life"﴾: that is, "How?" ﴿this﴾: that is, the people of this (town).

﴿after its death. So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾: that is, gave him life.

﴿He said﴾: a king (*malik*) said to him, ﴿"How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day"﴾, based on assumption, and in it is evidence for the permissibility of *ijtihad* (independent reasoning, the exertion of personal judgment in matters not settled by explicit text). It was reported that he died in the forenoon, and was raised after a hundred years before the sun had set. So he said, before looking at the sun, ﴿a day﴾; then he turned and saw some of the sun remaining, so he said, ﴿or part of a day﴾. ﴿He said, "No, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink"﴾. It was reported that his food was figs and grapes, and his drink was juice and milk. He found the figs and grapes as they had been when picked, and the drink in its original state.

﴿has not spoiled﴾: has not changed. The *ha'* (ه) is either an original radical or the *ha' al-sakt* (the silent ha' added at pause). Its derivation from *sunnah* (سنة, year) is according to both views: because its final radical is a ha', since the original form is *sanahah*, and the verb is *sanahtu fulanan* (سانهت فلانًا), meaning "I dealt with him for a year." Or it is a waw, since the original form is *sanawah*, and the verb is *sanaytu* (سانيت). Its meaning: the years did not change it. *Lam yatasannah* (لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ) with the ha' dropped in connected speech and retained in pause is recited by Hamzah and Ali.

﴿And look at your donkey﴾: how its bones were scattered and crumbled. He had a donkey which he had tied up, and it died, and its bones decayed. Or ﴿and look﴾ at it whole in its place, just as he had tied it. This is among the greatest signs: that it should live for a hundred years without fodder or water, just as He preserved his food and drink from change. ﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: We did that. It means reviving him after death and preserving what was with him. It is said the *waw* is a conjunction on an elided element, meaning: "so that you may take heed, and that We may make you a sign." It is said that he came to his people riding a donkey and said, "I am Uzayr," and they denied him. He said, "Bring the Torah," and began reciting it from memory. No one had recited the Torah openly before Uzayr, and that is the reason he was a sign. It is also said that he returned to his house and saw his children as elderly men while he was young.

﴿And look at the bones﴾: that is, the bones of the donkey, or the bones of the dead whose revival he marvelled at.

﴿how We raise them﴾: We move them, and lift some of them to others for assembly. *Nunshiruha* (نَنْشُرُها) with the *ra'* (ر) is recited by the Hijazi and Basri readers, meaning: We give them life.

﴿Then We clothe them﴾: that is, the bones, ﴿with flesh﴾. He made the flesh like a garment, metaphorically. ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾: its subject is implied, its supposed full form being: "So when it became clear to him that God is powerful over all things." ﴿He said, "I know that God is powerful over all things"﴾: the first was elided because the second indicates it, like the expressions "He hit me" and "I hit Zayd." It is permissible that ﴿when it became clear to him﴾ refers to what had been unclear to him, namely the matter of reviving the dead. He said, *a'lam* (اعْلَمْ, "know!") in the imperative form, recited by Hamzah and Ali, meaning: God said to him, "Know!" or he addressed himself.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 260:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ *Arinī* means *baṣṣirnī* (make me see). The position of ﴿*kayfa*﴾ (how) is in the accusative, governed by ﴿*tuḥyī*﴾ (You give life). ﴿He said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾ He said to him, "Have you not believed?" although He knew that he was the people's most firm in faith, so that he would answer with what he answered, because of the great benefit this holds for the listeners. ﴿*Balā*﴾ (yes) affirms what follows a negation. Its meaning is: "Yes, I believe, but I want to increase in tranquillity and assurance by combining necessary knowledge (*ʿilm al-ḍarūra*, knowledge that arises without need of proof) with knowledge acquired through reasoning (*ʿilm al-istidlāl*, knowledge gained by inference from evidence). The convergence of proofs is more soothing to the hearts and more increasing of insight." Knowledge acquired through reasoning admits of doubt, unlike necessary knowledge. The *lām* in ﴿*liyaṭmaʾinna*﴾ (so that it may be at rest) is connected to an omitted element, whose implied sense is: "But I asked for this desiring the tranquillity of the heart."

﴿He said: "Take four birds and make them incline toward you."﴾ They were a peacock, a rooster, a crow, and a dove. ﴿*Faṣurhunna ilayka*﴾ is read with a *kasra* on the *ṣād* by Ḥamzah, meaning: incline them to you and gather them toward yourself.

﴿Then place on every hill a portion of them﴾ Then cut them into pieces and distribute their parts over the hills that are in your presence and in your land. There were four hills, or seven. (*Juzʾan*) is read with two *ḍammas* and a *hamza* by Abū Bakr.

﴿Then call them﴾ Say to them: "Come, by God's permission."

﴿They will come to you running﴾ *Saʿyan* is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: hastening and running, in their flight, or in their walking on their feet. He was commanded to gather them to himself after taking them so that he could examine them, recognise their forms and shapes, and mark them, lest they be confused for him after being brought back to life and he imagine they were other than those. It is related that he was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, cut them up, separate their parts, mix their feathers, blood and flesh, and hold their heads. Then he was ordered to place their parts on the hills, a quarter from each bird on every hill, and then call out to them: "Come, by the permission of God, Exalted." So each part began flying toward the others until they became bodies, then they came and joined themselves to their heads, each body to its head.

﴿And know that God is Mighty﴾ nothing He wills is beyond His reach ﴿Wise﴾ in what He arranges; He does nothing except what contains wisdom.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 261:

When he (Allah) proved His power to give life, He exhorted (people) to spend in the way of Allah, and informed them that whoever spends in His way, there is for his expenditure a great reward, while He is able to do so. So He said: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. It is necessary to posit an omitted modifier (mudaf), meaning: the likeness of their expenditure.

﴿Is like a grain﴾, or their likeness is like the likeness of one who sows a grain, ﴿that produces seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains﴾. The one who causes growth is Allah, but since the grain is a cause, the growing is attributed to it, just as it is attributed to the earth and to the water. The meaning of its producing seven ears is that it sends forth a stalk from which seven branches sprout, each with an ear. This illustration is a depiction of multiplication, as if it were present before the eyes of the beholder. What is illustrated is found in millet and sorghum, and perhaps (p-217) a wheat stalk sprouts in strong, fertile land, so that its grain reaches this measure. Moreover, the illustration is valid even if it is not found except as a supposition and assumption. Placing "sanābil" (ears) in the place of "sunbulāt" (ears) is like placing "qurū'" in the place of "aqrā'" (menstrual periods/ cycles).

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾: that is, He multiplies that multiplication for whom He wills, not for every spender, due to the differences in the states of the spenders; or He increases beyond seven hundred for whom He wills. ("Yuḍā'if") is read by Shami, and ("Yuḍa''if") is read by Makki.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, abundant in bounty and generosity, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intentions of the spenders.

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity﴾ means that they boast over the one to whom they have done good, showing him that they have made him dependent on them and placed a right upon him for themselves. They used to say: "When you do a favour, forget it."

﴿Nor with injury﴾ means that they act arrogantly toward him on account of what they have given him. The meaning of "then" (thumma) is to show the difference between spending and leaving off reminders and injury, and that abandoning these two is better than the spending itself, just as He made steadfastness in faith better than entering into it, in His words: ﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾, that is, the reward for their spending.

﴿No fear shall be upon them﴾ of any diminishing of the reward, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over its loss. Or: no fear of punishment, and no grief over the loss of reward. He said here "for them is their reward" and later "then for them is their reward" because the relative construction (al-mawsul, the relative clause) here was not given the sense of a condition (shart), whereas it was given that sense in the other place.

﴿A kind word﴾: a gracious reply. ﴿And forgiveness﴾: pardon toward the petitioner when he says something that burdens the one who is asked. Or it means attaining forgiveness from God through the gracious reply.

﴿Better than charity followed by harm﴾: it is valid to report about an indefinite subject (mubtada' nakira, an indefinite grammatical subject) because it is specified by its qualifier. ﴿And God is Rich﴾: He has no need of a giver who reminds and harms. ﴿Forbearing﴾: He does not hasten to punish him. This is a warning to him. Then He reinforced that with His saying: (p-218)

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury, like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in God and the Last Day.﴾ The *kāf* is in the accusative (*naṣb*) as a qualifier (*ṣifa*) of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The estimated meaning is: "a nullifying like the nullifying of the one who..." That is, do not nullify the reward of your charities with reminders and injury, as the hypocrite (*munāfiq*) nullifies his, the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people, and does not intend by his spending the pleasure of God or the reward of the Hereafter. "*Riʾāʾa*" is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*).

﴿So his parable is like the parable of a smooth rock with dust upon it.﴾ His parable, and his expenditure from which he gains absolutely nothing, is like a smooth stone with dust on it. ﴿Then a heavy rain struck it⌋﴾ meaning a rain of great downpour.

﴿And left it bare⌋﴾ bare, clean of the dust that had been on it. ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned.﴾ They find no reward for anything of what they spent. Alternatively, the *kāf* is in the position of the accusative as a circumstantial (*ḥāl*), meaning: do not nullify your charities while being like the one who spends. He said "they have no power" after "like the one who spends" because by "the one who spends" he intended the category (*jins*), or the group that spends.

﴿And God does not guide the disbelieving people⌋﴾ as long as they choose disbelief.

The example of those who spend their wealth seeking God's pleasure and for the firming of their own souls﴾. That is, and for confirming (tasdiq) Islam, and for realizing the reward from the very root of their souls, because when a Muslim spends his wealth in the way of God, he knows that his affirmation and his faith in the reward come from the root of his own soul and from the sincerity of his heart. "Min" (مِن) is for the starting point of the action (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), and it is coordinated with the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu), meaning: for the seeking and for the firming. The sense is: the example of the spending of these people, in its growth, in the sight of God.

﴿like the example of a garden﴾, an orchard, ﴿on a hillside﴾, a raised place. He specified it because the trees in it are purer and their fruit is better. (بِرَبْوَةٍ) is read by ʿĀṣim and Shāmī (Ibn ʿĀmir).

﴿A heavy rain strikes it, so it yields its produce﴾ (p. 219) its fruit. (أُكْلَها) is read by Nāfiʿ, Makkī, and Abū ʿAmr.

﴿double﴾, twice what it used to yield before, because of the heavy rain.

﴿But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain﴾, a drizzle of small drops that suffices it because of the goodness of its soil. Or, he gave the likeness of their condition in the sight of God to the garden on the hillside, and their abundant and their meager spending to the heavy rain and the drizzle. Just as each of the two rains multiplies the yield of the garden, so their spending, whether abundant or meager, after they seek by it the pleasure of God Most High, is pure in the sight of God and increases their nearness and the goodness of their state with Him. ﴿And God is seeing of what you do﴾, He sees your deeds whether in abundance or in scarcity, and He knows your intentions in them, whether they be showing-off (riyaʾ) or sincerity.

The alif of interrogation in ﴿Would any one of you wish﴾ is for denial. ﴿That there should be for him a garden﴾, an orchard, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow, for him﴾, for the owner of the orchard, ﴿therein﴾, in the garden, ﴿of all the fruits﴾. By "fruits" he means the benefits that used to come to him from it. Or, since the palm trees and grapevines are the noblest and most beneficial of trees, they were singled out for mention, and the garden was described as containing them, even though it includes other trees, by way of taghlib (giving precedence to these two over the rest). Then he followed them with mention of all fruits. ﴿And old age has overtaken him﴾: the waw is for the circumstantial state (ḥāl). Its meaning is: that there should be for him a garden, while old age has overtaken him. The waw in ﴿and he has weak offspring﴾, young children, is also for the circumstantial state, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state relative to the pronoun in "overtaken him". ﴿Then there struck it a whirlwind﴾, a wind that spins over the ground and then rises toward the sky like a pillar. ﴿In it﴾, in the whirlwind, ﴿is fire﴾, and the word "fire" is in the nominative as the subject of the prepositional phrase (ẓarf), since the prepositional phrase functions as a descriptive modifier of "whirlwind". ﴿So it was burned﴾, the garden.

This is a parable for one who performs good deeds out of riya' (showing off in worship). When the Day of Resurrection comes, he will find them nullified, and he will then feel the regret of one who had a comprehensive garden of fruits, who reached old age with weak children whose livelihood depended on it, and then it was destroyed by a thunderbolt.

﴿Thus﴾, like this clarification which was made in what preceded,

﴿Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, concerning the Oneness of God and the religion, ﴿that you may give thought﴾, so that you may take heed.

(p-220)

O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned (مِن جِيادِ مَكْسُوباتِكم: from the choice things of what you have acquired). And from this is the evidence for the obligation of zakat on trade goods. ﴿And from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾ (from grain, fruit, and minerals, and other things). The sense is: "and from the good things of what We have brought forth for you," but it omitted [the second mention] because the "good things" has been mentioned.

﴿And do not intend the wicked﴾ (do not aim at the bad wealth) ﴿from it you spend﴾ (you single it out for spending). It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "and do not intend the wicked while spending," i.e., "determining to give charity." ﴿while you would not take it yourselves﴾ (and your condition is that you would not accept it in your own rights).

﴿Unless you overlook in it﴾ (unless you are lenient in accepting it and make concessions regarding it). From your saying: "Fulan overlooked part of his right" when he lowered his gaze. It is said to the seller: "Ughmiḍ" (overlook), i.e., do not insist strictly, as if you do not see. And from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: they used to give in charity the worst and most defective dates, so they were forbidden from that.

﴿And know that Allah is Ghanī﴾ (free of need) of your charities, ﴿Ḥamīd﴾ (deserving of praise, or praiseworthy).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 268:

﴿The Shaytan promises you﴾ poverty in spending, and says to you: indeed the outcome of your spending is that you will become poor. The word "wa'd" (promise) is used for both good and evil.

﴿And he commands you to indecency﴾ and urges you to stinginess, withholding charity, and the instigation of the one who commands toward the one commanded. Al-fahish (the indecent one) among the Arabs is the miser.

﴿And Allah promises you﴾ in spending ﴿forgiveness from Him﴾ for your sins, and an expiation for them.

﴿And bounty﴾: that He will replace for you something better than what you have spent, or a reward for it in the Hereafter.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, He expands [provision] for whom He wills, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your actions and your intentions.

Qur'anic quotations are rendered in ﴿ ﴾ markers as instructed.

﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾: the knowledge of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, or beneficial knowledge that leads to the pleasure of Allah, together with acting upon it. The wise person (al-hakim) in the sight of Allah is the one who has knowledge and acts upon it.

﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾ (wa-man yu'ti) is read by Ya'qub (al-Hadrami) as (wa-man yu'ti), meaning: and whoever Allah gives wisdom to.

﴿then he has indeed been given much good﴾: the indefinite form (tankir) here is one of magnification, meaning: he has been given good, that is, a great good.

﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾: none is admonished by the admonitions of Allah except those who possess sound intellects, or the scholars who act. The purpose of this is to urge acting upon what the verses contain concerning the matter of spending (infaq).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 270:

﴿And whatever expenditure you spend﴾ in the way of Allah, or in the way of Shaytan.

﴿Or whatever vow you vow﴾ in obedience to Allah, or in His disobedience.

﴿Indeed, Allah knows it﴾ it is not hidden from Him, and He will reward you for it.

﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾ those who withhold the charities, or who spend their wealth in sinful acts, or who make vows in sinful matters, or who do not fulfil their vows,

﴿there are no helpers﴾ from among those who would help them against Allah and protect them from His punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 271:

﴿If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are.﴾ "Fa-ni'ma" (how excellent) is an indefinite noun (nakira) that is neither a relative clause (mawsulah) nor a descriptive (mawsufah), and the thing being praised (al-makhsus bi-l-madh) is "hiya" (they). ("Fa-ni'imma hiya") with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the ayn: Abu 'Amr, and the Medinan reciters other than Warsh. With a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ayn: the Syrian reciters, Hamza, and 'Ali. With a kasra on both the nun and the ayn: the rest.

﴿But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you.﴾ And you would hit their right recipients along with concealment, so concealment is better for you. They said: what is meant is voluntary charities (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), and openly giving obligatory charities (al-jahr fi l-fara'id) is better, to dispel suspicion. However, if the one paying zakat is someone not known for wealth, then concealing it is better. And if the one giving voluntary charity wishes to be emulated, then making it public is better. ("Wa-nukaffir") with a nun and a jazm on the ra': Medinan, Hamza, and 'Ali. With a ya' and a raf' on the ra': the Syrian reciters and Hafs. With a nun and raf': the rest. Whoever reads it with jazm has made it a conjunction (ataf) upon the place (mahall) of the fa' and what follows it, since it is the answer of the conditional. Whoever reads it with raf' has made it a new sentence (isti'naf). The ya' is according to the meaning: "Allah will expiate."

﴿from you of your misdeeds.﴾ The nun is according to the meaning: "We will expiate."

﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾ of disclosing and concealing. ﴿Khabir﴾ means knowing (alim).

(p-222)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 272:**

﴿Their guidance is not your responsibility﴾. It is not obligatory for you to make them rightly guided to refraining from what they were forbidden: from reminding others of favours given (al-mann), from harming (al-adha), from spending of what is bad (al-khabith), and other things. Your only duty is to convey the prohibitions to them, nothing more.

﴿But God guides whom He wills﴾. Or: it is not your responsibility to grant them success in guidance, or to create guidance; that belongs to God alone.

﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, of wealth, ﴿it is for your own selves﴾. It benefits your own selves; no one other than you profits from it. So do not remind people of it with favour, and do not harm them by looking down on them.

﴿And you spend only seeking the face of God﴾. Your spending is only for the sake of seeking the face of God, that is, seeking His pleasure and desiring what is with Him. Why then do you remind people of it and spend what is bad, the kind of thing that is not offered to God? Or this is a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, that is: do not spend except seeking the face of God.

﴿And whatever good you spend will be repaid to you﴾, its reward multiplied manifold. So you have no excuse for turning away from spending it, or for not making it in the best and most beautiful manner.

﴿And you will not be wronged﴾, that is, you will not be diminished, like His saying: ﴿and wronged him not at all﴾ (al-Kahf 18:33), meaning: did not diminish.

The preposition in ﴿لِلْفُقَراءِ﴾ (*lil-fuqara'*, "for the poor") is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "Spend for the poor." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "These charities are for the poor."

﴿Those who are confined in the way of Allah﴾: they are those whom jihad confined and prevented from moving about freely.

﴿They cannot⁠﴾: because they are occupied with it. ﴿travel through the land﴾: to earn a living. It is said that they are the People of the Suffah (*Ahl al-Suffah*, the people of the bench, the companions who lived in the veranda of the mosque), who were about four hundred men of the emigrants from Quraysh. They had no dwellings in Madinah and no tribes. So they stayed in the Suffah of the mosque, which was its shaded porch. They studied the Qur'an at night and cracked date-stones by day. They would go out with every expedition (*sariyyah*, a small military detachment) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out, and whoever had a surplus would bring it to them in the evening.

﴿The ignorant man thinks them﴾ to be wealthy because of their condition. The verb *yahsabuhum* (يَحْسَبُهُمْ, "he thinks them") with the vowel on the *sin* being *fatha* (يَحْسَبُ) is in the pattern of al-Shami, Yazid, Hamza, Asim (except al-A'sha) and Hubayra. The rest read it with a *kasra* on the *sin* (يَحْسِبُهُمْ).

﴿wealthy because of their chastity﴾: considered self-sufficient because of their restraint from begging. ﴿You recognise them by their marks﴾: from the paleness of their faces and the shabbiness of their state.

﴿They do not ask people persistently⁠﴾: *ilhafan* means insistently. It is said that this is a denial of both asking and insistence together, like the line of poetry:

*Over a road whose landmarks cannot guide one by its signposts*

He means the denial of the signpost and of being guided by it. Insistence (*al-ilhaf*) is clinging on and not leaving until one is given something. In a hadith: "Allah loves the modest, the forbearing, the chaste, and dislikes the vulgar, the constant beggar, the one who insists." It is also said that the meaning is: if they ask, they ask gently and do not press.

﴿Whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it⁠﴾: it is not lost with Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾. Both are circumstantial expressions (*hal*), meaning: they are spending secretly and openly. That is, they generalize the times and circumstances with charity, because they are restricted to good, so whenever the need of a needy person arises, they hasten to meet it and do not delay it, and they do not make excuses of a time or a circumstance. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he gave charity of forty thousand dinars: ten at night, ten by day, ten in secret, and ten openly. Or it was revealed concerning ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, who possessed only four dirhams. He gave one dirham at night, one dirham by day, one dirham in secret, and one dirham openly. (p-٢٢٤) ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 275:

﴿Those who consume interest (ribā)﴾ is an excess of wealth that is free of any counter-value in an exchange of wealth for wealth. The word "الرِبَوْا" is written with a waw in accordance with the dialect of those who pronounce it with emphasis (tafkhīm), just as "الصَلْوَةُ" (al-ṣalwah) and "الزَكْوَةُ" (al-zakwah) are written. An alif is added after it in imitation of the waw of the plural. ﴿They do not rise﴾ when they are raised up from their graves, ﴿except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾, that is, the one who is afflicted (al-maṣrūʿ), because he was confused (takhabbaṭa) in transactions, so he was recompensed in kind. Al-khabṭ is striking without balance, like the khabṭ of the blind camel (ʿashwāʾ).

﴿By the touch﴾: from madness. It is connected to ﴿do not rise﴾, meaning: they do not rise from the touch that is upon them except as the afflicted one rises. Or it is connected to ﴿rises﴾, meaning: as the afflicted one rises from his madness. The meaning is that they will rise on the Day of Resurrection bewildered like the afflicted, and that is their mark by which they are recognized by the people of the place of standing. It was said: those who come out of their graves hastening, except the devourers of interest, for they rise and fall like the afflicted, because they consumed interest, so God increased it in their bellies until it weighed them down, and they cannot hasten.

﴿That﴾ punishment is ﴿because they said: trade is only like interest﴾. He did not say "interest is only like trade," although the discussion is about interest and not trade, because it was phrased in the manner of exaggeration, meaning that their belief in the permissibility of interest had reached the point that they made it a principle and a rule of permissibility, to the extent that they likened trade to it.

﴿And God has permitted trade and forbidden interest﴾: a denial of their equating the two, since permissibility and prohibition are opposites, so how can they be alike? It is also an indication that analogy (qiyās) is overridden by the text (naṣṣ), because He made the proof of the invalidity of their analogy the permission and prohibition of God.

﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord﴾: whoever has been reached by an exhortation from God and a warning by the prohibition of interest.

﴿And desists﴾: he follows the prohibition and refrains. ﴿He may keep what is past﴾: he is not held accountable for what passed from him, because he took it before the revelation of the prohibition.

﴿And his affair is with God﴾: He judges his matter on the Day of Resurrection, and none of his affair is up to you, so do not demand it from him.

﴿And whoever returns﴾: to considering interest permissible, according to al-Zajjaj. Or to interest while considering it permissible.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾: because by considering it permissible they became disbelievers, since whoever deems permissible what God, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden is a disbeliever, and therefore he deserves eternity. By this it becomes clear that the Mu'tazilah have no connection to this verse regarding the eternal damnation of sinners.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 276:

﴿Allah destroys usury﴾ — He takes away its blessing, and destroys the wealth into which it enters. ﴿And He causes charities to grow﴾ — He multiplies them and increases them, i.e., He increases the wealth from which the charity was given, and blesses it. And in a hadith: "No wealth has ever been diminished by zakat" ﴿And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾ — one who is greatly disbelieving (kufr) by deeming usury lawful (istihlal) ﴿sinful﴾ — persisting in sin by consuming it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 277:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, establish prayer, and give zakat, they will have their reward with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

It is said: What is meant by it is: those who believed in the prohibition of *ribā* (usury, interest).

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and give up what remains of the riba (usury/interest)﴾. They had taken what they had stipulated from people as riba, but some remainders still existed for them, so they were commanded to leave them and not to demand them. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Thaqif, who had money owed to them by some people of Quraysh, and they demanded from them, when the due date (al-mahall) arrived, the principal and the riba.

﴿If you are believers﴾: perfect in faith. For indeed the proof of its perfection is compliance with what one has been commanded.

[p. 226]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 279:

﴿Then if you do not do it, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger.﴾ Know of it. "Adhina bi al-shay'" means: when one knows it. It is supported by the reading of al-Hasan: (fa-ayqinu) fa-adhinu, and by Hamzah and Abu Bakr (other than Ibn Ghalib): fa-a'limu bi-ha ghayrakum (let others know of it).
